hist_human_evolution.label: Human Evolution
hist_human_evolution.subject: history
hist_human_evolution.detail: The process by which modern humans (Homo sapiens) developed from earlier primates over millions of years. Africa is considered the cradle of humankind. Evidence comes from fossils, stone tools, and cave art. Key stages include Australopithecus, Homo habilis, Homo erectus, and Homo sapiens.

hist_australopithecus.label: Australopithecus
hist_australopithecus.subject: history
hist_australopithecus.detail: Early hominid genus that lived in Africa around 4-2 million years ago. Bipedal but with smaller brain capacity than later humans. The famous fossil 'Lucy' (Australopithecus afarensis) was discovered in Ethiopia in 1974. They were not tool-makers in the systematic sense.

hist_homo_habilis.label: Homo habilis
hist_homo_habilis.subject: history
hist_homo_habilis.detail: The first real 'Homo' or human (hence 'habilis' = 'handy/skilful'). Lived in eastern and southern Africa about 2.6–1.5 million years ago. First real stone-tool maker — fractured pieces of stone and sharpened them to use as tools. Fractured stones have been found alongside Homo habilis bones. Braincase 500–700 cc, lightly built.

hist_homo_erectus.label: Homo erectus
hist_homo_erectus.subject: history
hist_homo_erectus.detail: Human species that lived roughly 1.8 million to 200,000 years ago. Braincase 800–1200 cc (vs Homo habilis 500–700 cc). First hominid to make the hand axe — the most distinctive tool of the species. Credited with the discovery and controlled use of fire, which enabled warmth in cold climates, protection from predators, and wider geographical expansion. First hominid to migrate out of Africa — remains found in China, South Asia, and Southeast Asia.

hist_homo_sapiens.label: Homo sapiens
hist_homo_sapiens.subject: history
hist_homo_sapiens.detail: Modern humans. Archaic Homo sapiens appears around 230,000–30,000 years ago (resembling Neanderthals, found in Europe, Near East, Old World). Full modern Homo sapiens sapiens traceable to ~115,000 years ago in southern Africa, in the Upper Palaeolithic. Braincase 1200–2000 cc. In India: Hathnora (Narmada valley) skull (found 1982) is archaic Homo sapiens; Fa Hien Cave (Sri Lanka) has modern Homo sapiens sapiens fossils ~34,000 years old. Earliest modern humans reached India via coastal migration from Africa ~50,000 years ago (from the south, not the north).

hist_neanderthals.label: Neanderthals
hist_neanderthals.subject: history
hist_neanderthals.detail: Species of archaic humans (Homo neanderthalensis) who lived in Europe and western Asia from about 400,000 to 40,000 years ago. Had large brains, made sophisticated tools, and buried their dead. Went extinct after Homo sapiens arrived in Europe, though some interbreeding occurred.

hist_africa_cradle.label: Africa as Cradle of Humankind
hist_africa_cradle.subject: history
hist_africa_cradle.detail: Africa is where the earliest hominids evolved and where the oldest fossils have been found. Key sites include Olduvai Gorge (Tanzania), Hadar (Ethiopia), and Sterkfontein (South Africa). The 'Out of Africa' theory holds that Homo sapiens originated in Africa and then migrated globally.

hist_olduvai_gorge.label: Olduvai Gorge
hist_olduvai_gorge.subject: history
hist_olduvai_gorge.detail: Archaeological site in Tanzania's Great Rift Valley, one of the most important sites for understanding human evolution. Louis and Mary Leakey discovered fossils of early hominids here. Rich in stone tools from Oldowan and Acheulian traditions spanning 2 million years.

hist_stone_tools.label: Stone Tool Traditions
hist_stone_tools.subject: history
hist_stone_tools.detail: Three major stone-tool traditions in India, each tied to a Palaeolithic phase: Oldowan (simple flaked pebbles, from 2.6 MYA globally), Acheulian (hand axes and cleavers, from 1.7 MYA), and Middle/Upper Palaeolithic blade-and-burin industries. Neolithic stone tools are distinct — polished axes and implements — with three Indian regional types by axe shape: NW rectangular+curved-edge, NE rectangular-butt+shouldered, Southern oval+pointed. Parashurama, the axe-wielding legendary hero, is a cultural echo of this.

hist_neolithic_revolution.label: Neolithic Revolution
hist_neolithic_revolution.subject: history
hist_neolithic_revolution.detail: Transition from hunting-gathering to agriculture and settled life, beginning around 10,000 BCE. First occurred in the Fertile Crescent (West Asia). Led to domestication of plants and animals, permanent settlements, pottery, and eventually urbanisation. One of the most transformative changes in human history.

hist_cave_art.label: Cave Art
hist_cave_art.subject: history
hist_cave_art.detail: Paintings and engravings made by early Homo sapiens in caves, dating from about 40,000 years ago. Famous sites include Lascaux and Chauvet (France) and Altamira (Spain). Depicted animals, hunting scenes, and abstract symbols. Suggests symbolic thinking, ritual, and aesthetic sense.

hist_lascaux.label: Lascaux Cave
hist_lascaux.subject: history
hist_lascaux.detail: Prehistoric cave in southwestern France containing some of the most famous Palaeolithic cave paintings, dating to about 17,000 years ago. Features over 600 paintings of animals including horses, deer, and bulls. Discovered in 1940.

hist_lucy_fossil.label: Lucy (Fossil)
hist_lucy_fossil.subject: history
hist_lucy_fossil.detail: A remarkably complete Australopithecus afarensis fossil discovered in Hadar, Ethiopia in 1974 by Donald Johanson. Dated to approximately 3.2 million years ago. About 40% of skeleton was recovered, showing bipedal locomotion. One of the most famous fossils in palaeoanthropology.

hist_out_of_africa.label: Out of Africa Theory
hist_out_of_africa.subject: history
hist_out_of_africa.detail: Theory that modern Homo sapiens evolved in Africa and then migrated to other continents, replacing earlier hominid populations. Supported by genetic evidence (mitochondrial DNA). Contrasts with the multiregional hypothesis which posits parallel evolution in different regions.

hist_language_origins.label: Origins of Language
hist_language_origins.subject: history
hist_language_origins.detail: Language is considered a defining feature of Homo sapiens. Earlier estimated ~35,000 BCE; now pushed back to ~50,000 BCE (per Sharma, Upper Palaeolithic). Made possible by anatomical changes in the vocal tract and brain development. Probably facilitated the formation of bands and alliances among Upper Palaeolithic hunter-gatherers.

hist_fire_use.label: Controlled Use of Fire
hist_fire_use.subject: history
hist_fire_use.detail: Evidence of controlled fire use dates to about 1 million years ago, associated with Homo erectus. Fire provided warmth, protection from predators, enabled cooking (which improved nutrition), and became a social focus. Cooking may have contributed to brain development.

hist_sulaiman_kirthar_hills.label: Sulaiman and Kirthar Hills
hist_sulaiman_kirthar_hills.subject: history
hist_sulaiman_kirthar_hills.detail: Hills in the northwest of the subcontinent where women and men first began to grow crops such as wheat and barley about 8000 years ago. Early agriculture also involved rearing of sheep, goat and cattle.

hist_hunter_gatherers.label: Hunter-Gatherers
hist_hunter_gatherers.subject: history
hist_hunter_gatherers.detail:
Earliest people of the subcontinent who hunted wild animals and gathered plant produce for food. They lived along rivers and in rock shelters, moving from place to place following resources.

[merged from hist_hunting_gathering]: The primary mode of subsistence for most of human history. Groups were small, mobile, and egalitarian. Division of labour existed, with gathering (often by women) providing majority of food. Knowledge of environment, seasons, and animal behaviour was crucial.

hist_beginning_agriculture.label: Beginning of Agriculture
hist_beginning_agriculture.subject: history
hist_beginning_agriculture.detail: Fundamental shift from gathering to producing food. In India: plant cultivation began ~7000–6000 BCE in the Sulaiman-Kirthar area and Rajasthan (Sambhar salt lake). Mature farming settlement at Mehrgarh from ~7000 BCE with wheat and barley. Animal rearing followed at Bagor and Adamgarh ~5000 BCE. By the Neolithic phase proper, settled agricultural villages spread across Kashmir, the Vindhyas, south India, and eastern India.

hist_mesolithic_period.label: Mesolithic
hist_mesolithic_period.subject: history
hist_mesolithic_period.detail: Middle Stone Age. In India, ~9000–4000 BCE. Transitional phase between Palaeolithic and Neolithic. Characteristic tools: microliths (tiny stone tools fitted onto bone/wood handles to make composite tools like saws and sickles). Post-ice-age climate warmer and wetter. People lived on hunting, fishing, and food gathering, and at later stages also domesticated animals. Key sites: Bagor (Rajasthan, occupied 5 millennia from 5000 BCE onwards, well-excavated), Adamgarh (MP). Bagor + Adamgarh provide the earliest evidence of animal domestication in India (~5000 BCE). Mesolithic sites abound in Rajasthan, southern UP, central and eastern India, and south of the Krishna river.

hist_neolithic_period.label: Neolithic
hist_neolithic_period.subject: history
hist_neolithic_period.detail: New Stone Age. Globally begins ~9000 BCE in western Asia; in India starts ~7000 BCE (Mehrgarh). North-Indian Vindhyan Neolithic sites ~5000 BCE; south-Indian Neolithic 2400–1000 BCE. Tools: polished stone axes and implements. Three Indian Neolithic regional groups based on axe types: (1) NW: rectangular axes with curved cutting edge (Baluchistan + Kashmir); (2) NE: rectangular-butt polished axes, occasional shouldered hoes (Vindhyas, Assam, Meghalaya); (3) Southern: oval sides, pointed butt (Karnataka/AP/TN, 850+ settlements). Neolithic innovations: polished stone tools, agriculture (wheat, barley, rice, ragi, horse gram), settled villages, domesticated animals, pottery (handmade → foot-wheel), mud/reed houses. Parashurama, the axe-wielding hero in Indian legend, symbolically links to the stone axe.

hist_microliths.label: Microliths
hist_microliths.subject: history
hist_microliths.detail: Tiny stone tools characteristic of the Mesolithic period. They were probably stuck on handles of bone or wood to make composite tools such as saws and sickles for harvesting wild grasses.

hist_bhimbetka.label: Bhimbetka
hist_bhimbetka.subject: history
hist_bhimbetka.detail: A prehistoric site in the Vindhyan range, 45 km south of Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh — over 500 painted rock shelters distributed across about 10 sq km. Discovered by V.S. Wakankar in 1957-58. UNESCO World Heritage Site (2003). Oldest paintings ~30,000 years old. Continuity of occupation from 100,000 BCE to 1000 CE — with paintings layered over each other across periods. Paintings span Upper Palaeolithic, Mesolithic, Chalcolithic, early historic and medieval periods — most are Mesolithic. Called 'Zoo Rock Shelter' for depictions of bison, elephant, rhinoceros, tiger, cattle, snake, spotted deer, barasingha. Also shows Lower Palaeolithic stone-tool features in the lower layers. Themes: hunting, dancing, music, everyday life. Pigments: haematite (red ochre), purple, brown, white, yellow, green.

hist_hunsgi.label: Hunsgi
hist_hunsgi.subject: history
hist_hunsgi.detail: An early Palaeolithic site in Karnataka where a large number of tools were found. Most tools were made from locally available limestone. Sites included both habitation and factory sites near springs.

hist_factory_sites.label: Factory Sites
hist_factory_sites.subject: history
hist_factory_sites.detail: Places where good quality stone was found and where people made tools. Identified by blocks of stone, discarded imperfect tools and chips of waste stone. Some were habitation-cum-factory sites.

hist_rock_paintings.label: Rock Paintings
hist_rock_paintings.subject: history
hist_rock_paintings.detail: Paintings on rock surfaces made by prehistoric people, found at many Indian sites. Rock engravings (as distinct from paintings) are called Petroglyphs. Three major phases identified in Indian rock art: (1) Upper Palaeolithic (40,000–10,000 BCE) — large animals (bison, elephant, rhino, tiger); white/dark red/green for animals, red for hunters, green for dancers. (2) Mesolithic (10,000–4,000 BCE) — smaller paintings, predominantly red; group hunting, grazing, riding scenes. (3) Chalcolithic — increased green and yellow; battle scenes, men on horses/elephants, bow-and-arrow. Key sites: Bhimbetka (MP), Jogimara (Chhattisgarh), Mirzapur (UP), Panchmarhi/Pachmarhi (MP), Narsinghgarh (MP). Pigments from natural minerals — haematite (red), ochre/geru, lime. Bhimbetka was discovered by V.S. Wakankar in 1957-58.

hist_climate_change_12000.label: Climate Change 12,000 Years Ago
hist_climate_change_12000.subject: history
hist_climate_change_12000.detail: Around 12,000 years ago major climate changes led to warmer conditions, development of grasslands, and increase in deer, antelope, goat, sheep and cattle. Led people to think about herding and farming.

hist_habitation_sites.label: Habitation Sites
hist_habitation_sites.subject: history
hist_habitation_sites.detail: Places where people lived, including natural caves and rock shelters found in the Vindhyas and Deccan plateau. People chose these for shelter from rain, heat and wind.

hist_earliest_grain_grasses.label: Wild Grain-Bearing Grasses
hist_earliest_grain_grasses.subject: history
hist_earliest_grain_grasses.detail: Wheat, barley and rice grew naturally in different parts of the subcontinent. People collected these grains as food and gradually learnt to cultivate them, leading to the beginnings of agriculture.

hist_domestication.label: Domestication
hist_domestication.subject: history
hist_domestication.detail: The process by which people grow plants and keep animals. Began globally around 12,000 years ago. In India: earliest plant cultivation evidence from Sambhar (Rajasthan salt-lake deposits) ~7000–6000 BCE; earliest animal domestication from Bagor (Rajasthan) and Adamgarh (MP) ~5000 BCE. At Mehrgarh (c. 7000 BCE), domesticated wheat, barley, cattle, sheep, goats. Selective breeding made domesticated plants and animals different from their wild counterparts.

hist_mehrgarh.label: Mehrgarh
hist_mehrgarh.subject: history
hist_mehrgarh.detail: One of the earliest known farming settlements (c. 7000 BCE), on the Bolan river in the Kochi plain of Baluchistan — the 'bread basket of Baluchistan', on the edge of the Indus plains. Called one of the largest Neolithic settlements between the Indus and the Mediterranean. Grew wheat and barley from the outset; domesticated cattle, sheep, and goats (goats predominated initially, then cattle outnumbered others). Compartmented mud-brick granaries; rectangular mud-brick houses. Disrupted by floods ~5500 BCE, agriculture resumed ~5000 BCE. Potter's wheel introduced ~4500 BCE (from western Asia); pottery rapidly multiplied and was painted. Agricultural expansion into the Indus plain 4500–3500 BCE paved the way for the Harappan culture. In the dried Hakra basin (a tributary of the Indus), 47 Later Neolithic settlements have been found.

hist_burzahom.label: Burzahom
hist_burzahom.subject: history
hist_burzahom.detail: A Neolithic site in Kashmir, 16 km north-west of Srinagar. The name means 'place of birch'. People lived in pit-houses dug into the ground with steps leading in, on a lake-side; hunting/fishing economy with some agriculture. Earliest date ~2700 BCE. Coarse grey pottery, polished stone tools, extensive bone tools (made from antlers). The Kashmiri Neolithic is distinguished by pit dwellings, wide ceramic range, and the complete absence of microliths. Unique to Burzahom among Indian Neolithic sites: domestic dogs were buried with their masters in their graves.

hist_daojali_hading.label: Daojali Hading
hist_daojali_hading.subject: history
hist_daojali_hading.detail: A Neolithic site on the hills near the Brahmaputra Valley, close to routes into China and Myanmar. Stone tools including mortars and pestles found, along with jadeite possibly from China and fossil wood tools.

hist_pit_houses.label: Pit Houses
hist_pit_houses.subject: history
hist_pit_houses.detail: Houses dug into the ground with steps leading into them, found at sites like Burzahom in Kashmir. May have provided shelter in cold weather. Represent early settled architecture.

hist_neolithic_tools.label: Neolithic Tools
hist_neolithic_tools.subject: history
hist_neolithic_tools.detail: Polished stone tools with fine cutting edges, including mortars and pestles for grinding grain. Different from earlier Palaeolithic tools. Some tools were also made of bone.

hist_earliest_crops.label: Earliest Domesticated Crops
hist_earliest_crops.subject: history
hist_earliest_crops.detail: Wheat and barley were among the first plants to be domesticated. Rice was grown in areas north of the Vindhyas. Millets were cultivated in southern India. Different crops suited different climates.

hist_earliest_animals_domesticated.label: Earliest Domesticated Animals
hist_earliest_animals_domesticated.subject: history
hist_earliest_animals_domesticated.detail: Dog was the first animal to be tamed. Sheep and goat were among the earliest domesticated animals. Cattle, pigs and buffalo were also reared. They provided milk, meat and served as stores of food.

hist_tribal_societies.label: Tribal Societies
hist_tribal_societies.subject: history
hist_tribal_societies.detail: Groups of families forming a tribe, usually two to three generations living together. Land, forests and water were shared wealth. No sharp rich-poor differences. Women did most agricultural work.

hist_pottery_invention.label: Pottery
hist_pottery_invention.subject: history
hist_pottery_invention.detail: Pottery first appears in the Neolithic phase when settled communities needed containers for storing, cooking, eating, drinking grains. Initially handmade; potter's wheel appeared at Mehrgarh ~4500 BCE (from western Asia), then spread across the subcontinent. Indian Neolithic pottery types: black-burnished ware, grey ware, mat-impressed ware. Painted pottery becomes common from ~2000 BCE onwards (Chalcolithic).

hist_koldihwa.label: Koldihwa
hist_koldihwa.subject: history
hist_koldihwa.detail: A Neolithic site in present-day Uttar Pradesh where evidence of rice cultivation and fragmentary animal bones was found. One of the important early farming sites in the subcontinent.

hist_chirand.label: Chirand
hist_chirand.subject: history
hist_chirand.detail: A Neolithic site 40 km west of Patna on the northern bank of the Ganges, at the junction of four rivers — Ganges, Son, Gandak, and Ghaghra. Open-land availability made settlement possible despite the riverine tract's paucity of stone. Distinguished by extensive bone and antler implements (from deer horns) — one of only two Indian Neolithic sites with a significant bone-tool industry (the other being Burzahom). Late Neolithic dates ~2000 BCE, possibly late Neolithic phase. Wheat, green gram, barley, buffalo and ox remains — showing the spread of agriculture into the eastern Gangetic plain.

hist_early_burials.label: Early Burials
hist_early_burials.subject: history
hist_early_burials.detail: Several burial sites found at Mehrgarh where dead were buried with goats, probably meant as food in the afterlife. Indicates belief in life after death and social rituals around death.

hist_cotton_cultivation.label: Cotton Cultivation
hist_cotton_cultivation.subject: history
hist_cotton_cultivation.detail: Cotton was probably grown at Mehrgarh from about 7000 years ago. Actual cloth pieces were found attached to objects at Mohenjodaro. Spindle whorls of terracotta and faience were used to spin thread.

hist_lower_paleolithic.label: Lower Palaeolithic
hist_lower_paleolithic.subject: history
hist_lower_paleolithic.detail: Earliest phase of the Stone Age. Globally begins ~2.6 million BCE (Oldowan); in India it is not older than ~600,000 BCE, with Bori (Maharashtra) being the earliest known Lower Palaeolithic site. In India the phase runs ~600,000–150,000 BCE. Characterised by hand axes, cleavers, and choppers (Acheulian and pre-Acheulian traditions). Associated with Homo erectus and Homo habilis. Indian sites: Bori, Soan/Sohan valley (Punjab/Pakistan), Belan valley (UP), Didwana (Rajasthan), Nagarjunakonda (AP), Bhimbetka (lower layers), Attirampakkam (TN), Hunsgi (Karnataka), Chirki-Nevasa (Maharashtra, 2000 tools). People were primarily food-gatherers with small-game hunting.

hist_middle_paleolithic.label: Middle Palaeolithic
hist_middle_paleolithic.subject: history
hist_middle_paleolithic.detail: Middle phase of the Stone Age. In India, ~150,000–35,000 BCE. Tools become smaller and more refined — flakes rather than cores (Levallois technique). Principal tools: blades, points, borers, scrapers, all made from flakes. Associated with Neanderthals globally and archaic Homo sapiens. Indian sites: Narmada valley, Nevasa (Maharashtra), Didwana (Rajasthan), Belan valley (UP), and several south of Tungabhadra river. The Belan valley has stone tools plus animal fossils (cattle, deer).

hist_upper_paleolithic.label: Upper Palaeolithic
hist_upper_paleolithic.subject: history
hist_upper_paleolithic.detail: Final phase of the Stone Age. In India, ~35,000–10,000 BCE, with 566 sites identified. Characterised by blade-and-burin tools and the first bone tools. Earliest cave/rock art appears (Bhimbetka upper layers, Lascaux globally). Associated with modern Homo sapiens sapiens. Sites in AP, Karnataka, Maharashtra, central MP, southern UP, Jharkhand, Gujarat sand dunes. Earliest Upper Palaeolithic site in the subcontinent: Fa Hien Cave (Sri Lanka, ~31,000 BCE artefacts). Climate was less humid during this phase (last phase of the ice age).

hist_pre_cultural.label: Pre-Cultural Hominins
hist_pre_cultural.subject: history
hist_pre_cultural.detail: Era before stone tools, when the hominin lineage emerged and diversified. Spans from the chimpanzee–hominin split (~6–7 million years ago) to the earliest Oldowan stone tools (~2.6 million years ago). Key developments: bipedalism, early Australopithecus species (e.g. Lucy, Australopithecus afarensis at ~3.2 mya in Ethiopia). No material culture yet — recognised only through fossils. Ends with the emergence of Homo habilis and the first flaked stone tools.

hist_chalcolithic_period.label: Chalcolithic
hist_chalcolithic_period.subject: history
hist_chalcolithic_period.detail: Copper-Stone Age: cultures using copper and stone implements together (low-grade bronze and occasional iron appear too). In India, spans c. 3000-500 BCE with strong regional variation - technologically, the Chalcolithic stage applies to pre-Harappan cultures, but in many regions Chalcolithic cultures in fact followed the Bronze Age Harappan. Chalcolithic peoples were primarily rural (contrast: the Harappans urbanized using Indus flood-plain surplus). Key Indian Chalcolithic cultures and type-sites: Ahar-Banas (Rajasthan, type-sites: Ahar, Gilund; c. 2100-1500 BCE); Kayatha (Malwa, MP; c. 2000-1800 BCE); Malwa (Navdatoli/Eran/Nagda; 1700-1200 BCE); Jorwe (Maharashtra, type-site Jorwe; major settlements Daimabad and Inamgaon; c. 1400-700 BCE); Prabhas-Rangpur (Gujarat). Characteristic pottery: black-and-red ware (from ~2000 BCE), often painted with white linear designs.

hist_jogimara_caves.label: Jogimara Caves
hist_jogimara_caves.subject: history
hist_jogimara_caves.detail: Ancient caves in the Ramgarh hills, Surguja district of Chhattisgarh. Paintings dated to around 1000 BCE. Contains what is often described as the world's oldest theatre/amphitheatre room — murals in this room mark a transition between prehistoric rock art and historic-period murals. Adorn a non-sacred space (the theatre), unusual for paintings of this era.

hist_mirzapur_rock_paintings.label: Mirzapur Rock Paintings
hist_mirzapur_rock_paintings.subject: history
hist_mirzapur_rock_paintings.detail: Prehistoric rock paintings in the Vindhyan sandstone shelters of Mirzapur district, southern Uttar Pradesh. Among the standard-reference sites for Indian rock art alongside Bhimbetka and Panchmarhi. Paintings span Mesolithic to Chalcolithic with hunting and everyday-life themes.

hist_panchmarhi.label: Panchmarhi
hist_panchmarhi.subject: history
hist_panchmarhi.detail: Pachmarhi (also Panchmarhi) in the Satpura range of Madhya Pradesh. Contains extensive prehistoric rock paintings spanning Upper Palaeolithic to Chalcolithic. Key reference site for Indian rock art alongside Bhimbetka and Mirzapur. Also MP's only hill station.

hist_petroglyphs.label: Petroglyphs
hist_petroglyphs.subject: history
hist_petroglyphs.detail: Rock engravings — images carved, chipped, or abraded into stone surfaces. Distinct from rock paintings (which use pigments applied to the rock). A key prehistoric art technique, often found alongside paintings at the same sites (including Bhimbetka). The term covers all forms of physical rock-surface marking as opposed to painted rock art.

hist_inamgaon.label: Inamgaon
hist_inamgaon.subject: history
hist_inamgaon.detail: A site on the river Ghod, tributary of the Bhima, occupied between 3600 and 2700 years ago. Adults were buried with food vessels. One man was buried in a large four-legged clay jar in the largest house.

hist_ahar_site.label: Ahar
hist_ahar_site.subject: history
hist_ahar_site.detail: Type-site of the Ahar culture in the dry Banas valley of southeastern Rajasthan (near Udaipur). Original name: Tambavati ('place of copper'). People here practised smelting and metallurgy from the outset, producing flat copper axes, bangles, and sheets. Unusually for a Chalcolithic site, Ahar virtually used no microlithic tools - stone axes and blades are essentially absent. Dated c. 2100-1500 BCE. Spread over about 4 hectares. Along with Gilund (a regional centre), these are the two major Ahar-culture sites.

hist_kayatha.label: Kayatha
hist_kayatha.subject: history
hist_kayatha.detail: Type-site of the Kayatha culture in Malwa (western Madhya Pradesh), near Ujjain. Dated c. 2000-1800 BCE, coexisting with the late phase of the Harappan civilisation. Shows both pre-Harappan and Harappan influences in its pottery. Notable find: one house yielded twenty-nine copper bangles and two unique copper axes - evidence of metal accumulation by specific households. Along with Eran, one of the earliest Chalcolithic settlements of central India; Kayatha was later superseded at the same region by the Ahar culture and then the Malwa culture.

hist_ramapithecus_sivapithecus.label: Ramapithecus & Sivapithecus
hist_ramapithecus_sivapithecus.subject: history
hist_ramapithecus_sivapithecus.detail: Early hominid skulls found in the Siwalik hills (India–Pakistan border region) — specifically in the Potwar plateau of Pakistani Punjab (developed on sandstone). Dated ~2.2 million years ago. Ramapithecus was female; both belonged to the same group. Possess some hominid features but represent apes. A related Greek fossil is dated ~10 million years ago. This Siwalik hominid line came to a dead end in the subcontinent — became extinct without spreading further.

hist_hathnora.label: Hathnora (Narmada Man)
hist_hathnora.subject: history
hist_hathnora.detail: A site in the middle valley of the Narmada in Madhya Pradesh where an almost-complete fossilized hominid skull was discovered in 1982. Initially called Homo erectus, now anatomically recognised as archaic Homo sapiens. The most significant hominid fossil find in India — evidence that archaic humans inhabited central India in the Middle Pleistocene (~700,000 BCE). Often called 'Narmada Man'.

hist_bori.label: Bori (Maharashtra)
hist_bori.subject: history
hist_bori.detail: Site in Maharashtra considered the earliest Lower Palaeolithic site in the Indian subcontinent (~600,000 BCE). Bori artefacts give the starting date for the Indian Lower Palaeolithic. Establishes that while Lower Palaeolithic began ~2 million years ago in Africa, in India it is no older than ~600,000 years.

hist_soan_valley.label: Soan Valley
hist_soan_valley.subject: history
hist_soan_valley.detail: Valley of the Son/Sohan river in Punjab (now Pakistan) — classic Lower Palaeolithic site of the subcontinent. Yielded early stone tools (hand axes, cleavers, choppers) of the Acheulian tradition. Along with Kashmir and the Thar desert, forms one of the best-known Early Old Stone Age regions of the subcontinent.

hist_belan_valley.label: Belan Valley
hist_belan_valley.subject: history
hist_belan_valley.detail: Valley in southern Uttar Pradesh at the foothills of the Vindhyas. Rich in stone tools and animal fossils (cattle, deer). Contains evidence spanning both Lower and Middle Palaeolithic ages, making it an important multi-period archaeological landscape.

hist_didwana_paleo.label: Didwana (Paleo)
hist_didwana_paleo.subject: history
hist_didwana_paleo.detail: A desert site in Rajasthan (distinct from the Didwana saline lake of modern geography). Yielded stone tools of all three Palaeolithic phases — Lower, Middle, and Upper — a rare stratified record making it key for understanding the progression of stone tool technologies in western India.

hist_fa_hien_cave.label: Fa Hien Cave
hist_fa_hien_cave.subject: history
hist_fa_hien_cave.detail: Cave in Sri Lanka with fossils of Homo sapiens sapiens (modern humans) dated ~34,000 years old; artefacts ~31,000 years old. Earliest Upper Palaeolithic site in the Indian subcontinent. Supports the hypothesis that the earliest modern humans arrived in India via an early coastal migration from Africa ~50,000 years ago — from the south, not the north.

hist_bagor.label: Bagor
hist_bagor.subject: history
hist_bagor.detail: Well-excavated Mesolithic site in Rajasthan. Distinctive microlithic industry. Inhabitants subsisted on hunting and pastoralism. Occupied continuously for 5,000 years from the 5th millennium BCE onwards. Along with Adamgarh (MP), provides the earliest evidence for animal domestication in India (~5000 BCE).

hist_adamgarh.label: Adamgarh
hist_adamgarh.subject: history
hist_adamgarh.detail: Mesolithic site in Madhya Pradesh. Along with Bagor (Rajasthan), provides the earliest evidence for the domestication of animals in the Indian part of the subcontinent (~5000 BCE). Key site for understanding the transition from hunting-gathering to pastoralism in central India.

hist_sambhar.label: Sambhar
hist_sambhar.subject: history
hist_sambhar.detail: A former salt lake in Rajasthan whose deposits suggest plant cultivation in the region as early as 7000–6000 BCE — earliest evidence of plant cultivation in India. Important for understanding the transition from gathering to agriculture at the Mesolithic–Neolithic interface.

hist_gufkral.label: Gufkral
hist_gufkral.subject: history
hist_gufkral.detail: Neolithic site 41 km south-west of Srinagar, Kashmir. Name means 'cave of the potter'. People practised both agriculture and animal husbandry. Part of the Kashmiri Neolithic group along with Burzahom — distinguished by pit dwellings, wide ceramic range, stone and bone tools, and the complete absence of microliths.

hist_piklihal.label: Piklihal
hist_piklihal.subject: history
hist_piklihal.detail: Important Neolithic site in Karnataka. Inhabitants were cattle-herders who domesticated cattle, sheep, and goats. Set up seasonal camps surrounded by cowpens made of posts and stakes; accumulated dung which was burned when abandoning camp — producing the characteristic 'ash mounds' of the south Indian Neolithic. Both ash mounds and habitation sites have been excavated.

hist_brahmagiri.label: Brahmagiri
hist_brahmagiri.subject: history
hist_brahmagiri.detail: A megalithic site where one skeleton was buried with 33 gold beads, 2 stone beads, 4 copper bangles and a conch shell, while others had only a few pots. Shows early social stratification.

hist_maski.label: Maski
hist_maski.subject: history
hist_maski.detail: Neolithic site in Karnataka (southern Neolithic group). Famously also the site of a Minor Rock Edict of Ashoka — the first edict where Ashoka's personal name 'Devanampiya Asoka' was identified, confirming the identity of 'Devanampiya Piyadassi' mentioned in other edicts as Ashoka Maurya.

hist_hallur.label: Hallur
hist_hallur.subject: history
hist_hallur.detail: Neolithic site in Karnataka (southern group). Notable for yielding some of the earliest evidence of iron in India (~1200 BCE in its later layers), marking the Neolithic-to-Iron-Age transition in peninsular India. Part of the same cluster as Maski, Brahmagiri, and Piklihal.

hist_senuwar.label: Senuwar
hist_senuwar.subject: history
hist_senuwar.detail: Important Neolithic site in the Rohtas district of Bihar, in the Kaimur hilly area. Part of the eastern Neolithic group along with Taradih (near the Bodh-Gaya temple). Shows Neolithic settlement patterns in eastern India.

hist_sargon_of_akkad.label: Sargon of Akkad
hist_sargon_of_akkad.subject: history
hist_sargon_of_akkad.detail: Founder of the Akkadian Empire (c. 2334-2279 BCE), often regarded as the first empire-builder in history. Rose from humble origins to conquer all of Sumer and expand territory from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean. Established Akkad as his capital.

hist_rigveda.label: Rigveda
hist_rigveda.subject: history
hist_rigveda.detail: The earliest composition in Sanskrit, dated to about 3500 years ago. Contains more than a thousand hymns (suktas) in praise of gods like Agni, Indra and Soma. Composed by sages and transmitted orally. Sharma: 10 mandalas (books); Books II-VII are the earliest core (family books); Books I and X are latest additions. ~1500 BCE (some parts to 1000 BCE). Collection of prayers to Agni, Indra, Mitra, Varuna etc. by various poet families. Written in Sanskrit but contains many Munda and Dravidian loanwords (from Harappan languages). Horse mentioned 215 times (most of any animal), cow 176, bull 170. Shudra varna first mentioned in Book X (the latest). Term "arya" occurs 36 times.

hist_harappan_script.label: Harappan Script
hist_harappan_script.subject: history
hist_harappan_script.detail: Remains undeciphered to this day. Written right to left with 375-400 signs, not alphabetical. Found on seals, copper tools, pottery rims, tablets, jewellery and even an ancient signboard. A bilingual inscription could help resolve the language question. Despite many attempts, scholars have not been able to decipher it. The signs are not alphabetic but logo-syllabic. First specimen noticed 1853 (Cunningham); complete script documented by 1923. ~4000 inscribed objects recovered; 250-400 pictographs. Not alphabetic — largely pictographic (each sign = a sound, idea, or object). Written right-to-left (Brahmi later left-to-right). Not deciphered; proposed links to Dravidian, Sanskrit, Sumerian — none satisfactory. Singhania: ~70% of seals bear short inscriptions in the still-undeciphered pictographic script. Writing direction is mostly right-to-left, but boustrophedon (alternating R-to-L and L-to-R on successive lines) is also attested.

hist_vedic_tradition.label: Vedic Sacrificial Tradition
hist_vedic_tradition.subject: history
hist_vedic_tradition.detail: Rigveda (c. 1500-1000 BCE) contains hymns to Agni, Indra, Soma. Sacrifices performed for cattle, sons, health. Later elaborate sacrifices like rajasuya and ashvamedha performed by kings with Brahmana priests. Upanishadic thinkers questioned the significance of sacrifices. Sharma: Rig Vedic period emphasized prayer; later Vedic period replaced prayer with elaborate sacrifices (yajna). Yajamana = sacrificer; success depended on magical power of words correctly uttered. Private (household) and public (royal) sacrifices coexisted. Cattle slaughtered on massive scale — guest was called "goghna" (fed on cattle). Rise of brahmana priests as monopolists of ritual knowledge. Reaction against sacrificial excess gave rise to the Upanishads (c. 600 BCE) in Panchala and Videha.

hist_harappan_agriculture.label: Harappan Agriculture
hist_harappan_agriculture.subject: history
hist_harappan_agriculture.detail: Crops included wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea, sesame; millets in Gujarat; rice relatively rare. Evidence of ploughed fields at Kalibangan. Irrigation through canals (Shortughai), wells and water reservoirs (Dholavira). Oxen likely used for ploughing. Crops: wheat, barley, pulses, peas, rice, sesame, linseed, mustard. Irrigation was used. Cotton was grown from about 7000 years ago at Mehrgarh. Sharma: no hoe or ploughshare found, but furrows in pre-Harappan Kalibangan show ploughing; wooden ploughs drawn by oxen (camels possibly). Stone sickles for harvest. Flood-plain sowing in November, harvest April. Gabarbands (dammed nalas) used in Baluchistan; no canal irrigation. Rice cultivated at Lothal from ~1800 BCE. Earliest cotton producers — Greeks called the area Sindon (from Sindh).

hist_social_differences_burials.label: Social Differences in Burials
hist_social_differences_burials.subject: history
hist_social_differences_burials.detail: Objects found with skeletons suggest differences in status. At Brahmagiri, one burial had 33 gold beads while others had few pots. Megaliths with multiple skeletons indicate family burial sites with portholes for re-entry.

hist_indus_river_cities.label: Earliest Cities on the Indus
hist_indus_river_cities.subject: history
hist_indus_river_cities.detail: About 4700 years ago, some of the earliest cities in the subcontinent flourished on the banks of the Indus and its tributaries. These were the Harappan cities with planned layouts and advanced drainage.

hist_janapadas.label: Janapadas
hist_janapadas.subject: history
hist_janapadas.detail: Literally 'the land where the jana set its foot and settled down'. Territorial units associated with specific peoples. Settlements included huts, cattle, and crops like rice, wheat, barley and sugarcane. Sharma: term "janapada" does NOT appear in the Rig Veda (where "jana" occurs 275 times). First appears in the Brahmanas, not earlier than 800 BCE. Marks the transition from tribal identity (jana) to territorial political unit (janapada) — tribal authority became territorial. The raja came to be called janapadin.

hist_harappan_bricks.label: Standardised Bricks
hist_harappan_bricks.subject: history
hist_harappan_bricks.detail: Bricks across all Harappan settlements maintained a standardised ratio where length and breadth were four times and twice the height respectively. Both sun-dried and baked bricks were used. This uniformity from Jammu to Gujarat indicates centralised planning. Burnt bricks were standard — in sharp contrast to Egypt (which primarily used dried bricks) and Mesopotamia (used baked bricks but far less extensively). This is one of the distinctive markers of Harappan material culture. Singhania: bricks were laid in multiple layers of well-baked brick joined with gypsum mortar. The standardised ratio (1:2:4 for thickness:width:length) was used across Harappan sites — a marker of cross-site coordination.

hist_sanskrit_language.label: Sanskrit
hist_sanskrit_language.subject: history
hist_sanskrit_language.detail: An ancient Indo-European language in which many important texts were composed including the Vedas and epics. Part of a family that includes Hindi, Persian, Greek and English.

hist_ashvamedha.label: Ashvamedha (Horse Sacrifice)
hist_ashvamedha.subject: history
hist_ashvamedha.detail: A ritual where a horse was let loose to wander freely, guarded by the raja's men. If other rajas stopped it, they had to fight. Successful completion established the raja's supremacy over rivals. Sharma: rooted in Indo-European horse-sacrifice tradition (widespread in Europe/Central Asia from 2nd half of 5th millennium BCE). Two hymns in the 10th book of the Rig Veda; the later Vedic texts transform it into a formal royal ritual. Symbolism: the royal horse is set loose for a year, and all territory it crosses unopposed is claimed by the king — thus asserting unquestioned sovereignty over that domain.

hist_yajnas.label: Yajnas (Sacrifices)
hist_yajnas.subject: history
hist_yajnas.detail: Rituals involving offerings of ghee, grain and sometimes animals into fire, meant for gods and goddesses. Wealth obtained from battles was used for yajnas. Performed by priests with raja as central figure. Sharma: formulae and sacrifices were invented and elaborated by the brahmanas who claimed monopoly over priestly knowledge. Performer (yajamana) attained merit through correctly uttered mantras. Dakshina (sacrificial fee) could be as much as 240,000 cows for a rajasuya — though actual transfers of land were limited despite later texts sometimes recommending the whole territory as dakshina.

hist_code_of_hammurabi.label: Code of Hammurabi
hist_code_of_hammurabi.subject: history
hist_code_of_hammurabi.detail: One of the oldest known written law codes, compiled c. 1754 BCE. Contains 282 laws dealing with trade, property, family, labour, and crime. Notable for its principle of lex talionis ('eye for an eye') though punishments varied by social class. Reveals a stratified society of free men, dependants, and slaves.

hist_akkadian_empire.label: Akkadian Empire
hist_akkadian_empire.subject: history
hist_akkadian_empire.detail: Founded by Sargon of Akkad c. 2334 BCE, it was the first empire in Mesopotamia unifying Sumerian and Akkadian city-states. Extended from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean. Sargon is often called the first empire-builder in history. The empire lasted about 180 years.

hist_indo_european_languages.label: Indo-European Language Family
hist_indo_european_languages.subject: history
hist_indo_european_languages.detail: A family of languages including Sanskrit, Hindi, Persian, Greek, Latin and English. They share common word roots. Other Indian language families include Dravidian, Tibeto-Burman and Austro-Asiatic.

hist_black_red_ware.label: Black and Red Ware
hist_black_red_ware.subject: history
hist_black_red_ware.detail: Distinctive pottery found in megalithic burials across the Deccan and south India. The dead were generally buried with these pots along with iron tools and ornaments of stone and gold.

hist_lower_town.label: Lower Town
hist_lower_town.subject: history
hist_lower_town.detail: The eastern, larger but lower part of Harappan cities where most people lived. Houses were one or two storeys high with rooms around courtyards, separate bathing areas and wells.

hist_harappan_decline.label: Decline of Harappan Civilisation
hist_harappan_decline.subject: history
hist_harappan_decline.detail: By c. 1800 BCE most Mature Harappan sites abandoned. Marked by disappearance of seals, weights, script, long-distance trade and craft specialisation. Multiple causes proposed: climate change, deforestation, floods, river shifts. Wheeler's Aryan invasion theory challenged by George Dales in 1964. Around 1900 BCE (3900 years ago), many cities were abandoned: writing, seals and standardised weights fell out of use. Possible causes include dried rivers, deforestation, flooding, and loss of administrative control. Sharma timeline: mature phase ends ~1900 BCE; degenerate phase 1900-1500 BCE in Gujarat/Rajasthan/Haryana/western UP; post-urban 1900-1200 BCE. Causes: (1) Yamuna + Sutlej shifted away from the Sarasvati/Hakra ~1700 BCE — water loss; (2) rise of Elam ~2000 BCE interrupted Mesopotamia trade, collapsing bead/bronze crafts; (3) rainfall decline; (4) soil exhaustion; (5) some floods. No mass-confrontation evidence with Indo-Aryans.

hist_harappa_site.label: Harappa
hist_harappa_site.subject: history
hist_harappa_site.detail: First Harappan site to be discovered, located in Punjab (Pakistan). Badly damaged by brick robbers for railway construction. Alexander Cunningham noted it in 1875. Excavated by Daya Ram Sahni in early 20th century and R.E.M. Wheeler in 1946. Spans ~150 ha. Citadel had six granaries in two rows of six; each granary 15.23 x 6.09 m (total floor ~838 sq m). Circular brick platforms nearby for threshing — wheat and barley grains found in crevices. Two-roomed barracks likely housed labourers. Singhania finds list: stone symbol of lingam and yoni, mother goddess figurine, wheat and barley in wooden mortar, dice, copper scale and mirror, a bronze sculpture of a dog chasing a deer, and the red sandstone male torso — together establishing Harappa's rich range of art and craft artefacts.

hist_ur.label: Ur
hist_ur.subject: history
hist_ur.detail: One of the most important Sumerian city-states, located in southern Mesopotamia. Flourished c. 2600-2000 BCE. Famous for its Royal Cemetery with rich grave goods, the Great Ziggurat, and as one of the world's first major urban centres. Excavated by Leonard Woolley in the 1920s-30s.

hist_epic_of_gilgamesh.label: Epic of Gilgamesh
hist_epic_of_gilgamesh.subject: history
hist_epic_of_gilgamesh.detail: One of the earliest known works of literature, originating from Sumerian poems c. 2100 BCE, compiled into an Akkadian epic c. 1200 BCE. Tells the story of Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, his quest for immortality, and includes a flood narrative. Written in cuneiform on clay tablets.

hist_chanhudaro.label: Chanhudaro
hist_chanhudaro.subject: history
hist_chanhudaro.detail: Small Harappan settlement of less than 7 hectares, almost exclusively devoted to craft production including bead-making, shell-cutting, metal-working, seal-making and weight-making. Specialised drills for bead production found here. Third city of mature Harappan, about 130 km south of Mohenjo-daro in Sindh. Noted for bead-making and craft workshops.

hist_megaliths.label: Megaliths
hist_megaliths.subject: history
hist_megaliths.detail: Large stone boulders carefully arranged to mark burial sites, beginning about 3000 years ago. Found throughout the Deccan, south India, north-east and Kashmir. Burials included Black and Red Ware pottery and iron tools.

hist_dholavira.label: Dholavira
hist_dholavira.subject: history
hist_dholavira.detail: Major Harappan site in Kutch, Gujarat, discovered and excavated by R.S. Bisht from 1990. Entire settlement was fortified with sections separated by walls. Had elaborate water reservoirs for storing water in the arid zone. Uniquely divided into three parts with massive stone walls. Has a set of large letters carved in white stone from the Harappan script, and a large open area for ceremonies. Covers ~50 ha in Kutch (Gujarat). Stone-built citadel — most impressive Harappan citadel; dressed stone used with mud bricks in masonry. Three burial types; one has a stone circle above the grave resembling Megalithic tradition. All three Harappan phases (early, mature, late) present. Singhania: giant water reservoir; unique water-harnessing system with dams and embankments; a stadium-like structure. Inscription board comprising 10 large-sized Harappan signs — resembling an "advertisement board" (world's earliest known signboard).

hist_rakhigarhi.label: Rakhigarhi
hist_rakhigarhi.subject: history
hist_rakhigarhi.detail: Major Harappan site in Haryana, one of the largest Harappan settlements discovered in India. Part of post-partition efforts to locate Harappan sites within Indian territory after major sites went to Pakistan. Largest Harappan site at ~250 ha — larger than Mohenjo-daro (500 ha physical size is coverage area; Rakhigarhi is comparable). Situated on the Ghaggar in Haryana. All three Harappan phases present. Singhania: granary, cemetery, drainage system, and terracotta bricks documented; confirms its status as the largest Harappan site.

hist_gotra_system.label: Gotra System
hist_gotra_system.subject: history
hist_gotra_system.detail: Brahmanical practice from c. 1000 BCE of classifying people by gotras named after Vedic seers. Two rules: women must adopt husband's gotra on marriage, and same-gotra marriage prohibited (exogamy). Satavahana queens retained father's gotra, showing regional variation. Sharma: literally means "cow pen" (where clan cattle were kept). The institution appeared in later Vedic times. Over time it came to signify descent from a common mythical ancestor. Gotra exogamy was enforced — marriage prohibited between persons of the same gotra.

hist_iron_age_india.label: Beginning of Iron Use
hist_iron_age_india.subject: history
hist_iron_age_india.detail: Iron tools and weapons were found in megalithic burials including horse equipment, axes and daggers. Iron was not used in earlier Harappan cities. It enabled new agricultural and military capabilities. Sharma: pure iron first produced in Mesopotamia ~5000 BCE, Anatolia in 3rd millennium BCE. Until 1200 BCE iron was a precious metal in Western Asia. In India: Rajasthan and Karnataka in 2nd half of 2nd millennium BCE (Chalcolithic context); Gandhara by 1000 BCE; western UP by 800 BCE (arrowheads, spearheads); eastern UP by 7th century BCE. Called shyama ayas or krishna ayas ("black metal") in later Vedic texts. Iron axes enabled clearance of the Gangetic forests.

hist_harappan_crafts.label: Harappan Crafts
hist_harappan_crafts.subject: history
hist_harappan_crafts.detail: Specialists produced fine objects of copper, bronze, gold and silver. Carnelian beads were cut, shaped, polished and bored. Faience was artificially produced from sand or quartz with blue-green glaze. Singhania adds: bead factories operated at Chanhu-daro and Lothal. Beads made from carnelian, amethyst, quartz, steatite. Both men and women wore necklaces, fillets, armlets, finger rings; girdles/earrings/anklets were worn by women. Cotton and wool spun by both rich and poor — using faience (expensive) or clay (cheap) spindles/whorls.

hist_proto_shiva_seal.label: Proto-Shiva Seal
hist_proto_shiva_seal.subject: history
hist_proto_shiva_seal.detail: Seal depicting a figure seated cross-legged in yogic posture, sometimes surrounded by animals. Interpreted by some as early form of Shiva (Pashupati). However, this interpretation is debated as Rigvedic Rudra does not match this depiction. The three-horned figure sits cross-legged in yogic posture, surrounded by an elephant, tiger, rhinoceros, buffalo (below throne) and two deer (at feet). Identification as Pashupati Mahadeva is doubtful (no bull present; horned deities also appear in other ancient cultures). Phallus worship is separately attested via stone lingas at Harappa, echoed in Rigveda's reference to non-Aryan phallus-worshippers. Singhania placement detail: elephant and tiger on the left side of the figure; rhinoceros and buffalo on the right side; two antelopes shown below the seat.

hist_bharata_jana.label: Bharata Jana
hist_bharata_jana.subject: history
hist_bharata_jana.detail: A group of people mentioned in the Rigveda who lived in the northwest of the subcontinent. The name Bharata was later used for the country itself.

hist_shortughai.label: Shortughai
hist_shortughai.subject: history
hist_shortughai.detail: A Harappan settlement in far-off Afghanistan, established near the best source of lapis lazuli. Evidence of canals found here. Demonstrates the vast reach of Harappan trade and resource procurement networks.

hist_citadel.label: Citadel
hist_citadel.subject: history
hist_citadel.detail: The western, smaller but higher part of Harappan cities. Contained special buildings like the Great Bath and storehouses. Surrounded by walls of baked brick laid in interlocking pattern.

hist_agni_indra_soma.label: Vedic Gods: Agni, Indra, Soma
hist_agni_indra_soma.subject: history
hist_agni_indra_soma.detail: Three especially important gods in the Rigveda. Agni was the god of fire, Indra was a warrior god, and Soma was a plant from which a special drink was prepared for rituals. Sharma: Indra — called Purandara (destroyer of dwelling units); has 250 hymns; warlord leading Aryans to victory; rain god. Agni — 200 hymns; the intermediary god who carries oblations as smoke to the other gods. Soma — god of plants + intoxicating drink made from a plant (likely ephedra, based on finds at Togolok-21 temple in Margiana). Many Soma-preparation hymns describe processing methods.

hist_harappan_burials.label: Harappan Burial Practices
hist_harappan_burials.subject: history
hist_harappan_burials.detail: Dead generally laid in pits, some lined with bricks. Some graves contained pottery and ornaments for afterlife. Jewellery found in burials of both men and women. Overall, Harappans did not bury precious things extensively, showing relatively less social differentiation in death.

hist_prakrit_language.label: Prakrit
hist_prakrit_language.subject: history
hist_prakrit_language.detail: Languages used by ordinary people in ancient India. Several forms existed, named after regions. Magadhi was the form spoken in Magadha. Used by Buddha and Mahavira for their teachings.

hist_harappan_seals.label: Harappan Seals
hist_harappan_seals.subject: history
hist_harappan_seals.detail: Distinctive artefacts made of steatite, containing animal motifs and undeciphered script. Used to facilitate long-distance trade through sealings on goods. Script written right to left with 375-400 signs, not alphabetical. Longest inscription has about 26 signs. Generally rectangular, usually carved with an animal and the undeciphered script. The script is the earliest form of writing in the subcontinent. About 2000 seals recovered. Made of steatite or faience. Motifs: unicorns (most common), humped bull, tiger, rhinoceros, buffalo, goat, elephant, antelope, crocodile. Used both as authority stamps and as amulets. Unlike Mesopotamia/Egypt, few stamped objects (sealings) survive. Singhania: shapes include square (most common), triangular, rectangular, circular. Materials: steatite (most common), agate, chert, copper, faience, terracotta, gold, ivory. Writing direction mostly right-to-left but boustrophedon (bi-directional, alternating lines) instances exist. Typical seal has animal/human figure on one side and inscription on the other; some bear inscriptions on both sides or on a third side. Motifs include unicorn, humped bull, rhinoceros, tiger, elephant, buffalo, bison, goat, markhor, ibex, crocodile, and imagined half-man-half-animal figures. Cow is notably absent. Some seals bear swastika-like symbols and mathematical-looking images. Some holed seals found with dead bodies — used as amulets.

hist_faience.label: Faience
hist_faience.subject: history
hist_faience.detail: Material made of ground sand or silica mixed with colour and gum, then fired. Considered precious because difficult to make. Faience pots found mostly at Mohenjodaro and Harappa, rarely at smaller sites, indicating social stratification. An artificially produced material from sand or powdered quartz, shaped with gum and glazed to produce a shiny blue or sea-green surface. Used for beads, bangles, earrings, tiny vessels.

hist_harappan_drainage.label: Harappan Drainage System
hist_harappan_drainage.subject: history
hist_harappan_drainage.detail: Most complete ancient drainage system discovered. Streets laid out in grid pattern with drains. Every house connected to street drains through covered channels. Drains had sumps for cleaning at intervals. Found even in smaller settlements like Lothal. Covered drains laid in straight lines with gentle slopes. House drains connected to street drains, smaller feeding into larger; inspection holes at intervals for cleaning. Perhaps no other Bronze Age civilization gave drainage and public health the attention the Harappans did — no comparable system existed except arguably at Knossos (Crete). House → street drain chain, some covered with brick, some with stone slabs.

hist_vedic_society.label: Vedic Society
hist_vedic_society.subject: history
hist_vedic_society.detail: Society described in the Rigveda with brahmins performing rituals and rajas who were not hereditary rulers. People were called jana or vish. Battles were fought for cattle, land and water. Wealth distributed through yajnas. Sharma: Aryans divided into five tribes (panchajana). The Bharatas and Tritsu (supported by priest Vasishtha) were the dominant clans. The Battle of Ten Kings (Dasarajna) on the river Parushni (modern Ravi) established Bharata supremacy under Sudas against a coalition of ten chiefs (five Aryan, five non-Aryan); the defeated Purus later merged with Bharatas to form the Kurus, who combined with Panchalas and dominated the upper Gangetic basin in later Vedic times. Country name Bharatavarsha = derived from the Bharata tribe, first mentioned in the Rig Veda.

hist_babylonian_empire.label: Babylonian Empire
hist_babylonian_empire.subject: history
hist_babylonian_empire.detail: Centred on the city of Babylon on the Euphrates. The Old Babylonian period (c. 1894-1595 BCE) under Hammurabi unified Mesopotamia. The Neo-Babylonian Empire (626-539 BCE) under Nebuchadnezzar II built the Hanging Gardens and the Ishtar Gate. Fell to the Persian Achaemenids.

hist_vedic_rajas.label: Vedic Rajas
hist_vedic_rajas.subject: history
hist_vedic_rajas.detail: Early rulers mentioned in the Rigveda who did not have capital cities, palaces or armies, nor did they collect taxes. Sons did not automatically succeed fathers. They were chosen by jana for their bravery. Sharma: Rig Vedic rajan was tribal chief, largely hereditary but subject to election by samiti (assembly). Assisted by purohita (priest — Vasishtha, Vishvamitra), senani (commander), vrajapati (pasture officer), kulapa (family head), gramani (village/military head). No standing army — militia raised in wartime. In later Vedic times, vidatha disappeared; sabha/samiti survived but no longer admitted women. King performed rajasuya (coronation), ashvamedha (territorial claim), vajapeya (chariot race) to legitimize power. New officer sangrihitri collected taxes.

hist_harappan_craft_production.label: Harappan Craft Production
hist_harappan_craft_production.subject: history
hist_harappan_craft_production.detail: Specialised craft centres existed at sites like Chanhudaro (bead-making, shell-cutting, metal-working, seal-making). Materials included carnelian, jasper, steatite, copper, bronze, gold, shell, faience and terracotta. Nageshwar and Balakot specialised in shell objects.

hist_harappan_trade.label: Harappan Long-Distance Trade
hist_harappan_trade.subject: history
hist_harappan_trade.detail: Extensive trade network with Mesopotamia, Oman (Magan) and Bahrain (Dilmun). Mesopotamian texts refer to Meluhha (possibly Harappan region) and its products: carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper, gold, wood. Harappan jars found at Omani sites. Copper from Oman had nickel traces matching Harappan artefacts. NCERT raw-material sourcing: copper from Rajasthan and Oman, tin from Afghanistan and Iran, gold from Karnataka, precious stones from Gujarat, Iran and Afghanistan. Mesopotamian records from ~2350 BCE onwards refer to Meluha (= Indus region) with intermediate trading stations Dilmun (Bahrain) and Makan/Magan. No metal money — barter. Trading colony established in northern Afghanistan (Shortughai) for Central Asian trade. Used bullock-carts with solid wheels (ekka-like, not spoked).

hist_harappan_civilisation.label: Harappan Civilisation
hist_harappan_civilisation.subject: history
hist_harappan_civilisation.detail: Also called the Indus Valley Civilisation, dated c. 2600-1900 BCE. One of the earliest urban civilisations in the world, contemporaneous with Mesopotamia and Egypt. Named after Harappa, the first site discovered. Spread from Afghanistan to Gujarat. Characterised by planned cities, advanced drainage, standardised weights and seals. Sharma: extended from the Siwaliks to the Arabian Sea and from the Makran coast (Baluchistan) to Meerut — roughly 1,299,600 sq km, larger than contemporary Egypt or Mesopotamia. ~2800 sites identified overall; 1022 mature-phase sites (406 in Pakistan, 616 in India). Three phases: early, mature (2500-1900 BCE), late/post-urban (1900-1200 BCE). Singhania: notably no monumental temples or palaces (unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia) — suggests the civilisation was primarily mercantile rather than priest- or king-dominated.

hist_painted_grey_ware.label: Painted Grey Ware
hist_painted_grey_ware.subject: history
hist_painted_grey_ware.detail: A special type of pottery found at janapada sites. Grey pots with painted designs of simple lines and geometric patterns, extremely fine to touch with smooth surface. Used for special occasions. Sharma: ~700 PGW sites identified in upper Gangetic basin (western UP, Delhi, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan/Matsya), dated c. 1000-500 BCE. Bowls and dishes; used by emerging upper orders for rituals or eating. Alongside PGW the later Vedic period used three other wares: black-and-red ware, black-slipped ware, and red-ware (most popular). PGW overlaps with late Harappan pottery at Bhagwanpura (Haryana).

hist_great_bath.label: Great Bath
hist_great_bath.subject: history
hist_great_bath.detail: Large rectangular tank in the Citadel of Mohenjodaro, made watertight with bricks set on edge and gypsum mortar. Two flights of steps on north and south. Scholars suggest it was used for special ritual bathing. Lined with bricks, coated with plaster, and made watertight with natural tar. Had steps on two sides and rooms on all sides. Dimensions: 11.88 x 7.01 m, 2.43 m deep. Burnt-brick floor; water drawn from an adjacent well; outlet from a corner to a drain. Dholavira has a comparable large tank likely used for similar ritual purpose.

hist_mohenjodaro.label: Mohenjodaro
hist_mohenjodaro.subject: history
hist_mohenjodaro.detail: The best-known Harappan site, located in Sind (present-day Pakistan). Divided into Citadel and Lower Town. Featured the Great Bath, warehouse, planned drainage system, and about 700 wells. A planned urban centre covering 125 hectares. Famous for the stone statue of a "priest-king"; houses were planned around courtyards, with covered drains. Covers ~500 ha. Name literally means "mound of the dead". Largest building is a granary 45.71 x 15.23 m. Ancient massive floods destroyed a large part of the city. Excavated by R.D. Banerjee (initial), Marshall (1931), Mackay (1938). Singhania: post-cremation burial practice also attested here; steatite Priest-King bust and bronze Dancing Girl both excavated from Mohenjo-daro. Pashupati seal found here.

hist_ziggurat.label: Ziggurat
hist_ziggurat.subject: history
hist_ziggurat.detail: Massive stepped pyramid temple-towers built in ancient Mesopotamia. Served as religious centres dedicated to the patron deity of the city. The most famous is the Great Ziggurat of Ur. Made of mud-brick with baked brick facing. Symbolised a connection between earth and heaven.

hist_harappan_weights.label: Harappan Weights System
hist_harappan_weights.subject: history
hist_harappan_weights.detail: Precise system using cubical chert stones with no markings. Lower denominations were binary (1,2,4,8,16,32 up to 12,800), higher followed decimal system. Standardised across the entire civilisation, indicating unified authority. Base-16 system: 16, 64, 160, 320, 640 (the 16-anna rupee survived in India until recently). A bronze measuring stick with measure marks has also been found.

hist_hammurabi.label: Hammurabi
hist_hammurabi.subject: history
hist_hammurabi.detail: King of Babylon (r. c. 1792-1750 BCE) who unified much of Mesopotamia under Babylonian rule. Famous for his law code, one of the earliest written legal codes, inscribed on a black stone stele. The code included 282 laws covering property, trade, family, and criminal matters with varying penalties by social class.

hist_kalibangan.label: Kalibangan
hist_kalibangan.subject: history
hist_kalibangan.detail: Harappan site in Rajasthan excavated by B.B. Lal and B.K. Thapar from 1960. Evidence of ploughed field with two sets of furrows at right angles in Early Harappan levels. Also had fire altars suggesting ritual practices. Had fire altars where sacrifices may have been performed — unique among major Harappan sites. Located in northern Rajasthan; name means "black bangles". Fire altars unique to the site. Pre-Harappan furrow evidence indicates ploughing. Many houses had their own wells. Singhania: decorated bricks; bangle factory; toy carts; camel bones; citadel + lower town arrangement. Confirmed fire altar.

hist_vedas.label: The Vedas
hist_vedas.subject: history
hist_vedas.detail: Four sacred texts: Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda. The Rigveda is the oldest, composed about 3500 years ago, containing over 1000 hymns (suktas) in Vedic Sanskrit praising gods like Agni, Indra and Soma. Sharma: four Samhitas — Rig Veda (oldest, prayers), Sama Veda (Rig prayers set to tune for recitation), Yajur Veda (hymns + rituals), Atharva Veda (charms and spells; reflects non-Aryan tradition). Each Samhita was followed by associated Brahmanas (ritualistic commentary). All later Vedic texts compiled in the upper Gangetic basin between 1000-500 BCE.

hist_lothal.label: Lothal
hist_lothal.subject: history
hist_lothal.detail: Harappan site in Gujarat, near sources of carnelian, steatite and metal. Entire settlement was fortified. Citadel was not walled off but built at a height. Had specialised bead drills and fire altars. Houses were built of mud bricks but drains of burnt bricks. Located beside a tributary of the Sabarmati near the Gulf of Khambat. Had a dockyard and a bead-making workshop; important centre for stone, shell and metal objects. Located at the head of the Gulf of Cambay in Gujarat. Rice cultivation from ~1800 BCE — unique among Harappan sites. Doubtful terracotta horse figurine. Dockyard + bead-making workshop. Singhania: nicknamed the "Manchester of the Indus Valley". Finds include a terracotta horse figurine, terracotta ship, modern-chess-like pieces, and instruments for measuring 45°, 90°, and 180° angles. Practised burial of cremated remains. Fire altars and a painted jar also recovered. A bead factory operated here.

hist_aryas_dasas.label: Aryas and Dasas
hist_aryas_dasas.subject: history
hist_aryas_dasas.detail: The Rigveda composers called themselves Aryas and their opponents Dasas or Dasyus, who did not perform sacrifices and spoke different languages. Later dasa came to mean slave, people captured in war. Sharma: Dasas appear in ancient Iranian literature too — likely a branch of early Aryans themselves (the term features in the name Divodasa, an Aryan chief). Dasyus were the original Indian inhabitants; "dasyuhatya" (slaughter of dasyus) is a repeated Rigvedic phrase. Dasyus worshipped the phallus and did not husband cattle for dairy — a key cultural divider. Trasadasyu = Aryan chief famed for overpowering dasyus.

hist_assyrian_empire.label: Assyrian Empire
hist_assyrian_empire.subject: history
hist_assyrian_empire.detail: Powerful Mesopotamian empire centred in northern Iraq. The Neo-Assyrian Empire (911-609 BCE) was the largest empire the world had seen at its time, stretching from Egypt to Iran. Known for military prowess, administrative efficiency, and the great library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh.

hist_mesopotamia.label: Mesopotamia
hist_mesopotamia.subject: history
hist_mesopotamia.detail: Region between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers (modern Iraq). One of the earliest sites of urbanisation and writing. Successive civilisations including Sumerians, Akkadians, Babylonians, and Assyrians flourished here. Name means 'land between the rivers' in Greek.

hist_sumerians.label: Sumerians
hist_sumerians.subject: history
hist_sumerians.detail: The earliest known civilisation in southern Mesopotamia (c. 4500-1900 BCE). Invented cuneiform writing, the wheel, and the sexagesimal (base-60) number system. Built city-states like Ur, Uruk, and Lagash. Developed irrigation agriculture in an arid landscape.

hist_cuneiform.label: Cuneiform Writing
hist_cuneiform.subject: history
hist_cuneiform.detail: One of the earliest known writing systems, developed by Sumerians around 3200 BCE. Written on clay tablets using a wedge-shaped reed stylus. Initially pictographic, it evolved into a syllabic script. Used for record-keeping, literature, law, and diplomacy for over 3,000 years.

hist_urbanisation_mesopotamia.label: Mesopotamian Urbanisation
hist_urbanisation_mesopotamia.subject: history
hist_urbanisation_mesopotamia.detail: Among the world's first urban centres, Mesopotamian cities emerged around 4000-3000 BCE. Cities like Ur and Uruk had populations exceeding 40,000. Urbanisation was enabled by agricultural surplus from irrigation, specialisation of labour, and trade networks.

hist_uruk.label: Uruk
hist_uruk.subject: history
hist_uruk.detail: Sumerian city-state that may have been the world's first true city, with a population of up to 80,000 by 2900 BCE. Centre of the earliest known writing. Associated with the legendary king Gilgamesh. Had monumental architecture including temples and the White Temple.

hist_irrigation_mesopotamia.label: Mesopotamian Irrigation
hist_irrigation_mesopotamia.subject: history
hist_irrigation_mesopotamia.detail: Southern Mesopotamia received insufficient rainfall for farming, making irrigation essential. Elaborate canal systems diverted water from the Tigris and Euphrates. Required communal labour and central coordination, which contributed to the development of state authority and social hierarchy.

hist_trade_mesopotamia.label: Mesopotamian Trade
hist_trade_mesopotamia.subject: history
hist_trade_mesopotamia.detail: Mesopotamia lacked key resources like stone, metals, and timber, driving extensive long-distance trade. Traded with the Indus Valley (Meluhha), Dilmun (Bahrain), and Magan (Oman). Exported textiles and grain in exchange for metals, stones, and luxury goods. This trade fostered cultural exchange.

hist_social_hierarchy_mesopotamia.label: Mesopotamian Social Hierarchy
hist_social_hierarchy_mesopotamia.subject: history
hist_social_hierarchy_mesopotamia.detail: Society was stratified into free citizens (awilum), dependants (mushkenum), and slaves (wardum). Priests and kings held highest status. Scribes formed an educated elite. Women had some property rights in earlier periods but their status declined over time. Code of Hammurabi codified class-based punishments.

hist_clay_tablets.label: Clay Tablets
hist_clay_tablets.subject: history
hist_clay_tablets.detail: Primary writing medium in Mesopotamia. Made of wet clay inscribed with cuneiform using a reed stylus, then dried or baked. Hundreds of thousands have survived, preserving administrative records, letters, literature, and school texts. The durability of clay has given us an unparalleled record of ancient life.

hist_banawali.label: Banawali
hist_banawali.subject: history
hist_banawali.detail: Harappan city in Hissar district, Haryana. Contains two cultural phases — pre-Harappan and Harappan — similar to Kalibangan. Pre-Harappan features include mud-brick platforms, streets, and drains. Substantial barley discovery. Singhania: on the dried-up Sarasvati; finds include a toy plough, lapis lazuli, fire altars, barley grains. Oval-shaped settlement and the only known Harappan city with radial streets.

hist_surkotada.label: Surkotada
hist_surkotada.subject: history
hist_surkotada.detail: Harappan site in west Gujarat with a citadel. Controversial: claimed horse remains dated c. 2000 BCE — one of the few direct (though disputed) pieces of evidence for the horse in Harappan culture. Most scholars regard the identification as uncertain. A sling-stone heap and soldier depiction on a potsherd hint at a possible standing force.

hist_sutkagendor.label: Sutkagendor
hist_sutkagendor.subject: history
hist_sutkagendor.detail: Coastal Harappan city in Baluchistan (Pakistan), on the Makran coast. Marked by a citadel; served as a maritime outpost for long-distance trade with Mesopotamia via the Arabian Sea.

hist_meluha.label: Meluha
hist_meluha.subject: history
hist_meluha.detail: Ancient Mesopotamian name for the Indus region (from ~2350 BCE onwards in cuneiform records). Mesopotamian texts record trade with Meluha in carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper, gold, and wood. The identification with the Harappan civilisation is near-universally accepted — a cornerstone piece of evidence for direct Indus-Mesopotamia commerce.

hist_dilmun.label: Dilmun
hist_dilmun.subject: history
hist_dilmun.detail: Ancient trading station identified with modern Bahrain in the Persian Gulf. Intermediate between Mesopotamia and Meluha (Indus). Mesopotamian texts describe it as a transshipment point; thousands of graves survive awaiting excavation.

hist_magan.label: Magan / Makan
hist_magan.subject: history
hist_magan.detail: Ancient trading station, between Dilmun and Meluha. Generally identified with modern Oman (also called Makan in Sharma). Source of copper that reached Mesopotamia; nickel traces in Harappan copper artefacts match Omani sources, confirming the trade link.

hist_dancing_girl.label: Dancing Girl
hist_dancing_girl.subject: history
hist_dancing_girl.detail: Bronze figurine recovered from Mohenjo-daro — one of the finest specimens of Harappan metal art. Naked, wears a necklace and bangles on one arm, right hand on hip, head tilted back. Demonstrates advanced lost-wax casting technique. UPSC PYQ 2025: the figurine is made of BRONZE. Singhania: the world's oldest known bronze sculpture (~4 inches / 10.5 cm tall). Stands in a "tribhanga" (three-bends) dancing posture, right hand on hip, head tilted slightly. Ornamented with bangles on the left arm and an amulet + bracelet on the right arm. Cast via the lost-wax (cire perdue) technique.

hist_priest_king.label: Priest-King Sculpture
hist_priest_king.subject: history
hist_priest_king.detail: Steatite bust from Mohenjo-daro. Wears an ornamented robe passing over the left shoulder under the right arm like a shawl; short hair locks at the back are held by a woven fillet. Marshall nicknamed it the "priest-king", but the identification is speculative — there is no evidence of priest-rule in Harappan civilisation. Singhania: the steatite figure shows a bearded man draped in a shawl with trefoil patterns. Eyes are elongated and half-closed, as if in meditation. Armlet on the right hand, plain woven fillet tied across the head. Marshall's label "priest-king" is speculative.

hist_sarasvati_river.label: Sarasvati / Hakra-Ghaggar
hist_sarasvati_river.subject: history
hist_sarasvati_river.detail: The ancient Sarasvati is identified with the Hakra-Ghaggar river system (now largely dried up). In the third millennium BCE, the Yamuna and Sutlej flowed into it due to Himalayan tectonic shifts, creating a major water source supporting many Harappan sites. Around 1700 BCE both tributaries shifted away, drying up the Sarasvati — a major contributor to Harappan decline. Some scholars call the civilisation the "Sarasvati culture" for this reason.

hist_elam.label: Elam
hist_elam.subject: history
hist_elam.detail: Ancient state on the eastern border of Mesopotamia (covering much of Iran). Its rise around 2000 BCE disrupted the long-distance trade between the Indus region and Mesopotamia — cutting off tin supply to Harappan bronze-workers and bead/luxury exports to Mesopotamia. A major factor in Harappan urban decline.

hist_sama_veda.label: Sama Veda
hist_sama_veda.subject: history
hist_sama_veda.detail: The second Veda — Rig Vedic prayers set to melody ("saman") for ritual recitation. One of the four Samhitas. Considered the source of Indian music traditions (musical scales derived from saman chants).

hist_yajur_veda.label: Yajur Veda
hist_yajur_veda.subject: history
hist_yajur_veda.detail: The third Veda. Contains not only hymns but also the prose formulae (yajus) that accompany rituals — reflecting the elaboration of sacrifice in the later Vedic period. Divided into Shukla (white/Vajasaneyi) and Krishna (black) recensions.

hist_atharva_veda.label: Atharva Veda
hist_atharva_veda.subject: history
hist_atharva_veda.detail: The fourth Veda. Contains charms and spells to ward off evil and disease. Reflects a strong non-Aryan / folk tradition — often considered to have absorbed indigenous pre-Aryan practices. Also contains early speculation on philosophical and medical themes.

hist_brahmanas_texts.label: Brahmanas (Texts)
hist_brahmanas_texts.subject: history
hist_brahmanas_texts.detail: Prose texts attached to each Veda that explain the ritual and its symbolism. Compiled in the upper Gangetic basin c. 1000-500 BCE. Major examples: Shatapatha Brahmana (Yajur), Aitareya Brahmana (Rig). First use of the term "janapada" (c. 800 BCE).

hist_andronovo_culture.label: Andronovo Culture
hist_andronovo_culture.subject: history
hist_andronovo_culture.detail: Bronze Age archaeological culture covering almost the whole of Central Asia in the 2nd millennium BCE. Considered proto-Indo-Iranian: characterised by stock-breeding, widespread horse use, spoked-wheel chariots, cremation, pit-dwellings roofed with birch, and the soma drink. Likely ancestral cultural zone of the Vedic Aryans who migrated to India.

hist_bmac.label: Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex (BMAC)
hist_bmac.subject: history
hist_bmac.detail: Archaeological complex covering south Central Asia (Bactria/Afghanistan + Margiana/Turkmenistan+Uzbekistan), c. 1900-1500 BCE. Shows evidence of domestic horse, spoked-wheel chariots, partial cremation, and svastika motif by 1500 BCE. The migratory herdsmen who damaged its proto-urban settlements may have moved to the Indian subcontinent's borders — consistent with horse remains + post-cremation burials appearing in the Swat valley from c. 1400 BCE.

hist_indo_aryan_migration.label: Indo-Aryan Migration
hist_indo_aryan_migration.subject: history
hist_indo_aryan_migration.detail: Migration of Indo-Aryans into the Indian subcontinent from Central Asia, in several waves beginning c. 1500-1200 BCE. Evidence: genetic marker M17 present in 40%+ of Central Asian steppe populations and 35% of Hindi speakers (vs 10% of Dravidian speakers); linguistic links with Russian; archaeological trail through Andronovo and BMAC cultures. No inscriptional Indo-Aryan evidence survives in India itself from this period — all Indo-European inscriptions from this era come from West Asia (Kassite, Mitanni, Hittite).

hist_sapta_sindhu.label: Sapta Sindhu (Land of Seven Rivers)
hist_sapta_sindhu.subject: history
hist_sapta_sindhu.detail: Land of the Seven Rivers — the area where the Aryans first settled in the subcontinent, covering eastern Afghanistan, the North-West Frontier Province, Punjab, and fringes of western UP. The seven rivers centre on the Sindhu (Indus) and its five tributaries, plus the Sarasvati (Rig Vedic naditama, "best of rivers") which was identified variously with the Hakra-Ghaggar or the Avestan Harakhwati (Helmand, in south Afghanistan).

hist_battle_of_ten_kings.label: Battle of Ten Kings (Dasarajna)
hist_battle_of_ten_kings.subject: history
hist_battle_of_ten_kings.detail: Key conflict described in the Rig Veda. Fought on the river Parushni (modern Ravi) between the Bharatas (under king Sudas, supported by priest Vasishtha) and a coalition of ten chiefs — five Aryan tribes and five non-Aryan peoples. Bharatas won, establishing their supremacy. The defeated Purus later merged with Bharatas to form the Kurus.

hist_bharatas.label: Bharatas
hist_bharatas.subject: history
hist_bharatas.detail: Dominant Aryan ruling clan of the Rig Vedic period, first mentioned in the Rig Veda. Victorious at the Battle of Ten Kings under Sudas. Merged with the defeated Purus to form the Kurus. Source of the name "Bharatavarsha" for the Indian subcontinent.

hist_kurus.label: Kurus
hist_kurus.subject: history
hist_kurus.detail: Later Vedic ruling tribe formed by the merger of Bharatas and Purus.
