Initially settled between Sarasvati and Drishadvati, then occupied Delhi and the upper Ganga-Yamuna doab ("Kurukshetra"). Coalesced with Panchalas to form the dominant Kuru-Panchala realm. Mahabharata war (~950 BCE) fought between Kauravas and Pandavas — both Kuru branches.

hist_panchalas.label: Panchalas
hist_panchalas.subject: history
hist_panchalas.detail: Later Vedic tribe occupying the central Ganga-Yamuna doab (modern Bareilly, Badaun, Farrukhabad districts). Famous for its philosopher-kings and brahmana theologians. Combined with Kurus to form the Kuru-Panchala realm. Panchala (and Videha) was the home of the Upanishadic tradition c. 600 BCE.

hist_hastinapur.label: Hastinapur
hist_hastinapur.subject: history
hist_hastinapur.detail: Capital of the Kuru-Panchala realm in later Vedic times, situated in Meerut district (western UP). Archaeologically dated 900-500 BCE — shows early settlement and faint beginnings of town life (proto-urban). Tradition says it was flooded and the Kurus moved to Kaushambi near Allahabad. Central setting of the Mahabharata narrative.

hist_mahabharata_war.label: Mahabharata War
hist_mahabharata_war.subject: history
hist_mahabharata_war.detail: War between the Kauravas (Duryodhana's faction) and Pandavas (Yudhishthira's faction) — both branches of the Kuru clan — for succession to the throne of Hastinapur. Traditionally dated c. 950 BCE; the epic was finally compiled c. 4th century CE. The war effectively wiped out the Kuru ruling clan.

hist_vasishtha.label: Vasishtha
hist_vasishtha.subject: history
hist_vasishtha.detail: Conservative priestly sage of the Rig Vedic period. Author of many hymns (mandala VII is traditionally attributed to him and his family). Supported the Bharata ruler Sudas at the Battle of Ten Kings. Traditional rival of Vishvamitra.

hist_vishvamitra.label: Vishvamitra
hist_vishvamitra.subject: history
hist_vishvamitra.detail: Liberal Rig Vedic sage, traditionally a kshatriya who attained brahmana status through ascetic achievement. Composer of the Gayatri mantra (Rig Veda 3.62.10) which was conceived as a universal admission formula to the Aryan fold — though later priests restricted it to the three upper varnas only. Mandala III of the Rig Veda is traditionally attributed to him and his family.

hist_gayatri_mantra.label: Gayatri Mantra
hist_gayatri_mantra.subject: history
hist_gayatri_mantra.detail: A Rig Vedic verse (3.62.10) composed by Vishvamitra. Intended originally as a universal admission mantra into the Aryan fold. Later priests made it the exclusive privilege of the three upper varnas (brahmanas, kshatriyas, vaishyas) — shudras and women were prohibited from reciting it.

hist_rajasuya.label: Rajasuya
hist_rajasuya.subject: history
hist_rajasuya.detail: Royal coronation sacrifice of later Vedic times. Supposed to confer supreme power on the king. Accompanied by large-scale dakshina (sacrificial fee) — traditionally 240,000 cows. One of the three major royal rituals alongside Ashvamedha and Vajapeya.

hist_vajapeya.label: Vajapeya
hist_vajapeya.subject: history
hist_vajapeya.detail: Later Vedic royal ritual involving a chariot race in which the king's chariot was made to "win" against his kinsmen's. Reinforced the king's ritual supremacy. Cognate with Greek and Indo-European chariot-race traditions, suggesting deep Indo-European antiquity.

hist_prajapati.label: Prajapati
hist_prajapati.subject: history
hist_prajapati.detail: The creator god who rose to supreme position in the later Vedic pantheon, displacing Rig Vedic Indra and Agni. Associated with the ritual of creation through sacrifice.

hist_rudra.label: Rudra
hist_rudra.subject: history
hist_rudra.detail: The god of animals in later Vedic texts. Minor in the Rig Veda, rose in later Vedic times. Later identified with Shiva — a continuity from Rig Veda's Rudra into the later Puranic Shiva.

hist_vishnu_early.label: Vishnu (Early Vedic form)
hist_vishnu_early.subject: history
hist_vishnu_early.detail: Minor solar deity in the Rig Veda, known for the three strides covering the universe. In later Vedic times, came to be conceived as preserver and protector of settled people. This pattern evolves into the major Puranic Vishnu of post-Vedic Hinduism.

hist_upanayana.label: Upanayana (Sacred Thread)
hist_upanayana.subject: history
hist_upanayana.detail: Rite of investiture with the sacred thread (yajnopavita), marking the beginning of Vedic education. Entitlement of the three higher varnas (brahmana, kshatriya, vaishya) — known collectively as dvija (twice-born). Shudras and women were barred. The rite marked entry into the brahmacharya ashrama (student stage).

hist_dvija.label: Dvija (Twice-Born)
hist_dvija.subject: history
hist_dvija.detail: Term for the three upper varnas (brahmana, kshatriya, vaishya) — those entitled to upanayana (sacred thread) and therefore to Vedic study. Shudras and women were excluded. The concept formalized the religious hierarchy of the varna system.

hist_sabha_samiti.label: Sabha and Samiti
hist_sabha_samiti.subject: history
hist_sabha_samiti.detail: Tribal assemblies of the Rig Vedic period. Sabha was a smaller council (possibly of elders/nobles); samiti was a larger popular assembly with deliberative, military, and religious functions. Even women attended in early Vedic times. In later Vedic times, vidatha disappeared, and sabha/samiti became dominated by warriors and brahmanas — women were barred.

hist_ropar.label: Ropar
hist_ropar.subject: history
hist_ropar.detail: Harappan site on the banks of the Sutlej in Punjab (India). Distinctive find: a dog buried with a human in oval pit burials — unique evidence of human-dog companionship in burial practice. Copper axe also recovered.

hist_alamgirpur.label: Alamgirpur
hist_alamgirpur.subject: history
hist_alamgirpur.detail: Easternmost known site of the Indus Valley Civilisation, in Meerut district (western UP) on the Yamuna. Finds: broken copper blade, ceramic items, and impression of cloth on a trough (evidence of cotton textile use in the late Harappan phase).

hist_lost_wax_technique.label: Lost Wax Technique
hist_lost_wax_technique.subject: history
hist_lost_wax_technique.detail: Method for making bronze sculptures. Image made in wax, covered with clay, heated to drain wax, then molten metal poured in. After cooling, clay removed and image polished. Used by Chola sculptors. [UPINDER:] North Indian alloy: 8 metals (gold, silver, tin, lead, iron, mercury, zinc, copper). South Indian alloy: 5 metals (copper, silver, gold, tin, lead). Northern images hollow, southern solid. Sharada Srinivasan archaeometric analysis shows that the earliest bronze Natarajas were made in the Pallava period (7-9c), not the Chola period as previously believed.

hist_mother_goddess_figurine.label: Mother Goddess Figurine
hist_mother_goddess_figurine.subject: history
hist_mother_goddess_figurine.detail: Terracotta female figurines found at many Harappan sites. Standing female adorned with necklaces over prominent breasts, a loincloth with girdle, and a distinctive fan-shaped headgear. Crudely modelled — made by pinching. Likely worshipped for prosperity and fertility — evidence of an early mother-goddess / fertility cult.

hist_red_sandstone_torso.label: Red Sandstone Male Torso
hist_red_sandstone_torso.subject: history
hist_red_sandstone_torso.detail: A rock sculpture found at Harappa. Frontal posture; well-baked shoulders and a prominent abdomen. Socket holes in the neck and shoulders suggest the head and arms were made separately and attached. Notable for its sophistication compared to the simpler Mohenjo-daro Priest-King figure.

hist_harappan_painted_pottery.label: Harappan Painted (Red and Black) Pottery
hist_harappan_painted_pottery.subject: history
hist_harappan_painted_pottery.detail: Distinctive Harappan pottery featuring a red slip background with glossy black designs — trees, birds, animals, geometric patterns. Mostly wheel-made; rare handmade pieces. Also rare polychrome examples. Perforated pottery (large bottom hole, small side holes) likely used for straining liquor. Miniature vessels (<half-inch) exquisitely crafted for decoration. Distinct from later Vedic Black-and-Red Ware.

hist_period_sumerian.label: Sumerian Mesopotamia
hist_period_sumerian.subject: history
hist_period_sumerian.detail: Earliest urban civilisation in southern Mesopotamia (c. 4500-2334 BCE). Sumerians invented cuneiform writing (c. 3200 BCE), the wheel, and the sexagesimal (base-60) number system that still governs our time (60 min) and angles (360°). City-states like Ur, Uruk (80,000 people by 2900 BCE), and Lagash developed on irrigation agriculture. Temple-centred social hierarchy dominated by priests. Trade connections with Meluha (Indus region) from ~2350 BCE onwards — a major source of Harappan long-distance exports.

hist_period_akkadian.label: Akkadian Empire
hist_period_akkadian.subject: history
hist_period_akkadian.detail: World's first empire (c. 2334-2154 BCE). Sargon of Akkad conquered the Sumerian city-states from a northern base, establishing Semitic Akkadian rule over Mesopotamia. Akkadian language supplanted Sumerian as the lingua franca for centuries. Contemporaneous with the peak of mature Harappan trade. Ended with Gutian invasions from the Zagros mountains; followed by a brief Neo-Sumerian revival (Ur III, 2112-2004 BCE).

hist_period_babylonian.label: Old Babylonian Empire
hist_period_babylonian.subject: history
hist_period_babylonian.detail: Rose under Hammurabi (1792-1750 BCE), who unified Mesopotamia under Babylonian rule (c. 1894-1595 BCE). Code of Hammurabi — one of the earliest codified legal systems — inscribed on a stele with class-based punishments (awilum/mushkenum/wardum). Epic of Gilgamesh took its "standard" Akkadian form in this period. Ended with Kassite invasion 1595 BCE. Contemporaneous with late Harappan decline and early Vedic migration.

hist_period_assyrian.label: Neo-Assyrian Empire
hist_period_assyrian.subject: history
hist_period_assyrian.detail: Final flowering of Mesopotamian civilisation (c. 911-609 BCE). Powerful militaristic state based at Nineveh, expanding from Egypt to Persia at its peak. Overlaps with later Vedic and early Upanishadic / Mahajanapada India. Fell to a Babylonian-Median alliance — Nineveh sacked 612 BCE, empire ended 609 BCE.

hist_period_early_harappan.label: Early Harappan Phase
hist_period_early_harappan.subject: history
hist_period_early_harappan.detail: Formative phase of the Indus civilisation (c. 3300-2600 BCE). Agricultural settlements spread in the Hakra-Cholistan belt, Baluchistan, and the Indus plains — building on older Neolithic roots (Mehrgarh 7000 BCE onwards). Pre-Harappan furrow at Kalibangan shows ploughing in Rajasthan. Proto-urban towns like Rahman Dheri (Baluchistan, planned roads). Mud-brick platforms, painted pottery, and female terracotta figurines foreshadow mature Harappan features. Distinct pre-Harappan layers excavated at Banawali and Kalibangan.

hist_period_late_harappan.label: Late (Post-Urban) Harappan
hist_period_late_harappan.subject: history
hist_period_late_harappan.detail: Post-urban / degenerate Harappan phase (c. 1900-1300 BCE). Writing, seals, standardised weights, and monumental brickwork fall out of use. Sharma's causes: (1) Yamuna + Sutlej shifted away from Sarasvati/Hakra ~1700 BCE — water loss; (2) Elam's rise (~2000 BCE) disrupted Mesopotamia trade, cutting tin supply for bronze and bead exports; (3) rainfall decline; (4) soil exhaustion. Harappan elements persist in Gujarat (Rangpur, Rojdi), Haryana (Bhagwanpura), Punjab, and western UP (Alamgirpur). Overlaps chronologically with early Vedic migration (1500-1200 BCE) but no mass-confrontation evidence.

hist_period_rigvedic.label: Rigvedic Phase
hist_period_rigvedic.subject: history
hist_period_rigvedic.detail: First Indo-Aryan settlement in the subcontinent (c. 1500-1000 BCE). Migration from Central Asia (Andronovo, BMAC) through Afghanistan into Sapta Sindhu — the Land of Seven Rivers (eastern Afghanistan, NWFP, Punjab, western UP fringe). Pastoral, cattle-centred society (gavishthi = "search for cows" = the term for war). Tribal assemblies: sabha, samiti, vidatha. Rig Veda composed — 10 mandalas, prayers to Agni, Indra, Mitra, Varuna. Five-tribe Panchajana; Battle of Ten Kings on Parushni (Ravi); Bharatas under Sudas emerge dominant. Priestly rivalry of Vasishtha (conservative) and Vishvamitra (liberal, composer of Gayatri). Horse (asva) mentioned 215x — marker of Aryan identity.

hist_period_later_vedic.label: Later Vedic Phase
hist_period_later_vedic.subject: history
hist_period_later_vedic.detail: Expansion into the Ganga-Yamuna doab (c. 1000-600 BCE). Kuru-Panchala realm dominates the upper doab from Hastinapur (Meerut); Mahabharata war traditionally ~950 BCE. Iron age begins — "krishna/shyama ayas" (black metal). Painted Grey Ware culture: ~700 sites, mostly wheat-rice farming villages. Agriculture replaces pastoralism. Varna system formalises (brahmana-kshatriya-vaishya-shudra); upanayana + dvija concept emerge. Royal rituals — rajasuya (coronation), ashvamedha (territorial claim), vajapeya (chariot race). Three later Vedas composed: Sama, Yajur, Atharva. Brahmanas compiled in upper Gangetic basin. Upanishads composed ~600 BCE in Panchala + Videha — philosophical reaction against ritual excess. Jana → janapada transition: tribal identity becomes territorial polity.

hist_roman_empire.label: Roman Empire
hist_roman_empire.subject: history
hist_roman_empire.detail: One of the largest and most influential empires in history, spanning Europe, North Africa, and West Asia at its height. The Principate (27 BCE-284 CE) and Dominate (284-476 CE) phases. Controlled the entire Mediterranean. Its legal, cultural, and administrative legacy profoundly shaped Western civilisation.

hist_roman_republic.label: Roman Republic
hist_roman_republic.subject: history
hist_roman_republic.detail: The period of Roman government from 509 BCE to 27 BCE, characterised by elected magistrates, the Senate, and popular assemblies. Expanded Roman territory across the Mediterranean through military conquests. Ended with the civil wars and rise of Augustus as the first emperor.

hist_augustus.label: Augustus (Octavian)
hist_augustus.subject: history
hist_augustus.detail: First Roman Emperor (r. 27 BCE-14 CE), born Gaius Octavius. Defeated Mark Antony at Actium (31 BCE). Established the Principate system where the emperor ruled while maintaining republican forms. Initiated the Pax Romana, reformed taxation, built infrastructure, and patronised arts and literature.

hist_pax_romana.label: Pax Romana
hist_pax_romana.subject: history
hist_pax_romana.detail: Period of relative peace and stability across the Roman Empire lasting roughly from 27 BCE to 180 CE (about 200 years). Enabled trade, urbanisation, cultural exchange, and prosperity across the Mediterranean. Roads, aqueducts, and cities were built. Population of the empire reached 60-70 million.

hist_roman_provinces.label: Roman Provincial System
hist_roman_provinces.subject: history
hist_roman_provinces.detail: The empire was divided into provinces governed by appointed officials (proconsuls, legates). Provinces paid taxes to Rome but often retained local customs and elites. Romanisation spread Latin, law, and urban planning. The provincial system was key to governing diverse peoples across three continents.

hist_roman_army.label: Roman Army
hist_roman_army.subject: history
hist_roman_army.detail: The professional standing army that was the backbone of Roman power. Legions of about 5,000 soldiers each, supplemented by auxiliaries from conquered peoples. Soldiers served 25 years and received land or cash on retirement. The army also built roads, bridges, and fortifications.

hist_roman_slavery.label: Roman Slavery
hist_roman_slavery.subject: history
hist_roman_slavery.detail: Slavery was integral to the Roman economy. Slaves came from war captives, debt, and birth. They worked in agriculture, mines, households, and as gladiators. Some slaves gained freedom (manumission) and became freedmen with limited rights. Slave revolts occurred, most famously Spartacus (73-71 BCE).

hist_roman_economy.label: Roman Economy
hist_roman_economy.subject: history
hist_roman_economy.detail: Based on agriculture, trade, mining, and manufacturing. Used gold and silver coinage (denarius). Mediterranean trade routes connected the empire. Traded with India, China (via Silk Road), and sub-Saharan Africa. Olive oil, wine, grain, pottery, and metals were major commodities.

hist_roman_law.label: Roman Law
hist_roman_law.subject: history
hist_roman_law.detail: One of Rome's most enduring legacies. Evolved from the Twelve Tables (450 BCE) through jurists' interpretations. Distinguished between civil law (ius civile) and law of nations (ius gentium). Concepts like legal personhood, contracts, property rights, and due process influenced European legal systems for centuries.

hist_constantine.label: Constantine
hist_constantine.subject: history
hist_constantine.detail: Roman Emperor (r. 306-337 CE) who fundamentally transformed the empire. Issued the Edict of Milan (313 CE) granting religious tolerance to Christians. Founded Constantinople (modern Istanbul) as the new eastern capital in 330 CE. Convened the Council of Nicaea (325 CE). First emperor to convert to Christianity.

hist_diocletian.label: Diocletian
hist_diocletian.subject: history
hist_diocletian.detail: Roman Emperor (r. 284-305 CE) who ended the Crisis of the Third Century. Established the Tetrarchy (rule of four) dividing the empire into eastern and western halves. Reformed taxation, the army, and provincial administration. Persecuted Christians. His reforms prolonged the empire's life.

hist_christianity_rome.label: Christianity in Rome
hist_christianity_rome.subject: history
hist_christianity_rome.detail: Christianity spread within the Roman Empire despite periodic persecution. Gained official tolerance through Constantine's Edict of Milan (313 CE). Became the state religion under Theodosius I (380 CE). The Church's institutional structure mirrored Roman provincial administration.

hist_constantinople.label: Constantinople
hist_constantinople.subject: history
hist_constantinople.detail: Founded by Constantine in 330 CE on the site of ancient Byzantium (modern Istanbul). Became the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire. Strategically located at the crossroads of Europe and Asia, controlling the Bosphorus strait. Remained a major centre of trade, culture, and power for over a thousand years.

hist_fall_western_rome.label: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
hist_fall_western_rome.subject: history
hist_fall_western_rome.detail: The Western Roman Empire fell in 476 CE when the Germanic chieftain Odoacer deposed the last emperor Romulus Augustulus. Caused by a combination of military pressure from Germanic tribes, economic decline, overextension, political instability, and reliance on barbarian mercenaries. The Eastern Empire (Byzantine) survived until 1453.

hist_byzantine_empire.label: Byzantine Empire
hist_byzantine_empire.subject: history
hist_byzantine_empire.detail: The continuation of the Eastern Roman Empire after the fall of the west in 476 CE. Centred on Constantinople, it lasted until 1453 when it fell to the Ottoman Turks. Preserved Greek and Roman knowledge, developed Orthodox Christianity, and produced Justinian's Code of law. A bridge between ancient and medieval worlds.

hist_roman_architecture.label: Roman Architecture
hist_roman_architecture.subject: history
hist_roman_architecture.detail: Romans perfected the arch, vault, and dome, and invented concrete. Built aqueducts, roads, amphitheatres (Colosseum), baths, and forums. Monumental public architecture was used to display imperial power. The Pantheon's dome remained the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome for nearly 2,000 years.

hist_roman_social_structure.label: Roman Social Structure
hist_roman_social_structure.subject: history
hist_roman_social_structure.detail: Society was hierarchical: senators and equestrians at the top, followed by citizens, freedmen, and slaves. The patronage system (patron-client relations) was central to social and political life. Citizenship was gradually extended, culminating in the Edict of Caracalla (212 CE) granting citizenship to all free men.

hist_crisis_third_century.label: Crisis of the Third Century
hist_crisis_third_century.subject: history
hist_crisis_third_century.detail: Period of military, political, and economic upheaval in the Roman Empire from 235 to 284 CE. Saw rapid turnover of emperors (many assassinated), barbarian invasions, plague, economic collapse, and temporary breakaway states. Ended by Diocletian's reforms. Nearly destroyed the empire.

hist_germanic_invasions.label: Germanic Invasions
hist_germanic_invasions.subject: history
hist_germanic_invasions.detail: Migrations and invasions of Germanic peoples (Goths, Vandals, Franks, Angles, Saxons) into Roman territory from the 3rd-5th centuries CE. Driven by pressure from the Huns and attraction of Roman wealth. The Visigoths sacked Rome in 410 CE. These movements reshaped the political map of Europe.

hist_tetrarchy.label: Tetrarchy
hist_tetrarchy.subject: history
hist_tetrarchy.detail: System of government established by Diocletian in 293 CE dividing the Roman Empire among four co-rulers: two senior Augusti and two junior Caesars. Aimed to manage the vast empire more effectively and ensure orderly succession. Collapsed after Diocletian's abdication, leading to civil wars and Constantine's eventual sole rule.

hist_mauryan_empire.label: Mauryan Empire
hist_mauryan_empire.subject: history
hist_mauryan_empire.detail: First pan-Indian empire, covering virtually the entire subcontinent except Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and parts of the north-east. Founded 321 BCE by Chandragupta; apex under Ashoka (273-232 BCE); disintegrated after Ashoka and ended in 185 BCE. Military strength (per Pliny): 600,000 foot soldiers, 30,000 cavalry, 9,000 war elephants, 8,000 chariots, plus a navy — about three times the Nanda military. State monopolies over mining, sale of liquor, and manufacture of arms. Estimated ~6.5 million population in the Gangetic heartland. Administrative system described in Arthashastra and Megasthenes's Indika.

hist_ashoka.label: Ashoka
hist_ashoka.subject: history
hist_ashoka.detail: Greatest Maurya ruler, reigned 273-232 BCE. Son of Bindusara; Buddhist tradition says he killed 99 brothers to seize the throne (legendary). Known in his inscriptions as Devanampiya Piyadasi ("Beloved of the Gods, of gracious mien") — the name "Ashoka" appears only in four copies of Minor Rock Edict I (Maski/Gujarra/Nittur/Udegolam). Fought only one major war (Kalinga, ~261 BCE) and converted to Buddhism, replacing bherighosha with dhammaghosha. Convened the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra (~250 BCE). Sent Buddhist missions to Sri Lanka (through son Mahendra and daughter Sanghamitra), Myanmar, Central Asia, and the Hellenistic West. Undertook dhamma-yatras (Buddhist pilgrimages). Retired in 232 BCE; empire fragmented soon after.

hist_arthashastra.label: Arthashastra
hist_arthashastra.subject: history
hist_arthashastra.detail: Treatise on statecraft, economics, and military strategy attributed to Kautilya (Chanakya); compiled in final form a few centuries after Maurya rule but contains authentic core describing Maurya administration. Fifteen books (adhikaranas). Prescribes 27 adhyakshas over specific economic activities; mandates state-built and user-paid irrigation; instructs king to settle new land with vaishya cultivators and drafted shudra labourers with tax remissions and state supplies (cattle, seed, money); enumerates an exhaustive list of taxes; justifies state monopolies in mining, liquor, arms. The king should promulgate dharma when varna-ashrama collapses ("dharmapravartaka"). Mandala theory of inter-state relations. Rediscovered by R. Shamasastry in 1905.

hist_megasthenes.label: Megasthenes
hist_megasthenes.subject: history
hist_megasthenes.detail: Greek ambassador to the court of Chandragupta Maurya. His account (surviving in fragments) describes Mauryan administration including a military committee with six subcommittees for navy, transport, infantry, cavalry, chariots and elephants.

hist_gupta_empire.label: Gupta Empire
hist_gupta_empire.subject: history
hist_gupta_empire.detail: Imperial dynasty founded c. 275 CE, unifying north India politically for over 160 years (c. 319-543 CE). Guptas were possibly of vaishya origin (sharma/varman/gupta/dasa title scheme); based originally in UP-Bihar, centred on Prayag. Principal rulers: Srigupta (founder) → Ghatotkacha → Chandragupta I (319-34) → Samudragupta (335-80) → Chandragupta II "Vikramaditya" (380-412) → Kumaragupta I (412-55) → Skandagupta (455-67) → decline under Huna pressure and feudatory assertions. At peak under Chandragupta II, spanned from Bengal to Gujarat and from Himalayas to central India. Called the "classical" or "golden age" of Indian culture — flowering of Sanskrit literature (Kalidasa), mathematics (Aryabhata, decimal/zero), astronomy, temple architecture (Deogarh Dashavatara), metallurgy (Mehrauli iron pillar), and Vaishnava/Bhagavata religion. Issued the most gold coins of any ancient Indian dynasty. Fell to Huna invasions from 485 CE; Yashodharman of Malwa dealt decisive blow in 532 CE; effective end by 550 CE.

hist_satavahanas.label: Satavahana Dynasty
hist_satavahanas.subject: history
hist_satavahanas.detail: Dynasty ruling the Deccan and central India c. 1st century BCE to c. 230 CE, also called Andhras in the Puranas. Succeeded the Mauryas after a ~100-year gap; defeated the Kanvas ~28 BCE. Earliest base in north Maharashtra (upper Godavari valley); later capital at Paithan/Pratishthan on the Godavari. Core economy: iron tools, paddy transplantation, thirty walled towns, Roman trade via Broach. Official language Prakrit, Brahmi script (like the Mauryas). Claimed brahmana status despite tribal origins; made the first royal land grants (tax-free villages) to brahmanas and Buddhist monks. Three-tier feudatory structure (raja, mahabhoja, senapati). Matronymic naming (Gautamiputra, Vashishthiputra), though patriarchal succession. Conflict with western Shakas dominated their political history. Issued predominantly lead and potin coins.

hist_cholas_cheras_pandyas.label: Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas
hist_cholas_cheras_pandyas.subject: history
hist_cholas_cheras_pandyas.detail: The muvendar (three crowned monarchs) of early Tamilakam (Sangam age, c. 300 BCE - 300 CE), mentioned in Ashokan edicts as borderland kingdoms. Pandyas: southernmost, capital Madurai, famous for pearls; referenced by Megasthenes as ruled once by a woman; sent ambassadors to Augustus. Cholas: between Pennar and Velar rivers; capital Uraiyur (cotton trade), later Puhar / Kaveripattanam (port); Karikala the most famous early king. Cheras: Kerala coast, capital Vanji; dominated pepper trade with Rome, Muziris port with Roman garrisons and temple of Augustus. All three profited from monsoon-driven Roman trade; declined from the 3rd century as Indo-Roman trade decayed, cleared by Pallava rise.

hist_brahmi_script.label: Brahmi Script
hist_brahmi_script.subject: history
hist_brahmi_script.detail: Earliest deciphered post-Harappan Indian script; wrote left-to-right. Appears in its fully developed form in Ashokan inscriptions (3rd century BCE) across most of the subcontinent (Prakrit language), with Maurya Brahmi also reaching Bangladesh (Mahasthana inscription, Bogra district). In the NW, Prakrit Ashokan texts used Kharoshthi instead; Kandahar used Greek/Aramaic. Brahmi is the parent of almost all Indian scripts (Devanagari, Tamil, Sinhala, etc.) and of many SE Asian scripts. Deciphered by James Prinsep in 1837 working from Ashokan bilinguals.

hist_dharmasutras.label: Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras
hist_dharmasutras.subject: history
hist_dharmasutras.detail: Brahmanical law-books (~600-200 BCE) prescribing duties (dharma) for each varna and ashrama. Civil and criminal law based on varna division: higher the varna, higher the expected moral conduct and the purer the status. Shudras denied the sacred thread (upanayana) and Vedic study. Punishment severity was inversely proportional to the varna of the offender and directly proportional to the varna of the victim. Condemned lending at interest, which held back vaishya social status. Elaborated later into the Dharmashastras (e.g., Manusmriti).

hist_land_grants.label: Land Grants
hist_land_grants.subject: history
hist_land_grants.detail: Royal grants of tax-free land and villages to brahmanas, temples, and Buddhist/Jain monasteries (and later, to state officers). Pioneered by the Satavahanas in the Deccan (1st-2nd CE), became systematic under the Vakatakas and Guptas (4th-5th CE), and routine under Harsha and the Rashtrakutas. Recorded on copper plates (tamra-patra) with royal seal (often Garuda). Two main types: (a) brahmadeya / agrahara — grants to individual brahmanas or groups; (b) devadana — grants to temples. Recipients enjoyed fiscal immunity, judicial authority, and exemption from royal entry; peasants on granted land became sharecroppers of the grantee. Foundational to R.S. Sharma's "Indian feudalism" thesis: converted direct-revenue peasants into dependent tenants, decentralised authority, and enabled brahmanisation of tribal frontiers.

hist_prabhavati_gupta.label: Prabhavati Gupta
hist_prabhavati_gupta.subject: history
hist_prabhavati_gupta.detail: Gupta princess, daughter of Chandragupta II and Kuberanaga. Married the Vakataka king Rudrasena II c. 385 CE. After his early death (c. 390 CE), became queen-regent for her minor sons c. 390-410 CE. Her land-grant charters (in Prakrit and Sanskrit) betray Gupta scribal style — she effectively administered the Vakataka kingdom as an extension of Gupta influence. One of the few powerful ruling queens of ancient India and evidence of Gupta soft-power expansion via marriage alliance.

hist_indo_roman_trade.label: Indo-Roman Trade
hist_indo_roman_trade.subject: history
hist_indo_roman_trade.detail: Extensive maritime trade between India and the Roman empire from c. 1st century BCE, peaking 1st-2nd centuries CE. Enabled by Hippalus's discovery (or Roman adoption) of the southwest monsoon pattern c. 45 CE, cutting voyage time from Red Sea to Malabar. India exported pepper, cinnamon, cardamom, ivory, pearls, precious stones, silk (transit from China), muslin textiles, and steel cutlery; imported gold and silver coins (large hoards found south of Vindhyas), wine (amphorae), glassware, Arretine pottery, and tin/copper/lead. Key Indian ports: Broach (Barygaza) on west, Muziris and Tondi in south, Arikamedu and Kaveripattanam on east. Documented in the *Periplus of the Erythraean Sea* (c. 1st century CE) and Ptolemy's *Geography*. Two Indian embassies sent to Roman emperors (Augustus in 27-28 BCE; Trajan in 110-120 CE).

hist_pataliputra.label: Pataliputra
hist_pataliputra.subject: history
hist_pataliputra.detail: Magadha's second capital, founded as a fort at the confluence of Ganges and Son by Udayin (~460-444 BCE). Classic jaladurga (water-fort): surrounded by Ganga and Son on north/west, Poonpun on south/east; Ghaghra joined the Ganges nearby. Commanded river-communications in all four directions. Population ~270,000 by 300 BCE, largest city of ancient India. Megasthenes describes wooden walls and houses; later capital of Mauryas, Guptas. Modern Patna.

hist_samudragupta.label: Samudragupta
hist_samudragupta.subject: history
hist_samudragupta.detail: Second major Gupta emperor, reigned c. 335-380 CE, son of Chandragupta I. "Napoleon of India" (coined by historian V.A. Smith) for his relentless military expansion. His biography and conquests are detailed in the *Allahabad Pillar Inscription* (Prayag Prashasti) composed by his court poet and minister Harishena — inscribed on the same Ashokan pillar as earlier Mauryan edicts. The inscription catalogues conquests in five groups: (1) nine Ganga-Yamuna doab kings dispossessed (Achyuta, Nagasena, Ganapati-naga etc.); (2) frontier kingdoms (Nepal, Assam, Bengal, Samatata) paying tribute; (3) 18 Atavika (forest) kingdoms of Vindhya reduced to servitude; (4) 12 southern kings defeated and reinstated (dakshinapatha digvijaya to Kanchi and Pallava king Vishnugopa); (5) Shakas, Kushanas, and Saka-Murundas submitting. Meghavarman of Sri Lanka sent a mission requesting leave to build a Buddhist monastery at Bodh Gaya. Performed the ashvamedha. Coins show him as lyrist (vina-player) and archer — patron of Sanskrit learning. Reportedly composed Sanskrit poetry himself.

hist_numismatics.label: Numismatics
hist_numismatics.subject: history
hist_numismatics.detail: Study of coins including visual elements, scripts, images, metallurgical analysis and contexts of discovery. Indo-Greeks issued first coins with ruler names and images. Kushanas issued first gold coins. Gupta gold coins were noted for purity.

hist_patriliny.label: Patriliny
hist_patriliny.subject: history
hist_patriliny.detail: Tracing descent from father to son. Central theme of the Mahabharata. Most ruling dynasties from c. sixth century BCE claimed to follow this system. Sons could claim resources of their fathers. Women were expected to give up father's gotra on marriage.

hist_jati_system.label: Jati System
hist_jati_system.subject: history
hist_jati_system.detail: Sub-castes within varnas that became the basis for organising society. Each jati framed its own rules enforced by jati panchayat. Ranks varied by power, influence and resources. Not fixed permanently.

hist_manusmriti.label: Manusmriti
hist_manusmriti.subject: history
hist_manusmriti.detail: Most important Dharmashastra, compiled c. 200 BCE-200 CE. Laid down norms for social behaviour, marriage, inheritance and caste. Recognised eight forms of marriage. Paternal estate divided equally among sons with special share for eldest. Women could retain stridhana.

hist_chandalas.label: Chandalas (Untouchables)
hist_chandalas.subject: history
hist_chandalas.detail: Placed at the very bottom of social hierarchy. Performed 'polluting' tasks like handling corpses. Manusmriti prescribed they live outside villages, use discarded utensils, wear clothes of the dead. Chinese pilgrims Fa Xian and Xuan Zang recorded their marginalisation.

hist_buddhist_social_critique.label: Buddhist Critique of Caste
hist_buddhist_social_critique.subject: history
hist_buddhist_social_critique.detail: Buddhists recognised social differences but did not regard them as natural or inflexible. Rejected claims to status based on birth. Majjhima Nikaya dialogue about wealthy Shudra shows that economic power could override varna distinctions.

hist_sangam_literature.label: Tamil Sangam Literature
hist_sangam_literature.subject: history
hist_sangam_literature.detail: Body of early Tamil poetry and prose produced by assemblies (Sangams) held under Pandya patronage at Madurai, c. 300 BCE - 300 CE (compiled c. 300-600 CE). Two main bodies: Eight Anthologies (Ettuthokai) and Ten Idylls (Pattupattu) — the "Eighteen Major Works" (Melkannakku); plus the Eighteen Minor Works (Kilkanakku) of didactic verse. Key works: Tolkappiyam (earliest surviving Tamil grammar and poetics); Silappadikaram and Manimekalai (the twin epics, c. 5th-6th CE); Tirukkural (Valluvar's couplets on ethics). Depicts warrior society, pastoralism with emerging plough agriculture, Roman trade, muvendar politics, early brahmanisation. Primary source for early south Indian history.

hist_polyandry_draupadi.label: Polyandry in Mahabharata
hist_polyandry_draupadi.subject: history
hist_polyandry_draupadi.detail: Draupadi's marriage with all five Pandavas is a central episode. Multiple explanations offered: Kunti's command, incarnation theory, Shiva's boon. Suggests polyandry was prevalent among some ruling elites and in Himalayan regions. Gradually fell into disfavour among Brahmanas.

hist_stridhana.label: Stridhana (Women's Wealth)
hist_stridhana.subject: history
hist_stridhana.detail: Literally 'a woman's wealth' - gifts received at marriage that women could retain. Could be inherited by children without husband's claim. However, Manusmriti warned women against hoarding valuables without husband's permission. Upper-class women had some access to resources.

hist_metronymics_satavahana.label: Satavahana Metronymics
hist_metronymics_satavahana.subject: history
hist_metronymics_satavahana.detail: Distinctive Satavahana naming practice in which kings carried their mother's gotra name as a prefix — e.g., Gautami-putra Satakarni ("son of Gautami"), Vashishthi-putra Pulumayi, Yajna-Sri Satakarni. Indicates matrilineal traces in the Satavahana family — inscriptions sometimes issued jointly in the king's and mother's names; mothers acted as regents. Still patriarchal in succession (son inheriting from father). A key marker distinguishing Satavahana-period inscriptions from other dynasties.

hist_silk_weavers_mandasor.label: Silk Weavers of Mandasor
hist_silk_weavers_mandasor.subject: history
hist_silk_weavers_mandasor.detail: Guild (shreni) of silk weavers commemorated in the famous *Mandasor Inscription* of 473-74 CE (reign of Kumaragupta I, under the feudatory Bandhuvarman). The guild had migrated from Lata (Gujarat) to Dasapura (Mandasor, western Malwa); the inscription in chaste Sanskrit kavya records their repair and re-gilding of a sun-temple they had originally built. Mentions that some guild members changed professions (became warriors, bards, astrologers, monks) while the shreni maintained collective identity — a rare glimpse of guild-life mobility. Evidence of long-distance craft migration, guild self-governance, and declining west-coast silk trade after Byzantine silk self-sufficiency.

hist_ekalavya_story.label: Ekalavya Story
hist_ekalavya_story.subject: history
hist_ekalavya_story.detail: Mahabharata story of a nishada (forest-dwelling hunter) who taught himself archery using a clay image of Drona. Drona demanded his thumb as fee to maintain Arjuna's supremacy. Illustrates how Brahmanical texts enforced social hierarchy through narratives.

hist_gautama_buddha.label: Gautama Buddha
hist_gautama_buddha.subject: history
hist_gautama_buddha.detail: Siddhartha Gautama, born ~567 BCE in Lumbini (Nepal) into the Shakya republican kshatriya clan of Kapilavastu (= Piprahwa, Basti district); father was the elected Shakya chief, mother a Koshalan princess. Left home at 29; attained enlightenment at 35 under a pipal tree at Bodh-Gaya. Delivered first sermon (Dhammachakkapavattana) at Sarnath near Banaras. Preached 40 years across the mid-Gangetic cities, resting only during the rainy season. Died at 80 in 487 BCE at Kusinagara (Kasia in Deoria district). Archaeological settlement at his associated cities does not predate 500 BCE.

hist_buddhism.label: Buddhism
hist_buddhism.subject: history
hist_buddhism.detail: Founded by Gautama Buddha ~500 BCE. Does not recognise god or soul. Core teachings: Four Noble Truths (dukkha, its cause, cessation, path) and the Eightfold Path (ashtangika marga). Middle path — avoid both luxury and austerity. Three Jewels (triratna): Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha. Preached in Pali (Prakrit derivative), accepting all castes and women into the sangha. Spread rapidly via Magadha, Koshala, Kaushambi monarchies; transformed into a world religion by Ashoka. Declined in India by the 12th century CE.

hist_mahavira.label: Vardhamana Mahavira
hist_mahavira.subject: history
hist_mahavira.detail: Founder of Jainism in effective form, son of kshatriya chief Siddhartha (Jnatrika clan) and Trishala, sister of Lichchhavi chief Chetaka (whose daughter was married to Bimbisara). Born ~540 BCE (one tradition) near Vaishali at Basarh; another tradition places birth earlier (death 527 BCE). Abandoned householder life at 30, wandered 12 years, attained kaivalya (omniscience) at 42 — hence "Jina" (conqueror) and "Mahavira" (great hero). Preached 30 years across Koshala, Magadha, Mithila, Champa in Prakrit. Died at 72 at Pavapuri near Rajgir (468 BCE / 527 BCE per rival traditions).

hist_sanchi_stupa.label: Sanchi Stupa
hist_sanchi_stupa.subject: history
hist_sanchi_stupa.detail: Major Buddhist stupa in Madhya Pradesh, one of the best-preserved ancient monuments. Four elaborately carved gateways at cardinal points. Preserved thanks to Begums of Bhopal (Shahjehan Begum and Sultan Jehan Begum) who funded conservation. Declared UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1989.

hist_therigatha.label: Therigatha
hist_therigatha.subject: history
hist_therigatha.detail: Unique Buddhist text in the Sutta Pitaka, collection of verses composed by bhikkhunis. Provides insight into women's social and spiritual experiences. Includes Punna (a slave woman) challenging a Brahmana's bathing rituals with logic.

hist_mahayana_buddhism.label: Mahayana Buddhism
hist_mahayana_buddhism.subject: history
hist_mahayana_buddhism.detail: The "Great Vehicle" school of Buddhism which crystallised in post-Maurya times (formalised at the Fourth Buddhist Council under Kanishka). Departures from earlier Hinayana/Theravada: accepts the divinity of Buddha and reveres him as a savior; introduces the bodhisattva ideal (postponing nirvana to help all beings); permits image-worship of Buddha; admits lay devotion with easier path to salvation; canon in Sanskrit and Hybrid Sanskrit (not Pali); embraces a pantheon of bodhisattvas (Avalokiteshvara, Manjushri, Maitreya, Tara). Reflects monastic accommodation to wealth (cash donations from traders and artisans) in post-Maurya urban boom. Key philosophers: Nagarjuna (Madhyamaka — shunyata/emptiness), Asanga and Vasubandhu (Yogachara). Spread to China, Korea, Japan, Tibet, Vietnam; now dominant form.

hist_vaishnavism.label: Vaishnavism
hist_vaishnavism.subject: history
hist_vaishnavism.detail: Hindu tradition worshipping Vishnu as principal deity. Ten avatars recognised. Vasudeva-Krishna important in Mathura region, worship spread across subcontinent. Bond between devotee and god visualised as bhakti (love and devotion). Local deities absorbed as forms of Vishnu.

hist_shaivism.label: Shaivism
hist_shaivism.subject: history
hist_shaivism.detail: Hindu tradition with Shiva as chief god. Shiva symbolised by the linga, occasionally in human form. Kailashnatha temple at Ellora (8th century CE) carved from single rock, culmination of cave temple tradition. Influenced by Tantric practices in eastern, northern and southern regions.

hist_early_temples.label: Early Hindu Temples
hist_early_temples.subject: history
hist_early_temples.detail: Hindu temple architecture originates in the Gupta period (c. 4th-6th century CE), evolving from simple square flat-roofed garbhagriha (sanctum) to multi-level shikhara structures. Five stages in Gupta temple evolution (per Percy Brown classification): (1) flat-roofed square temple with shallow pillared porch (Sanchi Temple 17, Tigawa); (2) flat-roofed with ambulatory and second-storey (Parvati Temple, Nachna Kuthara); (3) square with low tower — first shikhara (Dashavatara Temple, Deogarh; Bhitargaon brick); (4) rectangular temple with apsidal end; (5) circular temple (rare). Introduced the iconographic program (Vishnu's ten avatars, Shiva-Parvati, river goddesses at doorjambs). Build materials: brick (Bhitargaon) and stone (Deogarh, Sanchi). Set the template for later nagara (north) and dravida (south) styles.

hist_amaravati_stupa.label: Amaravati Stupa
hist_amaravati_stupa.subject: history
hist_amaravati_stupa.detail: One of the largest Buddhist stupas, in Andhra Pradesh. Elaborately carved mound. Discovered 1796, but sculptures removed to Calcutta, Madras and London. Now a denuded mound. H.H. Cole advocated in situ preservation but was overruled for Amaravati.

hist_bodh_gaya.label: Bodh Gaya
hist_bodh_gaya.subject: history
hist_bodh_gaya.detail: Place where Siddhartha attained enlightenment under the Bodhi tree. One of four sacred Buddhist sites along with Lumbini (birth), Sarnath (first sermon) and Kusinagara (death/nibbana). Ashoka erected a pillar at Lumbini to mark his visit.

hist_shalabhanjika.label: Shalabhanjika Motif
hist_shalabhanjika.subject: history
hist_shalabhanjika.detail: Sculpture of woman whose touch caused trees to flower and bear fruit, found at Sanchi gateway. Regarded as auspicious symbol from pre-Buddhist popular traditions, integrated into stupa decoration. Shows how Buddhism absorbed local beliefs and practices.

hist_gandhara_art.label: Gandhara Art
hist_gandhara_art.subject: history
hist_gandhara_art.detail: School of Buddhist art flourishing c. 1st-5th century CE in the Gandhara region (NW Pakistan/Afghanistan — Taxila, Peshawar, Hadda, Bamiyan). Synthesis of Indian subject matter with Hellenistic/Graeco-Roman form, shaped by long post-Alexander Indo-Greek, Shaka, and especially Kushan cultural mixing. Distinctive features: Buddha in Apollo-like form with wavy hair (ushnisha as topknot), realistic drapery with Roman-style folds, muscular anatomy, grey-blue schist stone, Buddha depicted in human form (a departure from aniconic early Buddhism). First anthropomorphic Buddha images. Key patron: Kanishka. Contrasts with the contemporary indigenous Mathura school (red sandstone, Indian form).

hist_ajanta_paintings.label: Ajanta Paintings
hist_ajanta_paintings.subject: history
hist_ajanta_paintings.detail: Buddhist rock-cut paintings in the 30 caves at Ajanta (Aurangabad district, Maharashtra), painted over two phases: Hinayana Phase I (c. 2nd-1st century BCE, caves 9, 10, 12) and Mahayana Phase II (c. 5th-6th century CE, under Vakataka king Harishena and earlier Satavahana patronage — caves 1, 2, 16, 17, 19, 26). Depict Jataka stories (previous lives of Buddha), life of Buddha, courtly life, celestial beings, processions, and decorative motifs. Techniques: true fresco (fresco-buono) over a lime-plaster ground; mineral and vegetable pigments (red ochre, yellow ochre, terre verte, blue lapis lazuli); shading for three-dimensional effect. Masterpieces include the Padmapani and Vajrapani Bodhisattvas in Cave 1. UNESCO WHS 1983. Rediscovered by British officer John Smith in 1819.

hist_puranas.label: Puranas
hist_puranas.subject: history
hist_puranas.detail: Compiled by Brahmanas by mid-first millennium CE. Contained stories of gods and goddesses that had been in circulation for centuries. Written in simple Sanskrit verse, meant to be read aloud to all including women and Shudras excluded from Vedic learning.

hist_ajivikas.label: Ajivikas
hist_ajivikas.subject: history
hist_ajivikas.detail: A philosophical tradition often described as fatalist, believing everything is predetermined. Founded by Makkhali Gosala. Their texts have not survived. Ashoka built artificial caves for Ajivika renouncers in the Barabar hills (Bihar) in third century BCE.

hist_four_noble_truths.label: Four Noble Truths
hist_four_noble_truths.subject: history
hist_four_noble_truths.detail: Core Buddhist teaching: life involves suffering (dukkha), suffering arises from desire/craving, suffering can end, and the path to end suffering is the Eightfold Path (Middle Way). Buddha emphasised metta (fellow feeling) and karuna (compassion) as central values.

hist_ganga_valley_cities.label: Cities in the Ganga Valley
hist_ganga_valley_cities.subject: history
hist_ganga_valley_cities.detail: About 2500 years ago, cities developed on the banks of the Ganga and its tributaries, and along sea coasts. These became centres of the mahajanapadas.

hist_charaka.label: Charaka
hist_charaka.subject: history
hist_charaka.detail: A famous physician who lived about 2000 years ago and wrote the Charaka Samhita, a book on medicine. He stated the human body has 360 bones, counting teeth, joints and cartilage.

hist_bimbisara.label: Bimbisara
hist_bimbisara.subject: history
hist_bimbisara.detail: Founder of Magadha's prominence, Haryanka dynasty; ruled ~544-492 BCE, contemporary of Buddha. Pursued policy of conquest and diplomatic marriage. Three wives: (1) Kosala Devi — Koshalan princess, sister of Prasenajit, who brought a Kashi village worth 100,000 revenue as dowry; (2) Chellana — Lichchhavi princess from Vaishali (Mahavira's maternal cousin), mother of Ajatasattu; (3) Madra princess from Punjab. Annexed Anga (capital Champa), placing son Ajatasattu as viceroy. Sent royal physician Jivaka to cure the Avanti king Chanda Pradyota. Said to have held a council of 86,000 gramikas (village headmen).

hist_ajatasattu.label: Ajatasattu
hist_ajatasattu.subject: history
hist_ajatasattu.detail: Haryanka ruler of Magadha ~492-460 BCE. Killed his father Bimbisara to seize the throne. Prolonged war against uncle Prasenajit of Kashi-Koshala ended with Koshalan princess married to him and sole possession of Kashi. Ruthlessly broke Lichchhavi Vaishali over 16 years despite his own Lichchhavi maternal lineage, using siege-engines — a stone-hurling catapult (mahashilakantaka) and a mace-fitted chariot (rathamusala). Fortified Rajgir against Avanti invasion (walls still visible). Presided over the First Buddhist Council at Rajgir.

hist_rajagriha.label: Rajagriha (Rajgir)
hist_rajagriha.subject: history
hist_rajagriha.detail: Capital of Magadha for several years, located in present-day Bihar. Later the capital was shifted to Pataliputra (present-day Patna).

hist_alexander_invasion.label: Alexander's Invasion
hist_alexander_invasion.subject: history
hist_alexander_invasion.detail: Alexander of Macedonia's Indian campaign, 326-325 BCE. Crossed the Hindu Kush via the Khyber Pass in 326 BCE after conquering the Achaemenid empire. Ambhi, ruler of Taxila, submitted; Porus of the Jhelum-Chenab doab gave the stiffest resistance at the Battle of the Hydaspes (Jhelum), was defeated but restored as ally. Alexander advanced to the Beas, where his homesick army mutinied (partly fearing the Nanda military mass on the Ganga). Turned south; 19 months total in India. Dispatched Nearchus by sea to explore the Indus-to-Euphrates coast; founded Alexandria (Kabul), Boukephala (Jhelum), and Alexandria (Sindh). Left three Greek governors in conquered NW areas. Historians in his train (Nearchus, Aristobulus, later Arrian) left the first dated European accounts of India, enabling firm Indian chronology.

hist_mahapadma_nanda.label: Mahapadma Nanda
hist_mahapadma_nanda.subject: history
hist_mahapadma_nanda.detail: Founder of the Nanda dynasty (~344 BCE), first major non-Kshatriya king of Magadha (said to be of shudra origin). Claimed the title "ekarat" (sole sovereign) and "sarva-kshatrantaka" (destroyer of all Kshatriyas). Conquered Kalinga (bringing back an image of Jina as a victory trophy) and probably Koshala. Maintained 200,000 infantry, 60,000 cavalry, 2000-3000 four-horse chariots, and 3000-6000 war elephants — a force that deterred Alexander's advance eastward. Succeeded by weaker Nandas; dynasty overthrown by Chandragupta Maurya.

hist_iron_ploughshare.label: Iron Ploughshare
hist_iron_ploughshare.subject: history
hist_iron_ploughshare.detail: A major agricultural innovation around 2500 years ago. Heavy clayey soil could be turned over better than with wooden ploughshares, leading to increased grain production.

hist_transplanting_paddy.label: Transplanting Paddy
hist_transplanting_paddy.subject: history
hist_transplanting_paddy.detail: Instead of scattering seeds, saplings were grown and then planted in fields. Led to increased production but was backbreaking work done by slaves (dasas/dasis) and landless labourers (kammakaras).

hist_sarnath.label: Sarnath
hist_sarnath.subject: history
hist_sarnath.detail: Near Varanasi where the Buddha gave his first sermon (taught for the first time). A stupa was built to mark the place. Contains the famous lion capital now adopted as India's national emblem.

hist_viharas.label: Viharas (Monasteries)
hist_viharas.subject: history
hist_viharas.detail: Permanent shelters for Buddhist and Jain monks. Earliest were of wood, then brick, some carved from hillside caves in western India. Built with donations from kings, merchants and landowners.

hist_panini.label: Panini
hist_panini.subject: history
hist_panini.detail: Famous grammarian who prepared a grammar for Sanskrit, arranging vowels and consonants in special order and creating about 3000 formulae for language rules, similar to algebraic expressions.

hist_tanha.label: Tanha (Craving)
hist_tanha.subject: history
hist_tanha.detail: The Buddha's concept of constant craving or thirst that causes suffering. He taught that this craving could be removed by following moderation in everything - the Middle Path.

hist_karma_concept.label: Karma
hist_karma_concept.subject: history
hist_karma_concept.detail: The concept that results of our actions, good or bad, affect us in this life and the next. Central to both Buddhism and broader Indian philosophical thought. Buddha taught personal responsibility for actions.

hist_chandragupta_maurya.label: Chandragupta Maurya
hist_chandragupta_maurya.subject: history
hist_chandragupta_maurya.detail: Founder of the Maurya empire (~321 BCE), overthrew the Nandas with the counsel of Chanakya (Kautilya). Origin disputed: brahmanical tradition claims he was the son of Mura, a shudra woman in the Nanda court; earlier Buddhist tradition identifies the Mauryas as the ruling clan of the little republic of Pipphalivana near Gorakhpur (Nepalese terai). Justin reports he overran India with 600,000 troops. Waged war with Seleucus Nicator (~305 BCE); treaty ceded to Chandragupta eastern Afghanistan, Baluchistan, and the area west of the Indus in return for 500 war-elephants; also received Seleucus's daughter in marriage. Received Greek ambassador Megasthenes. Late tradition has him abdicating and dying as a Jain ascetic at Shravanabelagola under Bhadrabahu.

hist_chanakya.label: Chanakya (Kautilya)
hist_chanakya.subject: history
hist_chanakya.detail: Also known as Kautilya or Vishnugupta, brahmana teacher from Takshashila (Taxila). Orchestrated Chandragupta Maurya's overthrow of the Nandas and served as his chief minister. Traditional author of the Arthashastra. His political machinations after the Maurya founding are dramatised in Vishakhadatta's Sanskrit play Mudrarakshasa ("The Signet Ring of Rakshasa", c. 9th century CE), which depicts how he won over Nanda loyalist Rakshasa to Chandragupta's side. Embodies the classical Indian ideal of the brahmana statesman-strategist.

hist_kalinga_war.label: Kalinga War
hist_kalinga_war.subject: history
hist_kalinga_war.detail: Ashoka's only major war, c. 261 BCE, eighth year of his reign. Sole contemporary account is the 13th Major Rock Edict (significantly, omitted from the Kalinga versions of the edicts): 100,000 killed, 150,000 deported, many times that number perished. Triggered Ashoka's remorse and conversion to Buddhism — the edict declares "victory by dhamma" the foremost victory. Kalinga was annexed and retained. Despite the turn to dhamma, Ashoka did not disband the army or surrender conquered territories, and threatened tribal peoples with force if they violated dharma.

hist_dhamma.label: Ashoka's Dhamma
hist_dhamma.subject: history
hist_dhamma.detail: Ashoka's ethical and social code, proclaimed through his inscriptions after the Kalinga war. Not a narrow sectarian faith but a tolerant ethical framework spanning religion, morality, social order, and administration. Shift from bherighosha (war drum) to dhammaghosha (drum of dhamma). Key injunctions: respect parents, elders, and teachers; ahimsa towards animals; amity between sects; mercy to slaves and servants; truthfulness; firm devotion (dridha bhakti) to king. Enforced by a new class of officials — dhamma-mahamatras. Kandahar Greek inscription explicitly preaches inter-sectarian amity. Compared to Dharmashastras in scope but written in Prakrit under Buddhist influence.

hist_dhamma_mahamatta.label: Dhamma Mahamatta
hist_dhamma_mahamatta.subject: history
hist_dhamma_mahamatta.detail: Officials appointed by Ashoka who went from place to place teaching people about dhamma. Part of his system for spreading ethical governance across the vast empire.

hist_taxila.label: Taxila
hist_taxila.subject: history
hist_taxila.detail: An important Mauryan provincial capital that served as a gateway to the northwest including Central Asia. Ruled from a provincial capital with some autonomy while following local customs.

hist_ujjain.label: Ujjain
hist_ujjain.subject: history
hist_ujjain.detail: Major Mauryan provincial capital on the route from north to south India. One of the key centres through which the empire was administered, along with Pataliputra and Taxila.

hist_mauryan_administration.label: Mauryan Administration
hist_mauryan_administration.subject: history
hist_mauryan_administration.detail: Elaborate bureaucratic state apparatus described in Arthashastra and Indika. Centre: king assisted by mantri-parishad (council of ministers) with mantrin, purohita, senapati, yuvaraja each paid 48,000 panas; lowest officials ~10-60 panas. Twenty-seven adhyakshas (superintendents) regulated specific domains — agriculture, weights, trade, spinning, mines, etc. Samaharta (chief assessor-collector) was more important than the sannidhata (chief treasurer). Extensive espionage network under tirthas. Provinces governed by kumaras (princes of royal blood) from Tosali (Kalinga+Andhra), Suvarnagiri (Deccan), Ujjain (Avanti), and Taxila (NW frontier). Pataliputra run by six committees of five (sanitation, foreigners, birth-death registration, weights, trade, tax) per Megasthenes; similar six committees of five ran the armed forces.

hist_ashokan_inscriptions.label: Ashokan Inscriptions
hist_ashokan_inscriptions.subject: history
hist_ashokan_inscriptions.detail: Body of Ashoka's royal pronouncements (dhammalipi), the first direct royal communication with subjects in Indian history. Thirty-nine distinct inscriptions, classified into Major Rock Edicts (14), Minor Rock Edicts, Separate Rock Edicts (Dhauli/Jaugada), Major Pillar Edicts (7), and Minor Pillar Edicts. Found at 47 places across present-day India, Nepal, Pakistan, and Afghanistan (six Afghan sites); 182 total versions. Composed chiefly in Prakrit with regional variants, in Brahmi script; in the NW (Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra) Prakrit in Kharoshthi; in Afghanistan (Kandahar) in Greek and Aramaic. Polished stone pillars quarried at Chunar sandstone near Varanasi. Deciphered by James Prinsep (1837). Principal source for Ashoka's biography, policy, and empire extent.

hist_lion_capital.label: Lion Capital of Ashoka
hist_lion_capital.subject: history
hist_lion_capital.detail: Capital of the Ashokan pillar at Sarnath (Uttar Pradesh), where Buddha delivered his first sermon. Four addorsed Asiatic lions seated back-to-back atop an inverted bell-shaped lotus; the abacus depicts four animals (lion/bull/elephant/horse) separated by four Dharmachakras ("wheels of law"), with a great dharmachakra originally crowning the top. Carved from a single block of buff-coloured Chunar sandstone, with the characteristic mirror-like Mauryan polish. Bell-shape and stylised animal form show Persepolitan/Achaemenid influence. Adopted as the national emblem of India (1950); the abacus dharmachakra is on the national flag.

hist_iron_tools_agriculture.label: Iron Tools in Agriculture
hist_iron_tools_agriculture.subject: history
hist_iron_tools_agriculture.detail: Iron use began around 3000 years ago. By 2500 years ago iron axes cleared forests and iron ploughshares increased production. Found in megalithic burials and enabled expansion of agriculture.

hist_irrigation_systems.label: Ancient Irrigation Systems
hist_irrigation_systems.subject: history
hist_irrigation_systems.detail: Canals, wells, tanks and artificial lakes were built to irrigate crops. Kings and villagers took active interest in building and maintaining these works, which required organised labour and resources.

hist_grama_bhojaka.label: Grama Bhojaka
hist_grama_bhojaka.subject: history
hist_grama_bhojaka.detail: Village headman in northern India whose position was hereditary. Usually the largest landowner who used slaves and hired workers. Also served as tax collector, judge, and sometimes policeman for the king.

hist_mathura.label: Mathura
hist_mathura.subject: history
hist_mathura.detail: Important settlement for over 2500 years at the crossroads of major trade routes. Second capital of Kushanas. Religious centre with Buddhist monasteries, Jaina shrines and centre for Krishna worship. Produced fine sculpture.

hist_arikamedu.label: Arikamedu
hist_arikamedu.subject: history
hist_arikamedu.detail: Coastal town near Pondicherry, a major Indo-Roman trading emporium c. 2nd century BCE - 3rd century CE, excavated by Mortimer Wheeler in 1945. Yielded large quantities of Roman amphorae (Dressel 1 wine jars), Arretine red-slip pottery from Italy, Roman lamps, glassware, and Tamil-Brahmi inscribed sherds. Had brick-built dyeing vats for cotton and bead-making workshops. Identified with "Poduke emporion" of the Periplus. Primary archaeological evidence of direct Roman contact with the Tamil states.

hist_nbpw.label: Northern Black Polished Ware
hist_nbpw.subject: history
hist_nbpw.detail: Northern Black Polished Ware — a very glossy, shining deluxe pottery served as tableware for the rich, appearing from the 5th century BCE in the Gangetic plains. Marks the archaeological beginning of the Second Urbanization in India. Associated with iron implements, punch-marked coins, burnt bricks, and ring wells (ring wells from mid-NBPW phase, ~3rd century BCE). Sherds found at over 400 sites across Bihar, UP, MP, and Maharashtra.

hist_ring_wells.label: Ring Wells
hist_ring_wells.subject: history
hist_ring_wells.detail: Rows of pots or ceramic rings arranged one on top of another, found in many cities. Used as toilets, drains and garbage dumps. Usually found in individual houses.

hist_jatakas.label: Jatakas
hist_jatakas.subject: history
hist_jatakas.detail: Stories probably composed by ordinary people and preserved by Buddhist monks. Depict everyday life, occupations and social conditions. Scenes from Jatakas were carved on stupa railings and painted at Ajanta.

hist_vellalar.label: Vellalar
hist_vellalar.subject: history
hist_vellalar.detail: Large landowners in the Tamil region mentioned in Sangam literature. They exercised considerable control over the affairs of the nadu alongside uzhavar (ploughmen) and kadaisiyar (landless labourers).

hist_grihapatis.label: Grihapatis
hist_grihapatis.subject: history
hist_grihapatis.detail: Independent farmers in northern India who were smaller landowners. Alongside the grama bhojaka, they formed the class of landed cultivators. Distinct from the landless dasa karmakara.

hist_bharuch.label: Bharuch (Barygaza)
hist_bharuch.subject: history
hist_bharuch.detail: Bharuch (also Broach, Barygaza in Graeco-Roman texts) on the Gulf of Khambhat in Gujarat — the busiest west-coast port of ancient India, peaking during Shaka-Kushan-Satavahana times. Described in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea as the emporium of the Western Kshatrapa kingdom. Received goods from both the Shaka and Satavahana interiors via Ujjain. Imports: wine, copper, tin, lead, Roman coral, glass, gold and silver coins; exports: Himalayan spikenard, costus, bdellium, ivory, agate-carnelian from Ujjain, cotton, muslin, and long pepper. At the junction of land routes (uttarapatha from Taxila via Mathura-Ujjain) and the Arabian Sea.

hist_kanishka.label: Kanishka
hist_kanishka.subject: history
hist_kanishka.detail: Greatest Kushan emperor, reigned c. 78-102 CE (dates debated). Started the Shaka Era in 78 CE (still used by the Government of India). Empire stretched from Bactria to Pataliputra, from the Aral Sea to the Narmada. Capital at Purushapura (Peshawar), where he built a huge stupa/monastery (reported by Chinese pilgrims). Great patron of Mahayana Buddhism — convened the Fourth Buddhist Council at Kashmir (Kundalavana), which produced commentaries on the Tripitaka in Sanskrit (engraved on copper sheets in a stupa) and formalised the Mahayana-Hinayana split. Suffered defeats against the Chinese general Ban Chao. Patronised Ashvaghosha (author of Buddhacharita), Charaka (physician), Nagarjuna (Madhyamaka philosopher), Vasumitra, Sangharaksha, and the Gandhara-Mathura art schools. His headless standing stone statue at Mat (Mathura) carries his inscribed name.

hist_theravada_buddhism.label: Theravada Buddhism
hist_theravada_buddhism.subject: history
hist_theravada_buddhism.detail: The older form of Buddhism, more popular in Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand and other parts of Southeast Asia. Maintained the original emphasis on monastic discipline and individual enlightenment.

hist_bodhisattvas.label: Bodhisattvas
hist_bodhisattvas.subject: history
hist_bodhisattvas.detail: Persons who had attained enlightenment but chose to remain in the world to teach and help others rather than living in isolation. Their worship became very popular in Mahayana Buddhism.

hist_fa_xian.label: Fa Xian
hist_fa_xian.subject: history
hist_fa_xian.detail: Chinese Buddhist pilgrim (Faxian, 法顯) who travelled to India 399-414 CE, during the reign of Chandragupta II. Left Chang'an in 399, crossed the Pamirs and Hindu Kush to reach the Gandhara-Punjab region, travelled through the Gangetic plain (visiting Mathura, Kanauj, Kapilavastu, Kushinara, Bodh Gaya, Pataliputra, Nalanda), spent years studying and copying Sanskrit Buddhist texts at Pataliputra and Tamralipti, and returned by sea via Sri Lanka and Java (reaching China 414). His account *Fo Guo Ji* ("Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms") describes a prosperous and tolerant Gupta India, Mauryan ruins at Pataliputra, the condition of Buddhist monasteries, and Chandala untouchables. Primary source for Gupta-era society.

hist_nalanda.label: Nalanda
hist_nalanda.subject: history
hist_nalanda.detail: Preeminent Buddhist monastic university at Nalanda (Bihar), founded by Kumaragupta I in the 5th century CE. Expanded through Gupta, Vardhana (Harsha), and Pala patronage over 700 years, burnt by Bakhtiyar Khilji c. 1200 CE. At its peak: ~10,000 students and 2,000 teachers from across Asia (Xuanzang's estimate; Yijing says ~3,000), accommodated in 8 large compounds with temples, shrines, meditation halls, and a nine-storey library (Dharmaganja) that reportedly burned for months. Curriculum: Mahayana Buddhist philosophy (all 18 schools debated), grammar, logic, medicine, mathematics, astronomy. Maintained from the revenues of 100 (later 200) villages. Visited by Xuanzang (studied under Silabhadra, 5 years) and Yijing (7 years). Ruins UNESCO WHS since 2016.

hist_bhakti_movement_early.label: Early Bhakti Movement
hist_bhakti_movement_early.subject: history
hist_bhakti_movement_early.detail: Worship of deities like Shiva, Vishnu and Durga through personal devotion. Open to all regardless of caste or gender. Present in the Bhagavad Gita. Led to construction of temples with deity images.

hist_pepper_trade.label: Pepper Trade with Rome
hist_pepper_trade.subject: history
hist_pepper_trade.detail: South Indian pepper (called "yavanapriya" in Sanskrit, "black gold" in the West) was the single most lucrative Roman import from India. Roman writer Pliny complained in his *Natural History* (77 CE) that Rome was being drained of gold to pay for Indian pepper and other luxuries — as early as 22 CE the Roman Senate had objected to expenditure on Eastern imports. Chera ports Muziris (Cranganore) and Tyndis, and the Pandya port of Korkai were the main export points. Sourced from Malabar coast. Drove the Indo-Roman gold-coin flow (~6,000 Roman coins found in India, mostly south of Vindhyas); Rome eventually banned the trade to stem the outflow.

hist_ashvaghosha.label: Ashvaghosha
hist_ashvaghosha.subject: history
hist_ashvaghosha.detail: Poet who lived in Kanishka's court and composed the Buddhacharita, a biography of the Buddha. One of the Buddhist scholars who began writing in Sanskrit rather than Prakrit.

hist_gautamiputra_satakarni.label: Gautamiputra Shri Satakarni
hist_gautamiputra_satakarni.subject: history
hist_gautamiputra_satakarni.detail: Greatest Satavahana king, reigned c. 106-130 CE. Restored Satavahana fortunes after Shaka conquests in Deccan. Defeated and killed the Kshaharata Shaka king Nahapana of western India — over 8,000 silver coins of Nahapana found near Nasik were re-struck by him. Recovered Malwa, Kathiawar, Konkan, and brought under control Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Andhra. Called himself "Ekabrahmana" (unique brahmana) and "Kshatriyadarpamanamarda" (destroyer of the pride of kshatriyas). His mother Gautami Balashri set up the famous Nasik cave inscription praising him — a key source. Claimed to have re-established the fourfold varna system and ended intermixture of castes (caused by Shaka presence).

hist_chandragupta_ii.label: Chandragupta II
hist_chandragupta_ii.subject: history
hist_chandragupta_ii.detail: Gupta emperor at the dynasty's peak, reigned c. 380-412 CE, son of Samudragupta. Took the title Vikramaditya ("Sun of Valour") after defeating the Western Kshatrapa Shakas c. 400 CE — conquered Malwa, Gujarat, and Kathiawar, giving the empire direct access to western-coast trade and Ujjain as a second capital. Married his daughter Prabhavati into the Vakataka dynasty of central India, securing indirect control over the Deccan after her husband's death made her regent. The Mehrauli Iron Pillar inscription eulogises a king "Chandra" whose exploits (conquest of Vanga, Vahlikas) likely refer to him. Court ornamented by the traditional Navaratnas (Nine Gems): Kalidasa, Amarasimha, Varahamihira, Dhanvantari, Kshapanaka, Shanku, Vetalabhatta, Ghatakarpara, and Vararuchi — likely tradition rather than history. Chinese pilgrim Fa-Hien (Faxian) visited India during his reign (399-414 CE). Issued famous silver (Shaka-type) and gold (dinara) coins.

hist_prashasti.label: Prashasti
hist_prashasti.subject: history
hist_prashasti.detail: Sanskrit eulogistic court inscriptions praising royal patrons, composed by court poets. Became the dominant royal inscriptional form from Gupta times onwards, displacing earlier Prakrit edicts (Ashoka) and factual prose epigraphs. Classic model: the *Allahabad Prashasti* (Prayag Prashasti) by Harishena for Samudragupta. Typical structure: genealogy of the king, enumeration of his conquests in poetic stock epithets, comparison with mythical heroes and gods, and the patron's virtues. Style-setters for Indian court poetry; the earliest surviving chaste-Sanskrit prashasti is Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription (c. 150 CE).

hist_pallavas.label: Pallava Dynasty
hist_pallavas.subject: history
hist_pallavas.detail: Tamil dynasty with capital at Kanchi, ruling Tondaimandalam. Rose under Simhavishnu in late 6c, peak under Mahendravarman I (590-630) and Narasimhavarman I Mahamalla (630-668) who captured Badami from the Chalukyas and built Mamallapuram. Overthrown by Chola Aditya I in 893; Tondaimandalam passed to the Cholas. [SINGHANIA:] Temple architecture evolved through four stages: Mahendra group (rock-cut mandapas under Mahendravarman I), Narasimha group (monolithic rathas under Narasimhavarman I), Rajsimha group (structural stone temples under Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha), Nandivarman group (smaller shrines transitional to mature Dravida style).

hist_samantas.label: Samantas (Military Leaders)
hist_samantas.subject: history
hist_samantas.detail: Hereditary military chiefs / feudatory lords who emerged as a distinct political class from Gupta times (4th-6th CE) onwards. Received grants of land (rather than cash salaries) in exchange for military service and tribute to the paramount king. The Allahabad prashasti of Samudragupta uses "samanta" for subordinated kings paying tribute. Under Guptas and especially Harsha, they formed the ring of tributary principalities. In weak reigns, samantas declared independence, fragmenting empires. Became the pillar of early medieval Indian polity (the "Indian feudalism" debate, R.S. Sharma). Typical obligations: personal attendance at court, tribute, and offering daughters in marriage.

hist_hereditary_offices.label: Hereditary Administrative Posts
hist_hereditary_offices.subject: history
hist_hereditary_offices.detail: Important administrative posts became hereditary with sons succeeding fathers. Some individuals held multiple offices. This contributed to decentralization and eventual political fragmentation.

hist_sabha_assembly.label: Sabha Assembly
hist_sabha_assembly.subject: history
hist_sabha_assembly.detail: Assembly of brahmin landowners in Pallava inscriptions. Functioned through sub-committees handling irrigation, agriculture, roads and temples. Controlled by rich and powerful landowners.

hist_kalidasa.label: Kalidasa
hist_kalidasa.subject: history
hist_kalidasa.detail: Greatest Sanskrit poet-dramatist, traditionally dated to late 4th / early 5th century CE — Gupta court poet, associated with Chandragupta II's Navaratnas. Seven surviving works: three plays (*Abhijnanashakuntalam* — the Dushyanta-Shakuntala love story, first Sanskrit work translated into European languages in 1789; *Vikramorvashiyam* — Pururavas-Urvashi; *Malavikagnimitram* — Agnimitra-Malavika), two mahakavyas (*Raghuvamsha* — dynasty of Rama; *Kumarasambhava* — birth of Kartikeya), and two lyric poems (*Meghaduta* — cloud-messenger; *Rtusamhara* — seasons). Universally regarded as the "Shakespeare of India". Praised by Goethe for Shakuntala.

hist_harishena.label: Harishena
hist_harishena.subject: history
hist_harishena.detail: Court poet, minister, and military commander (mahadandanayaka) of Samudragupta. Composed the *Prayag Prashasti* (Allahabad Pillar Inscription, c. 350 CE) in chaste Sanskrit kavya style — the foundational text for Samudragupta's reign and the model for all subsequent royal prashastis in Sanskrit India. Mixed prose (gadya) and verse (padya). Harishena held the titles sandhivigrahika (minister of peace and war) and kumaramatya. His prashasti deliberately echoes the Ashokan Mauryan pillar it shares as its medium, contrasting the aggressive Samudragupta with peace-loving Ashoka.

hist_aihole.label: Aihole
hist_aihole.subject: history
hist_aihole.detail: Ancient town on the Malaprabha river in Bagalkot district, Karnataka — an early Chalukyan cultural and religious centre from the late Gupta period onwards (c. 5th-8th CE). Contains over 120 temples of the early Chalukyan phase — called the "cradle of Indian temple architecture" since Aihole temples illustrate experimentation across the nagara (north Indian), dravida (south Indian), and vesara (hybrid Deccan) styles. Notable temples: Durga (apsidal, late 7th CE), Lad Khan (c. 450 CE, one of the earliest), Meguti (634 CE Jain temple with Ravikirti's Aihole inscription eulogising Chalukyan Pulakesin II's defeat of Harsha). The Aihole inscription is one of the earliest references to Kalidasa and Bharavi.

hist_kanchipuram.label: Kanchipuram
hist_kanchipuram.subject: history
hist_kanchipuram.detail: Ancient capital of the Pallava dynasty in Tamil Nadu, continuously inhabited since at least 500 BCE. Already prominent in Sangam literature as a market town. Rose to political preeminence under the Pallavas (c. 4th-9th CE), who fought continually with the Chalukyas and Pandyas. Great centre of Tamil Vaishnavite (Varadaraja Perumal Temple) and Shaivite (Ekambareshvara, Kailasanatha) devotion; also a Jain and Buddhist centre in the early medieval period. Kanchi Kamakoti Pitham claimed by Smarta tradition to be founded by Adi Shankaracharya. One of the seven holy Hindu cities (Sapta Puris). Educational centre rivalling Nalanda in early medieval times.

hist_iron_pillar_delhi.label: Iron Pillar of Mehrauli
hist_iron_pillar_delhi.subject: history
hist_iron_pillar_delhi.detail: Seven-metre (6.5 t) wrought-iron pillar in the Qutb complex at Mehrauli, Delhi. Originally erected in the 4th-5th century CE, probably at Udayagiri in central India and moved to Delhi later (possibly by Iltutmish). Sanskrit inscription in Gupta Brahmi eulogises a king "Chandra" (identified by most scholars with Chandragupta II Vikramaditya) whose conquests reached from Vanga (Bengal) to Balkh (Bactria). World-famous for its rust-resistance over ~1,600 years, attributed to high phosphorus content and passive phosphate layer formation; arid Delhi climate also preserved it. A tribute to Gupta-era metallurgy.

hist_silappadikaram.label: Silappadikaram
hist_silappadikaram.subject: history
hist_silappadikaram.detail: One of the two great Tamil epics of the later Sangam era (c. 5th-6th century CE), by Ilango Adigal (a Chera prince-turned-Jain monk). "The Tale of the Anklet" — tragedy of Kovalan, who abandons his chaste wife Kannagi for the courtesan Madhavi of Kaveripattanam; wrongly executed for theft at Madurai by the Pandya king; Kannagi proves his innocence with her anklet and burns down the city. Uniquely spans all three Tamil kingdoms (Chola, Pandya, Chera), giving invaluable social-economic detail. Considered the pinnacle of early Tamil literature. Paired with Manimekalai (a Buddhist sequel by grain-merchant Sattanar about Kovalan's daughter).

hist_ramayana.label: Ramayana
hist_ramayana.subject: history
hist_ramayana.detail: Sanskrit epic about Rama, prince of Kosala, his exile, the abduction of Sita by Ravana of Lanka, and Rama's victory. Author is Valmiki. Several regional versions exist across the subcontinent.

hist_aryabhata.label: Aryabhata
hist_aryabhata.subject: history
hist_aryabhata.detail: Mathematician-astronomer born 476 CE at Kusumapura (near Pataliputra), though some traditions place his birth at Ashmaka. Composed the *Aryabhatiya* in 499 CE (age 23) — a versified treatise in four parts: Gitikapada, Ganitapada (mathematics), Kalakriyapada (time), and Golapada (sphere/astronomy). Revolutionary contributions: place-value decimal system and use of zero (shunya); accurate approximation of π to 3.1416; sine table; heliocentric hints (Earth rotates on its axis, not the sky); accurate cause of solar and lunar eclipses (Earth's shadow, not demon Rahu); formula for the area of a triangle and volume of a sphere; length of sidereal year (365.358 days). Influenced Islamic mathematics through translations (al-Khwarizmi). First Indian satellite (1975) named after him.

hist_panchatantra.label: Panchatantra
hist_panchatantra.subject: history
hist_panchatantra.detail: Sanskrit collection of interlinked animal fables compiled by the brahmana Vishnu Sharma, c. 300-500 CE — composed as a teaching tool of niti (political wisdom) for princes. Five tantras (books): Mitra-bheda (splitting friends), Mitra-labha (winning friends), Kakolukiyam (crows and owls), Labdhapranasha (loss of gains), Apariksitakaraka (rash actions). Adapted into Pahlavi under Khosrow I (6th CE), Arabic as *Kalila wa Dimna* (8th CE, Ibn al-Muqaffa'), Hebrew, Latin, and over 50 European languages — arguably the most widely translated Indian literary work. Inspired Aesop's fables, La Fontaine, and the Jataka tradition.

hist_zero_invention.label: Invention of Zero
hist_zero_invention.subject: history
hist_zero_invention.detail: Indian mathematical innovation of zero as a placeholder and a number in its own right, dated to c. 3rd-5th century CE. Gupta-era mathematicians, especially Aryabhata (*Aryabhatiya*, 499 CE), systematised the decimal place-value system treating zero as a number. Earliest surviving inscriptional use of a numeric zero: Gwalior inscription of 876 CE. Sanskrit term "shunya" (void) was translated through Arabic "sifr" (empty) to Latin "cephirum", finally becoming English "cipher" and "zero".
