Brahmagupta (628 CE) gave the first arithmetical rules for zero (addition, subtraction, multiplication — division by zero he correctly left undefined). Transformed world mathematics through Arabic transmission.

hist_metallurgy_ancient.label: Ancient Indian Metallurgy
hist_metallurgy_ancient.subject: history
hist_metallurgy_ancient.detail: Harappans had knowledge of copper metallurgy and made bronze. Successors developed advanced iron-forging including wrought iron and cast iron. Iron pillar of Delhi exemplifies this expertise.

hist_mahajanapadas.label: Sixteen Mahajanapadas
hist_mahajanapadas.subject: history
hist_mahajanapadas.detail: Sixteen states from c. sixth century BCE mentioned in early Buddhist and Jaina texts. Prominent ones: Vajji, Magadha, Koshala, Kuru, Panchala, Gandhara, Avanti. Each had a capital city, often fortified. Some were monarchies, others oligarchies (ganas/sanghas).

hist_punch_marked_coins.label: Punch-Marked Coins
hist_punch_marked_coins.subject: history
hist_punch_marked_coins.detail: Earliest coins of the Indian subcontinent, appearing ~500 BCE in the age of Buddha. Primarily silver (with some copper); pieces of metal punched with multiple symbols — hill, tree, fish, bull, elephant, crescent, geometric marks. Earliest hoards concentrated in eastern UP, Bihar (Magadha), with some at Taxila. Used to pay wages and buy goods; Pali texts show money used universally (even a dead mouse was priced). Continued through Mauryas, alongside cast coins and die-struck coins.

hist_iron_plough_agriculture.label: Iron Plough Agriculture
hist_iron_plough_agriculture.subject: history
hist_iron_plough_agriculture.detail: Spread in fertile alluvial river valleys of Ganga and Kaveri from c. sixth century BCE. Iron-tipped ploughshare used to turn alluvial soil. Paddy transplantation dramatically increased production in parts of Ganga valley. Irrigation through wells, tanks and canals.

hist_varna_system.label: Varna System
hist_varna_system.subject: history
hist_varna_system.detail: Four hierarchical categories: Brahmanas (study/teach Vedas), Kshatriyas (warfare/administration), Vaishyas (agriculture/trade), Shudras (serving others). Justified through Purusha Sukta of Rigveda. Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras prescribed occupations and norms for each varna.

hist_endogamy_exogamy.label: Endogamy and Exogamy
hist_endogamy_exogamy.subject: history
hist_endogamy_exogamy.detail: Exogamy: marrying outside the kin group, prescribed by Brahmanical texts for gotra. Endogamy: marrying within the group, prevalent in south Indian communities including Satavahana practice. Kanyadana (gift of daughter) considered important religious duty of the father.

hist_non_kshatriya_kings.label: Non-Kshatriya Kings
hist_non_kshatriya_kings.subject: history
hist_non_kshatriya_kings.detail: Despite Shastras prescribing only Kshatriyas as kings, many ruling lineages had different origins. Mauryas' origins debated (Kshatriya or low origin). Shungas and Kanvas were Brahmanas. Shakas were mlechchhas. Political power was effectively open to anyone with support and resources.

hist_jainism.label: Jainism
hist_jainism.subject: history
hist_jainism.detail: Philosophy predating Vardhamana Mahavira, the 24th tirthankara, who was preceded by 23 tirthankaras. Five vows (pancha mahavrata): non-violence (ahimsa), truthfulness, non-stealing, non-possession, and celibacy (brahmacharya; added by Mahavira to the four of Parshvanatha). Three jewels (triratna): right knowledge, right faith, right action. Central tenet: the entire world is animated; non-injury is paramount; karma shapes rebirth. Sectarian split after the Magadha famine of ~300 BCE produced Shvetambara (white-clad, Magadha-based) and Digambara (sky-clad/naked, southern returnees under Bhadrabahu) at the Pataliputra council. Jaina canon finally compiled at Valabhi in Gujarat in 6th century CE.

hist_upanishads.label: Upanishads
hist_upanishads.subject: history
hist_upanishads.detail: Philosophical texts from c. sixth century BCE onwards exploring meaning of life, afterlife, rebirth. Brihadaranyaka Upanishad contains teacher lineages with metronymics. Chhandogya Upanishad discusses nature of the self and true sacrifice. Part of later Vedic tradition.

hist_vajji_republic.label: Vajji (Gana/Sangha)
hist_vajji_republic.subject: history
hist_vajji_republic.detail: A republic with capital at Vaishali in Bihar. Had many rulers (rajas) who performed rituals together and made decisions through assemblies and debate. Women, dasas and kammakaras could not participate.

hist_gana_sangha.label: Gana or Sangha System
hist_gana_sangha.subject: history
hist_gana_sangha.detail: A form of government with not one but many rulers, each called a raja. They met in assemblies to discuss and decide matters through debate. Both Buddha and Mahavira belonged to such sanghas.

hist_ahimsa.label: Ahimsa
hist_ahimsa.subject: history
hist_ahimsa.detail: The principle of not hurting or killing any living being, central to Jainism. Mahavira said 'All beings long to live. To all things life is dear.' Farmers found it difficult to follow as they killed insects.

hist_ashrama_system.label: Ashrama System
hist_ashrama_system.subject: history
hist_ashrama_system.detail: Four stages of life developed by brahmins: brahmacharya (student), grihastha (householder), vanaprastha (forest dweller), and samnyasa (renunciation). For brahmin, kshatriya and vaishya men. Women excluded from Vedic study.

hist_satyakama_jabala.label: Satyakama Jabala
hist_satyakama_jabala.subject: history
hist_satyakama_jabala.detail: Named after his mother Jabali, a slave woman. Despite humble birth, he had a deep desire to learn about reality and was accepted by brahmin teacher Gautama, becoming a renowned thinker.

hist_gargi.label: Gargi
hist_gargi.subject: history
hist_gargi.detail: A woman thinker mentioned in the Upanishads, famous for her learning and participation in debates held in royal courts. One of the few women scholars in the otherwise male-dominated philosophical tradition.

hist_mahabharata.label: Mahabharata
hist_mahabharata.subject: history
hist_mahabharata.detail: Colossal Sanskrit epic of over 100,000 verses, traditionally attributed to Vyasa, composed over c. 1000 years from c. 500 BCE. Central story of Kauravas vs Pandavas war for the throne of the Kurus at Hastinapura. Critical Edition prepared 1919-1966 under V.S. Sukthankar. Contains narrative and didactic sections including the Bhagavad Gita.

hist_buddhist_sangha.label: Buddhist Sangha
hist_buddhist_sangha.subject: history
hist_buddhist_sangha.detail: Monastic order founded by Buddha; open to all castes irrespective of birth. Members called bhikkhus (monks) and bhikkhunis (nuns). Initially men-only; women admitted through Ananda's mediation, with Mahapajapati Gotami (Buddha's aunt and foster-mother) becoming the first bhikkhuni. Slaves, soldiers, and debtors were explicitly barred from admission. Vows of continence, poverty, and faith. Lived on alms. Internal decisions by consensus or vote, modelled on gana/sangha republican traditions. Rules codified in the Vinaya Pitaka.

hist_magadha.label: Magadha
hist_magadha.subject: history
hist_magadha.detail: Most powerful mahajanapada, situated in modern Bihar along Ganga and Son rivers. Advantages underlying its supremacy: rich iron ores near Rajgir (and Avanti) for weapons, fertile alluvial soil with heavy rainfall, river-fortified strategic capitals (Rajgir surrounded by 5 hills; Pataliputra at Ganga-Son-Gandak-Ghaghra confluence), eastern access to elephants, and a recently Vedicized frontier population with expansionary energy. Ruled successively by Haryanka (Bimbisara, Ajatasattu, Udayin), Shishunaga, and Nanda dynasties; supplanted by Mauryas.

hist_shrenis.label: Shrenis (Guilds)
hist_shrenis.subject: history
hist_shrenis.detail: Associations/guilds of artisans and merchants organised under their own headmen. Eighteen guilds mentioned in Pali texts, including smiths, carpenters, leather workers, and painters; crafts were typically hereditary. Functions: training, raw-material procurement, product distribution, regulation of quality, and banking (deposits and loans). Continued to thrive through post-Maurya times, with ivory-workers and other guilds financing parts of stupas (seen in Sanchi votive inscriptions).

hist_parshvanatha.label: Parshvanatha
hist_parshvanatha.subject: history
hist_parshvanatha.detail: 23rd tirthankara of Jainism and immediate predecessor of Mahavira, traditionally placed in the 9th-8th century BCE. Hailed from Banaras (Kashi), son of king Ashvasena; abandoned royal life to become an ascetic. Taught four vows — non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, non-possession — to which Mahavira later added celibacy (brahmacharya) as the fifth. Asked his followers to cover the upper and lower body (unlike Mahavira's nudity prescription).

hist_digambara_shvetambara.label: Digambara and Shvetambara Split
hist_digambara_shvetambara.subject: history
hist_digambara_shvetambara.detail: Sectarian split of Jainism triggered by the 12-year Magadha famine (~300 BCE). Bhadrabahu led a group of Jains to south India (Karnataka) to escape the famine, while Sthulabahu stayed in Magadha. On the returnees' return, a council was convened at Pataliputra to compile the canon; the southern returnees boycotted it. From this point, southerners were called Digambaras ("sky-clad", naked) and Magadhans Shvetambaras ("white-clad"). Difference also over stricter Mahavira practice vs Parshvanatha-style clothed practice.

hist_bhadrabahu.label: Bhadrabahu
hist_bhadrabahu.subject: history
hist_bhadrabahu.detail: Jain acharya and last shruta-kevalin (possessor of knowledge of all Jain scriptures). Led the southern migration of Jains to Shravanabelagola in Karnataka during the 12-year Magadha famine (~300 BCE). Late tradition associates Chandragupta Maurya with him — the emperor is said to have abdicated, become a Jain ascetic under Bhadrabahu, and spent his last years in Karnataka (uncorroborated by other sources). His split with Sthulabahu's Magadhan Jains led to the Digambara-Shvetambara divide.

hist_kharavela.label: Kharavela
hist_kharavela.subject: history
hist_kharavela.detail: Kalinga king of the Mahameghavahana dynasty, 1st century BCE, major Jain patron. Known almost entirely through his Hathigumpha (Udayagiri, Odisha) rock inscription in Prakrit — one of the most important early epigraphs. Claimed to have defeated princes of Andhra and Magadha, recovered a Jina image that the Nandas had taken from Kalinga as war trophy, and patronised Jain monks.

hist_triratna_jain.label: Jain Triratna (Three Jewels)
hist_triratna_jain.subject: history
hist_triratna_jain.detail: Three jewels of Jainism prescribed as the path to liberation (moksha): samyak darshana (right faith / perception), samyak jnana (right knowledge), and samyak charitra (right action / conduct). No ritual is required — liberation is attained through cultivation of these three. Distinct from the Buddhist Triratna of Buddha-Dhamma-Sangha.

hist_eightfold_path.label: Eightfold Path (Ashtangika Marga)
hist_eightfold_path.subject: history
hist_eightfold_path.detail: Buddha's prescription for ending suffering, attributed to him in texts of around 3rd century BCE. The eight limbs: right view (samyak drishti), right intention/determination, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness/awareness, and right concentration. Forms the fourth of the Four Noble Truths. Leads to the "middle path" avoiding both luxury and extreme austerity.

hist_three_jewels_buddhist.label: Buddhist Triratna (Three Jewels)
hist_three_jewels_buddhist.subject: history
hist_three_jewels_buddhist.detail: Three refuges of Buddhism, the core elements of the religion: Buddha (the teacher), Dhamma (his teaching), and Sangha (the monastic community). Reciting "Buddham sharanam gachchhami, Dhammam sharanam gachchhami, Sangham sharanam gachchhami" marks acceptance into the Buddhist fold. Not to be confused with the Jain Triratna (right knowledge, faith, action).

hist_tripitaka.label: Tripitaka
hist_tripitaka.subject: history
hist_tripitaka.detail: The three "baskets" of the Buddhist (Theravada/Pali) canon, compiled at the early Buddhist councils and finalised by the third council at Pataliputra under Ashoka. Sutta Pitaka — sermons and discourses of the Buddha. Vinaya Pitaka — rules and regulations for monastic discipline of the sangha. Abhidhamma Pitaka — philosophical and systematic analysis of dhamma. Written in Pali. Mahayana traditions later added their own sutras in Sanskrit.

hist_buddhist_councils.label: Four Buddhist Councils
hist_buddhist_councils.subject: history
hist_buddhist_councils.detail: Four major councils convened to preserve and codify Buddhist teachings. (1) First Council, Rajagriha, ~483 BCE, shortly after Buddha's death, presided by Mahakasyapa under Ajatasattu's patronage — Ananda recited Sutta, Upali recited Vinaya. (2) Second Council, Vaishali, ~383 BCE, over the Ten Points dispute; led to the first schism (Sthaviravada vs Mahasanghika). (3) Third Council, Pataliputra, ~250 BCE, under Ashoka, presided by Moggaliputta Tissa — finalised Tripitaka; sent missions abroad. (4) Fourth Council, Kashmir (Kundalavana), ~72-100 CE, under Kanishka — Sanskrit canon, marked formalisation of Mahayana Buddhism.

hist_second_urbanization.label: Second Urbanization
hist_second_urbanization.subject: history
hist_second_urbanization.detail: Revival of urban life in the Gangetic plains from c. 500 BCE, about 1400 years after the decline of Harappan cities (~1900 BCE). Driven by iron-ploughshare agriculture, paddy transplantation, surplus food grain, long-distance trade, the use of punch-marked coins, and the NBPW pottery phase. Cities of the mahajanapadas — Rajgir, Vaishali, Kaushambi, Shravasti, Varanasi, Pataliputra, Champa, Ujjain — arose in this phase, becoming seats of government, markets, artisan quarters, and trade nodes. Prepared the material base for the rise of large territorial states.

hist_haryanka_dynasty.label: Haryanka Dynasty
hist_haryanka_dynasty.subject: history
hist_haryanka_dynasty.detail: First major dynasty of Magadha (~544-412 BCE), established in prominence by Bimbisara. Rulers: Bimbisara (544-492) → Ajatasattu (492-460) → Udayin (460-444) → minor successors. Expanded Magadha through conquest (Anga) and marriage diplomacy; fortified Rajgir; built Pataliputra fort at the Ganga-Son confluence. Contemporary of Buddha and Mahavira; hosted the First Buddhist Council under Ajatasattu. Supplanted by the Shishunagas.

hist_shishunaga_dynasty.label: Shishunaga Dynasty
hist_shishunaga_dynasty.subject: history
hist_shishunaga_dynasty.detail: Dynasty that supplanted the later Haryankas of Magadha, ruling ~412-344 BCE. Founded by Shishunaga (a minister/viceroy), who temporarily moved the capital to Vaishali. Greatest achievement: destruction of the 100-year rival Avanti (Ujjain), absorbing it into the Magadhan empire permanently. His son Kalashoka convened the Second Buddhist Council at Vaishali (~383 BCE). Overthrown by Mahapadma Nanda.

hist_nanda_dynasty.label: Nanda Dynasty
hist_nanda_dynasty.subject: history
hist_nanda_dynasty.detail: Ruled Magadha ~344-321 BCE. Founded by Mahapadma Nanda, of non-Kshatriya (traditionally shudra) origin — an example of the "non-Kshatriya kings" pattern. Claimed the title ekarat ("sole sovereign"). Vastly rich and militarily formidable (~200,000 infantry, 60,000 cavalry, 3000-6000 war elephants), which deterred Alexander from advancing beyond the Beas. Conquered Kalinga, bringing back a Jina image. Last nine Nandas (Dhana Nanda etc.) were unpopular; overthrown by Chandragupta Maurya with Chanakya's counsel.

hist_lichchhavis.label: Lichchhavis
hist_lichchhavis.subject: history
hist_lichchhavis.detail: Most powerful of the eight republican clans of the Vajji confederacy, with capital at Vaishali (Basarh, north Bihar). Texts refer to an assembly of 7707 rajas (ruling oligarchs) seated in the motehall — each maintaining his own storehouse and apparatus. Chetaka, the Lichchhavi chief, was maternal uncle of Mahavira and father-in-law of Bimbisara. Ajatasattu broke Lichchhavi power through sixteen years of intrigue and warfare, sowing dissension through his minister Vassakara. Later, the Gupta empire was linked to the Lichchhavis through Chandragupta I's marriage to Kumaradevi.

hist_shakyas.label: Shakyas
hist_shakyas.subject: history
hist_shakyas.detail: Buddha's republican clan, based in the foothills of the Himalayas with capital at Kapilavastu (identified with Piprahwa in Basti district, UP). Gautama's father Suddhodana was the elected raja; his mother Mahamaya was from the neighbouring Koliya clan. Lumbini (15 km from Piprahwa, in Nepal) served as a subsidiary capital and was where Buddha was born. The Shakyas were nominally under Koshalan suzerainty; Viudabha, son of Prasenajit, later massacred them.

hist_mallas.label: Mallas
hist_mallas.subject: history
hist_mallas.detail: Republican clan whose territory touched the northern border of the Vajji state. Had two capitals — Pava (Pavapuri, where Mahavira died in 468 BCE per one tradition) and Kushinara (Kasia in Deoria district, UP, where Buddha died in 487 BCE). Both founders of the heterodox traditions thus passed away in Malla territory. Eventually absorbed into the Magadhan empire.

hist_pali.label: Pali
hist_pali.subject: history
hist_pali.detail: A middle Indo-Aryan Prakrit language that became the scriptural language of Theravada Buddhism. Came into use around 500 BCE, roughly contemporary with Buddha. Chosen by the Buddha (and similarly by Mahavira who used Ardhamagadhi) over Sanskrit to make his teachings accessible to common people, which greatly aided the spread of Buddhism. The Tripitaka and the Jatakas were composed in Pali. From the 1st century CE onwards, Buddhist monks increasingly adopted Sanskrit and Hybrid Sanskrit, which Sharma identifies as one cause of Buddhism's decline.

hist_stupa_architecture.label: Stupa Architecture
hist_stupa_architecture.subject: history
hist_stupa_architecture.detail: Buddhist sepulchral mound structures containing relic caskets of the Buddha or important followers. Components: anda (hemispherical dome / egg), harmika (railed balcony above anda), yashti (central mast), chhatri (tiered parasol), medhi (circular terrace), pradakshina patha (circumambulation path), vedika (railing separating sacred from secular), and toranas (elaborately carved gateways at cardinal directions). Originated in Mauryan times (Ashoka reportedly built 84,000 stupas over redistributed Buddha relics); finest surviving examples at Sanchi, Bharhut, Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda. Narrative reliefs depict Jataka stories and life of Buddha.

hist_achaemenid_india.label: Achaemenid Conquest of NW India
hist_achaemenid_india.subject: history
hist_achaemenid_india.detail: Darius I of the Achaemenid (Iranian) empire annexed the Indus valley, Sindh, and Punjab west of the Indus in 516 BCE as the twentieth satrapy — the most fertile and populous of the empire's 28 satrapies. Paid an annual tribute of 360 talents of gold, about one-third of Iran's total Asian revenue. Indian subjects were enrolled in the Iranian army; Xerxes used them against the Greeks. Direct result: entry of the Kharoshthi script into India, Iranian influence on Maurya court art (bell-capitals), Iranian diplomatic terminology (dipi → lipi). Indo-Iranian contact lasted about 200 years until Alexander's invasion.

hist_kharoshthi_script.label: Kharoshthi Script
hist_kharoshthi_script.subject: history
hist_kharoshthi_script.detail: Right-to-left script derived from Aramaic, brought into India by Iranian scribes in the 5th-4th centuries BCE. Used in NW India (Gandhara region) for writing Prakrit; appears in Ashokan inscriptions at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra (Prakrit in Kharoshthi), and at Kandahar (bilingual Greek-Aramaic with Kharoshthi). Used on Indo-Greek, Indo-Scythian, and Kushan coins. Continued in use in NW India until c. 3rd century CE, then died out; deciphered by James Prinsep.

hist_darius_i.label: Darius I
hist_darius_i.subject: history
hist_darius_i.detail: Achaemenid (Persian) emperor, reigned 522-486 BCE. Annexed NW India (Gandhara, Sindh, Punjab west of Indus) in 516 BCE, converting it into the 20th satrapy. His inscriptions at Behistun, Persepolis, and Naqsh-e-Rustam list "Hi(n)dush" and Gandhara among his dominions. Son Xerxes deployed Indian troops against the Greeks at Thermopylae.

hist_porus.label: Porus (Puru)
hist_porus.subject: history
hist_porus.detail: King of the Paurava kingdom between the Jhelum (Hydaspes) and Chenab (Acesines) rivers. Gave the stiffest resistance to Alexander at the Battle of the Hydaspes in May 326 BCE. Defeated but, when asked by Alexander how he wished to be treated, replied "as a king should be treated"; Alexander was impressed and restored him to his kingdom as an ally, even enlarging his territory. Served as a Greek vassal until his assassination (c. 317 BCE) by Eudemus.

hist_ambhi.label: Ambhi (Omphis)
hist_ambhi.subject: history
hist_ambhi.detail: King of Taxila at the time of Alexander's invasion (326 BCE). Rivalry with Porus drove him to submit to Alexander without resistance on his arrival at the Indus, augmenting the Greek army with troops and replenishing its treasury. Retained his kingdom as a Greek ally.

hist_seleucus_nikator.label: Seleucus I Nicator
hist_seleucus_nikator.subject: history
hist_seleucus_nikator.detail: Macedonian general and one of Alexander's diadochi; founded the Seleucid empire ruling Asia Minor, Iran, and the east. Attempted to reconquer Alexander's Indian possessions but was defeated by Chandragupta Maurya (~305 BCE). Treaty: ceded to Chandragupta eastern Afghanistan (Arachosia, Paropamisadae), Baluchistan (Gedrosia), and the area west of the Indus in exchange for 500 war elephants (which Seleucus used decisively at the Battle of Ipsus, 301 BCE). Sealed by a marriage alliance (Seleucus's daughter to Chandragupta). Sent Megasthenes as ambassador to Pataliputra.

hist_bindusara.label: Bindusara
hist_bindusara.subject: history
hist_bindusara.detail: Second Mauryan emperor, son of Chandragupta Maurya and father of Ashoka. Reigned c. 297-273 BCE. Greek sources call him "Amitrochates" / "Amitraghata" (slayer of foes), suggesting military campaigns in south India / Deccan. Maintained Hellenistic diplomatic ties — received Greek ambassador Deimachus from Antiochus I (Seleucid), and Dionysius from Ptolemy II (Egypt). Reportedly requested Antiochus to send him sweet wine, dried figs, and a sophist. Patronised the Ajivika sect. During his reign Taxila rose in revolt and was pacified by prince Ashoka.

hist_rajukas.label: Rajukas
hist_rajukas.subject: history
hist_rajukas.detail: Class of Ashokan officers appointed across rural districts, vested with authority both to reward and to punish. Responsible for administration of justice. Introduced principles of vyavaharasamata (uniformity of judicial procedure) and dandasamata (uniformity of punishment) across varnas — a reform annoying to brahmanas since the Dharmashastras mandated varna-graded punishment. Also propagated dhamma among rural populations.

hist_indika.label: Indika (Megasthenes)
hist_indika.subject: history
hist_indika.detail: Account of India by Megasthenes, Greek ambassador of Seleucus Nicator at Chandragupta Maurya's court at Pataliputra. Original now lost; survives only in fragments quoted by later Greek writers (Arrian, Strabo, Diodorus, Pliny). Describes Pataliputra's fortifications (wooden palisades, 570 towers, 64 gates, 9.33 miles long × 1.75 miles wide), the six committees of five governing the city and the armed forces, seven-caste division of Indian society, absence of slavery (disputed), state-administered farms, and administrative hierarchy. Together with the Arthashastra, the foundational source for Maurya administration.

hist_barabar_caves.label: Barabar Caves
hist_barabar_caves.subject: history
hist_barabar_caves.detail: Earliest surviving rock-cut caves in India, in the Barabar and Nagarjuni hills about 30 km north of Gaya (Bihar). Four caves carved under Ashoka (Karna Chaupar, Lomas Rishi, Sudama, Vishvakarma), three more under his grandson Dasharatha. Dedicated to Ajivika monks per Ashokan inscriptions. Hewn from hard granite with mirror-like Mauryan polish inside. The Lomas Rishi cave's facade is carved to imitate a wooden chaitya arch — prototype for all later rock-cut chaitya halls (Bhaja, Karla, Ajanta). Setting for E.M. Forster's "Marabar caves" in A Passage to India.

hist_didarganj_yakshi.label: Didarganj Yakshini
hist_didarganj_yakshi.subject: history
hist_didarganj_yakshi.detail: Life-sized (nearly 7 ft) free-standing stone statue of a fly-whisk-bearing yakshi (chauri-bearer), discovered at Didarganj on the Ganga near Patna in 1917. Carved from Chunar buff sandstone with flawless Mauryan polish. Considered one of the finest early Indian stone sculptures — embodies the plasticity, voluminous hip-and-breast treatment, and polished surface that define Mauryan court art. Now in the Bihar Museum.

hist_mudrarakshasa.label: Mudrarakshasa
hist_mudrarakshasa.subject: history
hist_mudrarakshasa.detail: Sanskrit political drama by Vishakhadatta, c. 8th-9th century CE, in seven acts. "The Signet Ring of Rakshasa" — dramatises Chanakya's political machinations to secure Chandragupta Maurya's throne after the Nanda overthrow, culminating in winning over Rakshasa (the former Nanda minister) to the Maurya side. Only major Sanskrit drama with an entirely political (not romantic or mythological) plot. Principal literary source for the legend of Chanakya-Chandragupta partnership.

hist_pushyamitra_shunga.label: Pushyamitra Shunga
hist_pushyamitra_shunga.subject: history
hist_pushyamitra_shunga.detail: Brahmana commander-in-chief (senapati) of the last Maurya ruler Brihadratha; assassinated him in public in 185 BCE and usurped the throne of Pataliputra, founding the Shunga dynasty. Fought off Yavana (Indo-Greek, Demetrius / Menander) invasions. Performed the Vedic ashvamedha (horse sacrifice) — commemorated in an inscription at Ayodhya of his grandson — to mark the brahmanical revival after Maurya Buddhist patronage. Buddhist texts (Divyavadana) accuse him of persecuting Buddhists and destroying monasteries, though this is debated by modern historians. Reigned ~185-149 BCE.

hist_shunga_dynasty.label: Shunga Dynasty
hist_shunga_dynasty.subject: history
hist_shunga_dynasty.detail: Brahmana dynasty ruling Pataliputra and central India c. 185-73 BCE (~112 years, ten kings). Founded by Pushyamitra; capitals shifted between Pataliputra and Vidisha. Major cultural patrons: expansion of the Sanchi Stupa (railings and the famous four toranas), the Bharhut Stupa, and early Bharhut-Sanchi narrative sculpture marking the transition from Mauryan court art to a more organic popular style. Resisted Indo-Greek incursions (Menander's push into the Gangetic basin). Vedic sacrifices revived. Overthrown by their own brahmana ministers, the Kanvas.

hist_kanva_dynasty.label: Kanva Dynasty
hist_kanva_dynasty.subject: history
hist_kanva_dynasty.detail: Short-lived brahmana dynasty that succeeded the Shungas at Pataliputra, ruling c. 73-28 BCE. Four rulers: Vasudeva Kanva, Bhumimitra, Narayana, Susharman. Continued the Shunga tradition of Vedic revival. Overthrown by the Satavahana king Simuka in 28 BCE, marking the end of meaningful Magadhan imperial continuity.

hist_mauryan_art.label: Mauryan Art
hist_mauryan_art.subject: history
hist_mauryan_art.detail: Distinctive imperial art of the Maurya period (~321-185 BCE), introducing stone masonry on a wide scale. Two strands: (a) court/imperial art — monolithic buff-sandstone (Chunar) polished pillars with animal capitals (Sarnath Lion, Rampurva Bull, Sankissa Elephant), the Didarganj Yakshi, Ashoka's 84-pillared hall at Kumrahar; (b) popular art — unpolished hand-modelled terracottas (mother goddesses, elephants), wooden palisades, ring wells. Rock-cut architecture begins at Barabar Caves with the chaitya-arch facade of Lomas Rishi. Characterised by the distinctive "Mauryan polish" (mirror-like finish) and Achaemenid (Persepolitan) bell-capital influence.

hist_kushan_empire.label: Kushan Empire
hist_kushan_empire.subject: history
hist_kushan_empire.detail: Central Asian empire founded by a branch of the Yuezhi (Tocharian/Scythian) nomads. Consolidated under Kujula Kadphises (c. 30 CE) who displaced the Indo-Greeks and Shakas in the Kabul valley. Expanded across the Hindu Kush into Gandhara and the Gangetic basin under Vima Kadphises (copper coins imitating Roman, gold coins) and especially under Kanishka (c. 78-102 CE), greatest ruler. At its height spanned from the Oxus to Pataliputra and from Khorasan to eastern UP — a true Central Asian empire. Capitals: Purushapura (Peshawar, primary) and Mathura (second). Controlled the Silk Route, collected tolls, issued the largest gold coinage of ancient India before the Guptas, patronised Mahayana Buddhism (4th Buddhist Council in Kashmir under Kanishka), Gandhara and Mathura art schools. Some successors had Indian names (Vasudeva). Ended in India c. 230 CE; western branch absorbed by Sassanians c. 250 CE.

hist_silk_road.label: Silk Road
hist_silk_road.subject: history
hist_silk_road.detail: Network of overland and maritime trade routes connecting China through Central Asia and Iran to the Roman Mediterranean, with branches to India. Main overland route flourished under Kushan control (1st-3rd c. CE) — Kushans levied heavy tolls and built their prosperity on it. Goods: Chinese silk westward; Roman gold and glassware, horses, wool, and precious stones eastward; Indian pepper, ivory, cotton, spices, and steel going both directions. Parthian Iran's rise obstructed overland silk flow to Rome, diverting some traffic through north-western Indian ports. Also carried ideas (Buddhism into Central Asia and China under Kanishka-era missions), faiths, artisans (Gandhara art synthesis), and pathogens. Indian termini linked to the uttarapatha at Taxila.

hist_indo_greeks.label: Indo-Greeks (Bactrian Greeks)
hist_indo_greeks.subject: history
hist_indo_greeks.detail: Greek dynasties ruling NW India from Bactria after c. 200 BCE, pushed south by Scythian pressure. First foreigners to invade post-Maurya India (Demetrius I, c. 200-180 BCE). Held a larger area than Alexander, reportedly pushing as far as Ayodhya and Pataliputra. Never unified — two Greek houses ruled in parallel. Key contributions: first coins attributable to named kings (silver, gold); first gold coinage in India; Hellenistic art motifs (foundation of Gandhara school); theatre curtain (yavanika); Greek terminology in astronomy (horashastra, Sanskrit for astrology, from Greek horoskopos). Patronised Buddhism (Menander) and Vaishnavism (via envoys like Heliodorus). Absorbed by Shakas c. 1st century BCE.

hist_menander.label: Menander (Milinda)
hist_menander.subject: history
hist_menander.detail: Most famous Indo-Greek king, reigned c. 165-130 BCE with capital at Sakala (Sialkot). Ruled from Hindu Kush to at least the Yamuna, at one point reaching Mathura and reportedly Pataliputra. Converted to Buddhism by the monk Nagasena; their dialogue is preserved in the *Milindapanho* ("Questions of Milinda"), a Pali Buddhist classic. Widely circulated silver and copper coins (bilingual Greek-Kharoshthi). Greek historian Plutarch notes his ashes were divided among Greek cities like a Buddha relic.

hist_milindapanho.label: Milindapanho
hist_milindapanho.subject: history
hist_milindapanho.detail: "The Questions of Milinda" — Pali Buddhist text in dialogue form, recording questions put by Indo-Greek king Menander to the Buddhist monk Nagasena on doctrinal points (self, soul, karma, nirvana). Probably composed c. 100 BCE - 200 CE. Key source for post-Maurya Buddhist thought and for Indo-Greek-Buddhist interaction.

hist_heliodorus_pillar.label: Heliodorus Pillar
hist_heliodorus_pillar.subject: history
hist_heliodorus_pillar.detail: Stone pillar at Besnagar (near Vidisha, MP), erected c. 110 BCE by Heliodorus, a Greek ambassador from Indo-Greek king Antialkidas of Taxila to the Shunga king Bhagabhadra. Dedicated to Vasudeva (Vishnu), calling Heliodorus a "Bhagavata" — earliest inscriptional evidence of a foreigner embracing Vaishnavism/Bhagavatism and of the early Bhagavata cult. Crowned by a Garuda capital.

hist_shakas.label: Shakas (Indo-Scythians)
hist_shakas.subject: history
hist_shakas.detail: Scythian nomads from Central Asia who displaced the Indo-Greeks in the 1st century BCE, ruling parts of NW India for four centuries (western branch until ~4th century CE). Five branches: Afghanistan, Taxila/Punjab, Mathura, western India (longest-lasting, "Western Kshatrapas"), and the Deccan. The Western Kshatrapas of Gujarat issued the earliest datable silver coinage in India (with regnal years). Constant conflict with Satavahanas over western Deccan and Malwa. Introduced satrapy system, cavalry tactics, turban, tunic, trousers, long coat (ancestor of sherwani). Assimilated into Indian society as "fallen kshatriyas" per Manusmriti. Famously defeated by Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) c. 400 CE.

hist_rudradaman.label: Rudradaman I
hist_rudradaman.subject: history
hist_rudradaman.detail: Greatest ruler of the Western Kshatrapa (Shaka) dynasty, reigned c. 130-150 CE. Ruled Sindh, Gujarat, Konkan, Narmada valley, Malwa, and Kathiawar. Defeated the Satavahanas twice but spared them due to matrimonial ties. Repaired the Sudarshana Lake reservoir in Kathiawar (originally built under Chandragupta Maurya), damaged by storm. His Junagadh Rock Inscription (c. 150 CE) is the earliest long inscription in chaste Sanskrit, marking the shift from Prakrit to Sanskrit in royal epigraphy. Great patron of Sanskrit despite Central Asian ancestry.

hist_junagadh_inscription.label: Junagadh Rock Inscription
hist_junagadh_inscription.subject: history
hist_junagadh_inscription.detail: Inscription by Rudradaman I at Junagadh (Kathiawar, Gujarat), c. 150 CE — the first substantial royal inscription in chaste Sanskrit, marking the linguistic shift from Prakrit to Sanskrit in inscriptions. Records his territorial conquests and the repair of the Sudarshana reservoir (originally built under Chandragupta Maurya, expanded by Ashoka via provincial governor Yavanaraja Tushaspha). Also has two later additions: a Skandagupta (Gupta) inscription recording Sudarshana's further repairs, and Ashokan Major Rock Edicts 1-14 — making the rock a palimpsest of three imperial eras.

hist_sudarshana_lake.label: Sudarshana Lake
hist_sudarshana_lake.subject: history
hist_sudarshana_lake.detail: Large artificial reservoir at Girnar (Kathiawar, Gujarat), built under Chandragupta Maurya by provincial governor Pushyagupta Vaishya, enlarged under Ashoka through Yavanaraja Tushaspha. Damaged by a severe storm in ~150 CE; repaired by Shaka ruler Rudradaman I (recorded in Junagadh inscription). Again damaged and repaired under Skandagupta (c. 457 CE) — commemorated in a second Junagadh inscription. Rare example of continuous imperial irrigation patronage spanning Mauryan, Shaka, and Gupta dynasties over 800 years.

hist_vikrama_samvat.label: Vikrama Samvat
hist_vikrama_samvat.subject: history
hist_vikrama_samvat.detail: Hindu calendar era beginning 58/57 BCE, traditionally reckoned from the victory of king Vikramaditya of Ujjain over invading Shakas. Widely used across north India (notably in Nepal and parts of India). 57 years ahead of the Gregorian calendar. The name Vikramaditya ("Sun of Prowess") became a coveted title adopted by as many as 14 later kings — the most famous being Chandragupta II of the Gupta dynasty, who also defeated the (Western) Shakas c. 400 CE.

hist_shaka_era.label: Shaka Era (Saka Samvat)
hist_shaka_era.subject: history
hist_shaka_era.detail: Calendar era beginning 78 CE, started by Kushan emperor Kanishka. Adopted by the Government of India in 1957 as the national civil calendar (Shaka Samvat). 78 years behind the Gregorian calendar. Widely used across South and Southeast Asia (Java, Bali, Cambodia) through Indian cultural influence. Many later Deccan inscriptions (Satavahana, Chalukya) are dated in this era.

hist_parthians.label: Parthians (Pahlavas)
hist_parthians.subject: history
hist_parthians.detail: Iranian people who followed the Shakas into NW India in the 1st century CE, occupying a small portion of the NW. Often paired with Shakas in Indian texts as "Shaka-Pahlavas". Most famous king: Gondophernes (c. 19-46 CE); Christian tradition holds that St. Thomas the Apostle visited his court to preach Christianity. Assimilated into Indian society like the Shakas before them.

hist_gondophernes.label: Gondophernes
hist_gondophernes.subject: history
hist_gondophernes.detail: Most famous Indo-Parthian king, reigned c. 19-46 CE over NW India (Gandhara/Punjab). St. Thomas Acts (apocryphal Christian text) has him as the patron who invited the apostle to India — the traditional basis for the St. Thomas Christians of Kerala, though historicity debated. Issued bilingual Greek-Kharoshthi coins. Taxila Sirkap excavations date largely to his period.

hist_fourth_buddhist_council.label: Fourth Buddhist Council
hist_fourth_buddhist_council.subject: history
hist_fourth_buddhist_council.detail: Held in Kashmir (Kundalavana) under patronage of Kushan emperor Kanishka, c. 72-100 CE, presided over by Vasumitra (assisted by Ashvaghosha). Produced extensive commentaries (300,000 words) on the Tripitaka in Sanskrit, which Kanishka had engraved on copper sheets and enclosed in a stupa. Formalised the split between Mahayana (Sanskrit canon, bodhisattva doctrine, image-worship) and Hinayana (Pali canon, arhat ideal). A parallel tradition places it at Jalandhar. Not accepted by Theravada Buddhism.

hist_nagarjuna_philosopher.label: Nagarjuna (Madhyamaka)
hist_nagarjuna_philosopher.subject: history
hist_nagarjuna_philosopher.detail: Mahayana Buddhist philosopher, c. 150-250 CE, founder of the Madhyamaka ("Middle Way") school. Developed the doctrine of shunyata (emptiness) — all phenomena are without inherent essence. Principal work: *Mulamadhyamakakarika*. Regarded by Mahayana Buddhists as a second Buddha. Associated with Nagarjunakonda in Andhra (likely named after him). Distinct from Nagasena of the Milindapanho (Sharma's text conflates them).

hist_buddhacharita.label: Buddhacharita
hist_buddhacharita.subject: history
hist_buddhacharita.detail: Sanskrit epic poem by Ashvaghosha (court poet of Kanishka), c. 1st-2nd century CE — biography of the Buddha from birth to enlightenment and parinirvana in 28 cantos (partially lost; Chinese and Tibetan translations preserve full text). The earliest surviving complete Sanskrit kavya (court poem). Ashvaghosha's *Saundarananda*, about Buddha's half-brother Nanda's conversion, is the second major surviving kavya.

hist_mathura_school_of_art.label: Mathura School of Art
hist_mathura_school_of_art.subject: history
hist_mathura_school_of_art.detail: Indigenous school of art flourishing at Mathura (UP) in the early centuries CE, contemporaneous with the Gandhara school but stylistically distinct. Used local red spotted sandstone. Made the earliest Buddha images independently of Gandhara (in fleshy, fully Indian form with close-cropped hair — usnisha as shell-shape, shaven head, smiling face, broad shoulders). Also produced the headless standing statue of Kanishka (inscribed at the base), Jain tirthankara images, and Kushan royal portraits. Depicted yakshis and yakshas in full volumes. Contrast with Gandhara's Graeco-Roman realism.

hist_kamasutra.label: Kamasutra
hist_kamasutra.subject: history
hist_kamasutra.detail: Sanskrit treatise on kama (desire, pleasure) by Vatsyayana, c. 3rd century CE. Seven books covering social conduct, courtship, marriage, the nagaraka (sophisticated urban gentleman), courtesans, and erotics. Valuable source for life of city-dwelling elite classes during post-Maurya/early Gupta urban prosperity. Just one of the four purusharthas (life-aims) — dharma, artha, kama, moksha — each with its authoritative text.

hist_natyashastra.label: Natyashastra
hist_natyashastra.subject: history
hist_natyashastra.detail: Comprehensive Sanskrit treatise on the performing arts attributed to sage Bharata Muni, composed between 200 BCE and 200 CE. 36 chapters covering dramaturgy, acting, dance, music, stage construction, aesthetics (rasa theory — the nine rasas), and prosody. Foundational text for all subsequent Indian classical dance, drama, and music traditions. First work to articulate the rasa-sthayi bhava theory of aesthetic emotion.

hist_sushruta.label: Sushruta
hist_sushruta.subject: history
hist_sushruta.detail: Ancient Indian surgeon, composer of the *Sushruta Samhita* — foundational Sanskrit treatise on surgery. Dated variously from 6th century BCE to 4th century CE; the extant redaction is from c. 1st-2nd century CE by Nagarjuna (a different Nagarjuna). Describes over 300 surgical procedures and 120 instruments, including rhinoplasty, cataract couching, lithotomy, cesarean-like operations, and bone-setting. Founder of the "Shalya-chikitsa" (surgery) tradition of Indian medicine, alongside Charaka's Ayurveda (internal medicine).

hist_yavanas.label: Yavanas
hist_yavanas.subject: history
hist_yavanas.detail: Indian term for Greeks (and later, by extension, Muslims/foreigners of the west). Derived from Sanskritized "Ionian" (the Ionian Greeks of Anatolia with whom the Achaemenids had contact). Used in Ashokan inscriptions for the Greeks on the empire's NW border; continued through Sangam literature for Roman traders. Yavanika = "curtain" in Sanskrit drama, borrowed from Greek stagecraft. A Yavanaraja named Tushaspha served as Ashoka's provincial governor in Kathiawar.

hist_nahapana.label: Nahapana
hist_nahapana.subject: history
hist_nahapana.detail: Western Kshatrapa (Shaka) ruler of the Kshaharata lineage, early 2nd century CE. Controlled Gujarat, Malwa, western Deccan (Nasik area). His Nasik cave inscription records large religious gifts. Defeated and killed by Gautamiputra Satakarni — 8,000+ silver coins of Nahapana were recovered near Nasik re-struck with Satavahana symbols.

hist_vashishthiputra_pulumavi.label: Vashishthiputra Pulumavi
hist_vashishthiputra_pulumavi.subject: history
hist_vashishthiputra_pulumavi.detail: Satavahana king c. 130-154 CE, son and successor of Gautamiputra Satakarni. Reign saw Satavahana power extended into coastal Andhra, where his coins and inscriptions appear. Made Paithan (Pratishthan) on the Godavari the primary capital. Defeated twice by Shaka ruler Rudradaman I but not destroyed (matrimonial alliance — Rudradaman's daughter married into the Satavahana family).

hist_yajna_sri_satakarni.label: Yajna Sri Satakarni
hist_yajna_sri_satakarni.subject: history
hist_yajna_sri_satakarni.detail: Last great Satavahana king, reigned c. 165-194 CE. Recovered north Konkan and Malwa from the Shakas. Enthusiastic patron of trade and navigation — his coins appear in Andhra, Maharashtra, MP, and Gujarat, and depict a ship on the reverse (rare indicator of maritime ambitions). After him the Satavahana kingdom declined sharply, ending by c. 220 CE.

hist_paithan.label: Paithan (Pratishthan)
hist_paithan.subject: history
hist_paithan.detail: Principal Satavahana capital on the Godavari river in Aurangabad district, Maharashtra. Established as capital by Vashishthiputra Pulumavi in the 2nd century CE. Major inland terminus of the uttarapatha trade route. Continued as a cultural and trade centre; birthplace of Paithani silk weaving tradition.

hist_ikshvakus_andhra.label: Ikshvakus (Andhra)
hist_ikshvakus_andhra.subject: history
hist_ikshvakus_andhra.detail: Successors of the Satavahanas in the eastern Deccan, ruled c. 225-325 CE from Vijayapuri (modern Nagarjunakonda) on the lower Krishna. Major patrons of Buddhism — Nagarjunakonda became one of the most architecturally rich Buddhist sites of ancient India, with two dozen monasteries, the Mahachaitya stupa, and the earliest brahmanical brick temples. Queens (notably Chamtisiri) endowed many stupas. Matriarchal-leaning culture similar to Satavahanas. Overthrown by Pallavas.

hist_nagarjunakonda.label: Nagarjunakonda
hist_nagarjunakonda.subject: history
hist_nagarjunakonda.detail: Major Buddhist site in present-day Andhra Pradesh, prospering c. 2nd-4th century CE under the Ikshvakus. Named after philosopher Nagarjuna. Contains the Mahachaitya (great stupa) enshrining a tooth relic, about 30 monastic complexes, earliest brahmanical brick temples (Shiva, Karthikeya), amphitheatre, Ashokan-type pillar, and extensive inscriptions documenting royal and merchant donations. Since the site was submerged by the Nagarjunasagar dam in 1960, monuments were relocated to Nagarjunakonda Island.

hist_karle_chaitya.label: Karle Chaitya
hist_karle_chaitya.subject: history
hist_karle_chaitya.detail: The grandest rock-cut Buddhist chaitya hall (sacred prayer hall) in western India, near Lonavala in Maharashtra. Excavated c. 1st-2nd century CE under Satavahana patronage, partly by the Shaka king Nahapana's son-in-law Ushavadata. 40 m long, 15 m wide, 15 m high apsidal hall with 37 octagonal columns, a vaulted teak-ribbed roof (imitating wooden prototypes), and a monumental facade with a horseshoe chaitya arch and donor couple sculptures. Largest and best-preserved early chaitya.

hist_nasik_caves.label: Nasik Caves (Pandavleni)
hist_nasik_caves.subject: history
hist_nasik_caves.detail: Rock-cut Buddhist cave complex near Nashik, Maharashtra — 24 caves excavated c. 1st century BCE to 3rd century CE under Satavahana and Shaka patronage. Caves 3 and 10 contain inscriptions of Gautamiputra Satakarni and his mother Gautami Balashri praising his victories (key historical sources); other caves have inscriptions of Shaka Nahapana and his son-in-law Ushavadata. Mix of chaitya and vihara caves; show the transition from early Buddhist aniconic to Mahayana image-worship art.

hist_gathasaptasati.label: Gathasaptasati
hist_gathasaptasati.subject: history
hist_gathasaptasati.detail: Prakrit (Maharashtri Prakrit) anthology of 700 erotic and pastoral verses, attributed to Satavahana king Hala. One of the earliest extant works of Indian secular/profane poetry. Depicts village and rural life with psychological realism. Retouched/expanded after the 6th century. Shows the cultivated Prakrit literary culture of the Satavahana court.

hist_karikala.label: Karikala Chola
hist_karikala.subject: history
hist_karikala.detail: Famous early Chola king (Sangam era, c. mid-2nd century CE). Founded Puhar (Kaveripattanam), Chola capital and port. Built a 160-km flood embankment along the Kaveri river using 12,000 slaves captured from Sri Lanka. Maintained an efficient navy. Defeated Cheras and Pandyas at the legendary Battle of Venni. Lavished gold on Sangam poets (reportedly 1,600,000 gold pieces to one bard — exaggerated). Central hero of Sangam heroic poetry.

hist_puhar_kaveripattanam.label: Puhar (Kaveripattanam)
hist_puhar_kaveripattanam.subject: history
hist_puhar_kaveripattanam.detail: Capital and primary port of the early Cholas at the mouth of the Kaveri river. Founded by Karikala. Had a large artificial dock and customs warehouses documented in *Pattinappalai* (a Sangam idyll). A major node of Indo-Roman trade (Arretine pottery and Roman coins found nearby). Featured in the Tamil epic *Silappadikaram* as the home of Kovalan and Madhavi. Devastated by a tsunami or sea-surge c. 3rd century CE, ending its preeminence.

hist_uraiyur.label: Uraiyur
hist_uraiyur.subject: history
hist_uraiyur.detail: Early Chola capital, suburb of modern Tiruchirappalli. Famous for cotton trade; chief centre of Chola political power in the Sangam era before Puhar's rise. Dyeing vats excavated here attest the early textile industry. Archaeological evidence of occupation from c. 3rd century BCE.

hist_muziris.label: Muziris
hist_muziris.subject: history
hist_muziris.detail: Premier Chera port on the Malabar coast (identified with Pattanam near Kodungallur/Cranganore, Kerala) c. 1st century BCE - 4th century CE. Principal node of Indo-Roman pepper trade. Mentioned repeatedly in the *Periplus of the Erythraean Sea* and Ptolemy's *Geography*; depicted on the Roman *Tabula Peutingeriana*. Housed Roman trading colonies; Pliny says Rome had two cohorts stationed there to protect interests and a temple to Augustus. Famous for the Muziris papyrus (a 2nd century CE commercial contract for Red Sea trade). Recent Pattanam excavations confirm massive Mediterranean-pottery finds.

hist_madurai.label: Madurai
hist_madurai.subject: history
hist_madurai.detail: Ancient capital of the Pandya kingdom on the Vaigai river in Tamil Nadu, one of the oldest continually inhabited cities of India. Seat of the Sangam literary academies (3 traditional Sangams) under Pandya patronage. Meenakshi-Sundareshwara temple complex developed here later. Setting of *Silappadikaram's* tragic climax.

hist_tolkappiyam.label: Tolkappiyam
hist_tolkappiyam.subject: history
hist_tolkappiyam.detail: Earliest surviving work of Tamil literature, a treatise on Tamil grammar and poetics, attributed to Tolkappiyar. Three books: Eluttu (orthography), Sol (word/syntax), and Porul (semantics, poetics, cultural conduct — covering the Five Landscapes / tinai of akam love poetry). Dated variously from 3rd century BCE to 5th century CE; clearly pre-dates the main Sangam anthologies. Foundational text of Tamil linguistics and aesthetics.

hist_tirukkural.label: Tirukkural
hist_tirukkural.subject: history
hist_tirukkural.detail: Classical Tamil text of 1,330 couplets (kurals) by Tiruvalluvar, c. 3rd-5th century CE (disputed). Three books: Aram (virtue/dharma), Porul (wealth/artha), and Inbam (love/kama) — mirrors the trivarga of Sanskrit tradition but culturally distinct. Composed in venpa metre. Most revered Tamil ethical text; considered cross-sectarian (not tied to any one religion). Translated into over 40 languages.

hist_manimekalai.label: Manimekalai
hist_manimekalai.subject: history
hist_manimekalai.detail: Tamil Buddhist epic by Chithalai Chathanar (Sattanar), a grain merchant of Madurai, c. 5th-6th century CE. Sequel to *Silappadikaram*: tells the story of Manimekalai, daughter of Kovalan and Madhavi, who renounces courtesan life to embrace Buddhism and study philosophy. More religious than literary; important for post-Sangam Tamil Buddhism.

hist_periplus_erythraean.label: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea
hist_periplus_erythraean.subject: history
hist_periplus_erythraean.detail: Anonymous Greek merchant's manual of Indian Ocean trade, c. 40-70 CE. Describes ports, cargoes, prices, and sailing directions from Egyptian Red Sea ports to the east African coast, Arabia, and the Indian coast (Broach, Muziris, Nelkynda, Korkai). Key primary source for Indo-Roman trade, Indian ports, local rulers (mentions Nahapana, Satavahana king Siri Polemaios, Chera Kerobothros, Pandya Pandion, Chola dynasty), and the discovery/use of the monsoon for direct Red Sea-Malabar voyages.

hist_monsoon_discovery.label: Monsoon Trade (Hippalus)
hist_monsoon_discovery.subject: history
hist_monsoon_discovery.detail: Recognition of the seasonal reversal of the Arabian Sea monsoon winds (c. mid-1st century CE, traditionally attributed to Greek navigator Hippalus, though Arab/Indian seafarers had used it earlier). Allowed direct open-sea passage between Red Sea ports (Berenice, Myos Hormos) and Indian west coast (Muziris, Broach) — roughly 40 days each way — bypassing coastal and overland routes. Triggered the 1st-2nd century Indo-Roman trade boom.

hist_hindustan_term.label: Evolution of 'Hindustan'
hist_hindustan_term.subject: history
hist_hindustan_term.detail: 13th century: Minhaj-i-Siraj used it for Punjab, Haryana and Ganga-Yamuna areas under Delhi Sultan. 16th century: Babur used it for geography and culture of the subcontinent. Never originally included south India.

hist_gandhi_etymology.label: Gandhika → Gandhi
hist_gandhi_etymology.subject: history
hist_gandhi_etymology.detail: Sanskrit/Prakrit term *gandhika* originally meant perfumer (one who deals in scents), appearing as a frequent donor category in Satavahana-era Buddhist inscriptions (e.g., Karle, Nasik). By later medieval times *gandhika* broadened to mean all kinds of shopkeepers/grocers. The modern Indian surname *Gandhi* derives from this ancient term — a small linguistic thread tying Mahatma Gandhi's family name back to the trading classes of early historic India.

hist_roman_coins_india.label: Roman Coin Hoards in India
hist_roman_coins_india.subject: history
hist_roman_coins_india.detail: About 150 hoards of Roman gold and silver coins totalling ~6,000 coins have been found across India, overwhelmingly south of the Vindhyas (Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra) — evidence of the Indo-Roman trade balance favouring India. Pliny complained in 77 CE that Rome was being drained of gold by Indian trade. Roman coins were valued for intrinsic metal worth rather than for circulation; some re-struck by local rulers or kept as bullion. Concentration in the Coimbatore gap and along Cauvery indicates overland caravan routes feeding western-coast ports.

hist_uttarapatha.label: Uttarapatha
hist_uttarapatha.subject: history
hist_uttarapatha.detail: The "Northern Road", the great ancient trunk highway running from Taxila (Gandhara) through the Punjab, Mathura, Kanauj, Kaushambi, Varanasi, Pataliputra to Tamralipti at the Gangetic delta — and branches to Bactria in the NW and Burma in the east. Mentioned from late Vedic texts onward. Under the Mauryas it was the main imperial artery. Under the Kushans it linked into the Silk Route at Taxila. Paralleled by the Dakshinapatha (southern road) through the Deccan. Ancestor of the Grand Trunk Road.

hist_dakshinapatha.label: Dakshinapatha
hist_dakshinapatha.subject: history
hist_dakshinapatha.detail: The "Southern Road", trunk route from the Gangetic basin through Ujjain, Pratishthana (Paithan), and Tagar down to the south Indian states (Tamilakam). Valued by northern traders for gold, pearls, precious stones, and spices from the south. Key enabler of north-south cultural transmission — Jain, Buddhist, and brahmanical missionaries followed it; Megasthenes knew of the Pandya state through reports along it.

hist_chandragupta_i.label: Chandragupta I
hist_chandragupta_i.subject: history
hist_chandragupta_i.detail: Founder of Gupta imperial power, reigned c. 319-335 CE. Grandson of the dynasty founder Sri Gupta. Started the Gupta Era in 319-20 CE (date of his accession), used in dated inscriptions for centuries after. Married the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi (likely of Nepal), an alliance commemorated on rare "Chandragupta-Kumaradevi" type gold coins showing both figures — indicating the Lichchhavi match was politically momentous (possibly the Guptas as vaishyas gained kshatriya-princely legitimacy). His kingdom covered Magadha, Saketa (Ayodhya), and Prayag. Took the title Maharajadhiraja, marking the imperial pretension.

hist_gupta_era.label: Gupta Era (Samvat)
hist_gupta_era.subject: history
hist_gupta_era.detail: Calendar era beginning 319-320 CE, reckoned from the accession of Chandragupta I. Used in Gupta-dynasty inscriptions and persisted in Gujarat-Saurashtra (Valabhi era) long after the Guptas fell. 319-320 years behind Gregorian calendar. Along with Vikrama Samvat (57 BCE) and Shaka Era (78 CE), one of the three canonical eras of ancient Indian history.

hist_kumaragupta_i.label: Kumaragupta I
hist_kumaragupta_i.subject: history
hist_kumaragupta_i.detail: Gupta emperor (c. 412-455 CE), son and successor of Chandragupta II, with the title Mahendraditya. Longest-reigning Gupta ruler; kept the empire intact. Performed the ashvamedha sacrifice. Founded Nalanda University in the 5th century. Initiated gold coinage depicting Kartikeya (Kumara) — source of the Karttikeya/Peacock-rider gold type. Towards the end of his reign, Pushyamitras (not to be confused with Pushyamitra Shunga) and early Huna pressure began threatening the empire; his son Skandagupta repulsed them in his father's lifetime.

hist_skandagupta.label: Skandagupta
hist_skandagupta.subject: history
hist_skandagupta.detail: Last great Gupta emperor, reigned c. 455-467 CE, son of Kumaragupta I. Repulsed the first major Huna (Hephthalite) invasion of India in the late 450s — a victory commemorated in the Junagadh rock inscription (which also records his repair of the Sudarshana lake after a storm damaged it) and the Bhitari pillar inscription. Took titles Vikramaditya and Kramaditya. However, the military effort strained Gupta gold reserves — his later coinage shows visibly debased gold content. His death was followed by disputed succession and rapid imperial decay.

hist_hunas.label: Hunas (Hephthalites / White Huns)
hist_hunas.subject: history
hist_hunas.detail: Central Asian nomadic people who invaded NW India from the late 5th century CE, contributing significantly to the Gupta empire's fall. Not the same as the European Huns of Attila, though possibly related. Pressed into the Oxus region, then across the Hindu Kush in the 470s-480s. First repulsed by Skandagupta (c. 458 CE), but under their kings Toramana (c. 500 CE) and his son Mihirakula (c. 515-540 CE), they occupied Punjab, Kashmir, western Malwa, and central India. Mihirakula, a fanatical Shaivite, persecuted Buddhists (destroyed 1,600 stupas per Xuanzang). Decisively defeated by Yashodharman of Malwa (c. 528 CE) and Narasimhagupta Baladitya. Assimilated into Indian society as one of the 36 Rajput clans (some still bear the title "Hun"). Ended Gupta paramountcy in the west.

hist_toramana.label: Toramana
hist_toramana.subject: history
hist_toramana.detail: First major Huna king in India, c. 490-515 CE. Established Huna supremacy over Punjab, Rajasthan, Malwa, and parts of central India. His Eran (MP) boar-pillar inscription (in Sanskrit) proclaims his paramount status. Issued gold and silver coins. Succeeded by his son Mihirakula.

hist_mihirakula.label: Mihirakula
hist_mihirakula.subject: history
hist_mihirakula.detail: Son of Toramana and the most notorious Huna king, c. 515-540 CE. Capital at Sakala (Sialkot). Fanatical Shaivite; persecuted Buddhists — destroyed 1,600 stupas and monasteries per Xuanzang's account; also per the Chinese pilgrim Song Yun. Decisively defeated by Yashodharman of Malwa c. 528 CE and by Narasimhagupta. Retreated to Kashmir where he died.

hist_yashodharman.label: Yashodharman
hist_yashodharman.subject: history
hist_yashodharman.detail: Aulikara feudatory ruler of Malwa who rose to paramount status in northern India c. 530 CE. Decisively defeated the Huna king Mihirakula (commemorated in his Sondani pillar inscription) and broke Gupta paramountcy through victory inscriptions boasting conquest of "all of northern India". Set up two pillars of victory at Mandasor (532 CE). His rule was brief but marked the final disintegration of the Gupta imperial order and the transition to the early medieval regional-kingdom phase.

hist_vakatakas.label: Vakataka Dynasty
hist_vakatakas.subject: history
hist_vakatakas.detail: Central Indian dynasty ruling over Vidarbha, parts of MP, Chhattisgarh, and northern Maharashtra c. 250-550 CE. Contemporary and allies of the Guptas. Two branches: Pravarapura-Nandivardhana (main) and Vatsagulma (Washim). Chandragupta II married his daughter Prabhavati Gupta to the Vakataka king Rudrasena II; after Rudrasena II's early death, Prabhavati served as regent (c. 390-410 CE), effectively bringing Vakataka territory under Gupta influence. Vakataka king Harishena (c. 460-480 CE) of the Vatsagulma branch was the great patron of the second (Mahayana) phase of the Ajanta paintings. Overthrown by Chalukyas and Rashtrakutas.

hist_bhagavatism.label: Bhagavatism / Vaishnavism
hist_bhagavatism.subject: history
hist_bhagavatism.detail: Theistic devotional tradition centred on Vishnu-Narayana-Vasudeva-Krishna, emerging in post-Maurya times from the synthesis of (a) Vedic Vishnu (solar, fertility deity), (b) non-Vedic tribal god Narayana, and (c) the Krishna-Vasudeva cult of the Vrishni clan of Mathura. Merged into one by ~200 BCE. Characterised by bhakti (loving devotion to a personal god) and ahimsa. Earliest epigraphic evidence: Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar (~110 BCE), where a Greek envoy calls himself a Bhagavata. Doctrinal text: *Bhagavad Gita* (inserted into the Mahabharata). Developed the avatara doctrine — Vishnu's ten incarnations (dashavatara) descend whenever dharma is threatened. Overshadowed Mahayana Buddhism by Gupta times. Elaborated in the Vishnu Purana, Bhagavata Purana, and the works of the Alvars and Acharyas in medieval times.

hist_bhagavad_gita.label: Bhagavad Gita
hist_bhagavad_gita.subject: history
hist_bhagavad_gita.detail: "Song of the Lord" — a 700-verse Sanskrit philosophical dialogue forming Chapters 23-40 of the Bhishma Parvan of the Mahabharata, composed/inserted c. 200 BCE - 200 CE. On the eve of the Kurukshetra battle, the warrior Arjuna despairs at having to kill kinsmen; Krishna (incarnation of Vishnu) counsels him through a synthesis of three yogic paths: karma yoga (selfless action / duty), jnana yoga (knowledge), and bhakti yoga (devotion). Key teachings: the soul (atman) is eternal; perform one's varna-dharma without attachment to results; Krishna-Vishnu is the supreme reality. Became central to Vaishnavism, Hindu theology, and later Bhakti movements. Among the earliest Indian texts translated into European languages (Charles Wilkins, 1785).

hist_dashavatara_concept.label: Dashavatara (Ten Avatars of Vishnu)
hist_dashavatara_concept.subject: history
hist_dashavatara_concept.detail: Classical Vaishnava doctrine of Vishnu's ten incarnations that descend to restore dharma when the cosmic order is threatened. Standard list (finalised in Gupta/post-Gupta Puranas): Matsya (fish), Kurma (tortoise), Varaha (boar), Narasimha (man-lion), Vamana (dwarf), Parashurama (warrior-brahmana), Rama (ideal king), Krishna, Buddha (absorbed c. 8th-10th CE), and Kalki (future saviour). Expressed in sculpture (Dashavatara Temple, Deogarh) and literature (Jayadeva's Gita Govinda). The Varaha and Narasimha incarnations are given special prominence in Gupta iconography.

hist_dashavatara_deogarh.label: Dashavatara Temple, Deogarh
hist_dashavatara_deogarh.subject: history
hist_dashavatara_deogarh.detail: Early Gupta stone temple (c. 500 CE) in Lalitpur district, UP, on the Betwa river. One of the earliest surviving shikhara-style (nagara) Hindu temples. Panchayatana layout (main shrine + four corner shrines — a prototype). Three famous narrative relief panels on the exterior walls: Vishnu reclining on Shesha (Anantashayana), Nara-Narayana tapasya, Gajendramoksha. Originally had a modest shikhara (now partly collapsed). Named "Dashavatara" from the incarnation depictions. Landmark of early Hindu temple architecture.

hist_bhitargaon_temple.label: Bhitargaon Temple
hist_bhitargaon_temple.subject: history
hist_bhitargaon_temple.detail: Brick Gupta-period temple (c. 5th century CE) in Kanpur district, UP — the tallest surviving Hindu brick temple of the Gupta era. Pyramidal shikhara with recessed courses and terracotta panels depicting Vishnu's avatars, Shiva, and Ganga-Yamuna river goddesses. Square plan with projecting porch. Preserves the transition from flat-roofed early Gupta temples to the nagara-style superstructure.

hist_sultanganj_buddha.label: Sultanganj Buddha
hist_sultanganj_buddha.subject: history
hist_sultanganj_buddha.detail: Life-size (2.3 m, 500 kg) Gupta-period copper standing Buddha image from Sultanganj near Bhagalpur, Bihar — the largest surviving metal sculpture of the Gupta age (c. late 5th / early 6th CE). Discovered 1861 during railway construction; now in the Birmingham Museum (UK). Exemplifies Gupta sculptural ideals — transparent clinging drapery, serene facial expression, graceful posture — and the advanced bronze/copper casting technology of the period.

hist_amarasimha.label: Amarasimha
hist_amarasimha.subject: history
hist_amarasimha.detail: Sanskrit lexicographer, one of the traditional Navaratnas (Nine Gems) of Chandragupta II's court. Composed the *Amarakosha* ("Amara's Treasury"), the oldest and most authoritative surviving Sanskrit thesaurus. Three-part organisation (heaven, earth, miscellany) with words grouped by subject and gender. Still memorised by traditional Sanskrit students; the most-commented-upon Sanskrit lexicon. Possibly a Buddhist.

hist_amarakosha.label: Amarakosha
hist_amarakosha.subject: history
hist_amarakosha.detail: Oldest surviving Sanskrit synonym-thesaurus, composed by Amarasimha c. 4th-6th century CE. Verse format for memorisation. Organised semantically: Svargadi kanda (heaven, celestial), Bhuvargadi kanda (earth, places, people, professions), Samanyadi kanda (common, abstract). Foundational text of Sanskrit lexicography, with over 80 commentaries. Essential reference for all subsequent Sanskrit literature.

hist_varahamihira.label: Varahamihira
hist_varahamihira.subject: history
hist_varahamihira.detail: Astronomer, mathematician, and astrologer at Ujjain, c. 505-587 CE. Major works: *Brihatsamhita* (encyclopaedic treatise on natural and social omens, gemmology, architecture, iconography); *Panchasiddhantika* (summary of five astronomical schools — Surya, Vasishtha, Paulisha, Romaka, Paitamaha); *Brihajjataka* (foundational text of Indian horoscopic astrology). One of the traditional Navaratnas; integrated Greek astronomical terminology (horashastra from Greek horoskopos). Accurate computation of planetary positions.

hist_bhasa.label: Bhasa
hist_bhasa.subject: history
hist_bhasa.detail: Early Sanskrit dramatist, probably 3rd-4th century CE (dated c. 200 BCE by some). Thirteen plays attributed to him (rediscovered 1912 by T. Ganapati Sastri in Kerala), including *Swapnavasavadatta* (widely regarded as his finest, also his best-known), *Pratijnayaugandharayana*, *Charudatta* (incomplete; later reworked by Shudraka into *Mrichchhakatika*), *Urubhanga*, *Pancharatra*, and *Dutavakya*. Innovated by depicting on-stage battles and deaths (forbidden in classical Sanskrit theatre). Praised by Kalidasa. Uses Prakrit dialogue for lower-class characters and women, as became standard.

hist_shudraka.label: Shudraka
hist_shudraka.subject: history
hist_shudraka.detail: Sanskrit playwright, date uncertain (c. 4th-6th CE). Composed the famous 10-act Sanskrit drama *Mrichchhakatika* ("The Little Clay Cart") based on Bhasa's incomplete *Charudatta*. Unusual plot for Sanskrit drama: love of poor brahmana Charudatta and the courtesan Vasantasena, set against political intrigue in Ujjain. Notable for realistic detail of urban life, cross-class romance, and a happy ending after high tension. Sudraka himself is a legendary king-author figure.

hist_mrichchakatika.label: Mrichchakatika
hist_mrichchakatika.subject: history
hist_mrichchakatika.detail: "The Little Clay Cart" — ten-act Sanskrit prakarana drama by Shudraka, c. 4th-6th CE; a reworking of Bhasa's *Charudatta*. Tells the love of impoverished brahmana merchant Charudatta and the courtesan Vasantasena in the city of Ujjain, complicated by the villainous Samsthanaka (brother-in-law of the king) and political upheaval. Noted for its depiction of ordinary urban life — gamblers, thieves, courtesans, brahmanas — and Prakrit dialogue for lower characters. Mounted on European stages since the 1890s (as "The Toy Cart"). The term *yavanika* for stage-curtain appears here.

hist_abhijnanashakuntalam.label: Abhijnanashakuntalam
hist_abhijnanashakuntalam.subject: history
hist_abhijnanashakuntalam.detail: "The Recognition of Shakuntala" — Sanskrit play in seven acts by Kalidasa (c. 4th-5th CE), generally considered his masterpiece and the greatest work of Sanskrit drama. Dushyanta, king of the Puru dynasty, meets and secretly marries Shakuntala (daughter of sage Vishvamitra) in a forest hermitage; a curse makes him forget her when she arrives pregnant at his court, until a signet ring (abhijnana) recovered from a fish's belly restores his memory. Their son Bharata grows up to be the eponymous founder of Bharatavarsha. Translated by William Jones (1789) — the first Sanskrit work translated into European languages; hugely influential on Goethe and Herder.

hist_sati_origin.label: First Epigraphic Sati
hist_sati_origin.subject: history
hist_sati_origin.detail: The earliest inscriptional record of sati (widow immolation on husband's funeral pyre) comes from the Eran pillar inscription of 510 CE, during the Gupta period — recording the sati of a certain Bhanugupta's wife or the wife of his commander Goparaja. Sati practice had been rare or absent in earlier Indian texts (Sharma notes that Gupta patriarchal shift and polygamy among land-holding classes enabled it). Became more common under Rajputs; banned by Lord Bentinck in 1829 via Regulation XVII on the initiative of Raja Rammohan Roy.

hist_niyoga.label: Niyoga
hist_niyoga.subject: history
hist_niyoga.detail: Ancient Indian practice whereby a widow could bear a son by her deceased husband's younger brother or an approved brahmana, to ensure continuation of the male line. Allowed in Vedic and Dharmasutra texts for kshatriyas and brahmanas (illustrated in the Mahabharata — Vyasa with the wives of Vichitravirya). Forbidden to the higher varnas by Gupta-period law-books (continuing for shudras, who also practiced widow remarriage). Reflects the late-Dharmashastra tightening of upper-varna female sexuality.

hist_sanskrit_court_language.label: Shift to Sanskrit as Court Language
hist_sanskrit_court_language.subject: history
hist_sanskrit_court_language.detail: Transition from Prakrit (official language under Mauryas, Satavahanas) to Sanskrit as the language of royal inscriptions and court literature, c. 150 CE onwards. Marked by Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription (150 CE, first substantial Sanskrit kavya inscription) and consolidated under the Guptas, whose inscriptions, coins, and court literature are overwhelmingly in Sanskrit. Shift paralleled brahmanical resurgence, land-grants to brahmana priests, and the coding of Dharmashastra texts. Prakrit survived in drama (spoken by women and lower-class characters) and in Jain canonical literature.

hist_puranas_detail.label: Puranic Compilation
hist_puranas_detail.subject: history
hist_puranas_detail.detail: Final compilation of the major Puranas — vast encyclopaedic Sanskrit texts synthesising myth, cosmology, dynasty lists, ritual, geography, and popular Hinduism — occurred principally during the Gupta period (4th-6th CE). Eighteen Mahapuranas are traditionally listed (divided into three sets of six, emphasising Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva respectively): Brahma, Padma, Vishnu, Shiva, Bhagavata (the most popular, on Krishna), Narada, Markandeya, Agni, Bhavishya, Brahma-Vaivarta, Linga, Varaha, Skanda, Vamana, Kurma, Matsya, Garuda, Brahmanda. Contain the principal avatara mythology, tirthas (pilgrimage geographies), and genealogies of Gupta and post-Gupta kings.

hist_harshavardhana.label: Harshavardhana
hist_harshavardhana.subject: history
hist_harshavardhana.detail: Last great "Hindu" emperor of north India, reigned c. 606-647 CE from the Pushyabhuti/Vardhana dynasty of Thanesar. Took the throne at age 16 after his elder brother Rajyavardhana was killed by Gauda king Shashanka. Moved capital from Thanesar (Haryana) to Kanauj (UP), making it the new centre of north Indian political power — a shift reflecting the declining Gangetic trade and rising importance of fortified strategic locations. Empire stretched over Punjab, UP, Bihar, Orissa, and parts of Bengal; tributary Kamarupa (Assam under Bhaskaravarman). Southern expansion stopped by Chalukyan Pulakesin II at the Narmada (c. 618 CE). Originally Shaivite, converted to Mahayana Buddhism under Xuanzang's influence; held grand religious assemblies at Kanauj and Prayag. Patron of poet Banabhatta; himself credited with three Sanskrit plays (*Priyadarshika*, *Ratnavali*, *Nagananda*). After his death without heir, empire disintegrated into feuding kingdoms — marking the end of ancient India.

hist_banabhatta.label: Banabhatta
hist_banabhatta.subject: history
hist_banabhatta.detail: Court poet and biographer of Harshavardhana, c. 7th century CE. Composed the *Harshacharita* (the first Sanskrit historical biography — ornate prose-poetry account of Harsha's accession and early reign) and *Kadambari* (often called the first Sanskrit novel — a romance in highly ornate gadyakavya prose, left incomplete and finished by his son Bhushanabhatta). His style of prose-poetry (gadya-kavya) set the standard for subsequent Sanskrit biography and fiction. Also attributed: *Chandikashataka*. Supplied the information framework historians use to reconstruct Harsha's early career.

hist_harshacharita.label: Harshacharita
hist_harshacharita.subject: history
hist_harshacharita.detail: "Deeds of Harsha" — first surviving Sanskrit biographical text (akhyayika), by Banabhatta c. 640 CE. Covers Harsha's early life and accession through ornate prose-poetry (gadya-kavya). Structure: eight ucchvasas (chapters); autobiographical introduction by Bana; narrative of the Pushyabhuti dynasty; the murder of Harsha's elder brother Rajyavardhana by Shashanka; Harsha's accession and initial campaigns. Stops before Harsha's full reign (the remaining history is known from Xuanzang). Model for later Sanskrit charitas (Ramacharita, Vikramankadevacharita, etc.).

hist_xuanzang.label: Xuanzang (Hsuan Tsang)
hist_xuanzang.subject: history
hist_xuanzang.detail: Chinese Buddhist pilgrim who visited India 630-645 CE, during Harsha's reign. Left Chang'an in 629; travelled the Silk Road via the Tarim Basin, Samarkand, Bactria, the Hindu Kush, and Gandhara into Kashmir and the Gangetic plain. Studied at Nalanda for 5 years under Silabhadra, mastering Yogacara Mahayana. Travelled the length and breadth of India, attending Harsha's grand Kanauj and Prayag assemblies. Returned to China 645 CE with 657 Sanskrit manuscripts, relics, and Buddha images. Spent the rest of his life translating 75 of these texts into Chinese — foundational for East Asian Buddhism. His travelogue *Da Tang Xiyu Ji* ("Great Tang Records of the Western Regions") is the single most important primary source for 7th century Indian society, polity, and Buddhist institutions. Fictionalised as Tang Sanzang in *Journey to the West*.

hist_yijing.label: Yijing (I-tsing)
hist_yijing.subject: history
hist_yijing.detail: Chinese Buddhist pilgrim and scholar, c. 635-713 CE. Travelled to India by sea (673 CE) via Srivijaya (Sumatra), spent 10 years at Nalanda University (671-695 CE, some years at Srivijaya en route). Returned via sea with 400 Sanskrit texts. Composed *A Record of the Buddhist Religion as Practised in India and the Malay Archipelago* and *Memoirs of Eminent Monks*. Describes Nalanda's curriculum, discipline, and 3,000 monks (more conservative than Xuanzang's 10,000). Translated ~60 works into Chinese. Primary source for post-Harsha India and maritime Asian Buddhism.

hist_pulakesin_ii.label: Pulakesin II
hist_pulakesin_ii.subject: history
hist_pulakesin_ii.detail: Greatest Chalukyan emperor of Badami, reigned c. 610-642 CE. Decisively defeated Harshavardhana at the Narmada river c. 618 CE, stopping Harsha's southward expansion — commemorated in the *Aihole Inscription* (634 CE) by his court poet Ravikirti (modelled on the Allahabad Prashasti, with comparisons to Kalidasa and Bharavi). Took the title Parameshvara after the victory. Extended Chalukyan power over much of the Deccan; received embassies from Persian Sassanid king Khusrau II (depicted in Ajanta Cave 1 mural); defeated Pallava Mahendravarman I but was later killed by Pallava Narasimhavarman I Mamalla in 642 CE (Vatapi sacked). His defeat of Harsha is a landmark south-north check in Indian political history.

hist_shashanka.label: Shashanka of Gauda
hist_shashanka.subject: history
hist_shashanka.detail: Early 7c king of Gauda (Bengal), rival to Harshavardhana. According to Banabhatta Harshacharita, killed Harsha elder brother Rajyavardhana through a stratagem, triggering the Pushyabhuti vengeance. Remembered in Buddhist tradition for allegedly destroying the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya.

hist_kanauj.label: Kanauj
hist_kanauj.subject: history
hist_kanauj.detail: Strategic city in the Gangetic doab (Farrukhabad district, UP) on an elevated plateau, rising to political prominence from late 6th century CE. Capital of Harsha (from c. 606 CE onwards), then contested by Gurjara-Pratiharas, Palas, and Rashtrakutas in the Tripartite Struggle (8th-10th CE). Elevated, easily fortified position — suited to the feudal military polity that succeeded the trade-based Pataliputra order. Xuanzang describes it as a great city with Buddhist monasteries. Its symbolic importance made it the archetypal imperial capital of medieval north India — "he who holds Kanauj holds Aryavarta". Fell to Muhammad of Ghor in 1194.

hist_thanesar.label: Thanesar
hist_thanesar.subject: history
hist_thanesar.detail: Capital of the Pushyabhuti/Vardhana dynasty before Harsha moved the imperial seat to Kanauj. Located in Haryana near Kurukshetra. Excavated "Harsha ka Tila" mound contains brick structures from the period. Major Shaivite pilgrimage centre (Sthanishvara).

hist_maukharis.label: Maukhari Dynasty
hist_maukharis.subject: history
hist_maukharis.detail: Late Gupta feudatory clan that rose to independent power in the mid-6th century CE with capital at Kanauj, ruling eastern UP and western Bihar. Key kings: Isanavarman, Sarvavarman, Avantivarman, Grahavarman. Grahavarman married Rajyashri, Harsha's sister — when Grahavarman was killed by the Malwa (Later Gupta) king Devagupta (who was allied with Shashanka of Gauda), Harsha's family intervened; Rajyavardhana was killed by Shashanka, bringing Harsha to the throne. The Maukhari-Vardhana union under Harsha effectively merged Thanesar and Kanauj.

hist_bhaskaravarman.label: Bhaskaravarman
hist_bhaskaravarman.subject: history
hist_bhaskaravarman.detail: Varman dynasty king of Kamarupa (Assam), reigned c. 600-650 CE. Long-time ally of Harshavardhana against Shashanka of Gauda; after Shashanka's death, Bhaskaravarman and Harsha partitioned Gauda. Attended the Kanauj assembly convened by Harsha. Xuanzang visited his court — he is depicted receiving the pilgrim, and is said to have given him a map of Kamarupa.

hist_valabhi.label: Valabhi
hist_valabhi.subject: history
hist_valabhi.detail: Port city and capital of the Maitraka dynasty (c. 475-776 CE) in Saurashtra (Gujarat), emerging after Skandagupta's death. Major Buddhist and Jain learning centre — Valabhi University rivalled Nalanda; Xuanzang and Yijing both visited. Site of the final redaction of the Jain Shvetambara canon (6th century CE council). Rich sea-trade port. Destroyed c. 775 CE by Arab raids.

hist_bharhut_stupa.label: Bharhut Stupa
hist_bharhut_stupa.subject: history
hist_bharhut_stupa.detail: Early Buddhist stupa at Bharhut, Madhya Pradesh, built 3rd-2nd century BCE (Mauryan original, Shunga-era toranas and railings added c. 150-100 BCE). The earliest fully-sculpted Indian Buddhist narrative art — stone railings (vedika) and gateway (torana) carved with Jataka stories, life of Buddha (depicted aniconically via wheel, tree, footprints), yaksha and yakshi figures (Chulakoka, Sudarshana Yakshini), and labels in Prakrit-Brahmi.
