Dome destroyed; sculptures removed to the Indian Museum, Kolkata in 1874 by Alexander Cunningham. Transitional style between Mauryan imperial art and the more fluid Sanchi-Amaravati tradition.

hist_udayagiri_caves_mp.label: Udayagiri Caves (Madhya Pradesh)
hist_udayagiri_caves_mp.subject: history
hist_udayagiri_caves_mp.detail: Group of 20 rock-cut Hindu/Jain caves near Vidisha in MP, c. 400-500 CE, under Chandragupta II and Kumaragupta I — the earliest surviving monumental Hindu cave temples. Inscribed dates (Gupta Era 82 = 401 CE). Most famous: Cave 5 with a colossal Varaha (Boar avatar of Vishnu) relief rescuing the Earth goddess — allegory of Gupta empire rescuing India from chaos. Cave 6 has inscription of Chandragupta II. First sustained Hindu reception of the Buddhist rock-cut tradition.

hist_sarnath_buddha_gupta.label: Sarnath Buddha (Gupta)
hist_sarnath_buddha_gupta.subject: history
hist_sarnath_buddha_gupta.detail: Iconic seated Buddha image preaching the First Sermon (Dharmachakrapravartana mudra), c. 475 CE, from Sarnath. Chunar sandstone, perfect Gupta polish. Exemplifies the Sarnath school of Gupta sculpture — simplified, serene, transparent drapery without the heavy folds of Mathura, close-cropped curled hair, dharmachakra on the pedestal with flanking deer (Deer Park). Considered the archetype of the classical Indian Buddha and influenced all later Buddha iconography in Asia.

hist_mahabodhi_temple.label: Mahabodhi Temple
hist_mahabodhi_temple.subject: history
hist_mahabodhi_temple.detail: Buddhist temple at Bodh Gaya (Bihar) marking the spot of Buddha's enlightenment. Original vihara by Ashoka (3rd century BCE); present brick temple tower (~55 m) is Gupta-era (c. 5th-6th CE), extensively restored by Burmese Buddhists in 1880s and by Alexander Cunningham. Distinctive stepped-pyramid shikhara (unusual for India), panchayatana scheme (4 corner-spires), and the Vajrasana (diamond throne) marking the enlightenment spot. The Bodhi Tree beside it is descended from cuttings of the original tree (via Sri Lanka). UNESCO WHS 2002.

hist_mauryan_polish.label: Mauryan Polish
hist_mauryan_polish.subject: history
hist_mauryan_polish.detail: Distinctive mirror-like lustrous finish achieved on Mauryan-era stone sculpture (Ashokan pillars, Didarganj Yakshi, Barabar cave interiors), so shiny that early British observers initially thought the pillars were metal. Technique unknown to modern restorers; possibly achieved by prolonged rubbing with fine abrasives and oils on Chunar buff-sandstone. Unique to the Mauryan period; disappeared after 185 BCE. Together with the animal capitals and the imperial scale, the defining feature of Mauryan court art.

hist_ajivikas_barabar.label: Ajivika Sect
hist_ajivikas_barabar.subject: history
hist_ajivikas_barabar.detail: Heterodox ascetic sect contemporary with Jainism and Buddhism, founded by Makkhali Gosala (Sharma: Maskarin Goshala), a rival of Mahavira in Magadha. Denied free will — taught absolute determinism (niyati / fate); a soul passes through a fixed series of rebirths regardless of karma. Bindusara and Ashoka's grandson Dasharatha patronised them — dedicated the Barabar and Nagarjuni cave groups. Survived in south India (Karnataka, Tamil Nadu) into early medieval times but died out eventually. Our knowledge is mostly from Jain/Buddhist polemical texts.

hist_chalukyas.label: Chalukya Dynasty
hist_chalukyas.subject: history
hist_chalukyas.detail: Centred around the Raichur Doab between Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers. Capital at Aihole, an important trading and religious centre. Frequently clashed with Pallavas. Best-known ruler was Pulakeshin II. [UPINDER:] Pulakeshin I founded Vatapi (Badami); Kirtivarman I fought the Kadambas. Pulakeshin II (610-642) defeated Harshavardhana on the Narmada, captured Pishtapura, laid the foundation of the Aihole inscription (Ravikirti, 634). Killed by Pallava Narasimhavarman I who captured Badami. Revived but overwhelmed by the Rashtrakutas in the mid-8c.

hist_pandyas_madurai.label: Pandya Dynasty (Madurai)
hist_pandyas_madurai.subject: history
hist_pandyas_madurai.detail: Tamil dynasty of the far south based at Madurai. Kadungon (560-590) and Maravarman Avanishulamani (590-620) revived Pandya power by ending Kalabhra rule. Rajasimha I (735-765) bore the epithet Pallavabhanjana (breaker of Pallavas). Completely overpowered by the Cholas in the 10th century.

hist_alvars.label: Alvars
hist_alvars.subject: history
hist_alvars.detail: Earliest bhakti movement from c. sixth century CE in Tamil Nadu. 12 Alvars ('immersed in devotion to Vishnu') travelled singing hymns in Tamil. Compositions compiled as Nalayira Divyaprabandham ('Four Thousand Sacred Compositions'), described as Tamil Veda. Included woman saint Andal.

hist_nayanars.label: Nayanars
hist_nayanars.subject: history
hist_nayanars.detail: Devotees of Shiva in Tamil Nadu from c. sixth century. 63 Nayanars travelled singing Tamil hymns. Poems of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar form the Tevaram. Strongly opposed Buddhism and Jainism. Supported by Chola rulers who built magnificent Shiva temples.

hist_karaikkal_ammaiyar.label: Karaikkal Ammaiyar
hist_karaikkal_ammaiyar.subject: history
hist_karaikkal_ammaiyar.detail: Woman Nayanar devotee of Shiva who adopted extreme asceticism. Her compositions preserved in the Nayanar tradition. Depicted herself as a demoness (pey) with protruding eyes and shrunken stomach, presenting a deliberate contrast to traditional notions of feminine beauty.

hist_chahamanas_chauhans.label: Chahamanas/Chauhans of Shakambhari
hist_chahamanas_chauhans.subject: history
hist_chahamanas_chauhans.detail: Rajput dynasty of Shakambhari (Sambhar), initially subordinate to the Pratiharas. Claimed Agnikula origin. Vigraharaja IV conquered Delhi from the Tomaras in the mid-12th century. Dynasty reached peak under Prithviraja III before defeat by Muhammad Ghori in 1192.

hist_mahendravarman_i.label: Mahendravarman I
hist_mahendravarman_i.subject: history
hist_mahendravarman_i.detail: Pallava king (590-630 CE), son of Simhavishnu. Accomplished poet-playwright, author of the Sanskrit farce Mattavilasa Prahasana. Patron of early Pallava cave architecture. His reign saw the start of the Pallava-Chalukya conflict.

hist_badami_caves.label: Badami Cave Temples
hist_badami_caves.subject: history
hist_badami_caves.detail: Four rock-cut caves carved into red sandstone hills at Vatapi (Badami), capital of the Early Western Chalukyas. Cave 1 Shaiva, Caves 2-3 Vaishnava (with huge Vishnu avatara reliefs), Cave 4 Jain. Distinguished mithuna (amorous couple) bracket figures in Cave 3.

hist_brahmadeya.label: Brahmadeya
hist_brahmadeya.subject: history
hist_brahmadeya.detail: Land gifted to Brahmanas, leading to Brahmana settlements in the Kaveri valley and south India. Each brahmadeya was managed by a sabha of prominent Brahmana landholders whose decisions were inscribed.

hist_karkota_kashmir.label: Karkota Dynasty of Kashmir
hist_karkota_kashmir.subject: history
hist_karkota_kashmir.detail: Kashmir dynasty established in early 8th century. Lalitaditya Muktapida (c. 724-760) the most powerful ruler -- defeated Yashovarman of Kanauj and launched military campaigns from Sindh to the Himalayas. Patron of the Martand Sun Temple. Dynasty ended 855-56 CE.

hist_devi_mahatmya.label: Devi-Mahatmya (Durga-Saptashati)
hist_devi_mahatmya.subject: history
hist_devi_mahatmya.detail: 700-verse composition inserted into the Markandeya Purana around the 7c. Narrates the goddess exploits, especially her slaying of the buffalo-demon Mahisha (Mahishasura-mardini). Declares local goddesses as manifestations of the one great Devi. Foundational text of the Shakta tradition.

hist_badami_murals.label: Badami Cave Temple Murals
hist_badami_murals.subject: history
hist_badami_murals.detail: Among the earliest surviving Hindu paintings, belonging to 6-7c Chalukya patronage. Although partially lost, the surviving murals in the Badami caves (especially Cave 3) depict Chalukyan kings, Jain saints giving up worldly life, Shiva and Parvati, Puranic events, and a beautiful four-armed Brahma on his swan. Stylistically resemble the Ajanta and Bagh tradition.

hist_aihole_inscription.label: Aihole Inscription of Pulakeshin II
hist_aihole_inscription.subject: history
hist_aihole_inscription.detail: 19-line Sanskrit prashasti by the Jain poet Ravikirti at the Meguti temple, Aihole, dated Shaka 556 (634-35 CE). Eulogises Chalukya Pulakeshin II; records his defeat of Harshavardhana at the Narmada, victories over Latas, Malavas, Gurjaras, and his siege of Vanavasi. Major early medieval political document.

hist_appar.label: Appar (Tirunavukkarasar)
hist_appar.subject: history
hist_appar.detail: One of the three muvar (supreme Nayanmar saints). Originally a Jain, he converted to Shaivism. Many of his hymns appear in the Tevaram. Emphasised personal devotion over ritualism, caste, and ceremonial purity.

hist_aihole_temples.label: Aihole Temple Complex
hist_aihole_temples.subject: history
hist_aihole_temples.detail: Early Chalukya temple site (Bagalkot, Karnataka), a laboratory of experimental temple forms. The Meguti Jaina temple (built by Ravikirti) carries the famous Aihole inscription of Pulakeshin II. Other temples include the apsidal Durga temple and the pillared Lad Khan temple.

hist_narasimhavarman_i_mahamalla.label: Narasimhavarman I Mahamalla
hist_narasimhavarman_i_mahamalla.subject: history
hist_narasimhavarman_i_mahamalla.detail: Pallava king (630-668 CE) who avenged his father by invading the Chalukya kingdom and capturing Badami. Also defeated the Cholas, Cheras, and Kalabhras. Sent two naval expeditions to help Sri Lankan prince Manavarma. Built the port of Mamallapuram and its five rathas.

hist_mamallapuram_rathas.label: Pancha Rathas, Mamallapuram
hist_mamallapuram_rathas.subject: history
hist_mamallapuram_rathas.detail: Five monolithic rock-cut temples at Mamallapuram named after the Pandavas and Draupadi, carved during the reign of Narasimhavarman I Mahamalla. Each ratha experiments with a different plan and roof form. Also site of the Descent of the Ganga or Arjuna Penance open-air relief. [SINGHANIA:] Dharmaraja ratha (largest, square plan, terraced pyramidal tower) + Bhima ratha (longitudinal, barrel-vaulted roof) + Arjuna ratha (incomplete) + Draupadi ratha (smallest, hut-shaped curvilinear roof) + Nakula-Sahadeva ratha. Part of the UNESCO Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram (1984). Also the Descent of the Ganges (Arjuna Penance) open-air relief.

hist_pallava_temple_stages.label: Four Stages of Pallava Temple Architecture
hist_pallava_temple_stages.subject: history
hist_pallava_temple_stages.detail: Pallava temple development progressed through four dynastic stages. 1) Mahendra group (c. 600-630): rock-cut mandapa shrines under Mahendravarman I. 2) Narasimha group (c. 630-668): rock-cut + monolithic rathas under Narasimhavarman I Mahamalla (Pancha Rathas). 3) Rajsimha group (c. 700-728): structural stone temples under Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha (Shore Temple, Kailashanatha Kanchipuram). 4) Nandivarman group (late Pallava): smaller shrines transitional to the Dravida style that matured under the Cholas.

hist_sambandar.label: Tirugnana Sambandar
hist_sambandar.subject: history
hist_sambandar.detail: One of the muvar Nayanmars. A child-saint and Brahmana who wrote songs in praise of Shiva from the age of three. His hymns form part of the Tevaram.

hist_rajputs.label: Rajputs
hist_rajputs.subject: history
hist_rajputs.detail: Name derived from Rajaputra (son of a ruler). Between 8th-14th centuries applied to warriors claiming Kshatriya status. Included rulers, chieftains, soldiers and commanders. Known for chivalric code of valour and loyalty.

hist_islam_arrival.label: Arrival of Islam in India
hist_islam_arrival.subject: history
hist_islam_arrival.detail: Merchants and migrants brought Quran's teachings to India in the 7th century. Muslims included Shia (Ali's authority) and Sunni (early Khalifas' authority). Different schools of law: Hanafi and Shafi'i in India.

hist_gurjara_pratiharas.label: Gurjara-Pratihara Dynasty
hist_gurjara_pratiharas.subject: history
hist_gurjara_pratiharas.detail: Ruled over Gujarat and Rajasthan. Originally Brahmanas who took to arms. Participated in the tripartite struggle for control of Kanauj. Nagabhata was a notable ruler described in Gwalior prashasti. [UPINDER:] Nagabhata I offered successful resistance to Arab advances in the 8c. Bhoja (c. 836, 46-year reign) is identified with Arab Sulaiman Juzr -- a king of great military power and riches. Rashtrakuta Indra III devastated Kanauj in the early 10c. Wiped off the political map by the Ghaznavids in the early 11c. Powerful successor states: Chahamanas (Rajputana), Chaulukyas (Gujarat), Paramaras (Malwa).

hist_rajput_heroic_tradition.label: Rajput Heroic Tradition
hist_rajput_heroic_tradition.subject: history
hist_rajput_heroic_tradition.detail: From 8th century, Rajput rulers cherished the ideal of the hero choosing death over defeat. Stories recorded in poems and songs by minstrels. Also depicted sati. Strong emotions of loyalty, valour and love. [UPINDER:] The term Rajaputra for specific clans emerged by the 12c. B.D. Chattopadhyaya showed Rajput emergence was part of the wider early medieval phenomenon of lineage-based state proliferation. Agnikula myth (Pratiharas, Chaulukyas, Paramaras, Chahamanas claiming origin from Mount Abu sacrificial fire) is a later construction.

hist_paper_spread.label: Spread of Paper
hist_paper_spread.subject: history
hist_paper_spread.detail: Paper gradually became cheaper and widely available during 700-1750. Used for holy texts, chronicles, letters, judicial records, tax registers. Manuscripts collected by rulers, monasteries and temples.

hist_forest_clearing.label: Forest Clearing and Agriculture
hist_forest_clearing.subject: history
hist_forest_clearing.detail: Gradual clearing of forests and extension of agriculture throughout 700-1750. Forest-dwellers migrated or became peasants. New peasant groups influenced by markets, chieftains, priests and temples.

hist_trabeate_architecture.label: Trabeate (Corbelled) Architecture
hist_trabeate_architecture.subject: history
hist_trabeate_architecture.detail: Style using horizontal beams across vertical columns for roofs, doors and windows. Used from 7th-13th centuries for temples, mosques, tombs and stepped-wells (baolis).

hist_nagara_style.label: Nagara Style (North Indian Temple Architecture)
hist_nagara_style.subject: history
hist_nagara_style.detail: North-Indian temple architectural tradition associated with the land between Himalayas and Vindhyas. Square cruciform plan with curvilinear shikhara topped by an amalaka notched ring stone. Fully developed by 8c. Exemplified at Khajuraho, Bhubaneshwar, Mount Abu. [SINGHANIA:] Three regional sub-schools: Odisha/Kalinga (rekhadeul shikhara + jagmohan), Khajuraho/Chandel (erotic mithuna sculptures + triple chamber), Solanki/Maru-Gurjara (surya-kund step-tank, equinox alignment). Shikhara typology: Latina (curvilinear, most common), Phamsana (sloping broader base), Valabhi (wagon-vaulted rectangular). Vertical wall divisions: triratha > pancharatha > saptaratha > navaratha.

hist_dravida_style.label: Dravida Style (South Indian Temple Architecture)
hist_dravida_style.subject: history
hist_dravida_style.detail: South-Indian temple tradition between the Krishna and Kaveri rivers. Pyramidal shikhara of progressively smaller storeys topped by a stupika dome. Square sanctum set within larger walled enclosure, later marked by towering gopuram gateways. Exemplified at Mamallapuram, Kanchipuram, Tanjavur.

hist_vajrayana_buddhism.label: Vajrayana (Tantric Buddhism)
hist_vajrayana_buddhism.subject: history
hist_vajrayana_buddhism.detail: Tantric Buddhist tradition that ascended in early medieval India. Combined ritual, magic, and meditation; used mantras (especially Om mani padme hum), mandalas, and the vajra-sceptre. Earliest texts: Manjushrimulakalpa, Guhyasamaja (5-6c); Hevajra Tantra advocated the sublimation of sexual energy. Exponents were called Siddhas.

hist_sittanavasal_caves.label: Sittanavasal Cave Paintings
hist_sittanavasal_caves.subject: history
hist_sittanavasal_caves.detail: Rock-cut Jain cave temple 16 km northwest of Pudukkottai (Tamil Nadu), whose murals closely resemble the Ajanta-Bagh tradition. Attributed either to the Pallava Mahendravarman I (early 7c excavation) or Pandya renovation (7c). Paintings on walls, ceiling and pillars depict the Jain Samavasarana (preaching hall) theme: a lotus pond with monks, ducks, swans, fishes, apsaras gathering to hear the Tirthankara.

hist_narasimhavarman_ii_rajasimha.label: Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha
hist_narasimhavarman_ii_rajasimha.subject: history
hist_narasimhavarman_ii_rajasimha.detail: Pallava king (700-728 CE), patron of structural temple architecture after the rock-cut phase. Built the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram and the Kailashanatha (Rajasimheshvara) temple at Kanchipuram, which marked an important stage in the evolution of the Dravida style.

hist_muhammad_bin_kasim.label: Muhammad bin Qasim
hist_muhammad_bin_kasim.subject: history
hist_muhammad_bin_kasim.detail: Young Umayyad general, nephew and son-in-law of Hajjaj (governor of Iraq). Conquered Sindh in 712 CE -- captured Debal, defeated king Dahar at Raor, annexed Alor, Brahmanabad, and Multan. Foundational event for Islam in the Indian subcontinent, recounted in the 13c Persian Chachnama.

hist_arab_conquest_sindh.label: Arab Conquest of Sindh (712)
hist_arab_conquest_sindh.subject: history
hist_arab_conquest_sindh.detail: Muhammad bin Qasim Umayyad expedition captured Debal, defeated king Dahar at the fort of Raor, and annexed Alor, Brahmanabad, and Multan in 712 CE. Recounted in the 13c Persian Chachnama. Arab hold over Sindh remained precarious but the event is the first major Islamic political intrusion into the subcontinent.

hist_kailashanatha_kanchipuram.label: Kailashanatha (Rajasimheshvara) Temple, Kanchipuram
hist_kailashanatha_kanchipuram.subject: history
hist_kailashanatha_kanchipuram.detail: Pallava structural temple built under Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha. Square sanctum within a rectangular enclosure, surrounded by 50+ subsidiary shrines. Early example of the gopura enclosure wall. Important stage in the evolution of the South Indian temple.

hist_gaudapada.label: Gaudapada
hist_gaudapada.subject: history
hist_gaudapada.detail: Early Advaita Vedanta philosopher (7-8c), the parama-guru (grand-teacher) of Shankaracharya. Authored the Mandukyakarika, a verse commentary on the Mandukya Upanishad presenting the earliest formal exposition of non-dualistic Vedanta. Influenced by Madhyamika Buddhist thought.

hist_lalitaditya_muktapida.label: Lalitaditya Muktapida
hist_lalitaditya_muktapida.subject: history
hist_lalitaditya_muktapida.detail: Kashmir Karkota king (c. 724-760 CE) considered the most powerful ruler of his dynasty. Defeated Yashovarman of Kanauj and campaigned from Sindh to the Himalayas. Credited with the Martand Sun Temple at Anantnag.

hist_shore_temple_mamallapuram.label: Shore Temple, Mamallapuram
hist_shore_temple_mamallapuram.subject: history
hist_shore_temple_mamallapuram.detail: Structural temple on the Coromandel coast built under Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha. Three shrines -- two Shiva (one with a Somaskanda relief) and one Vishnu (Anantashayin). Marks the Pallava transition from rock-cut to structural temple building. [SINGHANIA:] Three shrines within a two-tier compound wall studded with images of Nandi bulls. Two shrines are Shiva (one with Somaskanda relief - Shiva with Uma and Skanda); the third houses Anantashayana Vishnu (Vishnu resting on Shesha). The terraced slender shikharas and seaside exposure create the emblematic Pallava structural silhouette.

hist_dantidurga.label: Dantidurga
hist_dantidurga.subject: history
hist_dantidurga.detail: Rashtrakuta king who overthrew his Chalukya overlord in the mid-8c and performed the hiranya-garbha ritual for rebirth as Kshatriya. Ascended the throne in 733 CE, assumed imperial titles, laid the foundations of Rashtrakuta paramountcy in the Deccan.

hist_pattadakal_temples.label: Pattadakal Temple Complex
hist_pattadakal_temples.subject: history
hist_pattadakal_temples.detail: UNESCO World Heritage Site near Badami. Cluster of 9 temples built under the Early Western Chalukyas. The Virupaksha temple (Queen Lokamahadevi, 745, Dravida style) commemorates victory over Pallavas; the Papanatha temple has a Nagara shikhara. Exemplifies fusion of North and South Indian styles.

hist_pala_dynasty.label: Pala Dynasty
hist_pala_dynasty.subject: history
hist_pala_dynasty.detail: Ruled Bengal and participated in the tripartite struggle for Kanauj. Along with Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas, formed the three parties in the long-drawn conflict for the Ganga valley. [UPINDER:] Gopala was elected by the people (per the Khalimpur plate) to rescue them from matsya-nyaya. Dharmapala (770-810) held a grand durbar at Kanauj, founded Vikramashila and Somapuri monasteries. Devapala (810-850) extended the empire Himalayas to Vindhyas, east to west oceans. Active patronage of Buddhism with Tibetan-monk exchanges. Revival under Mahipala I (late 10c).

hist_bengali_language.label: Growth of Bengali Language
hist_bengali_language.subject: history
hist_bengali_language.detail: Bengali is derived from Sanskrit but passed through several stages. Gupta rulers settled Brahmanas in Bengal from 4th century. By 15th century, western Bengal dialect united as literary Bengali. Includes non-Sanskrit words from tribal, Persian and European sources.

hist_mangalakavya.label: Mangalakavya
hist_mangalakavya.subject: history
hist_mangalakavya.detail: Literally 'auspicious poems' in Bengali literature dealing with local deities. Part of the category of Bengali literature indebted to Sanskrit, along with translations of epics and bhakti biographies.

hist_eastern_chalukyas_vengi.label: Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi
hist_eastern_chalukyas_vengi.subject: history
hist_eastern_chalukyas_vengi.detail: Andhra branch of the Chalukya family in the Vengi region, established second half of 8c. Vijayaditya II, III and Bhima I fought recurring wars with the Rashtrakutas. Ultimately conquered by Rajaraja Chola in 999 CE; matrimonial alliance with Cholas produced Kulottunga I, who united the two lineages.

hist_ellora_caves.label: Ellora Caves
hist_ellora_caves.subject: history
hist_ellora_caves.detail: UNESCO World Heritage Site in Aurangabad district, Maharashtra. 34 caves: Buddhist (1-12) at the southern end, Hindu (13-29) in the middle, Jaina (30-34) at the northern end -- a spectacular juxtaposition of three traditions excavated 6-10c. Cave 12 (Tin Thal) is a three-storeyed Buddhist marvel.

hist_tara_cult.label: Tara Cult
hist_tara_cult.subject: history
hist_tara_cult.detail: Female bodhisattva cult that rose to prominence in early medieval Vajrayana. Tara was said to have been born from Avalokiteshvara tears when he beheld the suffering of hell-beings. Many forms: Green Tara, White Tara, Khadiravani Tara, Ugra/Mahachina Tara. In Tantric Buddhism treated as the shakti (energy) of the Buddha.

hist_rashtrakutas.label: Rashtrakuta Dynasty
hist_rashtrakutas.subject: history
hist_rashtrakutas.detail: Initially subordinate to Chalukyas of Karnataka. Chief Dantidurga overthrew his Chalukya overlord in mid-8th century and performed hiranya-garbha ritual for rebirth as Kshatriya. Controlled western Deccan. [UPINDER:] Dantidurga (acc. 733) overthrew his Chalukya overlord and performed the hiranya-garbha ritual. Krishna I commissioned the rock-cut Kailashanatha temple at Ellora. Amoghavarsha (814-878) founded Manyakheta and authored the Kavirajamarga, the earliest Kannada poetics. Rashtrakuta armies defeated the Palas, Pratiharas, Eastern Chalukyas, and Cholas. Paramara sack of Manyakheta (late 10c) signalled the dynasty decline.

hist_gopala_pala.label: Gopala
hist_gopala_pala.subject: history
hist_gopala_pala.detail: Founder of the Pala dynasty. The Khalimpur copper plate of Dharmapala asserts that Gopala was elected by the people to rescue them from matsya-nyaya (chaos) -- a rare early-medieval instance of elective kingship.

hist_krishna_i_rashtrakuta.label: Krishna I
hist_krishna_i_rashtrakuta.subject: history
hist_krishna_i_rashtrakuta.detail: Rashtrakuta king who commissioned the magnificent Kailashanatha temple at Ellora -- a monolithic Shiva temple excavated out of a rocky hillside, marking the apex of rock-cut temple architecture in India.

hist_kailashanatha_ellora.label: Kailashanatha Temple, Ellora
hist_kailashanatha_ellora.subject: history
hist_kailashanatha_ellora.detail: Cave 16 at Ellora -- a monolithic Shiva temple carved top-down out of a single basalt cliff in the late 8c under Rashtrakuta Krishna I. Apex of Indian rock-cut architecture. Dravida-style superstructure with main shrine, Nandi pavilion, subsidiary shrines, and a relief of Ravana shaking Mount Kailasha.

hist_shankaracharya.label: Shankaracharya
hist_shankaracharya.subject: history
hist_shankaracharya.detail: Philosopher-saint born in Kerala, c. eighth century CE. Propounded Advaita (non-dualism) philosophy - Brahman alone is ultimate reality and individual soul is identical with Brahman. Established mathas at Sringeri, Dwarka, Puri and Joshimath. Toured the subcontinent debating scholars. [UPINDER:] Advaita (non-dualistic) Vedanta holds brahman as nirguna (without attributes) -- the sole reality; plurality is maya (illusion) born of avidya. Distinguished conventional from absolute reality (rope-snake analogy). Critics called him a hidden Buddhist. Traditionally credited with founding four mathas (Shringeri, Dwaraka, Puri, Jyotirmath), though these attributions may be later.

hist_dharmapala.label: Dharmapala
hist_dharmapala.subject: history
hist_dharmapala.detail: Pala king (770-810 CE) who conquered large parts of northern India and held a durbar at Kanauj installing his puppet Chakrayudha. Founded the great Buddhist monasteries at Vikramashila (Antichak, Bihar) and Somapuri (Paharpur, Bangladesh). Major patron of Buddhism.

hist_sundarar.label: Sundarar
hist_sundarar.subject: history
hist_sundarar.detail: Last of the muvar Nayanmars. Wrote the Tiruttondar Tokai (c. early 8c), the first list of 62 Nayanmars. His hymns are part of the Tevaram.

hist_vikramashila_monastery.label: Vikramashila Monastery
hist_vikramashila_monastery.subject: history
hist_vikramashila_monastery.detail: Great Buddhist monastic university founded by Pala king Dharmapala (r. 770-810) at Antichak (Bhagalpur district, Bihar). Along with Nalanda, the most important centre of Tantric Buddhist learning in the Pala period. Destroyed by Bakhtiyar Khalji c. 1193.

hist_odantapuri.label: Odantapuri Monastery
hist_odantapuri.subject: history
hist_odantapuri.detail: Pala Buddhist monastery in Bihar, founded by Gopala or Dharmapala. One of the major centres from which the Vajrayana tradition spread to Tibet. Destroyed during the Ghurid invasions.

hist_somapuri_paharpur.label: Somapuri Mahavihara (Paharpur)
hist_somapuri_paharpur.subject: history
hist_somapuri_paharpur.detail: Dharmapala-founded Buddhist monastery in Rajshahi district, Bangladesh (modern Paharpur). UNESCO World Heritage Site. Largest mahavihara south of the Himalayas. Cruciform monument with central stupa around which monastic cells were arranged.

hist_andal.label: Andal
hist_andal.subject: history
hist_andal.detail: Woman Alvar whose compositions are widely sung to this day. Saw herself as beloved of Vishnu. Her verses express love for the deity. One of the most striking features of Tamil bhakti was the presence of women saints who challenged patriarchal norms.

hist_tripartite_struggle.label: Tripartite Struggle for Kanauj
hist_tripartite_struggle.subject: history
hist_tripartite_struggle.detail: Long conflict between Gurjara-Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas and Palas for control over the strategically important city of Kanauj in the Ganga valley. The city was a prized possession for centuries.

hist_manigramam_nanadesi.label: Manigramam and Nanadesi Guilds
hist_manigramam_nanadesi.subject: history
hist_manigramam_nanadesi.detail: Most famous south Indian trading guilds from the 8th century onwards. Traded extensively within the peninsula and with Southeast Asia and China. Organised traders who needed collective protection.

hist_chera_kingdom.label: Chera Kingdom of Mahodayapuram
hist_chera_kingdom.subject: history
hist_chera_kingdom.detail: Established in 9th century in southwestern peninsula (Kerala). Introduced Malayalam language and script in official inscriptions. Drew upon Sanskritic traditions while developing regional identity.

hist_saguna_nirguna.label: Saguna and Nirguna Bhakti
hist_saguna_nirguna.subject: history
hist_saguna_nirguna.detail: Two broad categories of bhakti. Saguna (with attributes): worship of specific deities like Shiva, Vishnu, Devi in anthropomorphic forms. Nirguna (without attributes): worship of abstract formless god, rejecting idol worship. Kabir and Guru Nanak were nirguna saints.

hist_advaita_vedanta.label: Advaita Vedanta
hist_advaita_vedanta.subject: history
hist_advaita_vedanta.detail: Non-dualistic Vedanta philosophy systematised by Shankara in the late 8c. Holds that brahman (pure consciousness, nirguna) is the sole reality; the apparent plurality of the world is due to maya (illusion born of avidya/ignorance). Liberation consists of realising the oneness of atman with brahman. Built on Gaudapada Mandukyakarika.

hist_shaiva_siddhanta.label: Shaiva Siddhanta
hist_shaiva_siddhanta.subject: history
hist_shaiva_siddhanta.detail: Major South Indian Shaiva philosophical school. Authoritative texts include the Agamas and hymns of the Nayanmars. Recognises three eternal principles: Shiva (God), the universe, and souls. Shiva creates the world through his shakti (energy). Accepts Vedic authority via the lens of Shaiva bhakti.

hist_kapalikas_kalamukhas.label: Kapalikas and Kalamukhas
hist_kapalikas_kalamukhas.subject: history
hist_kapalikas_kalamukhas.detail: Two important Tantric Shaiva sects of early medieval India. Kapalikas were ascetics who carried a skull begging-bowl, associated with a mahavrata (great vow) and attributed with human sacrifice, self-mutilation, and cemetery rites. Kalamukhas, offshoot of the Pashupatas, active in Karnataka 11-14c with organised mathas and temple patronage.

hist_shakta_pithas.label: Shakta Pithas
hist_shakta_pithas.subject: history
hist_shakta_pithas.detail: Network of goddess-shrine pilgrimage sites organised around the myth of Sati dismembered body-parts falling across the subcontinent. The Kalika Purana lists 7 pithas; the Kularnava Tantra lists 18; the Kubjika Tantra 42. Eventually expanded to 51 or 108 pithas. Knit together the regional goddess cults into a pan-Indian sacred geography.

hist_tevaram.label: Tevaram
hist_tevaram.subject: history
hist_tevaram.detail: Canonical collection of Nayanar Shaiva devotional hymns, comprising songs of the muvar (Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar). Part of the larger 12-book canon Tirumurai compiled by Nambi Andar Nambi in the early 10c. Still chanted in Tamil Shaiva temples.

hist_ellora_cave_paintings.label: Ellora Cave Paintings
hist_ellora_cave_paintings.subject: history
hist_ellora_cave_paintings.detail: Mural paintings in five Ellora caves, mostly concentrated in the Kailasa temple (Cave 16). Early phase depicts Vishnu and Lakshmi on Garuda borne through clouds; later phase (painted centuries after the cave was carved) shows processions of Shaiva holy men in Gujarati style. Represent continuation of the Ajanta mural tradition into the early medieval Rashtrakuta period.

hist_armamalai_caves.label: Armamalai Cave Paintings
hist_armamalai_caves.subject: history
hist_armamalai_caves.detail: Natural caves in Vellore district, Tamil Nadu, converted into a Jain temple in the 8th century. Walls and ceilings bear colourful paintings depicting the Astathik Palakas (deities protecting the eight corners) and Jaina themes. Unbaked mud structures inside served as resting places for Jain saints.

hist_divya_deshams.label: Divya Deshams
hist_divya_deshams.subject: history
hist_divya_deshams.detail: 108 Vishnu abodes revered by the Alvar saints and enumerated in their hymns. 106 located across the Indian subcontinent, one in the cosmic ocean (Ksheera Sagara), and one in the spiritual realm (Vaikuntha). The sacred network gave the Sri Vaishnava tradition a pan-Indian pilgrimage geography mirroring the Shaiva Paadal Petra Sthalams.

hist_chandellas.label: Chandella Dynasty
hist_chandellas.subject: history
hist_chandellas.detail: Bundelkhand dynasty founded by Nannuka in the first quarter of the 9th century. Initially vassals of the Pratiharas. Dhanga was the first independent Chandella king. Built the Khajuraho temple complex (25+ temples). Defeated by Ghaznavids and later Chauhans.

hist_paramaras.label: Paramara Dynasty (Malwa)
hist_paramaras.subject: history
hist_paramaras.detail: Malwa dynasty with capital at Dhara. Traced origin to Mount Abu Agnikula myth. Munja (c. 985) sacked Rashtrakuta capital Manyakheta and was an accomplished poet-warrior. Bhoja Paramara (1010-1055) most famous scholar-king of the dynasty. Defeated by Chalukya Taila II.

hist_devapala.label: Devapala
hist_devapala.subject: history
hist_devapala.detail: Pala king (810-850 CE), son of Dharmapala. Expanded Pala empire to its greatest extent; inscriptions claim tribute from the Himalayas to the Vindhyas, and from the eastern to the western oceans. Continued royal patronage of Buddhism.

hist_bhoja_pratihara.label: Bhoja I (Mihira Bhoja)
hist_bhoja_pratihara.subject: history
hist_bhoja_pratihara.detail: Gurjara-Pratihara king, grandson of Nagabhata II. Ruled 46 years from Kanauj. After early reverses against Palas and Rashtrakutas, won victories against the Palas with help from Chedi and Guhila feudatories. The 9c Arab merchant Sulaiman refers to him as Juzr, king of great military power and riches.

hist_kalachuris_chedi.label: Kalachuris of Chedi
hist_kalachuris_chedi.subject: history
hist_kalachuris_chedi.detail: Central Indian dynasty with capital at Tripuri (near Jabalpur), ruling the Dahala-mandala. Kokkala I (845+) the earliest known king. Patronized poet Rajashekhara. Engaged in conflicts with Pratiharas, Chalukyas of Kalyani, and Paramaras.

hist_chola_empire.label: Chola Empire
hist_chola_empire.subject: history
hist_chola_empire.detail: Rose from minor chieftains to a major empire. Vijayalaya captured the Kaveri delta from Muttaraiyar in mid-9th century. Rajaraja I and Rajendra I expanded greatly, developing a navy for overseas expeditions. [UPINDER:] Vijayalaya captured Tanjavur from the Muttaraiyar chieftains in mid-9c. Aditya I ended Pallavas in 893. Parantaka I took Madurai. Rashtrakuta Krishna III defeated Cholas at Takkolam (949). Rajaraja I conducted a great land survey and reorganised the empire into valanadus. Rajendra I 1025 Sri Vijaya expedition and Chola tribute-missions to Song China (1015-1077) established a Chola thalassocracy.

hist_amoghavarsha.label: Amoghavarsha I
hist_amoghavarsha.subject: history
hist_amoghavarsha.detail: Rashtrakuta king (814-878 CE), scholar and patron of literature. Established a new capital at Manyakheta (Malkhed). Authored the Kavirajamarga, the earliest extant Kannada work on poetics. His long reign marked a cultural highpoint for the Rashtrakutas.

hist_manikkavachakar.label: Manikkavachakar
hist_manikkavachakar.subject: history
hist_manikkavachakar.detail: 9c Shaiva saint-poet (not among the 63 Nayanmars but ranked alongside the muvar). Minister at the Pandya court who renounced office. Authored the Tiruvachakam and Tirukkovaiyar -- celebrated for the metaphor of the devotee melting before the Lord.

hist_nammalvar.label: Nammalvar
hist_nammalvar.subject: history
hist_nammalvar.detail: Chief of the twelve Alvars and considered supreme among Vaishnava saints. Authored the Tiruvaymoli, considered the Tamil equivalent of the Sama Veda. His poems use akam (interior/love) conventions to express devotee-deity intimacy.

hist_anjuvannam.label: Anjuvannam
hist_anjuvannam.subject: history
hist_anjuvannam.detail: Association of foreign merchants (Arab, Jewish, Christian) active on the Kerala coast from the 9c. Expanded its operations to other areas. Alongside the Manigramam, among the corporate bodies of traders documented in Chola-period Tamil inscriptions.

hist_kashmir_shaivism.label: Kashmir Shaivism (Trika)
hist_kashmir_shaivism.subject: history
hist_kashmir_shaivism.detail: Non-dualistic Shaiva school. Atman and universe are identical with Shiva, who manifests the universe through his creative power (compared to a reflection in a mirror). Shakti is the feminine aspect of God. Shivasutras revealed to the sage Vasugupta (8-9c); elaborated by Kallata, Somananda, Utpala, and culminating in Abhinavagupta.

hist_kavirajamarga.label: Kavirajamarga
hist_kavirajamarga.subject: history
hist_kavirajamarga.detail: Earliest extant Kannada work on poetics, attributed to Rashtrakuta king Amoghavarsha. Lays the foundation of literary Kannada. Represents the emergence of Deccan vernaculars into formal literary production.

hist_mandapikas.label: Mandapikas (Trade Exchange Centres)
hist_mandapikas.subject: history
hist_mandapikas.detail: Local exchange centres intermediate between small periodic markets (hatta, hattika) and larger trade centres (pattana). Integrated into rural hinterlands. Key nodes in the monetised rural economy of early medieval India. Analogous to penthas in the Deccan and nagarams further south.

hist_utpala_kashmir.label: Utpala Dynasty of Kashmir
hist_utpala_kashmir.subject: history
hist_utpala_kashmir.detail: Kashmir dynasty founded by Avantivarman (855-883), credited with major irrigation works controlling Wular lake floods. Shankaravarman led campaigns into Punjab and Gujarat. Later years marked by rise of soldier-bodies (Tantrins, Ekangas) and landed Damara chiefs.

hist_chola_administration.label: Chola Administration
hist_chola_administration.subject: history
hist_chola_administration.detail: Villages (ur) formed larger units called nadu. Village councils and nadu handled justice and taxes. Brahmadeya lands managed by sabha. Uttaramerur inscription details sabha election by lottery.

hist_bhagavata_purana.label: Bhagavata Purana
hist_bhagavata_purana.subject: history
hist_bhagavata_purana.detail: One of the best-known Puranas, incorporating ideas of Tamil Vaishnava bhaktas into Sanskritic tradition. Composed c. 10th century CE. Central text for Krishna worship. Describes childhood and youth of Krishna in Vrindavan. Influenced bhakti movements across India.

hist_chola_temple_patronage.label: Chola Temple Patronage
hist_chola_temple_patronage.subject: history
hist_chola_temple_patronage.detail: Powerful Chola rulers (9th-13th centuries) supported Brahmanical and bhakti traditions. Built magnificent Shiva temples at Chidambaram, Thanjavur (Brihadishvara) and Gangaikondacholapuram. Introduced singing of Tamil Shaiva hymns (Tevaram) in temples. Consecrated metal images of Nayanar saints. [UPINDER:] Donative inscriptions at Tirupati: 11 Pallava-period, 31 Chola-period. Temples leased land out to tenants with fixed rice-rents. Devadana lands and tax exemptions. Merchant guilds (Manigramam, Ayyavole) made donations; artisan groups like the weavers of Kanchipuram were sometimes given temple management roles (Madras Museum plates of Uttama Chola).

hist_temple_towns.label: Temple Towns
hist_temple_towns.subject: history
hist_temple_towns.detail: Pattern of urbanisation where temples were central to economy and society. Rulers endowed temples with land and money. Pilgrims made donations. Temple authorities financed trade and banking.

hist_vishwakarma_community.label: Panchalas/Vishwakarma Community
hist_vishwakarma_community.subject: history
hist_vishwakarma_community.detail: Community of goldsmiths, bronzesmiths, blacksmiths, masons and carpenters essential for temple building. Also built palaces, tanks and reservoirs. Example of craft specialisation in medieval towns.

hist_ayyavole_guild.label: Ayyavole (Ainnurruvar) Merchant Guild
hist_ayyavole_guild.subject: history
hist_ayyavole_guild.detail: Powerful supra-regional merchant guild also called the Five Hundred of Aihole. Originally based in Aihole (Karnataka), operated across Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, southern Andhra Pradesh, and parts of Kerala. Inscriptions have been found as far afield as Sumatra (1088 Loboe Toewa) and Sri Lanka (Padaviya). Governed by the bananju-dharma code.

hist_nadu_assembly.label: Nadu and Nattar
hist_nadu_assembly.subject: history
hist_nadu_assembly.detail: The nadu was the key locality unit in early medieval South India consisting of several settlements, larger than a village but smaller than a district. Members of its assembly, the nattar, were influential landowners who handled revenue assessment, tax collection, irrigation management, and donations to temples. Subbarayalu counted 140 nadus in the Cholamandalam area.

hist_kayastha_caste.label: Emergence of Kayastha Caste
hist_kayastha_caste.subject: history
hist_kayastha_caste.detail: The kayasthas (scribes) transformed from an occupational group into a caste during the early medieval period. Their consolidation was driven by the massive growth in land-grant record-keeping, which made literate administrators invaluable. The karana group (professional scribes) underwent parallel caste-formation.

hist_sahajayana.label: Sahajayana
hist_sahajayana.subject: history
hist_sahajayana.detail: Buddhist path taught by the mahasiddha Saraha. Rejected rituals, mantras, obtuse philosophy, and image worship. Held that liberation could be attained while enjoying worldly life, through guru-instruction and intuition. Particularly influential in Bengal and influenced later Sahajiya traditions.

hist_chaunsat_yogini_temples.label: Chaunsat Yogini Temples
hist_chaunsat_yogini_temples.subject: history
hist_chaunsat_yogini_temples.detail: Hypaethral (open-roofed) circular temples dedicated to 64 Yoginis, attendants/manifestations of Durga. Major sites: Bheraghat (MP), Khajuraho, Hirapur (Odisha), Ranipur-Jharial (Odisha), Dudhai (Lalitpur). Reflect the Tantric-Shakta worship integrated with the mainstream Devi cult.

hist_nalayira_divya_prabandham.label: Nalayira Divya Prabandham
hist_nalayira_divya_prabandham.subject: history
hist_nalayira_divya_prabandham.detail: 10c compilation by Nathamuni of the four thousand hymns of the twelve Alvars -- the Vaishnava canon of Tamil bhakti. Organised into four sections, it is chanted in Vaishnava temples alongside Vedic recitation.

hist_indian_ocean_trade.label: Early Medieval Indian Ocean Trade Circuits
hist_indian_ocean_trade.subject: history
hist_indian_ocean_trade.detail: K.N. Chaudhuri three-segment model of Indian Ocean trade: (1) Red Sea and Persian Gulf to Gujarat/Malabar, (2) Indian coast to the Indonesian archipelago, (3) Southeast Asia to East Asia. Great emporia at junctions: Aden, Hormuz, Cambay, Calicut, Malacca, Guangzhou, Quanzhou. Principal commodities: silk, porcelain, sandalwood, black pepper.

hist_pala_school_painting.label: Pala School of Painting
hist_pala_school_painting.subject: history
hist_pala_school_painting.detail: Flourished 750-1150 AD in the Pala Buddhist milieu. Palm-leaf and vellum manuscript miniatures with sinuous lines and subdued tones, typically showing lonely single figures of Buddhist and Vajrayana deities. Patronised by Pala rulers and Buddhist monks using strictly non-violent materials (banana/coconut leaves). Leading painters: Dhimman and Vitapala.

hist_odisha_kalinga_school.label: Odisha (Kalinga) School of Architecture
hist_odisha_kalinga_school.subject: history
hist_odisha_kalinga_school.detail: Sub-school of Nagara architecture that flourished under the Kalinga empire in Odisha. Defining features: rekhadeul shikhara (almost vertical roof curving inwards sharply at top), jagmohan (mandapa), square ground plan, boundary walls, lavishly decorated exterior with plain interior, use of iron girders instead of porch pillars. Exemplars: Lingaraja (Bhubaneshwar), Jagannatha Puri, Konark Sun Temple.

hist_shikhara_types.label: Shikhara Types (Nagara Typology)
hist_shikhara_types.subject: history
hist_shikhara_types.detail: Three principal Nagara shikhara forms identified in Shilpashastra texts. Latina/rekha-prasad: square base with walls curving inward to a point (most common, e.g., Khajuraho). Phamsana: broader base, shorter height, straight sloping lines. Valabhi: rectangular base with roof rising into vaulted chambers (wagon-vaulted). The amalak (notched disc) and kalash (spherical finial) top the shikhara.

hist_uttaramerur.label: Uttaramerur Inscription
hist_uttaramerur.subject: history
hist_uttaramerur.detail: Inscription from Chingleput district detailing sabha organisation: separate committees for irrigation, gardens, temples. Members chosen by lottery from palm-leaf tickets. Strict eligibility criteria.

hist_rajashekhara.label: Rajashekhara
hist_rajashekhara.subject: history
hist_rajashekhara.detail: Sanskrit poet and dramatist associated with the Pratihara court of Mahendrapala and Mahipala, and later the Kalachuri court of Yuvaraja. His play Viddhashalabhanjika was staged in Yuvaraja court to celebrate a victory over the Rashtrakutas. Also authored Kavyamimamsa.

hist_chaulukyas_solankis.label: Chaulukyas/Solankis of Gujarat
hist_chaulukyas_solankis.subject: history
hist_chaulukyas_solankis.detail: Gujarat dynasty with capital at Anahilapataka (Anahilavada). Mularaja I (c. 940-995) founded the dynasty. Bhima I built the Modhera Sun Temple; the Vimal Vasahi at Dilwara was a Solanki Jain foundation. Kumarapala was the patron of Jain polymath Hemachandra.

hist_alptagin.label: Alptagin
hist_alptagin.subject: history
hist_alptagin.detail: Turkish slave-commander of the Samanids who rose to become governor of Balkh. Founded the Turkish principality of Ghazni in Afghanistan c. 962 CE, the nucleus of what became the Ghaznavid empire.

hist_al_biruni.label: Al-Biruni
hist_al_biruni.subject: history
hist_al_biruni.detail: Born 973 in Khwarizm (Uzbekistan). Brought to Ghazni by Sultan Mahmud in 1017. Versed in Syriac, Arabic, Persian, Hebrew and Sanskrit. Wrote Kitab-ul-Hind in Arabic covering 80 chapters on Indian religion, philosophy, astronomy, customs. Compared Indian society with other cultures. [UPINDER:] Brought to Ghazni c. 1017 after Mahmud invasion of Khwarizm. Studied Sanskrit and contacted Brahmana scholars in the Punjab (incorporated into the Ghaznavid empire). Kitab-ul-Hind (Tahqiq ma lil-Hind) is an objective ethnographic treatise on Indian religion, philosophy, science, and society -- the finest pre-modern outside account of India.

hist_chalukyas_kalyani.label: Later Western Chalukyas (Kalyani)
hist_chalukyas_kalyani.subject: history
hist_chalukyas_kalyani.detail: Deccan dynasty that overthrew the Rashtrakutas in 973 CE under Taila II. Held sway over Karnataka 973-1189 with capital at Kalyani. Rivalled the Cholas in peninsular India. Their temple architecture represents a high point of the Vesara (Karnata-Dravida) style.

hist_ghaznavid_dynasty.label: Ghaznavid Dynasty
hist_ghaznavid_dynasty.subject: history
hist_ghaznavid_dynasty.detail: Turkish dynasty founded at Ghazni in Afghanistan. Alptagin (slave of the Samanids) established an independent principality, succeeded by his slave/son-in-law Subuktagin (977-997), then Mahmud (997-1030) who launched 17 raids into India. Eclipsed by the Ghurids in the late 12th century.

hist_subuktagin.label: Subuktagin
hist_subuktagin.subject: history
hist_subuktagin.detail: Ghaznavid founder (977-997 CE), Alptagin slave and son-in-law. Consolidated Turkish rule over Ghazni and came into conflict with the Shahiyas of Gandhara and Punjab. Father of Mahmud of Ghazni.

hist_shravana_belagola.label: Shravana Belagola (Gommateshvara)
hist_shravana_belagola.subject: history
hist_shravana_belagola.detail: Jain pilgrimage site in Karnataka. Best known for the 17.5 m monolithic statue of Gommateshvara (Bahubali) carved in 983 CE at the orders of Chamunda Raya, a minister of the Ganga king Rachamalla. The mahamastakabhisheka (head anointment) is performed every 12 years.

hist_rajaraja_i.label: Rajaraja I
hist_rajaraja_i.subject: history
hist_rajaraja_i.detail: Most powerful Chola ruler, became king in 985. Expanded control over most of the southern regions and reorganised the empire's administration. Built the magnificent Rajarajeshvara temple at Thanjavur. [UPINDER:] Destroyed Anuradhapura and set up a Chola province in northern Sri Lanka. Conquered the Maldives. Initiated a massive land survey and revenue assessment from c. 1011 CE. Brihadishvara temple employed 600+ people from villages across the kingdom. Tripurantaka form of Shiva prominent in its iconography -- a political statement of conquest.

hist_munja_paramara.label: Munja (Vakpatiraja II)
hist_munja_paramara.subject: history
hist_munja_paramara.detail: Paramara king, also called Utpala. Sacked Rashtrakuta capital Manyakheta, defeated Kalachuris and Hunas, captured Mount Abu from Chahamanas. Accomplished poet-warrior finally defeated and executed by Chalukya Taila II.

hist_didda.label: Queen Didda
hist_didda.subject: history
hist_didda.detail: Kashmir queen who exercised political power for almost 50 years -- first as queen (reign of Kshemagupta), then as regent for her son Abhimanyu, then ruling in her own right from 980-1003 CE. Succeeded by her nephew Sangramaraja, founder of the Lohara dynasty. Described at length in Rajatarangini.

hist_alchi_tabo_monasteries.label: Alchi and Tabo Monasteries
hist_alchi_tabo_monasteries.subject: history
hist_alchi_tabo_monasteries.detail: Tibetan Buddhist monasteries in Ladakh (Alchi) and Spiti (Tabo), founded under the 10-11c Tibetan king Yeshe-O and the great translator Rinchen Zangpo. Preserve exquisite clay statuary and wall paintings. Represent the western-Himalayan outposts of Vajrayana that survived the collapse of mainland Buddhism.

hist_mahmud_ghazni.label: Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni
hist_mahmud_ghazni.subject: history
hist_mahmud_ghazni.detail: Ghaznavid sultan (r. 997-1030) ruling parts of Central Asia, Iran and north-west India. Raided the subcontinent almost annually, targeting wealthy temples including Somnath. Invaded Khwarizm in 1017 and brought scholars including Al-Biruni to Ghazni; Punjab's incorporation into the Ghaznavid empire enabled Al-Biruni's study of Sanskrit texts through contact with Brahmana scholars. Commissioned the Kitab-ul-Hind.

hist_kandariya_mahadeva.label: Kandariya Mahadeva Temple
hist_kandariya_mahadeva.subject: history
hist_kandariya_mahadeva.detail: Temple dedicated to Shiva at Khajuraho, built in 999 by Chandela king Dhangadeva. Features ornamented gateway, mahamandapa for dances, and garbhagriha. Royal temples with elaborate carved sculptures. [UPINDER:] Part of the Khajuraho temple complex (25+ surviving temples including the Lakshmana (930) and Vishvanatha (1002)). Chandella-patronised. Nagara-style shikhara at its most developed -- multiple urushringas clustered around a central spire. Famous for its erotic mithuna sculptures on outer walls. [SINGHANIA:] Three-chamber plan: garbhagriha (sanctum) + mandapa (assembly hall) + ardha-mandapa (half-hall), with antarala vestibule connecting mandapa to sanctum. Follows panchayatan layout with four subsidiary shrines. Multiple rekha-prasad shikharas cluster around the central spire creating a mountain-range effect. Built on a high platform. Exterior + interior both carved (rare combination).

hist_naths_jogis.label: Naths, Jogis and Siddhas
hist_naths_jogis.subject: history
hist_naths_jogis.detail: Religious leaders in north India who did not function within orthodox Brahmanical framework. Many came from artisanal groups including weavers. Questioned authority of the Vedas. Used languages spoken by ordinary people. Gained ground during emergence of new urban centres.

hist_chola_bronze.label: Chola Bronze Sculptures
hist_chola_bronze.subject: history
hist_chola_bronze.detail: Considered among the finest bronze images in the world. Made using the 'lost wax' technique. Mostly of deities, sometimes devotees. Associated with temple worship and craft centres.

hist_bangla_dome.label: Bangla Dome
hist_bangla_dome.subject: history
hist_bangla_dome.detail: Roof design developed by local rulers in Bengal resembling a thatched hut. Adopted by Mughals in their architecture due to its aesthetic appeal. Example of regional styles influencing imperial architecture.

hist_mahipala_i.label: Mahipala I
hist_mahipala_i.subject: history
hist_mahipala_i.detail: Pala king (c. 988-1038) who revived Pala power in the late 10c-early 11c after the nadir inflicted by the Rashtrakutas and Pratiharas. Represented the last significant Pala renaissance before the late 12c decline.

hist_abhinavagupta.label: Abhinavagupta
hist_abhinavagupta.subject: history
hist_abhinavagupta.detail: Major 10-11c Kashmir Shaiva philosopher, aesthetician, and mystic. His magnum opus Tantraloka systematised the Trika philosophy; his Dhvanyaloka-Lochana and Abhinavabharati (commentary on Natyashastra) shaped Indian aesthetics. Towering figure in Kashmir Shaivism.

hist_vesara_style.label: Vesara Style (Hybrid Deccan Style)
hist_vesara_style.subject: history
hist_vesara_style.detail: Hybrid temple style combining Nagara and Dravida elements, associated with the Deccan area between the Vindhyas and the Krishna. Best exemplified by Later Chalukya and Hoysala temples. Hardy prefers Karnata-Dravida for the Chalukya variant. Vesara literally means mule (hybrid).

hist_khajuraho_complex.label: Khajuraho Temple Complex
hist_khajuraho_complex.subject: history
hist_khajuraho_complex.detail: Group of ~25 surviving Nagara-style temples at Khajuraho (MP) built by the Chandellas between 950-1050 CE. Includes the Lakshmana (930), Vishvanatha (1002), and Kandariya Mahadeva (999) temples -- the Kandariya being the finest Nagara shikhara. Famous for erotic mithuna sculptures.

hist_krishi_parashara.label: Krishi-Parashara
hist_krishi_parashara.subject: history
hist_krishi_parashara.detail: Sanskrit manual on agriculture composed in Bengal between c. 950-1100 CE, ascribed to an author named Parashara. Gives instructions for rice cultivation, weather-forecasting through planetary movements, sowing, transplantation (ropanabidhi), and harvest rituals. Key source on early medieval eastern Indian agrarian practice.

hist_khajuraho_chandel_school.label: Khajuraho (Chandel) School of Architecture
hist_khajuraho_chandel_school.subject: history
hist_khajuraho_chandel_school.detail: Sub-school of Nagara architecture developed by the Chandellas in Bundelkhand. Defining features: both exterior and interior walls lavishly carved (including erotic mithuna sculptures drawing on Kamasutra), three-chambered plan (garbhagriha + mandapa + ardha-mandapa, sometimes with an antarala vestibule), made of sandstone, panchayatan layout with subsidiary shrines also carrying rekha-prasad shikharas, built on high platforms. Kandariya Mahadeva and Lakshmana are canonical examples.

hist_chola_temples.label: Chola Temples
hist_chola_temples.subject: history
hist_chola_temples.detail: Big temples at Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram were architectural marvels. Became nuclei of settlements, centres of craft production, endowed with land. Hub of economic, social and cultural life.

hist_rajarajeshvara_temple.label: Rajarajeshvara Temple at Thanjavur
hist_rajarajeshvara_temple.subject: history
hist_rajarajeshvara_temple.detail: Tallest shikhara among temples of its time. 90-tonne stone at top required an inclined path starting 4km away. Built by Rajaraja Chola. Named after both the king and the god, suggesting divine kingship. [UPINDER:] Vimana ~60m tall -- one of the largest structures of its age. Project took 7-8 years. Revenue from far-flung villages (including in Sri Lanka) assigned to its maintenance. 600+ employees included dancing women, teachers, drummers, tailors, goldsmiths, accountants. Inner ambulatory contains 30 representations of Shiva as Tripurantaka -- programmatically linking Shaiva theology to Chola political conquest.

hist_bhoja_paramara.label: Bhoja Paramara
hist_bhoja_paramara.subject: history
hist_bhoja_paramara.detail: Paramara scholar-king of Dhara (r. c. 1010-1055). Authored treatises on a remarkable range of subjects including architecture (Samaranganasutradhara), poetics (Shringara-Prakasha), yoga, and medicine. Founder of the intellectual Bhoja tradition and the Bhojshala.

hist_rajendra_i.label: Rajendra I
hist_rajendra_i.subject: history
hist_rajendra_i.detail: Son of Rajaraja I who continued expansion policies. Raided the Ganga valley, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asian countries. Developed a navy for these expeditions. Built temple at Gangaikondacholapuram. [UPINDER:] Campaigned to the Ganga valley, Sri Lanka, and in 1025 to Sri Vijaya in the Malay peninsula. Built the new capital Gangaikondacholapuram and a second (unfinished) Brihadishvara temple. Initiated the Cholaganga tank and canal irrigation network. Four tribute missions to the Song emperors between 1015 and 1077.

hist_temple_destruction.label: Temple Destruction in Medieval India
hist_temple_destruction.subject: history
hist_temple_destruction.detail: Not unique to Muslim rulers. Pandyan king looted Buddhist temples in Lanka. Chola Rajendra I seized statues from defeated rulers. Mahmud targeted Somnath. Part of political culture of demonstrating military success.

hist_ramanuja.label: Ramanuja
hist_ramanuja.subject: history
hist_ramanuja.detail: South Indian philosopher born c. 1017 CE. Propounded Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism). Accepted Brahman as ultimate reality but argued individual souls and matter are also real. Made bhakti accessible to all. Influence on later Vaishnavite bhakti movements. [UPINDER:] Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism) -- brahman is saguna, souls (chit) and matter (achit) are real modes of brahman. From the 11c, female devotees acquired a larger participatory role in Shaiva bhakti under his influence. Hagiographies describe him opening temple entry to untouchable devotees. [SINGHANIA:] Wrote Sri Bhasya and Gita Bhasya. Travelled widely, settled in Srirangam. Proposed three paths to salvation: karma, jnana, bhakti. His disciple Ramananda carried the Sri Vaishnava message to northern India, bridging the South Indian bhakti to the later nirguna saints.

hist_sati_practice.label: Sati Practice
hist_sati_practice.subject: history
hist_sati_practice.detail: Self-immolation of widows on husband's funeral pyre. Both Al-Biruni and Ibn Battuta recorded this practice. Bernier also described it. Different travellers offered varying perspectives: some described it as voluntary, others as coerced. Became major issue in colonial-era social reform.

hist_sri_vijaya_expedition.label: Chola Expedition to Sri Vijaya (1025)
hist_sri_vijaya_expedition.subject: history
hist_sri_vijaya_expedition.detail: Naval campaign despatched by Rajendra I in 1025 CE to the Malay peninsula and Indonesian archipelago, targeting the Shrivijaya kingdom which controlled the Straits of Malacca. Represented Chola thalassocratic peak. Motivated by control of Indian Ocean trade rather than simple plunder.

hist_solanki_maru_gurjara_school.label: Solanki / Maru-Gurjara School
hist_solanki_maru_gurjara_school.subject: history
hist_solanki_maru_gurjara_school.detail: Sub-school of Nagara architecture in Gujarat and Rajasthan under the Solankis. Defining features: plain exterior walls, garbhagriha connected to mandapa internally and externally, decorative arched gateways called torans, signature surya-kund step-tanks adjacent to the temple, east-facing alignment so that equinox sunrise strikes the central shrine. Materials: sandstone, black basalt, soft marble. Exemplars: Modhera Sun Temple, Dilwara.

hist_hoysalas.label: Hoysala Dynasty
hist_hoysalas.subject: history
hist_hoysalas.detail: Karnataka dynasty ruling from Dorasamudra (modern Halebid) 1026-1346. Peak under Vishnuvardhana (1108-1142) and Ballala II (1173-1220). Patrons of the Hoysaleshvara temple at Halebid, Chennakeshava at Belur, and Keshava at Somnathpur -- masterpieces of the Vesara style with intricate soapstone carving.

hist_modhera_sun_temple.label: Modhera Sun Temple
hist_modhera_sun_temple.subject: history
hist_modhera_sun_temple.detail: Surya temple built by Solanki Bhima I in Gujarat. Tripartite plan: surya kund (stepwell tank), sabhamandapa, and garbhagriha. Aligned so that the rising equinoctial sun directly strikes the Surya idol. Contemporary with Ghaznavid raids on Somnath. [SINGHANIA:] Solanki / Maru-Gurjara school. Three elements: surya-kund (step-tank with 108 small shrines on its steps) + sabhamandapa (assembly hall with decorative arched torans) + garbhagriha. East-facing so that the equinoctial sunrise strikes the central Surya idol directly. Built in 1026-27 CE by Bhima I.

hist_kitab_ul_hind.label: Kitab-ul-Hind
hist_kitab_ul_hind.subject: history
hist_kitab_ul_hind.detail: Al-Biruni's comprehensive work on India in Arabic, divided into 80 chapters. Each chapter structured: question, Sanskritic description, comparison with other cultures. Relied heavily on Brahmanical texts. Disapproved of caste-based pollution but described the varna system from Brahmanical perspective.

hist_dilwara_temples.label: Dilwara Jain Temples
hist_dilwara_temples.subject: history
hist_dilwara_temples.detail: Cluster of Jain temples at Mount Abu, Rajasthan. Vimal Vasahi (1031, built by Solanki minister Vimal Shah) and Luna Vasahi (1231, built by Vastupala-Tejapala brothers) are the most famous. Renowned for intricate marble carving -- every surface covered with delicate filigree.

hist_rajput_clans.label: Rajput Clans
hist_rajput_clans.subject: history
hist_rajput_clans.detail: New Rajput clans became powerful by 11th-12th centuries from lineages including Hunas, Chandelas and Chalukyas. Some had been tribes earlier. Replaced older rulers in agricultural areas and set example for tribal peoples.

hist_erivirappattanas.label: Erivirappattanas (Chola Protected Mercantile Towns)
hist_erivirappattanas.subject: history
hist_erivirappattanas.detail: Protected mercantile towns actively promoted by Chola kings. State provided armed security; emerged as important nodes in the trade networks of South India. Represent state-backed commerce contradicting the urban decay thesis of Indian feudalism.

hist_senas_bengal.label: Sena Dynasty of Bengal
hist_senas_bengal.subject: history
hist_senas_bengal.detail: Bengal dynasty that succeeded the declining Palas. Vijayasena founded the line; Ballalasena and Lakshmanasena were prominent rulers. Patronised Sanskrit scholarship (Jayadeva Gita Govinda composed at Lakshmanasena court). Lakshmanasena defeated by Bakhtiyar Khalji c. 1204.

hist_imperial_gangas_orissa.label: Imperial Gangas of Orissa
hist_imperial_gangas_orissa.subject: history
hist_imperial_gangas_orissa.detail: Orissa dynasty whose rapid rise in the 10c culminated in the unification of north and south Orissa under Anantavarman Chodaganga (1078-1150). Displaced the Somavamshis in lower Orissa. Anantavarman commissioned the Jagannatha temple at Puri.

hist_anantavarman_chodaganga.label: Anantavarman Chodaganga
hist_anantavarman_chodaganga.subject: history
hist_anantavarman_chodaganga.detail: Imperial Ganga king of Orissa (1078-1150). Unified north and south Orissa by displacing the Somavamshis. Commissioned the Jagannatha temple at Puri, elevating the Purushottama cult to imperial status. His mother and a queen were Chola princesses.

hist_miniature_painting.label: Miniature Painting Traditions
hist_miniature_painting.subject: history
hist_miniature_painting.detail: Small paintings in watercolour on cloth or paper. Earliest on palm leaves for Jaina texts in western India. Mughal style spread to Deccan and Rajput courts (Mewar, Jodhpur, Bundi, Kota, Kishangarh). Basohli and Kangra schools in hills.

hist_lingaraja_bhubaneshwar.label: Lingaraja Temple, Bhubaneshwar
hist_lingaraja_bhubaneshwar.subject: history
hist_lingaraja_bhubaneshwar.detail: Largest Shiva temple at Bhubaneshwar, built over three generations of Somavamshi kings (originally known as the Krittivasa temple). Classic example of the Orissa/Kalinga school of Nagara architecture with a curvilinear shikhara. [SINGHANIA:] Classic Odisha/Kalinga school with rekhadeul shikhara (almost vertical curving sharply inward at top) + jagmohan mandapa. Boundary walls surround the main shrine (unlike standard Nagara). Plain interior contrasts with the lavishly carved exterior walls.

hist_vishishtadvaita.label: Vishishtadvaita
hist_vishishtadvaita.subject: history
hist_vishishtadvaita.detail: Qualified non-dualism propounded by Ramanuja in the late 11c. While brahman is the sole reality, it has attributes (saguna) and the souls (chit) and matter (achit) are real modes of brahman. Opened devotional worship of a personal Vishnu to all castes and expanded bhakti theology.

hist_idangai_valangai.label: Idangai-Valangai (Left/Right Hand Castes)
hist_idangai_valangai.subject: history
hist_idangai_valangai.detail: Supra-caste dichotomy in late early-medieval and medieval South India. Valangai (right-hand) comprised mostly agricultural groups; Idangai (left-hand) comprised artisanal and trading groups. Initially non-antagonistic, became conflictual in later centuries.

hist_agnikula_myth.label: Agnikula Myth
hist_agnikula_myth.subject: history
hist_agnikula_myth.detail: Later-medieval Rajput origin myth -- the four fire-born clans (Pratiharas, Chaulukyas, Paramaras, Chahamanas) emerged from the sacrificial fire of sage Vasishtha on Mount Abu. Absent from early Paramara inscriptions; a later construction legitimising Rajput Kshatriya status.

hist_dakar_khanar_bachan.label: Dakar and Khanar Bachan
hist_dakar_khanar_bachan.subject: history
hist_dakar_khanar_bachan.detail: Earliest surviving Bengali-language works -- collections of short rhyming agricultural and astrological aphorisms. Popular tradition associates Khana with the daughter-in-law of Varahamihira. Still consulted as agricultural manuals in rural Bengal.

hist_apabhramsa_school_painting.label: Apabhramsa School of Painting
hist_apabhramsa_school_painting.subject: history
hist_apabhramsa_school_painting.detail: Western Indian school active 11-15c in Gujarat and Mewar (Rajasthan). Predominantly Jain themes (Kalpasutra, Kalakacharya Katha) with later Vaishnava appropriation introducing Gita Govinda themes. Early works on palm leaf, later on paper. Characterised by fish-shaped bulging eyes, pointed noses, angular faces in three-quarter profile, and stiff ornamented figures.

hist_basavanna.label: Basavanna
hist_basavanna.subject: history
hist_basavanna.detail: Founder of the Lingayat/Virashaiva movement (1106-68). Initially a Jaina, became a minister in the Chalukya court. Composed vachanas (sayings) in Kannada questioning ritualism. Followers called Virashaivas (heroes of Shiva) or Lingayats (wearers of the linga).

hist_keshava_belur.label: Chennakeshava Temple, Belur
hist_keshava_belur.subject: history
hist_keshava_belur.detail: Hoysala Vishnu temple commissioned by Vishnuvardhana in 1117 CE. Pillared mandapa cruciform in plan on a matching plinth. Renowned for intricate bracket figures (huntress, musicians, dancers) and madanika sculptures.

hist_vishnuvardhana_hoysala.label: Vishnuvardhana
hist_vishnuvardhana_hoysala.subject: history
hist_vishnuvardhana_hoysala.detail: Hoysala king (1108-1142). Built the Chennakeshava temple at Belur. Originally a Jain, he converted to Vaishnavism under the influence of Ramanuja during the latter exile from Chola country.

hist_hemachandra.label: Hemachandra
hist_hemachandra.subject: history
hist_hemachandra.detail: 12c Jain polymath at the Solanki court (particularly of Kumarapala). Son of a merchant of Dhandhuka. Authored works on grammar (Siddha-Hema-Shabdanushasana), poetics, lexicography, Jain philosophy, and the Dvyashrayakavya -- a historical poem disguised as a grammar treatise.

hist_hoysaleshvara_halebid.label: Hoysaleshvara Temple, Halebid
hist_hoysaleshvara_halebid.subject: history
hist_hoysaleshvara_halebid.detail: Twin-shrine Hoysala Shiva temple at Dorasamudra (Halebid), 12c. Two near-identical shrines with cruciform plan joined by a covered passage, each preceded by a Nandi pavilion. Extraordinarily detailed soapstone carvings. Shikharas are missing.

hist_periyapuranam.label: Periyapuranam
hist_periyapuranam.subject: history
hist_periyapuranam.detail: 12c hagiographical compilation by Sekkilar narrating the lives of the 63 Nayanmars. Forms the 12th and final book of the Shaiva canon Tirumurai. Patronised by Kulottunga II Chola.

hist_bengal_temples.label: Bengal Temple Architecture
hist_bengal_temples.subject: history
hist_bengal_temples.detail: Temple-building from late 15th to 19th century. Modest brick and terracotta temples built by 'low' social groups who prospered under European trade. Dochala (double-roofed) and chauchala (four-roofed) styles from thatched huts.

hist_kalhana.label: Kalhana
hist_kalhana.subject: history
hist_kalhana.detail: 12th-century author who composed Rajatarangini, a long Sanskrit poem containing the history of Kashmir's kings. Unique for using multiple sources and being critical of rulers, unlike prashasti writers.

hist_lingayats.label: Lingayats (Virashaivas)
hist_lingayats.subject: history
hist_lingayats.detail: Twelfth-century Karnataka movement led by Basavanna (1106-68), a Brahmana minister in the Chalukya court. Worship Shiva as linga worn around neck. Challenged caste system and rebirth theory. Bury their dead instead of cremation. Encouraged widow remarriage. Expressed through vachanas in Kannada.

hist_virashaiva_movement.label: Virashaiva (Lingayat) Movement
hist_virashaiva_movement.subject: history
hist_virashaiva_movement.detail: Movement in Karnataka in mid-12th century initiated by Basavanna. Strongly argued for equality, against caste, treatment of women, ritual and idol worship. Vachanas (sayings) are their key texts.

hist_jagannatha_cult.label: Jagannatha Cult at Puri
hist_jagannatha_cult.subject: history
hist_jagannatha_cult.detail: Cult of Jagannatha (lord of the world, a form of Vishnu) at Puri, Orissa. Wooden image made by local tribal people. Temple built by Ganga ruler Anantavarman. Anangabhima III dedicated his kingdom to the deity.

hist_jagannatha_puri_temple.label: Jagannatha Temple, Puri
hist_jagannatha_puri_temple.subject: history
hist_jagannatha_puri_temple.detail: Commissioned by the Imperial Ganga king Anantavarman Chodaganga in the early 12c, reportedly to surpass the Brihadishvara at Tanjavur. Elevated the local Purushottama cult to imperial status; Anangabhima III dedicated his empire to Jagannatha in 1230 CE as the deputy of the god. [SINGHANIA:] Odisha school temple. The kitchen (Anand Bazaar) is reputedly the largest temple kitchen in the world, feeding up to 100,000 pilgrims on festival days. The deities (Jagannatha, Balabhadra, Subhadra) are unique wooden images renewed in the Nabakalebara ceremony every 12-19 years. The Rath Yatra (chariot festival) is among the largest religious processions in India.

hist_pir_cult_bengal.label: Pir Cult in Bengal
hist_pir_cult_bengal.subject: history
hist_pir_cult_bengal.detail: Term pir included Sufi saints, colonisers, deified soldiers, Hindu and Buddhist deities, and animistic spirits. Shrines found everywhere in Bengal. Emerged as settlers sought order in new communities.

hist_ghurid_dynasty.label: Ghurid Dynasty
hist_ghurid_dynasty.subject: history
hist_ghurid_dynasty.detail: Afghan hill state that absorbed Ghazni and launched the decisive Turkish conquest of north India. Muhammad Ghori defeated at Tarain (1191) by Prithviraja III, victorious at second Tarain (1192). His commanders Qutb-ud-din Aibak and Bakhtiyar Khalji laid the groundwork for the Delhi Sultanate.

hist_muhammad_ghori.label: Muizzuddin Muhammad (Muhammad of Ghur)
hist_muhammad_ghori.subject: history
hist_muhammad_ghori.detail: Ghurid ruler (1173-1206) who established Turkish rule in north India. Conquered Multan and Uchch (1175), defeated by Gujarat ruler near Mount Abu (1178), captured Peshawar/Lahore/Sialkot by 1190. Defeated at 1st Tarain (1191) by Prithviraj III; decisive victor at 2nd Tarain (1192). Chandawar (1194) against Jaichandra of Kanauj extended Turkish rule to Ganga valley. Assassinated 1206 by a Muslim fanatic while suppressing the Khokhar rebellion. Political achievements in India greater than Mahmud Ghazni despite Mahmud's larger empire outside India.

hist_jayadeva.label: Jayadeva
hist_jayadeva.subject: history
hist_jayadeva.detail: Late-12c Sanskrit poet at the court of Sena king Lakshmanasena of Bengal. Composed the Gita Govinda, a lyrical Sanskrit poem celebrating the love of Radha and Krishna. Central to the elevation of Radha in Vaishnava devotion.

hist_gita_govinda.label: Gita Govinda
hist_gita_govinda.subject: history
hist_gita_govinda.detail: 12c Sanskrit lyric poem by Jayadeva, court poet of Sena king Lakshmanasena of Bengal. Celebrates the love of Radha and Krishna. Brought Radha into mainstream Vaishnava devotion. Blends high literary quality with powerful eroticism.

hist_caste_system_travellers.label: Caste System (Traveller Accounts)
hist_caste_system_travellers.subject: history
hist_caste_system_travellers.detail: Al-Biruni described the four varnas based on Sanskrit texts, finding parallels in Persian social categories. Disapproved of pollution concept as contrary to nature. Ibn Battuta and Bernier also commented on social stratification. Antyaja ('born outside system') provided labour.

hist_chishti_silsila.label: Chishti Silsila
hist_chishti_silsila.subject: history
hist_chishti_silsila.detail: Most influential Sufi order in medieval India. Full Delhi lineage: Muinuddin Chishti (Ajmer, d.1235) → Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki (Delhi, d.1235) → Baba Farid (Ajodhan/Pakpattan, d.1265) → Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi, d.1325) → Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Dehli (d.1356) → Bandanawaz Gisudaraz (Gulbarga, d.1422). Emphasised austerity, rejection of state patronage, use of sama (music) for devotion, simple living, and engagement with the lower classes and Hindus. After Chiragh-i-Dehli the order dispersed from Delhi to eastern and southern India.

hist_quwwat_al_islam.label: Quwwat al-Islam Mosque
hist_quwwat_al_islam.subject: history
hist_quwwat_al_islam.detail: Congregational mosque of the first city built by the Delhi Sultans. Built in the 1190s, enlarged by Iltutmish and Alauddin Khalji. Associated with the Qutb Minar. Earliest example of Sultanate architecture.

hist_chishti_order.label: Chishti Silsila
hist_chishti_order.subject: history
hist_chishti_order.detail: Most influential Sufi order in India. Lineage: Muinuddin Chishti (Ajmer), Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki (Delhi), Baba Farid (Punjab), Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi), Bandanawaz Gisudaraz (Gulbarga).

hist_sufism.label: Sufism
hist_sufism.subject: history
hist_sufism.detail: Muslim mysticism rejecting outward religiosity, emphasising love and devotion to God and compassion to all. Used methods like zikr, contemplation, sama (singing), raqs (dancing). Organised into silsilas under pirs.

hist_first_second_tarain.label: Battles of Tarain (1191 and 1192)
hist_first_second_tarain.subject: history
hist_first_second_tarain.detail: Two battles near Thanesar between Prithviraja III Chauhan and Muhammad of Ghor. In 1191, Prithviraja defeated the Ghurids. In 1192, Muhammad returned with a larger force and defeated a Rajput confederacy, opening the way for the Turkish conquest of north India and the foundation of the Delhi Sultanate.

hist_nalanda_destruction.label: Destruction of Nalanda
hist_nalanda_destruction.subject: history
hist_nalanda_destruction.detail: The great Buddhist monastic university at Nalanda was sacked by Bakhtiyar Khalji forces c. 1193. The library burned for months, and the monks were killed or scattered. Symbolic end of the Indian Buddhist monastic tradition of which Nalanda had been the intellectual apex for 800+ years.

hist_bakhtiyar_khalji.label: Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji
hist_bakhtiyar_khalji.subject: history
hist_bakhtiyar_khalji.detail: Khalji officer under Muhammad Ghori who conquered Bihar and Bengal (1204). Destroyed Buddhist monasteries of Nalanda and Vikramasila in Bihar raids. Attacked Sena capital Nadia disguised as horse-merchant; Sena ruler Lakshmana Sena fled to Sonargaon. Made Lakhnauti the new Muslim capital of Bengal. Died after disastrous Assam expedition against Magh rulers — stabbed by his own amir while sick and defeated.

hist_sufi_traditions.label: Sufi Traditions
hist_sufi_traditions.subject: history
hist_sufi_traditions.detail: Islamic mystical tradition emphasising love and devotion to God. Arrived in India with Turkish conquest. Major silsilas: Chishti, Suhrawardi, Qadiri, Naqshbandi. Sufis sought direct union with the Divine through zikr (remembrance), sama (music). Hospices (khanqahs) became centres of spiritual life.

hist_five_pillars_islam.label: Five Pillars of Islam
hist_five_pillars_islam.subject: history
hist_five_pillars_islam.detail: Universal practices accepted by all Muslims: shahada (declaration of faith), namaz/salat (five daily prayers), zakat (alms), sawm (fasting during Ramzan), hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca). In India, overlaid with local customs and sectarian practices (Sunni, Shia, Ismaili).

hist_shari_a_law.label: Sharia Law
hist_shari_a_law.subject: history
hist_shari_a_law.detail: Islamic law governing Muslim community based on Quran, hadis (Prophet's traditions), qiyas (reasoning by analogy) and ijma (community consensus). Ulama expected to ensure rulers governed by sharia. In Indian subcontinent, applied flexibly given diverse non-Muslim populations.

hist_dvaita_vedanta.label: Dvaita Vedanta
hist_dvaita_vedanta.subject: history
hist_dvaita_vedanta.detail: Strict dualism expounded by Madhvacharya (1199-1278). Sharply distinguishes God (Vishnu), souls (jivas), and matter as three eternally distinct categories. Roots in late early-medieval Karnataka; crystallised in early 13c. Boundary to era 5.

hist_keshava_somnathpur.label: Keshava Temple, Somnathpur
hist_keshava_somnathpur.subject: history
hist_keshava_somnathpur.detail: Late Hoysala triple-shrine temple (c. 1268). Each of the three shrines enshrines a form of Vishnu: Keshava (main), Venugopala, and Janardhana. Star-shaped plinth following intricate outlines. Represents the zenith of Hoysala temple architecture.

hist_varkari_panth.label: Varkari Panth
hist_varkari_panth.subject: history
hist_varkari_panth.detail: Marathi Vaishnava tradition centred on the worship of Vitthala (Vithoba, a form of Vishnu) at Pandharpur. Founded by the saint-poet Jnaneshwar (1275-1296), carried forward by Namdev, Eknath, Tukaram, Ramdas, and others. Composed abhangas (devotional poems) and conducted annual pilgrimage (wari) to Pandharpur. Core message: equality across caste, rejection of elaborate ritualism, direct bhakti via Vitthala.

hist_jnaneshwar.label: Jnaneshwar (Dnyaneshwar)
hist_jnaneshwar.subject: history
hist_jnaneshwar.detail: Earliest major bhakti saint of Maharashtra (1275-1296), founder of the Varkari Panth. Composed the Dnyaneshwari, a Marathi commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, and Amrutanubhav on yoga and philosophy. A follower of the Nath Yogi tradition, worshipper of Vithoba. His short life is considered a milestone in Marathi literature and regional-language bhakti.
