hist_feudalism.label: Feudalism
hist_feudalism.subject: history
hist_feudalism.detail: Political and economic system that dominated medieval Europe (9th-15th centuries). Based on exchange of land (fiefs) for military service and loyalty. Created a hierarchy from king to lords to vassals to serfs. Decentralised political power across numerous local lords rather than a strong central authority.

hist_three_orders.label: Three Orders of Medieval Society
hist_three_orders.subject: history
hist_three_orders.detail: Medieval European society was divided into three orders: those who pray (clergy), those who fight (nobility), and those who work (peasants). This division was seen as divinely ordained. The clergy provided spiritual guidance, the nobility military protection, and the peasants agricultural labour. This tripartite model justified social inequality.

hist_medieval_clergy.label: Medieval Clergy (First Order)
hist_medieval_clergy.subject: history
hist_medieval_clergy.detail: The first order comprised priests, monks, and bishops who administered the sacraments and maintained spiritual life. The Church was the largest landowner in medieval Europe. Monasteries were centres of learning, agriculture, and charity. The clergy were exempt from taxation and had their own courts.

hist_medieval_nobility.label: Medieval Nobility (Second Order)
hist_medieval_nobility.subject: history
hist_medieval_nobility.detail: The warrior aristocracy who held land (fiefs) from the king in exchange for military service. Lived in castles and followed a code of chivalry. Administered justice in their territories, collected taxes, and maintained armies. Knighthood was the ideal of this class, combining military prowess with courtly behaviour.

hist_medieval_peasants.label: Medieval Peasants (Third Order)
hist_medieval_peasants.subject: history
hist_medieval_peasants.detail: The vast majority of medieval population who worked the land. Included free peasants and serfs (who were bound to the land). Owed labour services (corvee), rent, and a tithe (one-tenth of produce) to the Church. Had limited legal rights and mobility. Their surplus sustained the other two orders.

hist_serfdom.label: Serfdom
hist_serfdom.subject: history
hist_serfdom.detail: A form of unfree labour where peasants (serfs) were bound to the land and subject to the lord's authority. Serfs could not leave the manor without permission, had to work on the lord's demesne, and paid various dues. Not quite slavery -- they had some rights and could not be sold. Declined after the Black Death.

hist_manor_system.label: Manor System
hist_manor_system.subject: history
hist_manor_system.detail: The basic economic unit of feudalism. A manor consisted of the lord's demesne (personal land), peasant holdings, common pastures, and forests. The lord's manor house or castle was the centre. Manors were largely self-sufficient, producing their own food, clothing, and tools. The lord held judicial authority.

hist_catholic_church_medieval.label: Catholic Church in Medieval Europe
hist_catholic_church_medieval.subject: history
hist_catholic_church_medieval.detail: The dominant institution of medieval Europe, headed by the Pope in Rome. Controlled vast lands, wealth, and education. Collected tithes from all Christians. Canon law governed moral and family matters. The Church legitimised the feudal order and provided the only unifying institution across fragmented Europe.

hist_crusades.label: Crusades
hist_crusades.subject: history
hist_crusades.detail: Series of religious wars (1095-1291) launched by European Christians to recapture the Holy Land from Muslims. The First Crusade (1096-99) captured Jerusalem. Though ultimately unsuccessful militarily, the Crusades stimulated trade with the East, cultural exchange, and weakened feudal lords. Pope Urban II launched the First Crusade.

hist_chivalry.label: Chivalry
hist_chivalry.subject: history
hist_chivalry.detail: Code of conduct for medieval knights emphasising bravery, loyalty, honour, courtesy toward women, and protection of the weak. Combined Christian ethics with martial values. Idealised in literature (Arthurian legends, troubadour poetry) though reality often fell short. Tournaments were public displays of chivalric skill.

hist_medieval_towns.label: Rise of Medieval Towns
hist_medieval_towns.subject: history
hist_medieval_towns.detail: From the 11th century, towns grew as trade revived in Europe. Merchants and artisans formed a new social class (burghers/bourgeoisie). Towns obtained charters of self-governance from lords. Guilds regulated trade and crafts. Towns challenged the feudal order by offering freedom to serfs ('town air makes you free').

hist_guilds.label: Guilds
hist_guilds.subject: history
hist_guilds.detail: Associations of merchants or craftsmen that regulated trade, set quality standards, fixed prices, and controlled entry into professions. Organised in a hierarchy of master, journeyman, and apprentice. Provided mutual aid and social welfare. Guilds were powerful in medieval towns and resisted outside competition.

hist_feudal_obligations.label: Feudal Obligations
hist_feudal_obligations.subject: history
hist_feudal_obligations.detail: The reciprocal duties binding lord and vassal. The lord granted a fief (land) and provided protection. The vassal owed military service (typically 40 days per year), counsel, and financial aid on occasions (ransoming the lord, knighting his son, marrying his daughter). Breach of these obligations could lead to forfeiture.

hist_cathedral_building.label: Cathedral Building
hist_cathedral_building.subject: history
hist_cathedral_building.detail: The construction of great Gothic cathedrals (12th-14th centuries) like Notre-Dame de Paris and Chartres. Demonstrated the power and wealth of the Church and civic pride of towns. Featured innovations like pointed arches, flying buttresses, ribbed vaults, and stained glass windows. Took decades or centuries to complete.

hist_fief.label: Fief (Land Grant)
hist_fief.subject: history
hist_fief.detail: A grant of land given by a lord to a vassal in exchange for loyalty and service, primarily military. The fief was the economic foundation of feudalism. It included the land, the peasants on it, and the right to collect dues. Fiefs became hereditary over time, weakening royal control over the nobility.

hist_mongol_empire.label: Mongol Empire
hist_mongol_empire.subject: history
hist_mongol_empire.detail: The largest contiguous land empire in history, founded by Genghis Khan in 1206. At its peak under his grandsons, it stretched from Korea to Hungary and from Siberia to Southeast Asia. United diverse nomadic tribes and connected East and West through trade and communication networks.

hist_genghis_khan.label: Genghis Khan (Chinggis Khan)
hist_genghis_khan.subject: history
hist_genghis_khan.detail: Born Temujin (c. 1162-1227), he unified the Mongol tribes and was proclaimed Genghis Khan ('universal ruler') in 1206. Created a disciplined army organised in decimal units. Conquered northern China, Central Asia, Persia, and parts of Russia. Established the Yasa (legal code) and promoted meritocracy over birth.

hist_mongol_military.label: Mongol Military Organisation
hist_mongol_military.subject: history
hist_mongol_military.detail: Genghis Khan organised his army in decimal units (10, 100, 1000, 10000 or tumen). Soldiers were drawn from different tribes to prevent tribal loyalties. Superb horsemen and archers. Used terror, psychological warfare, siege technology borrowed from China, and rapid mobility. Discipline was enforced through the Yasa.

hist_yasa.label: Yasa (Mongol Law Code)
hist_yasa.subject: history
hist_yasa.detail: Legal code attributed to Genghis Khan that governed the Mongol Empire. Covered military discipline, hunting regulations, trade, taxation, and social conduct. Emphasised loyalty, obedience, and meritocracy. Severe punishments for theft, adultery, and desertion. Remained influential even after the empire fragmented.

hist_nomadic_pastoralism.label: Nomadic Pastoralism
hist_nomadic_pastoralism.subject: history
hist_nomadic_pastoralism.detail: Lifestyle based on herding animals (horses, sheep, goats, cattle) and seasonal migration across grasslands. Steppe nomads lived in portable felt tents (ger/yurt). Economy supplemented by trade with and raiding of settled societies. Nomads developed exceptional military skills through hunting and herding.

hist_mongol_administration.label: Mongol Administration
hist_mongol_administration.subject: history
hist_mongol_administration.detail: Despite their nomadic origins, Mongols developed sophisticated governance. Used census-taking for taxation and military conscription. Employed literate administrators from conquered peoples (Chinese, Persians, Uighurs). Practiced religious tolerance. The postal relay (yam) system enabled rapid communication across the empire.

hist_mongol_religious_tolerance.label: Mongol Religious Tolerance
hist_mongol_religious_tolerance.subject: history
hist_mongol_religious_tolerance.detail: The Mongols initially followed shamanism but were remarkably tolerant of other religions. Genghis Khan's court hosted Buddhists, Christians, Muslims, and Taoists. This tolerance facilitated governance of diverse populations. Different khanates eventually adopted the dominant religion of their region -- Islam in the west, Buddhism in the east.

hist_chinese_printing.label: Chinese Printing Tradition
hist_chinese_printing.subject: history
hist_chinese_printing.detail: China pioneered printing with earliest known book Diamond Sutra (868 AD). Used woodblock printing for textiles, playing cards and paper money. Civil service examinations created huge demand for printed materials.

period_north_india.label: North India (Pratihara → Ghurid conquest)
period_north_india.subject: history
period_north_india.detail: Northern Indian political arena c. 700-1206 CE. Gurjara-Pratiharas dominate from Kanauj (700-1036); Chandellas, Kalachuris, Paramaras, Chahamanas carve out regional kingdoms. Tripartite struggle with Palas and Rashtrakutas for Kanauj. Arab conquest of Sindh (712) begins Islamic contact; Ghaznavid raids from 1000; Ghurid conquest 1192 ends the era.

period_east_pala.label: Eastern India (Pala → Sena)
period_east_pala.subject: history
period_east_pala.detail: Bengal-Bihar under Pala rule (750-1161) and Sena succession (1070-1204). Palas elected by people, founded Vikramashila, Odantapuri, Somapuri monasteries. Mature Bengali language, agricultural manuals (Krishi-Parashara, Dakar-Khanar Bachan). Senas end with Bakhtiyar Khalji invasion c. 1204.

period_deccan.label: Deccan (Chalukya → Rashtrakuta → Hoysala)
period_deccan.subject: history
period_deccan.detail: Deccan peninsula across three successive dynasties: Chalukyas of Badami (543-753), Rashtrakutas of Manyakheta (753-982), Later Chalukyas of Kalyani (973-1189), Hoysalas (1026-1346). Temple masterpieces at Badami, Aihole, Pattadakal, Ellora (Kailashanatha), Halebid, Belur, Somnathpur. Vesara/Karnata-Dravida architectural style matures here.

period_south_chola_pallava.label: Tamil South (Pallava + Chola + Pandya)
period_south_chola_pallava.subject: history
period_south_chola_pallava.detail: Tamil imperial core. Pallavas of Kanchi (575-893) with Mamallapuram; Cholas of Tanjavur (850-1279) at imperial peak under Rajaraja I and Rajendra I. Chola thalassocracy extended to Sri Lanka, Maldives, Sri Vijaya (1025). Nadu-Sabha-Ur village institutions, Brahmadeya, Uttaramerur, Ayyavole and Manigramam merchant guilds. Pandyas at Madurai; Cheras in Kerala.

period_west_solanki_paramara.label: Western India (Solanki + Paramara)
period_west_solanki_paramara.subject: history
period_west_solanki_paramara.detail: Western Indian kingdoms c. 820-1200. Paramaras of Dhara (Malwa) with scholar-king Bhoja; Chaulukyas/Solankis of Anahilapataka (Gujarat) patrons of Dilwara Jain temples and Modhera Sun Temple; Jain polymath Hemachandra. Maru-Gurjara architectural school with signature surya-kund step tanks.

period_frontier_kashmir_orissa.label: Kashmir + Orissa frontier
period_frontier_kashmir_orissa.subject: history
period_frontier_kashmir_orissa.detail: Kashmir and Orissa — peripheral but culturally rich. Kashmir: Karkotas (Lalitaditya), Utpalas (Avantivarman), Lohara (Didda), Kalhana's Rajatarangini, Kashmir Shaivism (Abhinavagupta). Orissa: Shailodbhavas, Bhauma-Karas, Imperial Gangas (Anantavarman Chodaganga) built Jagannatha Puri. Lingaraja temple at Bhubaneshwar.

period_religion_philosophy.label: Bhakti + Philosophy + Religion
period_religion_philosophy.subject: history
period_religion_philosophy.detail: The religious-intellectual spine of the era, cutting across all regions. South Indian bhakti (Alvars, Nayanars, muvar, Manikkavachakar, Nammalvar); Shankara's Advaita, Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita, Madhva's Dvaita; Lingayats (Basavanna); Varkari (Jnaneshwar, 1275+); Sanskrit lyric (Jayadeva's Gita Govinda). Vajrayana Buddhism at Pala monasteries; Shakta cult with Chaunsat Yogini temples and Shakta pithas; Jainism at Shravana Belagola and Dilwara. Sufism arrives at era's end.

period_parallel_medieval_europe.label: Medieval Europe (parallel)
period_parallel_medieval_europe.subject: history
period_parallel_medieval_europe.detail: Medieval European parallel track 800-1150 CE. Feudalism, three orders (clergy + nobility + peasants), serfdom, manor system, fief-grants. Catholic Church dominates; Crusades from 1095; rise of medieval towns and guilds; cathedral-building age.

period_parallel_mongol_eurasia.label: Mongol / Yuan / Ilkhanate (parallel)
period_parallel_mongol_eurasia.subject: history
period_parallel_mongol_eurasia.detail: Parallel: Mongol Eurasia. Chagatai Khanate (Trans-Oxiana), Ilkhanate (Iran), Golden Horde (Russia-steppe), Yuan dynasty (China, Kublai Khan). Pax Mongolica stabilises Silk Road; Marco Polo's 1271 journey. Mongol sack of Baghdad (1258) ends the Abbasid caliphate. Black Death travels Mongol trade routes 1346-48, reshaping Eurasian demography.

hist_khwaja_muinuddin_chishti.label: Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti
hist_khwaja_muinuddin_chishti.subject: history
hist_khwaja_muinuddin_chishti.detail: Founder of the Chishti silsila in India (d. 1235). Arrived in India around 1192, shortly after Prithviraj Chauhan's defeat. Settled in Ajmer (already with a sizeable Muslim population) after initial stays in Lahore and Delhi. Did not write books; fame rose with that of his successors. His dargah at Ajmer attracts devotees of all creeds — a pattern repeated across Chishti dargahs. Mughal emperors from Akbar onwards made pilgrimage to the Ajmer dargah.

hist_suhrawardi_silsila.label: Suhrawardi Silsila
hist_suhrawardi_silsila.subject: history
hist_suhrawardi_silsila.detail: Sufi order active mainly in Punjab, Multan, and Sindh during the Sultanate period. Famous saints: Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan, Shihabuddin Suhrawardi, Hamid-ud-Din Nagori. Unlike Chishtis, Suhrawardis accepted state patronage and held important ecclesiastical posts. Did not believe in extreme poverty or mystic excesses. Entered India at roughly the same time as the Chishtis.

hist_qutbuddin_bakhtiar_kaki.label: Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki
hist_qutbuddin_bakhtiar_kaki.subject: history
hist_qutbuddin_bakhtiar_kaki.detail: Chishti Sufi saint of Delhi (d. 1235), disciple of Muinuddin Chishti. Major preceptor in the Delhi Chishti lineage between Muinuddin and Baba Farid. His dargah in Mehrauli is an important pilgrimage site. Popular debate whether the Qutb Minar is named after him — unlikely, since the tower was originally part of the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque complex and called by that name; the association with Bakhtiyar Kaki is later.

hist_baba_farid.label: Baba Farid (Farid-ud-Din Ganj-i-Shakar)
hist_baba_farid.subject: history
hist_baba_farid.detail: Major Chishti Sufi saint (1173-1265) based at Ajodhan (modern Pakpattan, Pakistani Punjab) and Hansi. Disciple of Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki. Preceptor of Nizamuddin Auliya. Deeply respected in Delhi — crowds thronged on his visits. His verses (in Punjabi) were later included in the Adi Granth of the Sikhs — the only Chishti saint whose words entered Sikh scripture.

hist_maharashtra_saints.label: Maharashtra Saints
hist_maharashtra_saints.subject: history
hist_maharashtra_saints.detail: Maharashtra bhakti saint-poets spanning 13th-17th centuries, centred on Vitthala of Pandharpur (Varkari tradition). Era 5 figures: Jnaneshwar (c.1275-96, Jnaneshwari commentary on Gita in Marathi), Namdev (1270-1350, tailor-poet, travelled to Delhi, verses in Adi Granth), Chokhamela (14th c, Mahar saint), Janabai (14th c, women saint). Later figures — Eknath (1533-99), Tukaram (1608-50), Sakhubai — belong to Mughal era. All focused on Vitthala temple at Pandharpur; rejected ritualism and birth-based social differences.

hist_namadeva.label: Namadeva (Namdev)
hist_namadeva.subject: history
hist_namadeva.detail: Maharashtra bhakti saint (1270-1350). A tailor by trade (some accounts say a bandit before becoming a saint). Composed in Marathi with intense love and devotion to Vitthala of Pandharpur. Travelled widely; is said to have engaged with Sufi saints at Delhi. His verses later included in the Adi Granth of the Sikhs. Pioneer of Marathi bhakti literature alongside Jnaneshwar.

hist_nathpanthis_siddhas.label: Nathpanthis, Siddhas and Yogis
hist_nathpanthis_siddhas.subject: history
hist_nathpanthis_siddhas.detail: Religious groups criticising conventional religion using logical arguments. Advocated renunciation, meditation on formless Ultimate Reality. Used yogasanas, breathing exercises. Many came from artisanal groups including weavers. Questioned authority of the Vedas. Popular among 'low' castes. Gained ground during emergence of new urban centres in the Sultanate period. Influenced Kabir and north Indian nirguna bhakti.

hist_nasiruddin_chiragh_dehli.label: Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Dehli
hist_nasiruddin_chiragh_dehli.subject: history
hist_nasiruddin_chiragh_dehli.detail: Chishti Sufi saint (d. 1356), successor to Nizamuddin Auliya at Delhi. Called 'Chiragh-i-Dehli' (Lamp of Delhi). After his death the Chishtis no longer had a commanding figure at Delhi — as a result Chishti saints dispersed to eastern and southern India, greatly extending the order's reach.

hist_rishi_silsila.label: Rishi Silsilah (Kashmir)
hist_rishi_silsila.subject: history
hist_rishi_silsila.detail: Indigenous Sufi order of Kashmir combining features of Hinduism and Islam. Founded by Sheikh Noor-ud-din Noorani (Nund Rishi, 1377-1440); spiritually rooted in the earlier Shaiva mystic Lalleshwari (Lal Ded, 14th c). Rishis preached in Kashmiri, mingled with Hindu and Muslim devotees, used yogic practices. Promoted religious synthesis in Kashmir during a period of mass conversion.

hist_ramananda.label: Ramananda
hist_ramananda.subject: history
hist_ramananda.detail: North Indian bhakti saint (late 14th-early 15th c), follower of Ramanuja tradition. Substituted Rama for Vishnu as primary object of devotion. Born Prayag (Allahabad), based at Banaras. Taught bhakti to all four varnas; disregarded ban on inter-caste dining. Disciples drawn from all castes: Ravidas (cobbler), Kabir (weaver), Sena (barber), Sadhana (butcher), Pipa (raja), Dhanna (cultivator). Pioneer of north Indian vernacular bhakti.

hist_vallabhacharya.label: Vallabhacharya
hist_vallabhacharya.subject: history
hist_vallabhacharya.detail: Tailang Brahman philosopher-saint (1479-1531) who propounded Shuddhadvaita (pure non-dualism). Founded the Pushtimarga path of Krishna devotion centred on Srinathji at Govardhan. Followers (Vallabha sampradaya) emphasise grace (pushti) over personal effort. Influenced the saint-poets including Surdas, one of his ashtachhap disciples.

hist_chaitanya.label: Chaitanya Mahaprabhu
hist_chaitanya.subject: history
hist_chaitanya.detail: Bengal Vaishnava saint (1486-1534). Born in Nadia (a centre of Vedantic rationalism), initiated into Krishna cult at Gaya at age 22. Popularised kirtan (musical congregational worship) as a mystic path — the outside world 'disappeared by dwelling on God's name'. Toured widely including Vrindavan, where he revived the Krishna cult; spent much of later life at Puri. Called God Hari; god-intoxicated ecstatic devotion. Attracted Hindu and some Muslim followers; close ties with Alauddin Hussain Shah's Bengal court. Gaudiya Vaishnavism traces to him.

hist_dargah_culture.label: Dargah Culture
hist_dargah_culture.subject: history
hist_dargah_culture.detail: Tombs/shrines of Sufi saints became pilgrimage centres attracting people of all faiths. Major dargahs: Ajmer (Muinuddin Chishti), Delhi (Nizamuddin Auliya), Fatehpur Sikri (Salim Chishti). Urs (death anniversary) celebrations drew thousands. Kings often sought blessings of Sufi saints.

hist_guru_nanak.label: Guru Nanak
hist_guru_nanak.subject: history
hist_guru_nanak.detail: Founder of Sikhism (1469-1539). Born at Talwandi (now Nankana Sahib) on the Ravi, in a Khatri family. Trained in Persian for his father's accountancy profession but inclined to mysticism. After a mystic vision forsook the world; toured widely — said to have reached Sri Lanka in the south, Mecca and Medina in the west. Composed hymns sung to the rabab played by his lifelong companion Bhai Mardana. Founded centre at Kartarpur with the langar (common kitchen). Taught nam (worship), dan (charity), isnan (purity). Rejected caste, creed, and gender distinctions. Advocated a middle path — spiritual life combined with householder duties. Appointed Lehna (Guru Angad) as successor. No intention of founding a new religion; his teachings birthed Sikhism.

hist_kabir.label: Kabir
hist_kabir.subject: history
hist_kabir.detail: Major nirguna bhakti saint (c.1398-1448, though dating uncertain). Brought up in a Muslim julaha (weaver) family in Banaras. Disciple of Ramananda. Drew from Nath, Sufi, and Vaishnava traditions. Rejected external worship of both Hinduism and Islam — idol-worship, pilgrimages, bathing in holy rivers, namaz, the authority of the Vedas and Quran. Denounced caste, especially untouchability. Emphasised reform of the individual under a true guru; not a social reformer per se. Verses in sakhis (couplets) and pads (songs); compiled in the Bijak by his followers (Kabir Panthis) and included in the Adi Granth of the Sikhs.

hist_nizamuddin_auliya.label: Nizamuddin Auliya
hist_nizamuddin_auliya.subject: history
hist_nizamuddin_auliya.detail: Greatest Chishti Sufi of Delhi (1238-1325). Preceptor Baba Farid. Emphasized love as basis of relationship with God; stressed compassion and generosity. Adopted yogic breathing exercises so thoroughly that yogis called him a sidh ('perfect'). Used local Hindawi dialect with common people. Practised sama (musical recitation) including Hindi verses to maximise impact. Contemporary of seven sultans (Balban to Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq); famously refused to meet Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq — the 'delhi hunuz dur ast' prophecy. Amir Khusrau was his chief devotee and musical companion. His dargah in Delhi remains a major pilgrimage site; adjacent tombs of Khusrau and Jahanara.

hist_shankaradeva.label: Shankaradeva of Assam
hist_shankaradeva.subject: history
hist_shankaradeva.detail: Late 15th century saint from Assam who emphasised devotion to Vishnu. Composed poems and plays in Assamese. Founded namghars (houses of prayer). Teaching called Eka Sarana Nama Dharma (supreme surrender).

hist_amir_khusrau.label: Amir Khusrau
hist_amir_khusrau.subject: history
hist_amir_khusrau.detail: Born 1252 at Patiali (Etah, UP); d. 1325, buried in the same compound as his pir Nizamuddin Auliya (whom he survived by less than a day). Served seven Delhi sultans including Balban, Kaiqubad, Jalaluddin, Alauddin Khalji, Qutbuddin Mubarak, Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, Muhammad Tughlaq. Called 'tuti-i-hind' (Parrot of India). Took pride in his Indian identity — 'Hindustan is like heaven... Brahmans here are as learned as Aristotle.' Created the sabaq-i-hindi style of Persian poetry. Large Persian output including historical romances. Credited with inventing the sitar (disputed) and introducing Perso-Arabic ragas (aiman, ghora, sanam). Composed the first detailed Persian account of the jauhar at Ranthambhor 1301.

hist_jagirdari_system.label: Jagirdari System
hist_jagirdari_system.subject: history
hist_jagirdari_system.detail: Revenue assignments given to mansabdars as salary. Unlike muqtis, most mansabdars did not reside in or administer jagirs. By Aurangzeb's reign, actual revenue was less than granted sums causing shortages.

hist_arcuate_architecture.label: Arcuate Architecture
hist_arcuate_architecture.subject: history
hist_arcuate_architecture.detail: From the 12th century, arches carried the weight of superstructure above doors and windows. Combined with limestone cement that hardened into concrete, enabling larger and faster construction.

hist_diwan_i_arz.label: Diwan-i-Arz (Military Department)
hist_diwan_i_arz.subject: history
hist_diwan_i_arz.detail: Military department of the Sultanate, headed by the ariz-i-mamalik. Responsible for recruiting, equipping and paying the army (the sultan retained chief command). First established as a separate department under Balban; elaborated by Alauddin Khalji — regular musters, dagh (horse branding), cash salaries (238 tankas/year for a cavalryman).

hist_diwan_i_insha.label: Diwan-i-Insha
hist_diwan_i_insha.subject: history
hist_diwan_i_insha.detail: Sultanate department of state correspondence — formal and confidential communications between the ruler and other sovereigns or subordinate officials. Important office of dabir-i-khas (chief scribe). Persian the standard language.

hist_diwan_i_risalat.label: Diwan-i-Risalat
hist_diwan_i_risalat.subject: history
hist_diwan_i_risalat.detail: Sultanate department dealing with religious matters, pious foundations, stipends for scholars and men of piety. Headed by the chief sadr, usually also the chief qazi. Handled judicial administration; Islamic civil law (sharia) dispensed through qazis across the empire.

hist_jizyah.label: Jizyah
hist_jizyah.subject: history
hist_jizyah.detail: Poll tax on non-Muslims (zimmis) originating from Arab rule. In Delhi Sultanate initially bundled with land revenue (hard to separate since most cultivators were Hindus). Firuz Tughlaq made it a distinct tax and imposed it on Brahmans (previously exempt). Sikandar Lodi re-imposed after some relaxation. Collected on graduated scale by means; women, children, disabled, indigent exempt. Abolished by Akbar 1564; re-imposed by Aurangzeb 1679.

hist_karkhanas.label: Royal Karkhanas
hist_karkhanas.subject: history
hist_karkhanas.detail: Royal workshops and stores of the Sultanate. Manufactured and stocked costly articles for the king and royal household — silk, gold/silver ware, jewelry, robes of honour. Muhammad Tughlaq's karkhanas produced 2,00,000 robes yearly to gift nobles. Firuz Tughlaq established a separate slave department with 1,80,000 slaves, many employed in karkhanas. A model continued under the Mughals on a grander scale.

hist_manipravalam.label: Manipravalam
hist_manipravalam.subject: history
hist_manipravalam.detail: Literally 'diamonds and corals', referring to a mix of Sanskrit and regional language (Malayalam). The 14th-century text Lilatilakam on grammar and poetics was composed in this style.

hist_amara_nayaka_system.label: Amara-Nayaka System
hist_amara_nayaka_system.subject: history
hist_amara_nayaka_system.detail: Major political innovation of Vijayanagara — likely derived from the Delhi Sultanate's iqta system. Military commanders (nayakas, palaiyagars) given territories (amaram) to govern. Collected taxes, retained part for personal use and for maintaining specified foot/horse/elephant forces, and sent fixed tribute/contingent to the king annually. Under Krishnadeva Raya, the central government received only about half the total revenue (12 million pardaos estimate). Nayaks eventually established independent kingdoms (Madurai, Tanjore, Ginjee after Talikota), hastening imperial collapse. Weakened the Chola-era tradition of village self-government.

hist_harihara_bukka.label: Harihara and Bukka
hist_harihara_bukka.subject: history
hist_harihara_bukka.detail: Founders of the Vijayanagara empire in 1336. Legend: feudatories of the Kakatiyas of Warangal, later ministers of the Kampili kingdom in Karnataka. When Muhammad Tughlaq overran Kampili for sheltering a Muslim rebel, they were imprisoned, converted to Islam, and sent back to administer — they then reverted to Hinduism at the guidance of guru Vidyaranya and declared independence. Harihara crowned 1336; Bukka succeeded in 1356 and ruled till 1377. Some modern scholars reject the conversion narrative, seeing them instead as Karnataka nayaks rebelling against Turkish rule. Together they established Vijayanagara as a kind of cooperative brotherly commonwealth.

hist_sangama_dynasty.label: Sangama Dynasty
hist_sangama_dynasty.subject: history
hist_sangama_dynasty.detail: First ruling dynasty of Vijayanagara founded by Harihara and Bukka in 1336. Exercised control until 1485 when supplanted by Saluva military commanders. Built the Hiriya canal drawing water from a dam across the Tungabhadra river.

hist_vidyaranya.label: Vidyaranya
hist_vidyaranya.subject: history
hist_vidyaranya.detail: Hindu sage and guru who (by tradition) re-admitted Harihara and Bukka to Hinduism after their conversion under Muhammad Tughlaq, and blessed the founding of the Vijayanagara empire in 1336. Associated with the Sringeri matha. Historicity of the reconversion narrative is debated.

hist_bahmani_kingdom.label: Bahmani Kingdom
hist_bahmani_kingdom.subject: history
hist_bahmani_kingdom.detail: Deccan sultanate (1347-1518) founded by Hasan Gangu (Alauddin Bahman Shah). Capital Gulbarga, shifted to Bidar under Ahmad Shah I Wali (1424). Rivals of Vijayanagara over Tungabhadra doab, Krishna-Godavari delta, and Konkan. Peak under Firuz Shah Bahmani (1397-1422) and later Mahmud Gawan (minister 1460-81). Split into five successor sultanates — Berar, Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar — after Mahmud Gawan's execution in 1481. Acted as cultural bridge between north and south India.

hist_deccan_sultanates.label: Deccan Sultanates
hist_deccan_sultanates.subject: history
hist_deccan_sultanates.detail: Five successor states of the Bahmani kingdom after Mahmud Gawan's execution 1481 and further fragmentation by 1518: Bijapur (Adil Shahi, Iranian-origin), Ahmadnagar (Nizam Shahi), Golconda (Qutb Shahi), Berar (Imad Shahi, earliest to fall — absorbed by Ahmadnagar 1574), Bidar (Barid Shahi). Allied at Talikota 1565 to defeat Vijayanagara. Absorbed one by one into Mughal empire during 17th century — Berar/Ahmadnagar under Akbar-Shah Jahan, Bijapur and Golconda under Aurangzeb 1686-87. Cultural centres — Bijapur's Gol Gumbaz, Golconda's Charminar, Bidar's architecture. Relations with Vijayanagara not always hostile despite religious differences.

hist_hasan_gangu.label: Hasan Gangu (Alauddin Bahman Shah)
hist_hasan_gangu.subject: history
hist_hasan_gangu.detail: Afghan adventurer who founded the Bahmani kingdom in 1347. Rose in service of a Brahman named Gangu (hence Hasan Gangu). As Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah, he traced descent from the mythical Iranian hero Bahman Shah — though Ferishta relates that 'Bahman' was actually a tribute to his Brahman patron. Capital at Gulbarga.

hist_firuz_shah_bahmani.label: Firuz Shah Bahmani
hist_firuz_shah_bahmani.subject: history
hist_firuz_shah_bahmani.detail: Most remarkable Bahmani sultan (1397-1422). Learned in religious sciences, botany, geometry, logic. Spoke Persian, Arabic, Turkish, Telugu, Kannada, Marathi. Built an observatory near Daulatabad. Patronised scholars from Iran and Iraq — wanted to make the Deccan the cultural centre of India. Inducted Hindus on a large scale — Deccani Brahmans rose to prominence in revenue administration. Developed Chaul and Dabhol as ports. Married daughter of Deva Raya I (1420) with legendary splendour. Defeated by Deva Raya I in 1419; abdicated to his brother Ahmad Shah I.

hist_horse_trade_vijayanagara.label: Horse Trade
hist_horse_trade_vijayanagara.subject: history
hist_horse_trade_vijayanagara.detail: Import of horses from Arabia and Central Asia was crucial for warfare. Initially controlled by Arab traders. Local kudirai chettis (horse merchants) also participated. Portuguese arrived 1498 with superior musket technology, becoming important players in regional politics.

hist_indo_islamic_architecture.label: Indo-Islamic Architecture at Vijayanagara
hist_indo_islamic_architecture.subject: history
hist_indo_islamic_architecture.detail: Vijayanagara rulers borrowed and developed Indo-Islamic techniques: arches and domes on gateways, style introduced by Turkish Sultans. Mosque architecture in urban core resembles Hindu mandapas. Shows cultural interaction despite political rivalry with sultanates.

hist_mahanavami_dibba.label: Mahanavami Dibba
hist_mahanavami_dibba.subject: history
hist_mahanavami_dibba.detail: Massive platform in the royal centre, base of 11,000 sq ft rising to 40 ft. Relief carvings on base. Used for Mahanavami/Dasara/Navaratri festival celebrations including worship, animal sacrifice, wrestling, processions. Kings displayed prestige and received tribute from nayakas.

hist_vijayanagara_fortification.label: Vijayanagara Fortifications
hist_vijayanagara_fortification.subject: history
hist_vijayanagara_fortification.detail: Seven concentric lines of forts noted by Abdur Razzaq. Massive masonry without mortar, using wedge-shaped stone blocks. Unique feature: agricultural tracts enclosed within walls to survive sieges. Second line around urban complex, third around royal centre.

hist_virupaksha_temple.label: Virupaksha Temple
hist_virupaksha_temple.subject: history
hist_virupaksha_temple.detail: Temple in the sacred centre of Hampi, dedicated to a form of Shiva. Priests of this temple provided initial information to Colin Mackenzie. One of the longest-surviving structures, with worship continuing to the present day.

hist_bidar.label: Bidar
hist_bidar.subject: history
hist_bidar.detail: Second capital of the Bahmani kingdom from 1424 under Ahmad Shah I Wali, shifted from Gulbarga after the annexation of Warangal. Bidri metalwork (silver/copper inlay on blackened zinc-copper alloy) originated here — named after the city. Mahmud Gawan's madarasa (1472) is a major monument. Became capital of the independent Bidar sultanate after the Bahmani breakup; later absorbed by Bijapur, then the Mughals.

hist_deva_raya_ii.label: Deva Raya II
hist_deva_raya_ii.subject: history
hist_deva_raya_ii.detail: Vijayanagara ruler (1425-46), considered greatest of the Sangama dynasty. Reorganised army to match Bahmani cavalry strength — enlisted 2000 Muslim cavalrymen with jagirs; ordered Hindu soldiers to learn archery from them. Ferishta records 60,000 Hindu archers, 80,000 cavalry, 2,00,000 infantry. Nicolo Conti (1420) and Abdur Razzaq (1440s) visited during his or his father's reign; both praised Vijayanagara's size and wealth. Succession confusion after his death led to the dynasty change (Saluva).

hist_mahmud_gawan.label: Mahmud Gawan
hist_mahmud_gawan.subject: history
hist_mahmud_gawan.detail: Iranian-born trader who rose to become Peshwa (prime minister) and Malik-ut-Tujjar of the Bahmani kingdom for almost 20 years (d. 1481). Militarily overran western coastal areas including Dabhol and Goa. Internal reforms — divided kingdom into 8 tarafs (provinces) with tarafdars; fixed salaries (1 lakh hun/year for 500 horses); set apart khalisa tracts for sultan; attempted land measurement. Built a three-storey madarasa at Bidar (1472) with tiled walls and free food/clothing for 1000 teachers and students. Executed in 1482 at over 70 — victim of Deccani-Afaqi factional strife.

hist_bijapur_deccan_school.label: Bijapur (Deccan) Architecture School
hist_bijapur_deccan_school.subject: history
hist_bijapur_deccan_school.detail: Adil Shahi Bijapur's provincial style (1489-1686) — developed after Bahmani breakup. Features: 3-arched facade, bulbous dome (almost spherical with narrow neck), cornices, iron clamps + strong mortar giving apparently-unsupported ceilings, rich wall carvings. Spans era 5/6 boundary. Major monument — Gol Gumbaz (mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah, completed 1656, 2nd largest dome in the world, famous whispering gallery) — era 6. Ibrahim Rauza (1627) also noteworthy.

hist_calico.label: Calico
hist_calico.subject: history
hist_calico.detail: Derived from Calicut (Kerala coast) where Portuguese first landed (1498). Became generic European term for Indian cotton textiles in trade.

hist_duarte_barbosa.label: Duarte Barbosa
hist_duarte_barbosa.subject: history
hist_duarte_barbosa.detail: Portuguese writer who provided detailed account of trade and society in south India after 1500. Part of a wave of European travellers including Jesuit Roberto Nobili and French jeweller Jean-Baptiste Tavernier who documented Indian society.

hist_lotus_mahal.label: Lotus Mahal
hist_lotus_mahal.subject: history
hist_lotus_mahal.detail: Beautiful building in the royal centre, named by British travellers. Possibly a council chamber per Mackenzie's map. Combines Hindu and Indo-Islamic architectural elements including arches. Nine towers: one high central tower and eight on sides.

hist_krishnadeva_raya.label: Krishnadeva Raya
hist_krishnadeva_raya.subject: history
hist_krishnadeva_raya.detail: Most famous Vijayanagara ruler (1509-29) of the Tuluva dynasty. Acquired Raichur doab (1512), subdued Orissa (1514), defeated Sultan of Bijapur (1520). Built fine temples and gopurams. Composed Amuktamalyada in Telugu on statecraft. Called 'establisher of the Yavana kingdom'.

hist_domingo_paes.label: Domingo Paes
hist_domingo_paes.subject: history
hist_domingo_paes.detail: Portuguese traveller who visited Vijayanagara in the 16th century during or just after Krishnadeva Raya's reign. Compared the city's size to Rome. Described the royal centre, mahanavami celebrations, water works and gardens in detail.

hist_rama_raja.label: Rama Raja
hist_rama_raja.subject: history
hist_rama_raja.detail: Real power in Vijayanagara under titular ruler Sadashiva Raya (1543-67). Played off the Deccan sultans against each other; concluded a commercial treaty with the Portuguese that stopped horse supply to Bijapur. Defeated Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar in sequence — but this drove them into alliance. The combined army of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda (+ Bidar) inflicted the final defeat at the Battle of Bannihatti (Talikota) in 1565 — Rama Raja was captured and executed on the field.

hist_battle_talikota.label: Battle of Talikota (1565)
hist_battle_talikota.subject: history
hist_battle_talikota.detail: Battle at Rakshasi-Tangadi where combined armies of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and Golconda routed Vijayanagara forces led by Rama Raya. City was sacked and totally abandoned. Empire shifted to Penukonda then Chandragiri under Aravidu dynasty. Rama Raya's policy of playing sultans against each other backfired.

hist_abdur_razzaq.label: Abdur Razzaq Samarqandi
hist_abdur_razzaq.subject: history
hist_abdur_razzaq.detail: Persian diplomat who visited south India in the 1440s. Provided one of the most important descriptions of Vijayanagara in the 15th century. Greatly impressed by the fortifications, noting seven lines of forts encircling the city.

hist_bidri_work.label: Bidri Work
hist_bidri_work.subject: history
hist_bidri_work.detail: Inlay work in copper and silver so famous from Bidar that it was named after the city. Represents the high-quality metalwork craftsmanship of medieval Indian towns.

hist_colin_mackenzie.label: Colin Mackenzie
hist_colin_mackenzie.subject: history
hist_colin_mackenzie.detail: Engineer, surveyor and cartographer who discovered Hampi ruins in 1800. First Surveyor General of India (1815-1821). Prepared first survey map of Vijayanagara based on memories of Virupaksha temple priests and Pampadevi shrine. Collected local histories for colonial governance.

hist_hampi.label: Hampi (Vijayanagara)
hist_hampi.subject: history
hist_hampi.detail: Capital of Vijayanagara Empire founded 1336 in natural basin of Tungabhadra river surrounded by granite hills. Three zones: sacred centre (Virupaksha + Vitthala temples), urban core (markets, mosques, merchant quarters), royal centre (Mahanavami Dibba, Lotus Mahal). Seven lines of fortifications, enclosing even agricultural tracts to survive sieges. Water drawn from Kamalapuram tank and Hiriya canal. Bustled with merchants, festivals (Mahanavami/Dasara). Sacked in 1565 after Battle of Talikota; abandoned. Rediscovered by Colin Mackenzie in 1800.

hist_vijayanagara_empire.label: Vijayanagara Empire
hist_vijayanagara_empire.subject: history
hist_vijayanagara_empire.detail: Founded 1336 by Harihara and Bukka at the guidance of guru Vidyaranya. City Hampi named after mother-goddess Pampadevi. Four dynasties — Sangama (1336-1485), Saluva (1485-1505), Tuluva (1505-1570, Krishnadeva Raya), Aravidu (1570-1646). Also called Karnataka Samrajyamu in contemporary Telugu sources. Reached extreme south of peninsula; major rival of Bahmani over Tungabhadra doab/Krishna-Godavari delta/Konkan. Sacked 1565 after Battle of Rakshasi-Tangadi (Talikota/Bannihatti). Empire shifted to Penukonda and Chandragiri under Aravidu dynasty but never recovered.

hist_prithviraja_iii.label: Prithviraja III (Prithviraj Chauhan)
hist_prithviraja_iii.subject: history
hist_prithviraja_iii.detail: Best-known Chahamana ruler (1168-1192) who controlled Delhi and Ajmer. Defeated Afghan ruler Muhammad Ghori in 1191 at the First Battle of Tarain but lost to him in 1192 at the Second Battle.

hist_arhai_din_ka_jhonpra.label: Arhai Din Ka Jhonpra (Ajmer)
hist_arhai_din_ka_jhonpra.subject: history
hist_arhai_din_ka_jhonpra.detail: Mosque at Ajmer, converted by Qutbuddin Aibak around 1199 from an older Sanskrit college/Jain temple (reusing Hindu/Jain pillars — many carvings still visible). Elaborately carved 7-arch screen of Quranic verses intertwined with floral motifs added in front of the earlier sanctum. Alongside Delhi's Quwwat-ul-Islam, among the earliest Sultanate mosques — defining monument of the Mameluke style. Popular name 'Two and a Half Day Shed' per folk etymology.

hist_qutb_minar.label: Qutb Minar
hist_qutb_minar.subject: history
hist_qutb_minar.detail: Tapering tower (originally 71.4 m high, 5 storeys) — ground storey by Qutbuddin Aibak, storeys 2-4 by Iltutmish, top (5th) storey added by Firuz Shah Tughlaq after lightning damage. Sikander Lodi repaired further earthquake damage. Part of the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque complex, not originally named for Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki. Effect derived from projected-yet-linked balconies, alternating red and white sandstone with marble panels, and ribbed vertical fluting. Alai Darwaza (1311) added by Alauddin Khalji as entrance. Alauddin planned a minar twice its height but died before it was begun.

hist_delhi_sultanate.label: Delhi Sultanate
hist_delhi_sultanate.subject: history
hist_delhi_sultanate.detail: Five dynasties ruling from Delhi (1206-1526): Early Turkish, Khalji, Tughluq, Sayyid and Lodi. Transformed Delhi from a commercial centre to capital controlling vast areas. Administration used Persian.

hist_mameluke_style.label: Mameluke Style (Slave Dynasty Architecture)
hist_mameluke_style.subject: history
hist_mameluke_style.detail: Indo-Islamic architectural style of the Slave/Ilbari dynasty (1206-1290). Mostly remodellings of existing Hindu structures. Qutb Minar begun by Aibak (ground floor), next three storeys by Iltutmish. Key examples: Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, Arhai-Din-ka-Jhonpra (Ajmer, converted from a Jain college). Decoration uses arabesque + intertwined Quranic script — no human/animal figures.

hist_qutbuddin_aibak.label: Qutbuddin Aibak
hist_qutbuddin_aibak.subject: history
hist_qutbuddin_aibak.detail: Turkish slave of Muhammad Ghori; first Sultan of Delhi (1206-10), ruling from Lahore. Severed Sultanate's links with Ghazni, enabling an India-based state. Began construction of Qutb Minar. Defeated Bhima III of Gujarat; conquered forts at Bayana, Gwaliyar, Kalinjar, Mahoba, Khajuraho. Died 1210 from injuries in a fall from horseback while playing chaugan (polo). Succeeded by his son-in-law Iltutmish.

hist_iltutmish.label: Shamsuddin Iltutmish
hist_iltutmish.subject: history
hist_iltutmish.detail: Sultan who ruled 1210-1236, consolidated the Delhi Sultanate. Favoured specially trained slaves (bandagan) for political offices. His daughter Raziyya became Sultan in 1236. Built parts of Qutb Minar.

hist_mongol_india_invasions.label: Mongol Invasions of India
hist_mongol_india_invasions.subject: history
hist_mongol_india_invasions.detail: Multiple Mongol incursions into the Indian subcontinent from the 13th to 14th centuries. Genghis Khan reached the Indus during Jalal-ud-din Khilji's reign (c. 1221). Later invasions were repelled by Alauddin Khilji. The Delhi Sultanate's military preparedness was significantly shaped by the Mongol threat.

hist_raziyya.label: Raziyya Sultan
hist_raziyya.subject: history
hist_raziyya.detail: Iltutmish's daughter who became Sultan in 1236, more able than her brothers. Chronicler Minhaj-i Siraj acknowledged her ability but was uncomfortable with a woman ruler. Removed from throne in 1240.

hist_bandagan.label: Bandagan (Slave Officers)
hist_bandagan.subject: history
hist_bandagan.detail: Specially purchased slaves trained for military service and important political offices. Favoured by Iltutmish because they were totally dependent on the Sultan. Loyal to master but not to heirs.

hist_ghiyasuddin_balban.label: Ghiyasuddin Balban
hist_ghiyasuddin_balban.subject: history
hist_ghiyasuddin_balban.detail: Sultan 1266-1287 who consolidated the Delhi Sultanate. A Sanskrit prashasti claimed his empire stretched from Bengal to Ghazni including south India, though historians regard these as exaggerated.

hist_chahalgani.label: Chahalgani (Group of Forty)
hist_chahalgani.subject: history
hist_chahalgani.detail: Group of forty privileged Turkish nobles/slaves who dominated early Delhi Sultanate politics after Iltutmish. Acted as kingmakers on his death, initially opposing Raziya. Balban (1266-87) systematically broke their power — first by excluding non-Turks to appease them, then by raising monarchy above all nobles, ultimately eliminating the group's kingmaking role.

hist_jalaluddin_khalji.label: Jalaluddin Khalji
hist_jalaluddin_khalji.subject: history
hist_jalaluddin_khalji.detail: Founder of the Khalji dynasty (1290-96), first non-Turk sultan. Warden of the marches in the northwest who had fought Mongols. Mild ruler — held that state should rest on the willing support of the governed, and that an Islamic state was impossible with a Hindu majority. Defeated Mongols under Abdullah (Halaku's grandson) near Tabarhinda 1292. Treacherously murdered by his nephew and son-in-law Alauddin Khalji at Kara 1296.

hist_alauddin_khalji.label: Alauddin Khalji
hist_alauddin_khalji.subject: history
hist_alauddin_khalji.detail: Sultan 1296-1316 who expanded into south India, raised a large standing army in Siri to counter Mongols, controlled market prices in Delhi, fixed taxes at 50% of produce, and cancelled chieftains' tax rights.

hist_iqta_system.label: Iqta System
hist_iqta_system.subject: history
hist_iqta_system.detail: Land-revenue assignment system brought from West Asia by the Turks. A Turkish chief was allotted a tract as iqta from which he collected revenue; in return he maintained troops for the sultan. Not hereditary — at the sultan's pleasure, transferable. The sultan drew revenue directly from khalisa lands. Evolved: initially muqtis kept almost all revenue (early Sultanate); Balban began tighter control; Alauddin abolished doab iqtas (cash salaries instead); Muhammad Tughlaq restored and expanded; Firuz Tughlaq made iqtas hereditary — weakening the system and undermining central control. Became the basis of the Mughal jagirdari system.

hist_kharaj_tax.label: Kharaj (Land Tax)
hist_kharaj_tax.subject: history
hist_kharaj_tax.detail: Tax on cultivation amounting to about 50% of the peasant's produce under Alauddin Khalji. One of three main taxes along with taxes on cattle and houses. Central to Sultanate revenue.

hist_seljuk_khalji_style.label: Seljuk Style (Khalji Architecture)
hist_seljuk_khalji_style.subject: history
hist_seljuk_khalji_style.detail: Architectural style of the Khalji dynasty (1290-1320), named for its Seljuk Turkish influences. Prominence of the arcuate (arch) method over the trabeate (lintel-beam). First widespread use of mortar as cementing agent. Red sandstone dominant. True dome first constructed on scientific principles at the Alai Darwaza. Alauddin built the fortress-city of Siri — his second capital — as part of the Mongol-defense infrastructure.

hist_mongol_invasions_delhi.label: Mongol Invasions of Delhi Sultanate
hist_mongol_invasions_delhi.subject: history
hist_mongol_invasions_delhi.detail: Sustained Mongol threat to north India from 1221 (Changez Khan pursuing Jalaluddin to Indus) through 1327 (Tarmashrin under Muhammad Tughlaq). Early attacks by Chagatai Mongols of Trans-Oxiana. Key invasions: 1292 — Abdullah (Halaku's grandson) defeated by Jalaluddin Khalji near Tabarhinda (4000 Mongol converts settled near Delhi). 1297-1303 — Dawa Khan's sustained campaigns; 1299 Qutlugh Khwaja's 2,00,000 entered Delhi streets; 1303 Mongols camped outside Siri two months during Alauddin's Chittor campaign. Prompted Alauddin's army reforms (market controls, dagh, 300,000 cavalry, construction of Siri). Mongol threat eased with Dawa Khan's death 1306 and civil war among Chagatais. 1327 Tarmashrin reached Meerut but was defeated by Muhammad Tughlaq near Jhelum.

hist_sultanate_market_controls.label: Alauddin's Market Controls
hist_sultanate_market_controls.subject: history
hist_sultanate_market_controls.detail: Alauddin Khalji's market regulations (c.1300) — three dedicated markets at Delhi (foodgrains; costly cloth; horses/slaves/cattle), each under a high officer (shahna) who maintained merchant registers and strictly controlled prices. Designed primarily to enable a large standing army against Mongols by keeping salaries low — cavalryman paid 238 tankas/year. Mechanics: doab land revenue raised to 50% of produce and collected directly (no iqta), forcing peasants to sell cheap to registered banjaras who brought grain to Delhi at fixed prices. State warehouses stocked against famine. Very harsh enforcement — false weights punished, no variation allowed even during famine. Barani: 'wheat 7½ jitals per man, the permanence of prices was a wonder of the age.' Collapsed with Alauddin's death.

hist_siri.label: Siri (Alauddin's capital)
hist_siri.subject: history
hist_siri.detail: Second city of Delhi, built by Alauddin Khalji as a base to counter Mongol invasions (from 1303 onwards). Strongly fortified; housed his standing army. Alauddin camped at Siri during the 1303 Mongol siege by Qutlugh Khwaja. Hazar Sutun (Palace of a Thousand Pillars) was here — described in detail by Ibn Battuta. Mostly ruined; remnants near modern Hauz Khas and Shahpur Jat.

hist_malik_kafur.label: Malik Kafur
hist_malik_kafur.subject: history
hist_malik_kafur.detail: Alauddin Khalji's slave general; captured at Cambay during the 1299 Gujarat campaign. Led two south Indian expeditions (1309-11): against Warangal (Kakatiyas/Telangana) and then Dwara Samudra (Hoysalas/Karnataka) and Mabar (Pandyas/Tamil Nadu), reaching Madurai — first Muslim forces that far south. Plundered Chidambaram temple. Made malik-naib (vice-regent). After Alauddin's death 1316 raised a minor son to throne, imprisoned/blinded the others; killed by palace guards.

hist_alai_darwaza.label: Alai Darwaza
hist_alai_darwaza.subject: history
hist_alai_darwaza.detail: Entrance gateway to the Qutb complex, built by Alauddin Khalji in 1311. Defining monument of the Seljuk/Khalji style — red sandstone with white marble inlay. Prominent use of the arcuate (arch) method; first building in India with a true dome constructed on correct scientific principles. Pleasing arch proportions; lotus-bud fringes on arch undersides. Alauddin had planned a minaret twice the height of Qutb Minar but died before work could begin.

hist_dagh_system.label: Dagh (Horse-branding) System
hist_dagh_system.subject: history
hist_dagh_system.detail: Mandatory branding of cavalry horses introduced by Alauddin Khalji to prevent soldiers from bringing poor-quality horses to muster. Combined with descriptive rolls (chehra) of each soldier. Part of Alauddin's army reforms that enabled his Mongol resistance and south Indian conquests. Revived and formalised by Sher Shah and Akbar (as part of the Mansabdari system).

hist_jauhar.label: Jauhar Ceremony
hist_jauhar.subject: history
hist_jauhar.detail: Rajput ritual of collective self-immolation by women (and suicidal last charge by warriors, called saka) when fort defeat was imminent. First Persian description: Ranthambhor 1301 (fall to Alauddin Khalji) by Amir Khusrau. Famous instances — Chittor 1303 (Padmini legend, Ratan Singh's queens), Chittor 1535 (Rani Karnavati), Champaner 1484, Chittor 1568 (under Akbar). Ranthambhor jauhar also saw the Mongol refugees die fighting alongside Hamirdeva.

hist_sumptuary_laws.label: Sumptuary Laws in France
hist_sumptuary_laws.subject: history
hist_sumptuary_laws.detail: From 1294 to 1789 French society had strict dress codes regulating what each social class could wear. Only royalty could wear ermine, silk, velvet and brocade. French Revolution ended these distinctions.

hist_petrarch.label: Petrarch
hist_petrarch.subject: history
hist_petrarch.detail: Italian scholar and poet (1304-1374) often called the 'Father of Humanism'. Rediscovered and promoted classical Latin texts by Cicero and others. His sonnets to Laura established a poetic tradition. Coined the idea of the 'Dark Ages' for the medieval period, looking back to classical antiquity as a golden age.

hist_hundred_years_war.label: Hundred Years' War
hist_hundred_years_war.subject: history
hist_hundred_years_war.detail: Series of conflicts between England and France (1337-1453) over territorial and dynastic claims. Saw the rise of infantry and longbow over mounted knights, undermining feudal warfare. Joan of Arc's role rallied French national sentiment. Ended with French victory and contributed to the decline of feudalism and rise of nation-states.

hist_black_death_europe.label: Black Death in Europe
hist_black_death_europe.subject: history
hist_black_death_europe.detail: Bubonic plague pandemic that devastated Europe between 1347-1353, killing an estimated one-third of the population (25 million). Arrived via trade routes from Central Asia. Led to acute labour shortage which empowered surviving peasants, raised wages, and weakened serfdom. Triggered social upheaval and religious crisis.

hist_decline_of_feudalism.label: Decline of Feudalism
hist_decline_of_feudalism.subject: history
hist_decline_of_feudalism.detail: Feudalism declined from the 14th century due to multiple factors: the Black Death empowered peasants through labour scarcity, the rise of towns and commerce created a money economy, centralising monarchs curbed noble power, gunpowder made castles and mounted knights obsolete, and the Crusades drained feudal resources.

hist_italian_city_states.label: Italian City-States
hist_italian_city_states.subject: history
hist_italian_city_states.detail: Wealthy, independent urban centres like Florence, Venice, Genoa, and Milan that were the cradles of the Renaissance. Prospered from Mediterranean trade, banking, and textile production. Governed as republics or by ruling families (like the Medici in Florence). Their wealth enabled patronage of art, architecture, and learning.

hist_renaissance.label: Renaissance
hist_renaissance.subject: history
hist_renaissance.detail: Cultural and intellectual movement that began in Italy in the 14th century and spread across Europe through the 16th century. Meaning 'rebirth', it revived interest in classical Greek and Roman art, philosophy, and literature. Marked the transition from medieval to modern worldview with emphasis on humanism, individualism, and secularism.

hist_peasant_revolts.label: Peasant Revolts
hist_peasant_revolts.subject: history
hist_peasant_revolts.detail: Uprisings by peasants against feudal lords and heavy taxation, particularly after the Black Death. The English Peasants' Revolt (1381) and the French Jacquerie (1358) were major examples. Triggered by attempts to reimpose pre-plague labour obligations. Though suppressed, they signalled the weakening of feudalism.

hist_classical_antiquity_revival.label: Revival of Classical Antiquity
hist_classical_antiquity_revival.subject: history
hist_classical_antiquity_revival.detail: Rediscovery and study of Greek and Roman texts, art, and philosophy that drove the Renaissance. Facilitated by the fall of Constantinople (1453) which sent Greek scholars and manuscripts westward. Scholars studied classical Latin and Greek, translating works of Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, and others. Universities became centres of classical learning.

hist_age_of_exploration.label: Age of Exploration
hist_age_of_exploration.subject: history
hist_age_of_exploration.detail: Period from the 15th-17th centuries when European nations explored and colonised distant lands. Driven by trade, religion, and curiosity. Portugal (under Henry the Navigator) led early exploration of Africa. Columbus reached the Americas (1492). Vasco da Gama reached India (1498). Magellan's expedition circumnavigated the globe (1522).

hist_humanism.label: Humanism
hist_humanism.subject: history
hist_humanism.detail: Intellectual movement at the core of the Renaissance emphasising the study of classical texts (studia humanitatis), human potential, and rational inquiry. Humanists like Petrarch, Erasmus, and Thomas More promoted education, critical thinking, and civic virtue. Shifted focus from purely theological concerns to human experience and achievement.

hist_printing_press.label: Printing Press (Gutenberg)
hist_printing_press.subject: history
hist_printing_press.detail: Johannes Gutenberg invented the movable type printing press in Mainz, Germany around 1440. Revolutionised the spread of knowledge by making books cheaper and more widely available. The Gutenberg Bible (1455) was among the first major works printed. Enabled the rapid spread of Renaissance ideas and later the Reformation.

hist_print_revolution.label: Print Revolution
hist_print_revolution.subject: history
hist_print_revolution.detail: Shift from hand-copied manuscripts to mechanical printing transformed knowledge access. Books became cheaper and available to wider population. Created new reading culture and spread of ideas across Europe.

hist_leonardo_da_vinci.label: Leonardo da Vinci
hist_leonardo_da_vinci.subject: history
hist_leonardo_da_vinci.detail: Italian polymath (1452-1519) often regarded as the ideal 'Renaissance man'. Painter of the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper. Also an engineer, anatomist, inventor, and scientist. His notebooks contain designs for flying machines, tanks, and anatomical studies. Epitomised the Renaissance spirit of curiosity and versatility.

hist_medici.label: Medici Family
hist_medici.subject: history
hist_medici.detail: Powerful banking family that effectively ruled Florence for much of the 15th-16th centuries. Lorenzo de' Medici ('the Magnificent', r. 1469-1492) was the most famous patron. The family supported artists like Michelangelo and Botticelli, funded libraries, and shaped Renaissance culture. Produced four popes.

hist_renaissance_art.label: Renaissance Art
hist_renaissance_art.subject: history
hist_renaissance_art.detail: Art underwent transformation with techniques like perspective, chiaroscuro (light and shadow), and anatomical accuracy. Shifted from religious iconography to include secular subjects, portraits, and classical mythology. Artists gained individual fame (unlike anonymous medieval craftsmen). Major figures: Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael, Botticelli.

hist_erasmus.label: Erasmus of Rotterdam
hist_erasmus.subject: history
hist_erasmus.detail: Dutch humanist scholar (1466-1536), the most influential intellectual of the Northern Renaissance. His 'In Praise of Folly' satirised Church corruption and superstition. Produced a critical edition of the Greek New Testament. Advocated reform within the Church rather than separation. Influenced both Catholics and Protestants.

hist_niccolo_machiavelli.label: Niccolo Machiavelli
hist_niccolo_machiavelli.subject: history
hist_niccolo_machiavelli.detail: Italian political philosopher (1469-1527) from Florence. His work 'The Prince' (1513) analysed political power with cold pragmatism, separating politics from morality. Argued that rulers should use any means to maintain power and stability. Considered the founder of modern political science.

hist_michelangelo.label: Michelangelo
hist_michelangelo.subject: history
hist_michelangelo.detail: Italian sculptor, painter, and architect (1475-1564). Created the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel and the sculpture of David. Designed the dome of St. Peter's Basilica. His work combined classical forms with emotional intensity. Considered one of the greatest artists of all time.

hist_columbian_exchange.label: Columbian Exchange
hist_columbian_exchange.subject: history
hist_columbian_exchange.detail: Post-1492 exchange of plants, animals, diseases, and peoples between Americas and Afro-Eurasia. Potato + maize transformed European diets. Smallpox decimated Americans. American silver financed European trade with Asia (incl India textiles).

hist_european_colonisation_americas.label: European Colonisation of Americas
hist_european_colonisation_americas.subject: history
hist_european_colonisation_americas.detail: Begins with Columbus 1492. Spanish/Portuguese/English/French/Dutch colonised. Spanish conquered Aztec + Inca. English coastal colonies became USA. Disease, enslavement, cultural destruction of indigenous peoples.

hist_plantation_economy.label: Plantation Economy (Americas)
hist_plantation_economy.subject: history
hist_plantation_economy.detail: Large agricultural estates producing sugar, tobacco, cotton, coffee for European markets. Relied on enslaved African labour after indigenous decline. Enriched colonial powers; fuelled slave trade; shaped racial + economic structures.

hist_atlantic_slave_trade.label: Atlantic Slave Trade
hist_atlantic_slave_trade.subject: history
hist_atlantic_slave_trade.detail: ~12-15M Africans transported to Americas 16c-19c. Triangular trade: Europe manufactures→Africa; African captives→Americas; American sugar/cotton/tobacco→Europe. Largest forced migration in history.

hist_martin_luther.label: Martin Luther
hist_martin_luther.subject: history
hist_martin_luther.detail: German monk and theologian (1483-1546) who initiated the Protestant Reformation by posting his 95 Theses in Wittenberg in 1517. Argued that salvation comes through faith alone (sola fide) and scripture alone (sola scriptura), not through Church rituals or papal authority. Translated the Bible into German, making it accessible to common people.

hist_reformation.label: Protestant Reformation
hist_reformation.subject: history
hist_reformation.detail: Religious movement begun by Martin Luther in 1517 that challenged Catholic Church doctrines and papal authority. Luther's 95 Theses criticised indulgences and corruption. Led to the establishment of Protestant churches (Lutheran, Calvinist, Anglican). Split Western Christianity and triggered religious wars across Europe.

hist_vernacular_literature.label: Rise of Vernacular Literature
hist_vernacular_literature.subject: history
hist_vernacular_literature.detail: Shift from Latin to local languages in literature and official communication. Dante's 'Divine Comedy' in Italian, Chaucer's 'Canterbury Tales' in English, and Luther's German Bible were landmarks. The printing press accelerated this shift. Vernacular languages became vehicles for national identity and wider literacy.

hist_chagatai_khanate.label: Chagatai Khanate
hist_chagatai_khanate.subject: history
hist_chagatai_khanate.detail: One of the four successor states of the Mongol Empire, named after Genghis Khan's second son Chagatai. Covered Central Asia including modern Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and parts of Afghanistan. Gradually converted to Islam. Eventually fragmented, with Timur emerging from its western portion.

hist_golden_horde.label: Golden Horde
hist_golden_horde.subject: history
hist_golden_horde.detail: The western Mongol khanate founded by Batu Khan (Genghis Khan's grandson) covering Russia, Ukraine, and parts of Central Asia. Ruled from Sarai on the Volga River. Imposed tribute on Russian principalities for over two centuries. Converted to Islam in the early 14th century. Declined by the 15th century.

hist_pax_mongolica.label: Pax Mongolica
hist_pax_mongolica.subject: history
hist_pax_mongolica.detail: Period of relative peace and stability across Eurasia under Mongol rule (c. 1250-1350). Enabled safe long-distance trade along the Silk Road. Facilitated exchange of goods, technologies, ideas, and diseases between China, Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. Also transmitted the Black Death.

hist_ilkhanate.label: Ilkhanate
hist_ilkhanate.subject: history
hist_ilkhanate.detail: Mongol khanate established by Hulagu Khan (Genghis Khan's grandson) in Persia and the Middle East after the sack of Baghdad (1258). Ended the Abbasid Caliphate. Rulers eventually converted to Islam. Fell in 1335. Facilitated cultural and scientific exchange between China, Persia, and Europe.

hist_sack_of_baghdad.label: Sack of Baghdad (1258)
hist_sack_of_baghdad.subject: history
hist_sack_of_baghdad.detail: Hulagu Khan's Mongol forces besieged and destroyed Baghdad in 1258, killing the last Abbasid Caliph al-Musta'sim. The destruction of the House of Wisdom and its libraries was a catastrophic loss for Islamic civilisation. Ended the Abbasid Caliphate and shifted the centre of Islamic power.

hist_kublai_khan.label: Kublai Khan
hist_kublai_khan.subject: history
hist_kublai_khan.detail: Grandson of Genghis Khan (r. 1260-1294), he completed the conquest of China and founded the Yuan Dynasty (1271-1368). Moved the capital to Khanbaliq (Beijing). Attempted invasions of Japan and Southeast Asia. Hosted Marco Polo. Under him the Mongol Empire effectively split into four khanates.

hist_silk_road_mongols.label: Silk Road under Mongols
hist_silk_road_mongols.subject: history
hist_silk_road_mongols.detail: The Mongol Empire revitalised the Silk Road by providing security and infrastructure across Eurasia. Established a postal relay system (yam) with rest stations. Merchants, missionaries, and diplomats travelled freely. Marco Polo's journey to Kublai Khan's court exemplifies this connectivity.

hist_marco_polo.label: Marco Polo
hist_marco_polo.subject: history
hist_marco_polo.detail: Venetian merchant and explorer (1254-1324) who travelled to Kublai Khan's China and spent about 17 years in the Mongol Empire. His account, 'The Travels of Marco Polo', introduced Europeans to the wealth and sophistication of Asia. While some details are disputed, it stimulated European interest in the East.

hist_yuan_dynasty.label: Yuan Dynasty
hist_yuan_dynasty.subject: history
hist_yuan_dynasty.detail: Mongol dynasty established by Kublai Khan in China (1271-1368). First foreign dynasty to rule all of China. Maintained Mongol identity while adopting Chinese administrative practices. Promoted trade along the Silk Road. Overthrown by the Ming Dynasty after peasant revolts.

hist_black_death_mongols.label: Black Death and Mongol Trade Routes
hist_black_death_mongols.subject: history
hist_black_death_mongols.detail: The bubonic plague (Black Death) spread along Mongol trade routes from Central Asia to Europe in the 1340s, killing an estimated one-third of Europe's population. The same connectivity that facilitated trade and cultural exchange also transmitted disease. This was an unintended consequence of the Pax Mongolica.

hist_mewar_kingdom.label: Mewar Kingdom
hist_mewar_kingdom.subject: history
hist_mewar_kingdom.detail: Rajput kingdom in southern Rajasthan. Virtual founder Bapa Rawal (Guhilot clan, 7th c). Chittor as capital. After Alauddin Khalji ousted Ratan Singh in 1303, the Sishodia branch (formerly Guhilot feudatories) took over. Rose to prominence under Rana Kumbha (1433-68) and Rana Sanga (1508-28). Survived as independent Rajput state through Sultanate and Mughal periods; eventually Mughal vassal after Akbar's Chittor siege 1568.

hist_kashmir_sultanate.label: Kashmir Sultanate
hist_kashmir_sultanate.subject: history
hist_kashmir_sultanate.detail: Muslim rule established in Kashmir c.1339 after Mongol leader Dalucha's devastating 1320 raid discredited the Hindu government. Baramulla route facilitated incursion of Muslim saints and Central Asian refugees. Sikandar Butshikan (1389-1413) persecuted Brahmans; Zainul Abidin 'Bud Shah' (1420-70) reversed policy and fostered cultural synthesis. Rishi silsilah combined Hindu and Muslim features. Annexed by Mughals under Akbar 1586.

hist_bengal_arch_school.label: Bengal Architecture School
hist_bengal_arch_school.subject: history
hist_bengal_arch_school.detail: Bengal Sultanate's provincial architectural style (14th-16th c). Characterised by use of bricks and black marble. Adopted 'Bangla roof' — sloping/curved roof resembling a thatched bamboo hut, originally a Pala-Sena temple feature, later carried into Mughal architecture as the bangla dome. Key monuments: Adina Mosque (Pandua, c.1375 — largest mosque in Indian subcontinent at its time), Qadam Rasul mosque (Gaur), Eklakhi Mausoleum (Pandua), Sixty Dome Mosque (Bagerhat).

hist_bengal_sultanate.label: Bengal Sultanate
hist_bengal_sultanate.subject: history
hist_bengal_sultanate.detail: Independent from Delhi from 1338 onwards; Ilyas Shahi dynasty founded 1342 by Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah. Capital Pandua, later Gaur. Distinct architectural style using stone and brick. Firuz Tughlaq failed twice to subdue Ilyas and his son Sikandar (who retreated to Ekdala fort). After 200 years of independence, Sher Shah conquered Bengal 1538. Major patron of Bengali literature. Brief Hindu interregnum under Raja Ganesh early 15th c.

hist_adina_mosque_pandua.label: Adina Mosque (Pandua)
hist_adina_mosque_pandua.subject: history
hist_adina_mosque_pandua.detail: Largest mosque of the Indian subcontinent at its time, built 1373-75 by Sultan Sikandar Shah of Bengal at Pandua. Reused stones from destroyed Hindu temples. Long rectangular plan with huge central courtyard; 260 pillars; uniquely large mihrab ornamented with mouldings. A signature Bengal School example — Islamic form with local brick-and-stone material.

hist_sikandar_butshikan.label: Sikandar Shah Butshikan
hist_sikandar_butshikan.subject: history
hist_sikandar_butshikan.detail: Kashmir sultan (1389-1413) known as 'butshikan' (idol-breaker). Ordered all Brahmans to convert to Islam or leave Kashmir; temples destroyed; gold/silver idols melted for currency. Policy implemented by his Hindu-convert minister Suha Bhatt. Led to mass exodus of Brahmans and Hindu learning from the valley. Reversed under his grandson Zainul Abidin.

hist_jaunpur_sharqi_school.label: Jaunpur (Sharqi) Architecture School
hist_jaunpur_sharqi_school.subject: history
hist_jaunpur_sharqi_school.detail: Sharqi provincial style at Jaunpur (1394-1484). Distinctive: bold forceful characters painted on huge screens at centre/side bays of prayer halls; no minars (like Pathan). Unlike Delhi style — emphasis on monumental propylons/facades with soaring arches. Key monuments: Atala Mosque (1408, earliest/most influential), Jami Masjid Jaunpur, Lal Darwaza Mosque.

hist_jaunpur_sultanate.label: Jaunpur Sultanate (Sharqis)
hist_jaunpur_sultanate.subject: history
hist_jaunpur_sultanate.detail: Independent sultanate (1394-1484) in eastern UP founded by Malik Sarwar — formerly wazir of Firuz Tughlaq, titled Malik-us-Sharq (Lord of the East), whence 'Sharqi'. Capital Jaunpur — 'Shiraz of the East'. Distinct architectural style with lofty gates and huge arches. Great patrons of learning. Malik Muhammad Jaisi composed Padmavat here. Great musical patronage under Husain Shah Sharqi. Annexed by Bahlul Lodi 1484 after long Delhi-Jaunpur rivalry for the Ganga-Yamuna valley.

hist_malwa_sultanate.label: Malwa Sultanate
hist_malwa_sultanate.subject: history
hist_malwa_sultanate.detail: Independent from 1401 after Timur's invasion; high plateau between Narmada and Tapti controlling trunk routes Gujarat↔North and North↔South. Capital shifted from Dhar to Mandu. Rival of Gujarat and Mewar in the cockpit struggle for north India. Peak under Mahmud Khalji (1436-69). Internal factionalism allowed Rana Sanga of Mewar to defeat Mahmud II at Khatoli 1517 and annex eastern Malwa. Finally absorbed by Mughals under Akbar 1562.

hist_malwa_pathan_school.label: Malwa (Pathan) Architecture School
hist_malwa_pathan_school.subject: history
hist_malwa_pathan_school.detail: Malwa Sultanate's provincial style centred at Mandu. Also known as 'Pathan School'. Features: coloured stones/marbles; large windows (some European influence); ornate arches and pillars; stairs used aesthetically; NO minars. Environmental adaptation — baulis in premises, lightly-arched airy pavilions, locally available materials, Tughlaq batter. Key monuments: Hindola Mahal, Jahaz Mahal, Rani Roopmati Pavilion, Ashrafi Mahal, Jami Masjid Mandu.

hist_mandu.label: Mandu
hist_mandu.subject: history
hist_mandu.detail: Second capital of Malwa Sultanate, shifted from Dhar. Highly defensible plateau location with natural beauty. Distinctive massive architecture on lofty plinths, using coloured/glazed tiles. Landmark buildings: Jama Masjid, Hindola Mahal, Jahaz Mahal, Hushang Shah's tomb (first marble tomb in India), Rewa Kund and Rupmati Pavilion.

hist_hushang_shah.label: Hushang Shah
hist_hushang_shah.subject: history
hist_hushang_shah.detail: Early Malwa sultan (1406-35) known for religious toleration. Allowed Rajput migration to Malwa (brothers of Rana Mokal of Mewar granted jagirs). Lalitpur temple inscription shows no restrictions on temple construction under him. Patronised Jain merchants; Nardeva Soni was his treasurer. His tomb at Mandu is among the earliest marble tombs in India — said to have been studied by Shah Jahan's architects before the Taj Mahal.

hist_gujarat_sultanate.label: Gujarat Sultanate
hist_gujarat_sultanate.subject: history
hist_gujarat_sultanate.detail: Independent sultanate from 1407 under Zafar Khan (Muzaffar Shah), whose father Sadharan was a Rajput convert whose sister had married Firuz Tughlaq. Initial capital at Patan, shifted to Ahmedabad (founded 1411). Peak under Mahmud Begarha (1459-1511). Annexed Girnar, Champaner; sacked Dwarka. Dealt with Portuguese naval threat through alliance with Ottomans. Rich ports (Cambay, Surat) and textile industry. Absorbed by Akbar 1572-73.

hist_atala_mosque_jaunpur.label: Atala Mosque (Jaunpur)
hist_atala_mosque_jaunpur.subject: history
hist_atala_mosque_jaunpur.detail: Earliest major Sharqi monument, built 1408 by Ibrahim Shah Sharqi at Jaunpur. Signature Sharqi style — towering central propylon with huge recessed arch dominating the facade; bold geometric patterns on screen. Built on the site of an earlier Hindu temple (reused materials). Model for later Sharqi monuments.

hist_ahmad_shah_gujarat.label: Ahmad Shah I of Gujarat
hist_ahmad_shah_gujarat.subject: history
hist_ahmad_shah_gujarat.detail: Gujarat sultan (1411-43), real founder of the kingdom. Shifted capital from Patan to the new city of Ahmedabad (foundation laid 1413). Developed a distinct Gujarat architectural style — slender turrets, exquisite stone-carving, highly ornate brackets — drawing on Jain temple architecture. Built Jama Masjid and Tin Darwaza at Ahmedabad. Imposed jizyah on Hindus (not levied earlier); levelled temples at Sidhpur. But inducted Hindu merchants Manik Chand and Motichand as ministers; had his own son-in-law executed for murder.

hist_ahmedabad.label: Ahmedabad
hist_ahmedabad.subject: history
hist_ahmedabad.detail: Capital of Gujarat Sultanate, founded 1411 by Ahmad Shah I (laid 1413). Distinct architectural style blending Gujarat Jain tradition with Sultanate forms. Landmark buildings: Jama Masjid, Tin Darwaza, later Sidi Saiyyed Mosque. Major centre of textile production — zari (gold lace) work. Renamed Karnavati briefly. Later a Mughal province capital.

hist_zainul_abidin.label: Zainul Abidin (Bud Shah)
hist_zainul_abidin.subject: history
hist_zainul_abidin.detail: Greatest Muslim monarch of Kashmir (1420-70), called 'Bud Shah' (Great Sultan). Reversed Sikandar Butshikan's anti-Hindu policies: cancelled Brahman persecution, restored temples and land grants, abolished jizyah and cow slaughter, even withdrew the ban on sati (in deference to Hindu wishes). Hindus held high office (Sriya Bhatt was chief justice). Sent envoys to Samarqand to learn paper-making and book-binding; fostered shawl-making, stone-cutting, musket-making, fireworks. Had Rajatarangini and Mahabharata translated to Persian. Built Zaina Lanka, an artificial island in Wular Lake. Unified Kashmir through Baltistan conquest. Three sons from two Hindu queens (daughters of Raja of Jammu).

hist_hindola_mahal.label: Hindola Mahal (Mandu)
hist_hindola_mahal.subject: history
hist_hindola_mahal.detail: 'Swing Palace' at Mandu, built c.1425 under Hushang Shah. Named for sloping outer walls that give the illusion of a swinging building. T-shaped hall; massive buttressed walls with fine stone screens. Used as durbar hall. Exemplifies the Malwa School's use of batter.

hist_rana_kumbha.label: Rana Kumbha
hist_rana_kumbha.subject: history
hist_rana_kumbha.detail: Mewar ruler (1433-68) who made it the premier Rajput state. Defeated internal rivals; conquered Bundi, Kotah, Dungarpur. Fought Malwa and Gujarat simultaneously; repulsed multiple Kumbhalgarh sieges by Gujarat. Built Kirti Stambha (Tower of Victory) at Chittor — 9-storey tower commemorating victory over Mahmud Khalji of Malwa. Also built 32 forts including Kumbhalgarh. Learned author; patron of arts. Murdered by his son Uda for the throne.

hist_mahmud_khalji_malwa.label: Mahmud Khalji of Malwa
hist_mahmud_khalji_malwa.subject: history
hist_mahmud_khalji_malwa.detail: Most powerful Malwa sultan (1436-69). Restless and ambitious — fought Gujarat, Gondwana, Orissa, Bahmanis, and Delhi. Principal struggle against Rana Kumbha of Mewar. Destroyed temples during these campaigns — a lapse from Malwa's earlier tolerance, though not a general policy of temple destruction.

hist_kirti_stambha.label: Kirti Stambha (Chittor)
hist_kirti_stambha.subject: history
hist_kirti_stambha.detail: 9-storey Tower of Victory built by Rana Kumbha at Chittor (c.1448) to commemorate his victory over Mahmud Khalji of Malwa. Covered in sculptures of Hindu deities. Contrast with the older Jain Kirti Stambha at the same site (Chittor has two famous Jain and Hindu victory towers). Architectural statement of Rajput resurgence.

hist_ashrafi_mahal.label: Ashrafi Mahal (Mandu)
hist_ashrafi_mahal.subject: history
hist_ashrafi_mahal.detail: 'Palace of Gold Coins' at Mandu, built by Mahmud Khalji next to the Jami Masjid — originally a madarasa, expanded into a victory tower commemorating his defeat of Rana Kumbha.
