The Seven-Storey Tower (mostly ruined) intended to parallel the Kirti Stambha of Chittor. Mostly in ruins today.

hist_mahmud_begarha.label: Mahmud Begarha
hist_mahmud_begarha.subject: history
hist_mahmud_begarha.detail: Most famous Gujarat sultan (1459-1511). Name 'Begarha' from capturing two major garhs — Girnar/Junagadh (1469) and Champaner (1484). Founded Mustafabad below Girnar and Muhammadabad near Champaner. Sacked Dwarka (cited pirate harbouring, also razed temples). Allied with Egypt against Portuguese naval threat. Striking appearance — beard to waist, moustache tied over head. Barbosa: nourished on poison from childhood (insects died on contact). Legendary appetite (10-15 kg/day). Made Gujarat powerful enough to later challenge Humayun.

hist_jahaz_mahal.label: Jahaz Mahal (Mandu)
hist_jahaz_mahal.subject: history
hist_jahaz_mahal.detail: 'Ship Palace' at Mandu, built by Ghiyas-ud-din Khalji (1469-1500). Long two-storey building (120m × 15m) between two artificial lakes (Munj Talao, Kapur Talao), appearing to float like a ship. Terraces, pavilions and cupolas on top. Showpiece of Malwa School's use of water and environmental adaptation.

hist_alauddin_hussain_shah.label: Alauddin Hussain Shah
hist_alauddin_hussain_shah.subject: history
hist_alauddin_hussain_shah.detail: Bengal sultan (1493-1519), presided over its brilliant cultural phase. Inducted Hindus in highest offices — wazir, physician, chief of bodyguard, mint-master were all Hindus. Rupa and Sanatana Goswami (Chaitanya's chief lieutenants) held senior posts before renouncing. Showed great respect to Chaitanya. Patronised Bengali literature — his son Nusrat Shah had Mahabharata translated to Bengali. Conquered Kamata (Cooch Bihar), wrested Chittagong from Arakan, annexed Tipperah.

hist_nimatnama.label: Nimatnama
hist_nimatnama.subject: history
hist_nimatnama.detail: 'Book of Delicacies' — illustrated cookery and pharmacy manuscript produced at Mandu during the reign of Nasir Shah Khalji (1500-10) and completed under Mahmud Shah II. Famous example of Sultanate miniature painting — synthesis of Persian Shiraz-school style with indigenous Indian elements. Depicts sultan supervising preparation of dishes and recipes for foods/remedies. Preserved in the British Library.

hist_rani_roopmati_pavilion.label: Rani Roopmati Pavilion (Mandu)
hist_rani_roopmati_pavilion.subject: history
hist_rani_roopmati_pavilion.detail: Hilltop pavilion at Mandu, originally a military observation post later associated with Rani Roopmati (wife of Baz Bahadur, last Malwa sultan, defeated by Akbar 1561). Affords views of the Narmada — Roopmati reportedly refused to eat until she had seen the river.

hist_rana_sanga.label: Rana Sanga (Sangram Singh)
hist_rana_sanga.subject: history
hist_rana_sanga.detail: Mewar ruler (1508-28), grandson of Rana Kumbha. Defeated Malwa's Mahmud II at Khatoli 1517, carried him prisoner to Chittor, annexed eastern Malwa including Chanderi. Defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Khatoli and Dholpur. Invited Babur to oust the Lodis, hoping to emerge as dominant north Indian power. Defeated by Babur at Khanwa 1527 (Babur's victory consolidated Mughal rule).

hist_qadam_rasul_gaur.label: Qadam Rasul Mosque (Gaur)
hist_qadam_rasul_gaur.subject: history
hist_qadam_rasul_gaur.detail: Single-domed mosque at Gaur (West Bengal) built 1530 by Nusrat Shah (son of Alauddin Hussain Shah). Houses an impression of the Prophet's footprint (qadam rasul) brought from Mecca. Late Bengal Sultanate style — brick construction with curved Bangla roof, stone veneer, blind arches.

hist_malik_muhammad_jaisi.label: Malik Muhammad Jaisi
hist_malik_muhammad_jaisi.subject: history
hist_malik_muhammad_jaisi.detail: Hindi/Awadhi Sufi poet of the Jaunpur tradition. Composed Padmavat (c.1540) — an allegorical Sufi masnavi set around Alauddin Khalji's siege of Chittor (1303), introducing the Padmini legend more than two centuries after the event. Representative of Sufi saints composing in Hindi to convey mystical concepts to common people.

hist_sayyid_dynasty.label: Sayyid Dynasty
hist_sayyid_dynasty.subject: history
hist_sayyid_dynasty.detail: Delhi dynasty (1414-51) that arose after Timur's 1398 invasion. Nominal rule — contemporaries quipped the sultan's writ ran 'from Delhi to Palam'. Khizr Khan (founder, claimed Sayyid descent from Prophet) and successors ruled a rump territory while regional governors broke away. Displaced by Bahlul Lodi who crowned himself in 1451 after the Sayyid king Alam Shah died in exile.

hist_bahlul_lodi.label: Bahlul Lodi
hist_bahlul_lodi.subject: history
hist_bahlul_lodi.detail: Founder of the Lodi dynasty (1451-89). Afghan noble of Sirhind who dominated Punjab after checking the Khokhars. Occupied Delhi 1451 when Sayyid king died in exile. Fought the Sharqis of Jaunpur across several decades; invited Afghans of Roh to India, changing the complexion of Muslim society. Annexed Jaunpur 1484. Divided kingdom among sons and relations — a partition later undone by Sikandar.

hist_lodi_dynasty.label: Lodi Dynasty
hist_lodi_dynasty.subject: history
hist_lodi_dynasty.detail: Afghan dynasty (1451-1526) founded by Bahlul Lodi; first non-Turkish dynasty of Delhi. Bahlul (1451-89), Sikandar Lodi (1489-1517), Ibrahim Lodi (1517-26). Expanded the Afghan element in north Indian Muslim society — many Afghans of Roh migrated on Bahlul's invitation. Annexed Sharqi kingdom of Jaunpur 1484. Ended at First Battle of Panipat 1526 (Babur).

hist_sikandar_lodi.label: Sikandar Lodi
hist_sikandar_lodi.subject: history
hist_sikandar_lodi.detail: Lodi sultan (1489-1517). Controlled Afghan nobles by requiring them to stand in durbar and show deference — a departure from their tradition of first-among-equals. Laid foundation of Agra (1506) to control eastern Rajasthan/Malwa/Gujarat routes. Introduced gazz-i-Sikandari (standard yard) which prevailed till Mughal times. Abolished octroi on grains. Bigoted in later reign — re-imposed jizyah, demolished temples (Nagarkot), executed a Brahman for teaching Hindu-Muslim scriptural equivalence. Patron of Persian scholars; many Sanskrit works (including music treatises) translated to Persian under him.

hist_double_dome.label: Double Dome (Lodi Innovation)
hist_double_dome.subject: history
hist_double_dome.detail: Architectural innovation of the Lodi period — a hollow inner dome beneath the outer dome. Reasons: (1) greater structural strength; (2) lowering inner ceiling for human scale while retaining commanding outer skyline. First full expression in Sikander Lodi's tomb at Lodi Garden. Adopted and refined by Mughals — Humayun's Tomb is the first major Mughal double dome, culminating in the Taj Mahal. Lodi tombs also feature hard/bare exteriors (octagonal, ~15m diameter) on sloping verandahs.

hist_lodi_architecture.label: Lodi Tomb Architecture
hist_lodi_architecture.subject: history
hist_lodi_architecture.detail: Lodi-era style (c.1451-1526): tombs placed on high platforms for better skyline; many octagonal (~15m diameter) on sloping verandahs. Signature innovation — the double dome (hollow inner dome beneath outer dome, giving strength + lowering inner ceiling). Hard, bare, less decorated exteriors. Some tombs set in gardens. Lodi Garden (Delhi) preserves Muhammad Shah's tomb, Sikandar Lodi's tomb, Bara Gumbad, Sheesh Gumbad. Features (double domes, octagonal plans, garden-tombs) adopted by Mughals — culminating in Humayun's tomb and the Taj Mahal.

hist_lodi_khuladar.label: Lodi Khuladar
hist_lodi_khuladar.subject: history
hist_lodi_khuladar.detail: Sultanate miniature painting style prevalent in the region between Delhi and Jaunpur during late 15th-early 16th c. Blended Persian illumination with indigenous Indian elements; formed the 'Sultanate formulae' that the later Mughal, Rajput, and Deccan schools all drew from. Less refined than the Nimatnama school of Mandu but historically important as precursor of Mughal painting.

hist_agra_founding.label: Agra (founded 1506)
hist_agra_founding.subject: history
hist_agra_founding.detail: Founded by Sikandar Lodi in 1506 after careful site survey. Intended to command eastern Rajasthan, Malwa, and routes to Gujarat. Became the second capital of the Lodis. Later chosen by the Mughals (Babur, Akbar, Shah Jahan) as imperial capital — site of the Taj Mahal and Agra Fort.

hist_sher_shah_sur.label: Sher Shah Sur
hist_sher_shah_sur.subject: history
hist_sher_shah_sur.detail: Afghan leader who defeated Humayun and drove him into exile (1540-45). Established efficient administration and revenue system during his brief rule. His administrative innovations influenced later Mughal governance. Built Grand Trunk Road from Peshawar to Bengal.

hist_bhils.label: Bhils
hist_bhils.subject: history
hist_bhils.detail: Large tribe spread across western and central India. By late 16th century many became settled agriculturists and some zamindars, though many clans remained hunter-gatherers. Adapted to changing conditions.

hist_mundas_santals.label: Mundas and Santals
hist_mundas_santals.subject: history
hist_mundas_santals.detail: Important tribal groups in present-day Bihar, Jharkhand, Orissa and Bengal. Along with Cheros, they represented significant tribal presence in eastern India that interacted with Mughal power.

hist_tribal_societies_medieval.label: Medieval Tribal Societies
hist_tribal_societies_medieval.subject: history
hist_tribal_societies_medieval.detail: Many subcontinent societies did not follow Brahmanical rules or divide into unequal classes. United by kinship bonds. Obtained livelihood from agriculture, hunting-gathering or herding. Controlled land jointly.

hist_nomadic_pastoralists.label: Nomadic Pastoralists
hist_nomadic_pastoralists.subject: history
hist_nomadic_pastoralists.detail: Mobile people who moved long distances with animals, living on milk and pastoral products. Exchanged wool, ghee with settled agriculturists. Included Gaddis in the western Himalaya.

hist_gond_kingdom.label: Gond Kingdom
hist_gond_kingdom.subject: history
hist_gond_kingdom.detail: Gonds lived in Gondwana practising shifting cultivation. Garha Katanga had 70,000 villages. Kingdom divided into garhs, chaurasi (84 villages) and barhots (12 villages). Rani Durgawati resisted Mughal forces in 1565.

hist_garha_katanga.label: Garha Katanga
hist_garha_katanga.subject: history
hist_garha_katanga.detail: Rich Gond state that earned wealth by trapping and exporting wild elephants. When Mughals defeated the Gonds, they captured precious coins and elephants. Part annexed, rest granted to Chandra Shah.

hist_rani_durgawati.label: Rani Durgawati
hist_rani_durgawati.subject: history
hist_rani_durgawati.detail: Capable ruler of Gond kingdom Garha Katanga, ruling on behalf of her young son Bir Narain. Expanded the kingdom considerably. Defeated by Mughal forces under Asaf Khan in 1565. Preferred death to surrender.

hist_ahom_kingdom.label: Ahom Kingdom
hist_ahom_kingdom.subject: history
hist_ahom_kingdom.detail: Mongoloid tribe from north Burma who established kingdom in Brahmaputra valley 1228. Gradually Hinduised — Suhungmung (1497-1539), considered greatest Ahom ruler, took name Svarga Narayana; his reign saw rapid Sanskritisation and Vaishnava reform (Shankaradeva). Used firearms from 1530s; made gunpowder by 1660s. Repulsed Bengal Sultanate attack (probably Nusrat Shah). Used paiks (forced labour) with census-based rotation and buranjis (historical works in Ahom then Assamese). Defeated Mughals at Battle of Saraighat 1671 (Lachit Borphukan). Kingdom lasted until Burmese invasion / British annexation 1826.

hist_banjaras.label: Banjaras
hist_banjaras.subject: history
hist_banjaras.detail: Most important trader-nomads. Caravans called tanda with up to 700 persons and 14,000 oxen. Carried grain for Alauddin Khalji and Mughal armies. Bought grain cheaply and sold where dearer.

hist_buranjis.label: Buranjis
hist_buranjis.subject: history
hist_buranjis.detail: Historical works written by the Ahoms, first in Ahom language then in Assamese. Represent sophisticated literary culture. Important works of Sanskrit were also translated into local language.

hist_paiks.label: Paiks (Ahom Forced Labour)
hist_paiks.subject: history
hist_paiks.detail: People forced to work for the Ahom state. Census taken to determine numbers. Villages sent paiks by rotation. Adults served in army during war, otherwise built dams, irrigation and public works.

hist_shifting_cultivation.label: Shifting Cultivation
hist_shifting_cultivation.subject: history
hist_shifting_cultivation.detail: Method where trees and bushes are cut and burnt, crops sown in ashes. When soil loses fertility, another plot is cleared. Practised by Gonds and other forest-dwelling tribal communities.

hist_ghiyasuddin_tughlaq.label: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq
hist_ghiyasuddin_tughlaq.subject: history
hist_ghiyasuddin_tughlaq.detail: Founder of Tughlaq dynasty (1320-25). Rose as officer by defeating Khusrau Khan. Died 1325 when a wooden pavilion hastily erected by his son Muhammad Tughlaq collapsed during an elephant parade — rumours of parricide followed. Built the massive palace-fortress complex Tughlaqabad near Delhi, with an artificial lake formed by blocking the Yamuna. His tomb introduced the marble-dome-on-high-platform style in Sultanate architecture.

hist_tughlaqabad.label: Tughlaqabad
hist_tughlaqabad.subject: history
hist_tughlaqabad.detail: Massive palace-fortress complex built by Ghiyasuddin and Muhammad Tughlaq near Delhi. Huge artificial lake created by blocking the Yamuna. Sloping walls (batter) gave an effect of strength and solidity — a Tughlaq hallmark. Ghiyasuddin's tomb within the complex — on a high platform with a marble dome, marking a new architectural trend. Abandoned after Muhammad Tughlaq shifted court to Daulatabad.

hist_muhammad_bin_tughlaq.label: Muhammad bin Tughlaq
hist_muhammad_bin_tughlaq.subject: history
hist_muhammad_bin_tughlaq.detail: Tughlaq sultan (1324-51), son of Ghiyasuddin. Called 'ill-starred idealist' — deeply read in philosophy and science, conversed with Muslim mystics, Hindu yogis, and Jain saints (Jinaprabha Suri); accused of 'rationalism' by theologians. Gave offices on merit, not lineage. Five major experiments: (1) transfer of capital to Daulatabad 1327 (~1500 km forced exodus); (2) bronze token currency 1329-30 (failed due to forgery); (3) increased doab taxation leading to peasant rebellion and famine; (4) diwan-i-amir-i-kohi development-bloc agricultural scheme; (5) Khurasan expedition army (disbanded) and Qarachil (Kumaon hills) expedition (disaster, 10 of 10,000 returned). Appointed Ibn Battuta qazi of Delhi. Died 1351 in Sind while suppressing rebellion. Vijayanagara (Harihara-Bukka) and Bahmani (Hasan Gangu) both emerged from rebellions against him.

hist_daulatabad_shift.label: Shift to Daulatabad
hist_daulatabad_shift.subject: history
hist_daulatabad_shift.detail: Muhammad Tughlaq's 1327 order shifting Delhi residents — especially officers, Sufi saints, and leading men — to Deogir (renamed Daulatabad) to better control the south. Road built with rest-houses for the 1500 km journey; liberal grants made; but summer-season exodus caused many deaths and homesickness. Ordinary population not moved; Delhi remained populous, coins minted there confirm. After a few years the shift was abandoned — couldn't control north from south either. Long-range consequences: brought north-south closer; religious and cultural ideas (Sufi saints) spread into Deccan; basis for Deccan Islamic culture (including the later Bahmani).

hist_token_currency.label: Muhammad Tughluq's Token Currency
hist_token_currency.subject: history
hist_token_currency.detail: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's bronze/brass coin (1329-30) intended to have the same value as the silver tanka — following the successful precedent of Qublai Khan of China and Ghazan Khan of Iran. Introduced due to shortage of silver in 14th-century world. The government failed to prevent forgery; devaluation in markets. Withdrawn; sultan promised to exchange silver for bronze — many did so, but forged coins (detectable by tests) weren't exchanged and 'lay heaped up outside the fort for many years' (Barani). Damaged prestige and treasury but the government recovered; Ibn Battuta in 1333 found no lasting harm.

hist_firuz_shah_tughlaq.label: Firuz Shah Tughlaq
hist_firuz_shah_tughlaq.subject: history
hist_firuz_shah_tughlaq.detail: Tughlaq sultan (1351-88), cousin of Muhammad bin Tughlaq. Appeased nobles by making iqtas hereditary; extended heredity to army. Dug extensive canals (longest Sutlej-Hansi, 200 km; Yamuna canal). Built new towns — Hissar-Firuzah, Firuzabad, Fatehabad, Jaunpur. Established karkhanas with 1,80,000 slaves. Made jizyah a separate tax; imposed it on Brahmans. Had Sanskrit works (music, medicine, Rajatarangini) translated to Persian. Set up free hospitals, banned mutilation punishments, provided dowries to poor girls. Orthodox on religion — persecuted Muslim sects deemed heretical; burnt a Brahman for preaching to Muslims.

hist_hauz_khas.label: Hauz Khas
hist_hauz_khas.subject: history
hist_hauz_khas.detail: Firuz Shah Tughlaq's pleasure resort around a large tank originally built by Alauddin Khalji. Contains a madarasa, pavilions, and Firuz's own tomb. Characteristic Tughlaq combination of arch-and-dome with lintel-and-beam. Used greystone (cheaper than red sandstone); minimal decoration apart from lotus motif. Now a South Delhi park.

hist_timur.label: Timur (Tamerlane)
hist_timur.subject: history
hist_timur.detail: Central Asian conqueror (1336-1405); Turk claiming blood relationship with Changez Khan. Unified Iran and Turan, extending empire from Volga to Indus and Syria to southern Russia. 1398 invasion of Delhi — plundering raid. Mercilessly sacked towns along the way; sacked Delhi without mercy, large numbers of Hindus and Muslims killed; took enormous wealth and many Indian artisans (masons, stone-cutters, carpenters) to Samarqand. Direct political effect on India small — but marked the end of strong Delhi Sultanate rule and triggered the rise of regional sultanates (Malwa, Gujarat, Jaunpur, Bengal) and the Sayyid/Lodi rumps.

hist_ibn_battuta.label: Ibn Battuta
hist_ibn_battuta.subject: history
hist_ibn_battuta.detail: Moroccan traveller born in Tangier, arrived in India 1333. Appointed qazi of Delhi by Muhammad bin Tughlaq. Travelled extensively across North Africa, West Asia, Central Asia, India, China. His Rihla records detailed observations of 14th-century Indian social life.

hist_mughal_postal_system.label: Sultanate Postal System (Dak Chauki)
hist_mughal_postal_system.subject: history
hist_mughal_postal_system.detail: (Described by Ibn Battuta during Tughlaq-era Delhi Sultanate, not Mughal. Relabelled for accuracy.) Ibn Battuta described an efficient postal system with horse relay (uluq) and foot relay stations at regular intervals. Enabled rapid communication across the empire. Foot carriers were considered even more reliable than horse system for important messages.

hist_persian_tawarikh.label: Persian Historical Texts (Tawarikh)
hist_persian_tawarikh.subject: history
hist_persian_tawarikh.detail: Persian historical writing developed strongly in Sultanate India. Major historians — Minhaj-i-Siraj Juzjani (Tabaqat-i-Nasiri, covering till Balban), Ziauddin Barani (Tarikh-i-Firuzshahi, Fatawa-i-Jahandari — covering Balban to early Firuz; key source for market controls and politics), Shams-i-Siraj Afif (second Tarikh-i-Firuzshahi, focused on Firuz), Isami (Futuh-us-Salatin, mid-14c, Bahmani court). Amir Khusrau's historical mathnavis (Qiranus-Sadain, Miftahul Futuh, Khazainul Futuh, Tughlaq Nama) blur poetry and history. Later — Yahya Sirhindi (Tarikh-i-Mubarakshahi, Sayyid period), Ferishta (17c but covers Sultanate).

hist_rihla.label: Rihla
hist_rihla.subject: history
hist_rihla.detail: Ibn Battuta's travel account written in Arabic, dictated after his return to Morocco. Records unfamiliar customs, foods (coconut, paan), the postal system (horse and foot relay), and dangers of travel. Journey from Multan to Delhi took 40 days, Sind to Delhi 50 days.

hist_ziyauddin_barani.label: Ziyauddin Barani
hist_ziyauddin_barani.subject: history
hist_ziyauddin_barani.detail: 14th-century chronicler who wrote his chronicle first in 1356 and a revised version in 1358. The first version remained lost until the 1960s. Important source for Delhi Sultanate history.

period_ghurid_slave.label: Ghurid & Slave Dynasty
period_ghurid_slave.subject: history
period_ghurid_slave.detail: Ghurid & Slave (Mamluk) Dynasty: 1192-1290. Muhammad Ghori's 2nd Tarain victory (1192) founds Turkish rule; Qutbuddin Aibak (1206) establishes the Sultanate at Delhi. Iltutmish consolidates; his daughter Raziyya briefly takes the throne; Balban breaks the power of the chahalgani Turkish nobles. Early Mongol pressure on the northwest frontier. Key monuments — Qutb Minar, Arhai-Din-ka-Jhonpra, Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque (Mameluke style).

period_khalji.label: Khalji Dynasty
period_khalji.subject: history
period_khalji.detail: Khalji Dynasty: 1290-1320. Jalaluddin Khalji ends the Turkish monopoly; Alauddin (1296-1316) imposes market controls in Delhi, abolishes doab iqtas for direct cash taxation, repels Mongol sieges of 1299 and 1303. Malik Kafur's southern campaigns reach Madurai. Seljuk-Khalji architecture — Alai Darwaza, Siri fortress.

period_tughlaq.label: Tughlaq Dynasty
period_tughlaq.subject: history
period_tughlaq.detail: Tughlaq Dynasty: 1320-1414. Ghiyasuddin founds Tughlaqabad. Muhammad bin Tughlaq's ambitious but failed experiments — Daulatabad transfer (1327), token currency (1330), Khurasan and Qarachil campaigns. Firuz Shah's canals, karkhanas, hereditary iqtas, jizyah as separate tax. Ibn Battuta qazi of Delhi. Barani's Tarikh. Timur sacks Delhi 1398 — effective end of Tughlaq strength.

period_sayyid_lodi.label: Sayyid & Lodi Dynasties
period_sayyid_lodi.subject: history
period_sayyid_lodi.detail: Sayyid & Lodi Dynasties: 1414-1540. Sayyid rump after Timur; Bahlul Lodi (1451) founds the Afghan Lodi dynasty, annexes Jaunpur (1484). Sikandar Lodi founds Agra (1506), introduces gazz-i-Sikandari, builds octagonal double-domed tombs. Ibrahim Lodi defeated by Babur at Panipat 1526 (era 6 boundary). Sher Shah's interregnum 1540-55 restores Afghan rule briefly.

period_deccan_empires.label: Vijayanagara & Bahmani
period_deccan_empires.subject: history
period_deccan_empires.detail: Vijayanagara & Bahmani: 1336-1565. Rebellions against Muhammad bin Tughlaq birth the Vijayanagara empire (Harihara-Bukka, 1336) and the Bahmani kingdom (Hasan Gangu, 1347). Four Vijayanagara dynasties — Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, Aravidu; peak under Krishnadeva Raya (1509-29). Bahmani peaks under Firuz Shah Bahmani and then minister Mahmud Gawan (8 tarafs, Bidar madarasa). Bahmani splits into five Deccan sultanates (1518). Combined Deccan armies crush Vijayanagara at Talikota (1565).

period_regional_sultanates.label: Regional Sultanates (N. India)
period_regional_sultanates.subject: history
period_regional_sultanates.detail: Regional Sultanates (North India): 1339-1540. Post-Tughlaq fragmentation — Bengal (Ilyas Shahi, Hussain Shahi), Gujarat (Muzaffar Shahi, peak under Mahmud Begarha), Malwa (at Mandu), Jaunpur (Sharqis, 'Shiraz of the East'), Kashmir (Zainul Abidin 'Bud Shah'), Mewar (Rana Kumbha, Rana Sanga). Distinctive provincial architecture schools — Bengal, Pathan (Malwa), Sharqi (Jaunpur), Bijapur (Deccan).

period_tribes_nomads.label: Tribes, Nomads & Settled Communities
period_tribes_nomads.subject: history
period_tribes_nomads.detail: Tribes, Nomads & Settled Communities. Ahom kingdom in Brahmaputra valley from 1228 (firearms by 1530s); Gond kingdom of Garha Katanga under Rani Durgawati; Rajput clans in western India; Bhils of central/western India; Mundas, Santals of eastern India. Banjaras — trader-nomads supplying grain to Sultanate armies. Shifting cultivation, pastoralism, and gradual sedentarisation.

period_bhakti_sufi.label: Bhakti & Sufi Movements
period_bhakti_sufi.subject: history
period_bhakti_sufi.detail: Bhakti & Sufi Movements: 1192-1526. Chishti silsila dominant — Muinuddin Chishti → Bakhtiyar Kaki → Baba Farid → Nizamuddin Auliya → Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Dehli; Suhrawardis accept state patronage; Kashmir Rishi order synthesises Hindu-Muslim elements. Nirguna bhakti (Kabir, Nanak) and saguna (Ramananda, Chaitanya, Vallabhacharya) flourish. Namdev + Maharashtra saints, Shankaradeva in Assam. Common humanist platform emerges across creeds.

period_culture_arts.label: Culture, Arts & Administration
period_culture_arts.subject: history
period_culture_arts.detail: Culture, Arts & Administration. Amir Khusrau creates the sabaq-i-hindi Persian style, attributed sitar innovation, praises Hindustan. Persian historiography (Barani, Afif, Isami). Sultanate administration — diwan-i-arz/risalat/insha, karkhanas, iqta→jagir evolution, jizyah as separate tax under Firuz, dagh branding, jauhar in Rajput politics. Trabeate yielding to arcuate architecture; social practices (sati, purdah).

period_parallel_european_renaissance.label: European Renaissance / Reformation
period_parallel_european_renaissance.subject: history
period_parallel_european_renaissance.detail: Parallel: European Renaissance & Reformation. Italian city-states (Medici Florence, Venice, Genoa); humanism (Petrarch, Erasmus); Gutenberg press (1440-48) enables print revolution. Art — Leonardo, Michelangelo. Machiavelli's statecraft. Hundred Years' War (1337-1453), Black Death (1347-51), peasant revolts, decline of feudalism. Protestant Reformation (Luther 1517). Age of Exploration — Columbus (1492), Vasco da Gama (1498). Columbian exchange, Atlantic slave trade, plantation economy.

hist_babur.label: Babur (1526-1530)
hist_babur.subject: history
hist_babur.detail:
Founder of Mughal Empire. Driven from homeland Farghana by Uzbeks. Established at Kabul, then entered India 1526. Related to Genghis Khan through mother. Wrote memoirs in Turkish (Babur Nama). Defeated Ibrahim Lodi at First Battle of Panipat. Spoke Turkish, wrote poetry.

Campaign sequence: Ferghana throne at age 12 (1494), forced out by Uzbegs under Shaybani Khan, seized Kabul 1504. Panipat-I 1526 used matchlocks and field artillery. Then Khanwa 1527 vs Rana Sanga of Mewar, Chanderi 1528 vs Medini Rai. Died 1530.

Ancestry context: Timur died 1405; grandson Shahrukh Mirza (d. 1448) held West Asia (Samarqand, Herat) as cultural centres. Timurid partitioning tradition weakened the dynasty. Babur succeeded Farghana at 12 (1494) but was ousted by Uzbek Shaibani Khan — later killed 1510 at Merv by Shah Ismail Safavid. Three-empire context: Uzbeks + Safavids + Ottomans contested Central/West Asia. Captured Bhira 1518-19 (first gunpowder use); Sialkot + Lahore 1520-21. Invited into India by Daulat Khan Lodi (via son Dilawar Khan) + Rana Sanga separately. Ottoman master-gunners Ustad Ali + Mustafa manned artillery at Panipat-I. Post-Panipat he fought Battle of Ghagra 1529 vs Nusrat Shah of Bengal + Afghans under Mahmud Lodi (Ibrahim's brother) — inconclusive, patched agreement. Wrote memoirs Tuzuk-i-Baburi / Babur Nama in Chaghtai Turkish — classic naturalist observation of Indian flora/fauna. Introduced chahar-bagh formal gardens with running water.

hist_humayun.label: Humayun
hist_humayun.subject: history
hist_humayun.detail:
Second Mughal ruler (1530-40, 1555-56). Expanded frontiers but lost empire to Afghan Sher Shah Sur. Took refuge at Safavid court of Iran. Defeated the Surs in 1555 but died a year later. Brought Persian artists Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad to Delhi.

Lost two decisive battles to Sher Khan (Suri): Chausa 1539 and Kanauj 1540. Fled to Iran via Sind. Safavid Shah Tahmasp provided military aid on condition of Shia allegiance. Retook Qandahar and Kabul in stages, defeated Sikandar Suri 1555 to recover Delhi. Died 1556 after falling down library stairs at Din Panah.

Brothers under Timurid partition: Kamran (Kabul/Qandahar, seized Punjab/Multan), Askari, Hindal (later rebelled). Defeated Afghans at Dadrah 1532. First Chunar siege 1532 — allowed Sher Khan retention of fort in return for loyalty + hostage son. Gujarat campaign 1535-37: Bahadur Shah fled Mandsor → Mandu → Champaner (Humayun was 41st up the wall); Malwa + Gujarat gained then lost within a year. Second Chunar siege 1537 took 6 months with master-gunner Rumi Khan; meanwhile Sher Khan captured Rohtas by treachery and took Bengal capital Gaur 1538. Battle of Chausa 1539 (Karmnasa river crossing) + Kanauj 1540 ended his first reign. Wandered Sindh 2.5 years; Maldeo Marwar refused asylum; accepted by Shah Tahmasp (Safavid) 1544 on condition of Shiite allegiance. Recovered Qandahar + Kabul 1545. Built Dinpanah (Delhi) 1533. Recovered Delhi 1555 from Sur civil war, defeating Sikandar Sur.

hist_babur_nama.label: Babur Nama
hist_babur_nama.subject: history
hist_babur_nama.detail: Memoirs of Babur, first Mughal emperor. Written in Turkish, translated to Persian. Records observations about Indian agriculture, irrigation devices, peasant mobility and settlement patterns. Noted that villages could be depopulated and set up 'in a moment'.

hist_chahar_bagh.label: Chahar Bagh Garden
hist_chahar_bagh.subject: history
hist_chahar_bagh.detail:
Formal gardens within rectangular walled enclosures divided into four quarters by artificial channels. Developed by Babur, the most beautiful built by Jahangir and Shah Jahan in Kashmir, Agra and Delhi.

Major surviving Mughal gardens by reign: Babur — Aram Bagh (Agra, 1526) + Lahore gardens. Akbar — Nishat Bagh (Kashmir). Jahangir — **Shalimar Bagh Kashmir 1619** for Nur Jahan, **Chashm-e-Shahi** (Kashmir, built around fresh spring, Persian style). Shah Jahan — Shalimar Bagh Lahore 1641, Pinjore garden (Punjab foothills, also called Yadavindra), garden of the Taj Mahal. Dara Shukoh — Pari Mahal (Kashmir, mid-17c) terraced on a Srinagar hill overlooking Dal Lake, with an observatory. All in chahar-bagh four-quadrant plan with running water, fountains, Persian-inspired terraces.

hist_mughal_empire.label: Mughal Empire
hist_mughal_empire.subject: history
hist_mughal_empire.detail: Founded by Babur in 1526, descended from Timur (paternal) and Genghis Khan (maternal). Called themselves Timurids, not Mughals. Major rulers: Babur, Humayun, Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan, Aurangzeb. After Aurangzeb's death (1707), regional powers gained autonomy. Last ruler Bahadur Shah Zafar II overthrown 1857.

hist_akbar.label: Akbar (1556-1605)
hist_akbar.subject: history
hist_akbar.detail:
Greatest Mughal emperor who expanded and consolidated the empire. Made Persian the court language. Abolished pilgrimage tax (1563) and jizya (1564). Promoted sulh-i kul (absolute peace). Composite nobility of Iranis, Turanis, Afghans, Rajputs, Deccanis. Patronised art and learning.

Reign in three phases: (1) 1556-60 regency of Bairam Khan — Second Battle of Panipat 1556 vs Hemu. (2) 1560-1585 consolidation — Chittor siege 1568 (Sisodiya), Ranthambhor 1569, Gujarat 1572-73, Bihar/Bengal/Orissa campaigns, Mirza Hakim revolt 1579-80. (3) 1585-1605 expansion — Qandahar seized from Safavids 1595, Kashmir and Kabul annexed, Deccan campaigns absorbed Berar, Khandesh, parts of Ahmadnagar. Last years disturbed by Prince Salim's rebellion.

Born 15 October 1542 at Amarkot fort (Rana Prasad Rao's refuge during Humayun's flight). Uncle Kamran captured young Akbar in Kabul; reunited with Humayun 1545. Crowned at Kalanaur (Punjab) 14 February 1556 at age 13 years 4 months while Humayun's body still lay at Delhi. Early court dominated by foster-mother Maham Anaga and her son Adham Khan (killed 1561 — Akbar threw him twice off Agra Fort parapet after stabbing of acting wazir Atgah Khan). Uzbek noble rebellions 1561-67 (Akbar vowed Jaunpur as capital until rebels crushed); Mirzas (Timurid relatives) rebelled 1567. Mirza Hakim (half-brother ruling Kabul) besieged Lahore 1581 during eastern revolt — crushed via Akbar's march from Jaunpur→Lahore→Kabul; Akbar handed Kabul to his sister as gesture. Abdullah Khan Uzbek seized Badakhshan 1584. Conquered Kashmir+Ladakh+Baltistan 1586 (called Tibet Khurd + Tibet Buzurg); Sindh 1590. Birbal killed in Khyber Yusufzai campaign 1586. Died 27 October 1605, buried at Sikandra.

Diplomatic context with Uzbeks: rejected Abdullah Khan Uzbek's 1577 proposal for tripartite Sunni alliance (with Ottomans) against Shia Iran — 'differences of religion could not be ground for conquest.' Circa 1585 agreement with Abdullah on Hindukush boundary — implicit partition: Mughals gave up Badakhshan/Balkh claim; Uzbeks gave up Kabul/Qandahar claim. Conquered Qandahar 1595 (not part of a partition deal with Uzbeks as some older historians argued — motivation was defensive frontier vs newly Uzbek-held Khurasan).

hist_mansab_system.label: Mansab System
hist_mansab_system.subject: history
hist_mansab_system.detail: Hierarchical ranking system for Mughal nobles. Each mansabdar assigned a rank (zat and sawar) determining status, pay and military obligations. Positions given purely on service and loyalty regardless of religion or ethnicity. Included Iranis, Turanis, Afghans, Rajputs, Deccanis.

hist_mansabdari_system.label: Mansabdari System
hist_mansabdari_system.subject: history
hist_mansabdari_system.detail:
Grading system fixing rank (zat), salary and military responsibilities (sawar/cavalrymen). Mansabdars from diverse backgrounds: Turanis, Iranians, Indian Muslims, Afghans, Rajputs, Marathas. Salaries paid through jagirs.

Scale data: under Akbar 29 mansabdars held 5,000 zat or higher; by Aurangzeb's reign 79 — indicating massive expansion of the noble class. Jagir crisis = central cause of decline: actual jagir revenue fell below granted salary by late 17c, combined with huge increase in claimants producing long waits (be-jagiri) and extractive behaviour from jagirdars holding temporary assignments. Mansabdars registered sawars, horses branded (dagh system, Sher Shah origin) before payment.

Mansabdars of 1,000 zat or higher ranked as nobles (umara, plural amir). Aurangzeb-era data: 79 mansabdars at 5,000 zat (vs Akbar's 29). Dagh (horse-branding) and chehra (soldier identification) continued Sher Shah tradition to prevent muster fraud. Akbar instituted spiritual master-disciple bond (murid) with select nobles. Recruitment: candidate petitioned through a noble who presented a tajwiz to emperor; mir bakhshi signed appointment orders. Nobles at court (tainat-i-rakab) = reserve force, mandatory twice-daily attendance at Diwan-i-Am. Ethnic composition: Turanis, Iranis, Afghans, Indian Muslims (Shaikhzadas, from 1560s), Rajputs (Bharmal Kachhwaha 1562), Marathas (substantial under Aurangzeb).

Zat+sawar bifurcation introduced 1594-95 (40th regnal year); earlier a single rank. Three categories per rank: first (sawars=zat), second (sawars ≥ half of zat), third (sawars < half). Ideal 10:20 horse ratio (rest+replacement). Max rank raised 5000→7000 late reign; only Man Singh + Aziz Koka awarded 7000. Hierarchy of titles: <500 zat = mansabdar, 500-2500 = amir, 2500+ = amir-i-umda / umda-i-azam. Iranis + Turanis paid higher than Rajputs + Hindustani Muslims. Ahadis: gentleman-troopers of noble lineage without their own contingent, paid ~Rs 800/month, reported directly to the emperor, had separate muster-master — comparable to European knights.

Jahangir-era modification: du-aspah sih-aspah system (literally, trooper with 2 or 3 horses) — doubled a mansabdar's sawar quota without raising zat rank. Shah Jahan era: noble expected to maintain only 1/3 of sawar rank obligation (1/4 in some cases) to ease fiscal strain; paired with month-scale mechanism (salaries and sawar obligations scaled to 10/8/6/5-month equivalents depending on jagir income class). Accounting convention — assessed revenue (jama-dami) recorded in dams (40 dams = 1 rupee), not rupees. Cavalry strength: ~2,00,000 under Shah Jahan, 2,40,000 under Aurangzeb; infantry ~40,000. Marathas inducted into Mughal service generally given mansabs on 5-month or less scale — fewer effective sawars than their zat rank suggested.

hist_sulh_i_kul.label: Sulh-i Kul (Absolute Peace)
hist_sulh_i_kul.subject: history
hist_sulh_i_kul.detail: Cornerstone of Akbar's enlightened rule as articulated by Abu'l Fazl. All religions and schools of thought had freedom of expression, provided they did not undermine state authority. Implemented through composite nobility and abolition of discriminatory taxes like jizya.

hist_farr_i_izadi.label: Farr-i Izadi (Divine Light)
hist_farr_i_izadi.subject: history
hist_farr_i_izadi.detail:
Concept that Mughal kingship received Divine Light from God, placing it at highest station. Inspired by Iranian sufi Shihabuddin Suhrawardi. Abu'l Fazl placed Mughal kings in hierarchy of objects receiving divine emanation. From 17th century, emperors portrayed with halos in paintings.

Legitimising legend: Mongol queen Alanqua impregnated by ray of sunshine while resting in her tent — her offspring carry Divine Light through generations, passed down to Timur and thence to the Mughals. Hierarchical theology: Divine Light transmitted to king who becomes spiritual-source for subjects. Intellectual lineage: Plato's Republic (God-as-sun) → Shihabuddin Suhrawardi (d.1191, Iranian sufi, Illuminationist/ishraqi philosophy) → Shaikh Mubarak → his sons Faizi and Abu'l Fazl. From 17c Mughal painting onward, emperors depicted wearing halo borrowed from European Christ/Mary iconography.

hist_zabt_system.label: Zabt Revenue System
hist_zabt_system.subject: history
hist_zabt_system.detail:
Revenue system developed by Akbar's minister Todar Mal. Based on 10-year survey of crop yields, prices and cultivated areas (1570-1580). Tax fixed in cash for each crop. Provinces divided into revenue circles.

Developed from Sher Shah's ray (crop rate). Akbar first tried reverting to annual assessment via qanungos (hereditary record-keepers) but many were corrupt. 1573 appointed karoris (revenue officers assigned 1 crore dams = Rs 2.5 lakh each). Dahsala bandobast instituted 1580: 10-year average of produce AND prices; 1/3 produce as state share, converted to cash at 10-year average price. Parganas grouped into assessment circles of similar productivity. Applied Lahore→Allahabad, Malwa, Gujarat. NOT a 10-year binding settlement nor permanent — state could revise. Peasants given choice between zabti and batai (under certain conditions). Cash crops (cotton, indigo, oilseed, sugarcane) invariably taken in cash. Nasaq = rough estimation method (also called jankut). Taccavi loans provided for seeds/implements/animals. Work of a team: Todar Mal + Muzaffar Khan Turbati + others (not Todar Mal alone).

hist_todar_mal.label: Todar Mal
hist_todar_mal.subject: history
hist_todar_mal.detail: Akbar's revenue minister who carried out careful survey of crop yields, prices and areas cultivated over 10 years (1570-1580). Developed the zabt system of land revenue assessment.

hist_abul_fazl.label: Abu'l Fazl
hist_abul_fazl.subject: history
hist_abul_fazl.detail:
Court historian of Akbar, author of Akbar Nama. Grew up in Agra, widely read in Arabic, Persian, Greek philosophy and Sufism. Shaped and articulated Akbar's ideology. Worked on Akbar Nama for 13 years from 1589. Murdered in 1602 by conspiracy of Prince Salim and Bir Singh Bundela.

Son of Shaikh Mubarak (rationalist scholar); elder brother poet-laureate Faizi. Trained in Suhrawardi's Illuminationist (ishraqi) philosophy — which he applied to formulating Mughal-kingship ideology. Widely read in Arabic, Persian, Greek philosophy and Sufism. Forceful debater against conservative ulama. Assassinated August 1602 en route back from Deccan by Bir Singh Bundela at Prince Salim's behest.

hist_akbar_nama.label: Akbar Nama
hist_akbar_nama.subject: history
hist_akbar_nama.detail:
Official chronicle of Akbar's reign by Abu'l Fazl, in three books. First two are chronological histories. Third is the Ain-i Akbari giving synchronic picture of the empire. Based on official records, documents and oral testimonies. Published by Asiatic Society of Bengal, translated by Henry Beveridge.

Abu'l Fazl worked on the text from 1589 for 13 years, repeatedly revising. Sources: official records (waqai), farmans, oral testimonies, his aunt Gulbadan Begum's memoirs. Volume 1 begins 'history of mankind from Adam' to one celestial cycle (30 years) of Akbar's life. Volume 2 closes at 46th regnal year (1601). Abu'l Fazl murdered August 1602 by Bir Singh Bundela, acting on Prince Salim's orders — Salim feared Abu'l Fazl's influence on succession. Translated into English by Henry Beveridge in early 20th century.

hist_ain_i_akbari.label: Ain-i Akbari
hist_ain_i_akbari.subject: history
hist_ain_i_akbari.detail:
Third book of Akbar Nama, authored by Abu'l Fazl. Most important chronicle for Mughal agrarian history. Meticulously records cultivation arrangements, revenue collection and zamindar relations. Agra produced 39 crop varieties, Delhi 43, Bengal 50 varieties of rice alone.

Five-daftar structure: (1) manzil-abadi — imperial household; (2) sipah-abadi — military and civil administration + biographical notices of mansabdars, poets, artists; (3) mulk-abadi — fiscal side with 8-column suba tables (pargana/qila/arazi/naqdi/suyurghal/zamindars/castes/troops); (4-5) religious, literary, cultural traditions + Akbar's 'auspicious sayings'. Completed 1598 (42nd regnal year) after 5 revisions. Aggregate Ain data: zamindar muster across empire = 384,558 cavalry + 4,277,057 infantry + 1,863 elephants + 4,260 cannons + 4,500 boats. Numeric data written in words to prevent transcription error. English translations: Vol 1 by Henry Blochmann (Calcutta 1873), Vols 2-3 by H.S. Jarrett (1891, 1894).

hist_humayun_tomb.label: Humayun's Tomb
hist_humayun_tomb.subject: history
hist_humayun_tomb.detail: Built 1562-1571, introduced the central towering dome and tall pishtaq gateway into Mughal architecture. Placed in centre of chahar bagh. Hasht bihisht (eight paradises) plan. Red sandstone edged with white marble.

hist_fatehpur_sikri.label: Fatehpur Sikri
hist_fatehpur_sikri.subject: history
hist_fatehpur_sikri.detail:
Akbar's capital in the 1570s where he held religious discussions in the ibadat khana. Buildings show architectural influence from Gujarat and Malwa. Contains the Govind Deva temple in Vrindavan style.

Ibadat Khana (House of Worship) built here 1575 — Akbar held religious debates among ulama, Brahmans, Jains, Parsis, and Portuguese Jesuit priests (first Jesuit mission 1580 under Rodolfo Acquaviva). These debates informed his Sulh-i-Kul doctrine and the 1582 Din-i-Ilahi. City abandoned c.1585 due to water shortage; court moved to Lahore.

Located on direct Agra-Ajmer road — Akbar wanted proximity to dargah of Shaikh Muinuddin Chishti at Ajmer, a pilgrimage he undertook repeatedly. White-marble Salim Chishti tomb adjacent to Friday mosque. Enormous Buland Darwaza (gateway) commemorates 1573 Gujarat victory. Ibadat Khana debates held 1575-82. Capital transferred to Lahore 1585 — Akbar stayed there 13 years to watch north-west frontier during Uzbeg threat.

Ibadat Khana built 1575 — initially Muslim-only theological debate; opened to all religions 1578 (Portuguese Jesuits, Hindus, Jains, Parsis, Zoroastrians). Debates closed 1582 due to acrimony among theologians. Replaced by bilateral consultations: Purushottam + Devi (Hindu), Maharji Rana (Zoroastrian), Hira Vijaya Suri (Jain saint from Kathiawar, spent 2 years at court).

Additional structures: **Panch Mahal** — five-storey open-pillared wind-catcher inspired by Persian badgir; each storey smaller than one below; supported by 176 columns showing mix of temple pillar traditions. **Jodha Bai's Palace** (Mariam-uz-Zamani's palace) — Hindu interior motifs (bells, flowers, lotus). **Hiran Minar** — tower with protruding elephant-tusk spikes, reportedly memorial to Akbar's favourite elephant Hiran; doubled as traveller's lighthouse. **Pachisi Court** — courtyard floor inlaid as pachisi board (Akbar reportedly played with human pieces). **Salim Chishti's tomb** (1581) — white marble with celebrated jaali screens + arabesque Quranic-verse inscriptions; further decorated by Jahangir 1606. **Tudor arch** (four-centred arch) architectural innovation introduced here.

hist_guru_granth_sahib.label: Guru Granth Sahib
hist_guru_granth_sahib.subject: history
hist_guru_granth_sahib.detail: Holy scripture of the Sikhs. Compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604 with compositions of Nanak and successors. Includes writings of Shaikh Farid, Kabir, Namdev. Authenticated by Guru Gobind Singh in 1706.

hist_jahangir.label: Jahangir (1605-1627)
hist_jahangir.subject: history
hist_jahangir.detail:
Mughal emperor who maintained father Akbar's empire. Revolted against Akbar as Prince Salim. Established Chain of Justice (pure gold, 30 gaz long, 60 bells) for direct petitions. Commissioned portraits with halos. His memoirs describe court life and natural history observations.

Key achievements: Sisodiya Amar Singh of Mewar accepted Mughal service 1615 ending long resistance (received watan jagir). Less successful against Sikhs, Ahoms, Ahmadnagar (Malik Ambar held out). Thomas Roe English embassy 1615-1619. Nur Jahan dominated court from 1620s. Prince Khurram (Shah Jahan) rebelled in last years.

Accession 1605 immediately challenged by son Khusrau (Akbar's favoured successor candidate) — rebellion defeated at Lahore; Khusrau blinded and imprisoned; later killed 1622 by Shah Jahan during his rebellion. Bengal pacification 1608-13 via Islam Khan (grandson of Shaikh Salim Chishti — Mughal patron saint). Capital of Bengal shifted Rajmahal → Dacca 1610. Afghan chief Usman Khan and Barah Bhuiyan (12 zamindars) confederacy including Musa Khan defeated. Mahabat Khan's coup June 1626: seized Jahangir at Jhelum crossing; Nur Jahan rescued via 6-month diplomatic maneuver. Died October 1627 near Lahore, buried at Shahdara.

hist_nur_jahan.label: Nur Jahan
hist_nur_jahan.subject: history
hist_nur_jahan.detail:
Wife of Jahangir who wielded enormous influence at court. Had silver coins struck bearing her name. Issued official orders (farmans) with her own seal. One of the most powerful women in Mughal history.

Originally Mehrunnisa, daughter of Persian noble Mirza Ghias Beg (Itimad-ud-Daulah). Married Jahangir 1611, given title Nur Jahan ('Light of the World'). Silver coins struck in her name with inscription 'struck in the name of the Queen Begum, Nur Jahan'. Issued farmans under own seal. Formed 'Junta' with father, brother Asaf Khan, and Prince Khurram. Later fell out with Khurram over Shahryar succession attempt; effectively sidelined after Jahangir's death 1627.

First marriage to Iranian noble Sher Afgan (died 1607 in clash with Qutbuddin Khan Koka, Bengal governor — sober historians reject Jahangir's direct role). Married Jahangir at Meena Bazar 1611, age 34. Family rise: father Mirza Ghiyas Beg (Itimad-ud-Daulah) became joint diwan, then chief diwan; brother Asaf Khan held khan-i-saman, then wakil. 'Junta' thesis (Beni Prasad): Nur Jahan + Itimad + Asaf + Khurram managed Jahangir's decisions. Later historians (Satish Chandra) argue this is overstated — most political decisions till 1622 were clearly Jahangir's per his Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri. Issued farmans under own seal; silver coins struck in her name; title Badshah Begum. After Jahangir's death 1627, Asaf Khan made her a virtual prisoner; she received fixed settlement and lived retired 18 more years at Lahore.

hist_shah_jahan.label: Shah Jahan (1628-1658)
hist_shah_jahan.subject: history
hist_shah_jahan.detail:
Mughal emperor who continued territorial expansion. Commissioned Badshah Nama written by Abdul Hamid Lahori. Built Shahjahanabad (Old Delhi), Red Fort and Taj Mahal. Issued grants for temple repair even after wars. Deposed by Aurangzeb in 1658.

Afghan noble Khan Jahan Lodi rebelled early in reign, defeated. Bundelas defeated, Orchha seized. Ahmadnagar annexed 1632, Bijapur sued for peace. North-west: Balkh campaign vs Uzbegs failed (1645-1647); Qandahar permanently lost to Safavids (1649 after three failed sieges). Succession war 1657-58: imprisoned at Agra by Aurangzeb for rest of life, died 1666. Mother was Rathor (Jodhpur) princess.

Rebellion 1622-26: refusal to lead Qandahar relief against Shah Abbas I escalated into full revolt. Defeated by Mahabat Khan near Delhi (saved by Mewar Rajput contingent from complete defeat). Fled Gujarat → Deccan → Orissa (surprise attack) → captured Bengal/Bihar → forced back to Deccan by Mahabat Khan → allied with Malik Ambar → submitted 1626, sent Dara + Aurangzeb as hostages. Ali Mardan Khan (Persian Qandahar governor) defected 1638, restoring Qandahar briefly. Balkh campaign 1646-47: aimed to place friendly Nazr Muhammad at Bokhara; Prince Murad mishandled; Prince Aurangzeb defeated Abdul Aziz's ~1,20,000 Uzbeks at Balkh 1647 — but strategic retreat October 1647 with heavy losses. Qandahar lost to Persia 1649; three failed recovery attempts (Aurangzeb 1649, Aurangzeb 1652, Dara 1653). Foreign-policy doctrine held Mughals to Hindukush frontier, with Qandahar as outer bastion; friendship with Iran as pivot despite Qandahar disputes.

hist_badshah_nama.label: Badshah Nama
hist_badshah_nama.subject: history
hist_badshah_nama.detail:
Official history of Shah Jahan's reign by Abdul Hamid Lahori, pupil of Abu'l Fazl. Three volumes of ten lunar years each. First two covering 1627-47 revised by wazir Sadullah Khan. Third volume by Waris. Gifted to King George III by Nawab of Awadh in 1799, now at Windsor Castle.

Author Abdul Hamid Lahori, pupil of Abu'l Fazl; Shah Jahan commissioned it on hearing of his talent. Three daftars of 10 lunar years each, modelled on Akbar Nama. Lahori wrote daftars 1-2 (1627-47); revised by Sadullah Khan (Shah Jahan's wazir). Old age prevented Lahori from third daftar — completed by historian Muhammad Waris. Gifted by Nawab of Awadh (Asaf-ud-Daulah) to King George III in 1799; held at Royal Collections, Windsor Castle. Taken apart for conservation 1994; paintings first exhibited 1997 (New Delhi, London, Washington). Full text still not translated to English.

hist_taj_mahal.label: Taj Mahal
hist_taj_mahal.subject: history
hist_taj_mahal.detail: Shah Jahan's grandest architectural achievement in white marble at Agra, completed 1643. Adapted the river-front garden layout with mausoleum on terrace by the Yamuna. Garden to its south.

hist_pietra_dura.label: Pietra Dura
hist_pietra_dura.subject: history
hist_pietra_dura.detail: Technique of placing coloured hard stones in depressions carved into marble or sandstone creating ornate patterns. Used extensively in Shah Jahan's constructions including depictions of Orpheus at Red Fort.

hist_shahjahanabad.label: Shahjahanabad (Old Delhi)
hist_shahjahanabad.subject: history
hist_shahjahanabad.detail: New city built by Shah Jahan in Delhi. Imperial palace commanded the river-front. Only favoured nobles like Dara Shukoh given river access. Contains the Red Fort and Jami Masjid.

hist_diwan_i_khas.label: Diwan-i Khas
hist_diwan_i_khas.subject: history
hist_diwan_i_khas.detail: Hall of private audience in Mughal palaces. Shah Jahan's hall resembled a mosque with the throne on a qibla-like pedestal. Series of pietra dura inlays of Orpheus behind the throne symbolised just rule.

hist_aurangzeb.label: Aurangzeb (1658-1707)
hist_aurangzeb.subject: history
hist_aurangzeb.detail:
Last great Mughal emperor, title Alamgir. Re-imposed jizya on non-Muslims. Despite reputation for orthodoxy, gave grants to Hindu and Jaina institutions and issued farmans for temple repair. Corresponded respectfully with Hindu Jogis. After his death, central authority declined rapidly.

Title Alamgir. Major campaigns: Ahoms defeated 1663 but rebelled 1680s (Battle of Saraighat 1671 lost to Lachit Borphukan). Yusufzai Pashtun revolt 1667. Sikh campaigns — executed Guru Tegh Bahadur 1675. Rathor-Marwar rebellion after Jaswant Singh's death 1678. Shivaji visit to Agra 1666, insulted, escaped, rebuilt state. Son Prince Akbar rebelled, fled to Marathas then Safavids. Bijapur annexed 1685, Golconda 1687. From 1698 Aurangzeb personally led Deccan campaigns vs Maratha guerrilla warfare until death 1707. Also faced Jat (Gokla 1669) and Satnami (1672) rebellions.

Religious policy execution: appointed muhtasibs (morality-enforcement officers) in provinces from 1666 to enforce shariat; issued zawabits (secular decrees supplementing shariat) compiled as Zawabit-i-Alamgiri; commissioned Fatawa-i-Alamgiri (30-volume Hanafi legal compendium) c. 1667-75. Discontinued jharoka darshan 1669 as superstitious; banned kalma-inscribed coins; suspended tula-dan ceremony in principle (exception made for sons on illness recovery). Destroyed Vishwanath temple Kashi 1669, Keshava Rai Mathura 1670 (latter built by Bir Singh Bundela under Jahangir); many Marwar/Udaipur temples demolished during 1679-80 Rajput war as punishment. Jizya reimposed 2 April 1679 — collected by specially-appointed Muslim amins, proceeds earmarked for ulama employment; caused Delhi merchant sit-ins and killing of collectors. Temple destruction abated post-1679 — no major south-India destruction 1681-1707. Hindu share of nobility rose to ~1/3 by late reign vs ~1/4 under Shah Jahan. Reputation as zinda pir (living saint); accomplished veena player himself despite banning court singing 1668-69. Banned musicians from court (but instrumental + naubat continued); pensioned off musicians. Died Aurangabad 3 March 1707.

hist_francois_bernier.label: Francois Bernier
hist_francois_bernier.subject: history
hist_francois_bernier.detail:
French doctor, political philosopher and historian in India 1656-1668. Physician to Prince Dara Shukoh, then associated with Danishmand Khan. Dedicated writings to Louis XIV. Constantly compared India unfavourably with Europe. His works reprinted 8 times in French by 1725.

Career detail (from NCERT 12p2 Ch 5): doctor + political philosopher + historian. In India 12 years (1656-1668). First physician to Prince Dara Shukoh, then associated with Danishmand Khan (Armenian noble at Mughal court) as intellectual-scientist. Dedicated major writing to Louis XIV. Published in France 1670-71 (Histoire de la Dernière Révolution des États du Grand Mogol + Voyage dans les États du Grand Mogol); translated to English, Dutch, German, Italian within 5 years. Reprinted 8 times in French (1670-1725), 3 times in English by 1684 — massive dissemination vs Arabic/Persian accounts that circulated only as manuscripts before 1800.

hist_bernier_land_ownership.label: Bernier's Land Ownership Theory
hist_bernier_land_ownership.subject: history
hist_bernier_land_ownership.detail:
Bernier argued the Mughal emperor owned all land, unlike Europe where private property existed. This created a 'bleak scenario' of ruin. His view influenced European thinkers including Montesquieu and Karl Marx who developed the concept of Oriental Despotism. Assessment was not always accurate.

Bernier observed Shah Jahan's artillery during 1664 Kashmir trip — praised the light artillery ('artillery of the stirrup'): 50 brass pieces on painted carriages drawn by 2 horses + 1 reserve. Even while critical of Mughal over-centralisation he noted this section as well-appointed.

hist_oriental_despotism.label: Oriental Despotism Concept
hist_oriental_despotism.subject: history
hist_oriental_despotism.detail: European political theory partly based on Bernier's observations. Montesquieu used Bernier's account to develop the idea. Karl Marx used it to argue Asiatic societies lacked private property. Later scholars challenged this characterisation as inaccurate oversimplification.

hist_khalsa.label: Khalsa
hist_khalsa.subject: history
hist_khalsa.detail:
Instituted by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699. The Sikh community became a political entity called Khalsa Panth. Believed their destiny was to rule (raj karega khalsa). Led to politicisation of Sikh movement.

Instituted by Guru Gobind Singh at Anandpur on Baisakhi 13 April 1699. Panj Piyare ('Five Beloved Ones') ritual — five volunteers from diverse castes drank amrit from a single steel bowl signifying caste abolition; all took surname Singh (men) or Kaur (women). Five K symbols (Panj Kakaar): kesh (uncut hair), kangha (comb), kara (steel bracelet), kirpan (sword), kachera (cotton undergarment). Khalsa Panth became political community pledged to rule (raj karega khalsa). Militarised after 1704 Anandpur siege + 1705 Chamkaur battle (Guru's two elder sons died in battle); two younger sons (Zorawar Singh + Fateh Singh, age 7 and 9) bricked alive at Sirhind by faujdar Wazir Khan. Sikh tradition commemorates 21 December as Shaheedi Saptah. Miri-Piri (temporal-spiritual dual authority) doctrine from Guru Har Govind underpinned militarisation.

hist_rajput_watan_jagirs.label: Rajput Watan Jagirs
hist_rajput_watan_jagirs.subject: history
hist_rajput_watan_jagirs.detail:
Rajput kings of Amber and Jodhpur enjoyed considerable autonomy in their hereditary territories. In 18th century claimed subadari of Gujarat and Malwa. Sawai Jai Singh founded Jaipur and built observatories.

Sisodiya Rajputs of Mewar (Chittor fort) were the longest holdouts — refused Mughal authority through Akbar's reign despite Chittor's 1568 fall and Haldighati 1576. Their 1615 submission to Jahangir (via Amar Singh I) marked the end of serious Rajput resistance. Defeated but honourably treated: returned watan (hereditary land) as watan jagir — a hereditary assignment distinct from the typical transferable jagir. Key institutional innovation enabling Mughal-Rajput stability.

Origin: Raja Bharmal Kachhwaha of Amber submitted 1562; gave daughter Harkha Bai (Mariam-uz-Zamani) to Akbar — mother of Jahangir. Chittor 1568: 30,000 massacre, Jaimal + Patta died heroically — Akbar installed stone statues on elephants outside Agra Fort main gate. Ranthambhor 1569. Haldighati 1576 held by Rana Pratap. Mewar holdout finally settled by Jahangir 1615 via Prince Khurram — terms preserved honour: no personal homage required, son Karan Singh attended court instead, 5000 rank given, Chittor restored but fortifications not to be repaired. Marwar: Chandrasen rebelled post-1562 → direct Mughal admin → later restored to his elder brother Udai Singh who married daughter Jagat Gosain/Jodha Bai to Prince Salim (she became mother of Shah Jahan) — traditional Hindu baraat rituals followed, unlike earlier dola-form transfers.

hist_mughal_decline.label: Decline of Mughal Empire
hist_mughal_decline.subject: history
hist_mughal_decline.detail:
After Aurangzeb's death in 1707, the empire fragmented. Causes: depleted resources from Deccan wars, inefficient administration, powerful mansabdars, peasant rebellions, and invasions by Nadir Shah (1739) and Ahmad Shah Abdali.

Primary structural cause: **jagirdari crisis**. Gap between paper income (jama-dami) and actual collection widened from mid-17c. Mansabdar count exploded: 2,069 at Jahangir's 1605 accession → 8,000 under Shah Jahan 1637 → 11,456 under Aurangzeb late reign — jagirs became 'one pomegranate among a hundred sick' per contemporary historian Khafi Khan. Deccan conquest strained rather than funded — best jagirs kept in khalisa to fund the war; Karnataka jagirs yielded nothing due to unsettlement. Aurangzeb's specific political misjudgments per Satish Chandra: refusal to befriend Shivaji 1666 (Jai Singh's advice ignored); execution of Sambhaji 1689 (removed negotiating partner); prolonged Marwar war 1679-1698; Guru Tegh Bahadur execution 1675 radicalised Sikhs; inability to trust Shahu 1703 negotiated settlement. Structural causes also include: mansabdari army obsolescence (cavalry-dominated vs emerging flint-gun infantry + mobile field artillery); zamindar empowerment across the empire producing local bases of resistance; breakdown of administrative checks-and-balances without competent monarch.

hist_banda_bahadur.label: Banda Bahadur
hist_banda_bahadur.subject: history
hist_banda_bahadur.detail: Led Khalsa revolt against Mughal authority after Guru Gobind Singh's death in 1708. Struck coins in names of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh. Established administration between Sutlej and Jamuna. Captured 1715, executed 1716.

hist_bengal_state.label: Bengal State
hist_bengal_state.subject: history
hist_bengal_state.detail: Under Murshid Quli Khan who was naib (deputy). Transferred Mughal jagirdars to Orissa, reassessed revenues. Revenue collected strictly in cash. Jagat Seth banking house prospered under Alivardi Khan.

hist_awadh_state.label: Awadh State
hist_awadh_state.subject: history
hist_awadh_state.detail: Founded by Burhan-ul-Mulk Sa'adat Khan in 1722. Controlled rich Ganga plain trade route. Combined subadari, diwani and faujdari offices. Reduced Mughal jagirdars. Used revenue farmers (ijaradars) and bankers.

hist_hyderabad_state.label: Hyderabad State
hist_hyderabad_state.subject: history
hist_hyderabad_state.detail: Founded by Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah (1724-1748). Appointed mansabdars, granted jagirs. Ruled independently though nominally under Mughal emperor. Struggled against Marathas, Telugu nayakas and British.

hist_ijaradari.label: Ijaradari (Revenue Farming)
hist_ijaradari.subject: history
hist_ijaradari.detail: Practice of selling tax collection rights to highest bidders. Bankers guaranteed payments. Revenue farmers given freedom in assessment. Disapproved by Mughals but spread across 18th-century India.

hist_nadir_shah_invasion.label: Nadir Shah's Invasion
hist_nadir_shah_invasion.subject: history
hist_nadir_shah_invasion.detail: Iranian ruler who sacked Delhi in 1739, looting the Peacock throne and immense wealth. Devastated the city and its residents. Many notables fled to Bharatpur. Accelerated Mughal decline.

hist_suraj_mal.label: Suraj Mal
hist_suraj_mal.subject: history
hist_suraj_mal.detail: Jat ruler who consolidated the state at Bharatpur (1756-1763). Provided refuge to Delhi notables during Nadir Shah's invasion. His son Jawahir Shah had 30,000 own troops plus hired Maratha and Sikh forces.

hist_sikh_state.label: Sikh Political Formation
hist_sikh_state.subject: history
hist_sikh_state.detail: Organised into jathas then misls. Combined forces called dal khalsa. Met at Amritsar for gurmatas. Rakhi system offered protection for 20% tax. Struck sovereign coins in 1765. Maharaja Ranjit Singh unified in 1799.

hist_jat_state.label: Jat State
hist_jat_state.subject: history
hist_jat_state.detail:
Prosperous agriculturists who consolidated power in late 17th-18th centuries. Under Churaman, dominated between Delhi and Agra. Under Suraj Mal, Bharatpur became a strong state with Lohagarh fort.

First revolt: Gokla, zamindar of Tilpat (Mathura region), 1669 — Aurangzeb marched in person to crush; 20,000 Jats no match for imperial army; Gokla captured and executed. Second revolt: Rajaram 1685 — used guerrilla tactics combined with plunder. Raja Bishan Singh Kachhwaha appointed faujdar of Mathura to crush; complicated by Rajput-Jat zamindari conflict (Rajputs as intermediary zamindars over primary Jat peasant-zamindars). Rajaram killed 1688; succeeded by nephew Churaman who submitted by 1691. Churaman then used 18c Mughal weakness to carve independent Jat principality 1695-1721 around Bharatpur — ancestor of Bharatpur state consolidated under Suraj Mal.

hist_sawai_jai_singh.label: Sawai Jai Singh
hist_sawai_jai_singh.subject: history
hist_sawai_jai_singh.detail: Ruler of Amber who founded Jaipur as his new capital. Governor of Agra (12 years) and Malwa (5-6 years). Built five astronomical observatories (Jantar Mantar) at Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Mathura and Varanasi.

hist_shivaji.label: Shivaji
hist_shivaji.subject: history
hist_shivaji.detail:
Founder of the Maratha kingdom (1627-1680). Used mobile peasant-pastoralist forces to challenge Mughals. Born to Shahji and Jijabai. After his death, Peshwas wielded effective power from Poona.

Early conquests: Rajgarh, Kondana (later Sinhagad), Torna forts near Poona 1645-47 at age 18. Javli conquest 1656 by treachery from Chandra Rao More — secured Mavala highlands; Mavali foot soldiers became backbone. 1659 killed Bijapur noble Afzal Khan at Pratapgarh with concealed bagh-nakh. Shaista Khan night raid April 1663 at Lal Mahal Poona — killed Khan's son + cut off Khan's own fingers. First sack of Surat January 1664 (Mughal premier port). Treaty of Purandar June 1665 with Raja Jai Singh — surrendered 23 of 35 forts. Agra visit May 1666 — insulted as 5,000-mansab (equal to his minor son's rank); escaped 19 August 1666 hidden in sweet-baskets with son Sambhaji. Second Surat sack 1670. Battle of Salher 1672 — first pitched-battle victory vs Mughals. Coronation at Raigarh 6 June 1674 — priest Gaga Bhatta declared kshatriya; titles Chhatrapati and Haindava-Dharmoddharak. Karnataka expedition 1676-78 via Qutb Shahi alliance (Madanna-Akkanna); captured Jinji, Vellore, Karnataka territories from half-brother Ekoji. Died at Raigarh April 1680. Administrative legacy: Ashtapradhan ministerial system; chauth + sardeshmukhi tribute system.

hist_maratha_empire.label: Maratha Empire
hist_maratha_empire.subject: history
hist_maratha_empire.detail:
Shivaji carved kingdom with warrior families (deshmukhs) and peasant-pastoralists (kunbis). Under Peshwas, expanded from Deccan to Delhi (1737). Collected chauth (25%) and sardeshmukhi (9-10%). Sardars: Sindhia, Gaekwad, Bhonsle.

Maratha rise was gradual, nurtured by Deccani Sultanates well before Shivaji. Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur employed ~30,000 Maratha bargis, introduced Marathi in revenue accounts. Leading Maratha families: Bhonsles (Ghorpade lineage), Mores, Nimbalkars, Ghatges, Dafles (Chavans). 'Peshwa' title was used in Ahmadnagar before Marathas — first given to Brahmin Kankoji Narsi. Malik Ambar's guerrilla-with-Marathas model against the Mughals directly inspired Shivaji's tactics. Father-in-law of Shahji Bhonsle was Jadhav Rao (murdered 1629) — this event drove Shahji to Mughal service.

hist_chauth.label: Chauth
hist_chauth.subject: history
hist_chauth.detail: 25% of land revenue claimed by zamindars, collected by Marathas in the Deccan. Along with sardeshmukhi (9-10%), formed the basis of Maratha revenue collection across expanding territories.

hist_peshwas.label: Peshwas
hist_peshwas.subject: history
hist_peshwas.detail: Chitpavan Brahmana family who served as principal ministers to Shivaji's successors. Made Poona the Maratha capital. Baji Rao I expanded beyond Vindhyas into Malwa, Bundelkhand and Gujarat.

hist_mughal_agrarian_system.label: Mughal Agrarian System
hist_mughal_agrarian_system.subject: history
hist_mughal_agrarian_system.detail:
85% of India's 16th-17th century population lived in villages. State derived bulk of income from agriculture. Revenue assessed and collected in cash. Two types of peasants: khud-kashta (resident) and pahi-kashta (non-resident cultivators). Two crop seasons: kharif (autumn) and rabi (spring).

Land classified (Akbar/Ain system): polaj — continuously cultivated every year; parauti — fallow 1-2 years to recover; chachar — fallow 3-4 years; banjar — uncultivated 5+ years. Three quality grades (good/middling/bad); average of three × 1/3 = royal due. Collection methods: kankut (crop-estimate), batai/bhaoli (post-harvest crop-share), khet-batai (pre-harvest field-division), lang batai (post-harvest heap-division). Two crop seasons: kharif (autumn) + rabi (spring); do-fasla (two crops) standard, three crops where irrigation sufficient. Production diversity: Agra produced 39 crops, Delhi 43, Bengal 50 rice varieties. Jama (assessed) vs hasil (actually collected). Forest cover averaged ~40%. Assessment officer = amin; collector = amil-guzar.

hist_mughal_zamindars.label: Mughal Zamindars
hist_mughal_zamindars.subject: history
hist_mughal_zamindars.detail: Rural elites who held extensive personal lands (milkiyat), collected revenue on behalf of the state and received financial compensation. Had fortresses and military resources. Some women were zamindars, including the famous Rajshahi zamindari in 18th-century Bengal.

hist_mughal_revenue_system.label: Mughal Revenue System
hist_mughal_revenue_system.subject: history
hist_mughal_revenue_system.detail: Revenue assessed in cash based on crop type and productivity. Collected through zamindars and state officials. Records maintained by patwari (village accountant). State demanded a share of agricultural produce. Excessive demands led to peasant resistance including village desertion.

hist_village_panchayat_mughal.label: Village Panchayat (Mughal Era)
hist_village_panchayat_mughal.subject: history
hist_village_panchayat_mughal.detail: Assembly of village elders, usually heterogeneous in mixed-caste villages. Headed by muqaddam/mandal chosen by consensus, ratified by zamindar. Functions: village accounts, caste boundary enforcement, dispute resolution, collecting common funds. Could expel members for caste violations.

hist_jins_i_kamil.label: Jins-i Kamil (Perfect Crops)
hist_jins_i_kamil.subject: history
hist_jins_i_kamil.detail: Term for high-value commercial crops that brought more revenue. Included cotton (central India, Deccan), sugarcane (Bengal), oilseeds and lentils. State encouraged their cultivation. Subsistence and commercial production were closely intertwined in average peasant holdings.

hist_mughal_irrigation.label: Mughal Irrigation
hist_mughal_irrigation.subject: history
hist_mughal_irrigation.detail: Monsoons were backbone of agriculture. Additional irrigation through wells, tanks and canals. Persian wheels (in Punjab), bucket systems (in Agra). State supported canal construction: shahnahr in Punjab during Shah Jahan's reign. Babur Nama describes various irrigation devices.

hist_new_world_crops.label: New World Crops in India
hist_new_world_crops.subject: history
hist_new_world_crops.detail: 17th century saw introduction of crops from the Americas: maize via Africa and Spain, tomatoes, potatoes, chillies, pineapple, papaya. Tobacco arrived in Deccan, spread to north India by early 1600s. Akbar encountered tobacco in 1604; Jahangir banned it (ineffectively).

hist_women_agrarian_society.label: Women in Mughal Agrarian Society
hist_women_agrarian_society.subject: history
hist_women_agrarian_society.detail: Worked alongside men: sowing, weeding, threshing, winnowing. Artisanal tasks: spinning, pottery, embroidery. Bride-price (not dowry) paid in many rural communities. Remarriage of widows was legitimate. Women zamindars existed. But male-headed households and menstrual taboos persisted.

hist_jajmani_system.label: Jajmani System
hist_jajmani_system.subject: history
hist_jajmani_system.detail: System where village artisans (potters, blacksmiths, carpenters, barbers, goldsmiths) provided services in return for share of harvest or land allotment decided by panchayat. In Maharashtra, such lands became hereditary miras or watan. Cash remuneration was also sometimes used.

hist_tribal_forest_communities.label: Forest and Tribal Communities
hist_tribal_forest_communities.subject: history
hist_tribal_forest_communities.detail: Huge swathes of forest (jangal) covered substantial territory beyond settled agriculture. Forest dwellers engaged in hunting-gathering, shifting cultivation and trade in forest products (honey, beeswax, gum). Mughal state attempted to bring them into agricultural economy.

hist_caste_rural_mughal.label: Caste in Mughal Rural Society
hist_caste_rural_mughal.subject: history
hist_caste_rural_mughal.detail: Deep inequities based on caste. Agricultural labourers (majur) from lowest castes had least resources. Muslim communities also had hierarchies: halalkhoran (scavengers) housed outside villages. Some castes rose through profitable activities: Ahirs, Gujars, Malis through cattle-rearing and horticulture.

hist_mughal_population_growth.label: Mughal Era Population Growth
hist_mughal_population_growth.subject: history
hist_mughal_population_growth.detail: India's population grew by about 50 million between 1600 and 1800, roughly 33% increase over 200 years. Driven by varied agricultural production and slow demographic growth despite periodic famines and epidemics.

hist_cotton_textile_mughal.label: Cotton and Textile Production
hist_cotton_textile_mughal.subject: history
hist_cotton_textile_mughal.detail: Cotton grown over central India and Deccan plateau. Bengal famous for sugar and fine textiles. Weavers producing for export received advances in cash. Cotton, silk and indigo were major commercial products. Artisans participated in both domestic and international markets.

hist_peasant_resistance_mughal.label: Peasant Resistance
hist_peasant_resistance_mughal.subject: history
hist_peasant_resistance_mughal.detail: Peasants petitioned panchayats against excessive taxation and begar (forced unpaid labour). When reconciliation failed, cultivators deserted villages - an effective weapon given available uncultivated land and competition over labour. Petitions from lowest social strata documented in Rajasthan and Maharashtra archives.

hist_coparcenary_inheritance.label: Coparcenary Inheritance
hist_coparcenary_inheritance.subject: history
hist_coparcenary_inheritance.detail: Mughal/Timurid custom dividing inheritance among all sons, not just the eldest (primogeniture). Led to frequent succession conflicts and rebellions by princes, weakening the dynasty over time.

hist_surat.label: Surat
hist_surat.subject: history
hist_surat.detail: Gujarat port that was the emporium of western trade during Mughal period. Gateway to Mecca for pilgrim ships. Textiles with gold lace borders (zari). Hundis honoured in Cairo, Basra and Antwerp. Declined as Bombay rose.

hist_masulipatnam.label: Masulipatnam (Machlipatnam)
hist_masulipatnam.subject: history
hist_masulipatnam.detail: Port on Krishna river delta, chief port of Golconda. Dutch built a fort there. Fierce competition among Golconda nobles, Persian merchants, Telugu Chettis and Europeans. Declined after Mughal annexation of Golconda.

hist_hundi_system.label: Hundi System
hist_hundi_system.subject: history
hist_hundi_system.detail: Notes recording deposits that could be claimed at another place. Used by Surat's mahajans (moneychangers). Surat hundis were honoured in far-off markets of Cairo, Basra and Antwerp.

hist_chintz.label: Chintz
hist_chintz.subject: history
hist_chintz.detail: From Hindi chhint — cotton printed with small flowery designs. From 1680s a craze in England and Europe for texture and relative cheapness. Prompted Calico Act 1720.

hist_muslin.label: Muslin
hist_muslin.subject: history
hist_muslin.detail: Term from Mosul (Iraq) where Europeans first saw fine Indian cotton via Arab traders. Came to mean any finely woven cloth. Dacca mulmul celebrated.

hist_indian_textile_trade.label: Indian Textile Trade (pre-1750)
hist_indian_textile_trade.subject: history
hist_indian_textile_trade.detail: Before 1750, India was world's largest cotton textile producer. Extensively traded to SE Asia, West + Central Asia, Europe. European companies bought Indian textiles (muslin, calico, chintz) and re-sold at large profits.

hist_dacca_textile_centre.label: Dacca Textile Centre
hist_dacca_textile_centre.subject: history
hist_dacca_textile_centre.detail: Foremost 18c East Bengal textile city, famous for mulmul and jamdani. Weaving industry devastated by British manufactured imports from 1830s — population fell sharply, weavers displaced.

hist_mughal_court.label: Mughal Court Culture
hist_mughal_court.subject: history
hist_mughal_court.detail:
Heart of empire where political alliances were forged, status defined. Capital cities shifted: Agra, Delhi, Lahore, Fatehpur Sikri. Court rituals included jharokha darshan (public appearance), formal salutations. Elaborate hierarchy with mansab system ranking nobles.

Takht (throne) conceived as axis mundi (world-pillar); canopy symbolically separated imperial radiance from sun's. Darbar etiquette: kornish (right palm to forehead + bow), sijda (complete prostration), chahar taslim (Shah Jahan's innovation — four back-of-hand-on-ground salutations), zaminbos (kissing the ground). Jharoka darshan was Akbar's innovation — daily sunrise appearance at east-facing balcony for public viewing, extending imperial authority into popular faith. Daily rhythm: jharoka (sunrise) → Diwan-i-Am (public audience, one hour) → Diwan-i-Khas (private audience, confidential matters). Three annual festivals: solar birthday, lunar birthday, Nauroz (Iranian New Year on vernal equinox). Tula-dan ceremony: emperor weighed against gold/silver/grain/cloth on birthdays, quantities distributed as charity.

hist_mughal_painting.label: Mughal Painting Tradition
hist_mughal_painting.subject: history
hist_mughal_painting.detail:
Miniature paintings accompanied chronicles. Called taswir by Abu'l Fazl who held it in high esteem. Akbar defended painting against orthodox ulama opposition. Artists from Iran (Mir Sayyid Ali, Abdus Samad) brought by Humayun. Hindu artists praised by Abu'l Fazl as surpassing conception.

Under Akbar: ~100+ painters employed at imperial karkhana. Masters Mir Sayyid Ali + Abdus Samad (brought from Safavid court by Humayun) trained Indian apprentices — leading Hindu painters Daswant, Basawan, Kesav Das, Miskin, Mukund, Lal. Multi-artist collaboration common (faces/bodies/feet by different specialists). Jahangir era: climax of portrait and natural-history painting — master Ustad Mansur ('Nadir-ul-Asr') celebrated for zebra, Siberian crane and floral studies. European perspective + foreshortening adopted from Jesuit-brought paintings. Shah Jahan era: formal, static idealised portraits. Aurangzeb's lack of interest dispersed artists to regional courts — Rajasthani schools flourished (Mewar, Kishangarh, Bundi, Kota, Marwar, Amber); Pahari schools developed (Basohli early, Guler mid, Kangra late). Tradition revived partially in 18c under Muhammad Shah.

**Tasvir Khana** = Akbar's formal salaried art studio (overlaps with kitabkhana atelier). Monumental illustrated manuscripts under Akbar: **Hamzanama** (1562-77, 14 volumes, 1400+ folios — largest Mughal atelier project ever); **Tutinama** (Tales of a Parrot, c. 1560-65 — early formative work); **Anvar-i-Suhaili** (illustrated fables); **Razmnama** (Persian Mahabharata, supervised by Faizi). Under Jahangir: decorated margins around paintings sometimes rivalled the paintings themselves; naturalistic studies of flora/fauna; **Ayar-i-Danish** (Touchstone of Knowledge, illustrated animal fable). Under Shah Jahan: shift to pencil drawing (from charcoal), increased gold + silver, brighter palette, but formal static idealisation replaced Jahangir's naturalism. Dispersal under Aurangzeb seeded regional Rajasthani + Pahari + Deccani schools.

hist_persian_language_mughals.label: Persian as Court Language
hist_persian_language_mughals.subject: history
hist_persian_language_mughals.detail: Akbar consciously elevated Persian to language of empire. Conferred power on those who commanded it. Used for administration at all levels. Influenced Rajasthani, Marathi and Tamil official records. Interaction with Hindavi created Urdu. Mahabharata translated as Razmnama.

hist_mughal_manuscripts.label: Mughal Manuscript Production
hist_mughal_manuscripts.subject: history
hist_mughal_manuscripts.detail: All books were handwritten manuscripts produced in imperial kitabkhana (scriptorium). Involved paper makers, calligraphers, gilders, painters, bookbinders. Akbar's favourite calligraphic style was nastaliq. Muhammad Husayn of Kashmir earned title zarrin qalam (golden pen).

hist_printing_india.label: Printing in India (pre-1857)
hist_printing_india.subject: history
