hist_printing_india.detail: Portuguese missionaries brought printing to Goa 1550s. First Tamil book printed at Cochin 1579. First Hindi print 1805. Missionaries printed scriptures in Indian languages. First Bengali newspaper Samachar Darpan 1818 (Serampore). Enabled Bengal Renaissance debates.

hist_tulsidas.label: Tulsidas
hist_tulsidas.subject: history
hist_tulsidas.detail: Conceived God as Rama. Wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi, important both as devotional work and literary achievement. Accepted existing beliefs but made them accessible to all people.

hist_surdas.label: Surdas
hist_surdas.subject: history
hist_surdas.detail: Ardent devotee of Krishna whose compositions were compiled in Sursagara, Surasaravali and Sahitya Lahari. Contemporary of Tulsidas and Mirabai in the north Indian bhakti movement.

hist_mirabai.label: Mirabai
hist_mirabai.subject: history
hist_mirabai.detail: Rajput princess devotee of Krishna, c. 16th century. Defied family and societal norms through her devotion. Compositions widely sung across North India. Her songs express intense personal devotion (prem bhakti) to Krishna, whom she regarded as her husband.

hist_kathak.label: Kathak Dance
hist_kathak.subject: history
hist_kathak.detail: Dance form derived from katha (story). Originally temple story-tellers in north India. Evolved through bhakti movement rasa lila. Developed in Mughal courts. Two gharanas: Jaipur and Lucknow under Wajid Ali Shah.

hist_basohli_painting.label: Basohli School of Painting
hist_basohli_painting.subject: history
hist_basohli_painting.detail:
Bold and intense style of miniature painting that developed in the Himalayan foothills by late 17th century. Most popular text painted was Bhanudatta's Rasamanjari. Preceded the Kangra school.

First patron Raja Kirpal Singh of Basohli commissioned paintings of Bhanudatta's Rasamanjari (Bouquet of Delight), Gita Govinda, Ramayana. Master painter **Devi Das** famous for Radha-Krishna scenes + portraits in white garments. Colour palette borrowed from Malwa paintings — primary red/yellow/green with strong contrast. Characteristic facial features: receding hairline, large lotus-petal eyes, expressive faces. Preceded Kangra chronologically and stylistically — stylistic parent of the broader Pahari tradition.

hist_kangra_school.label: Kangra School of Painting
hist_kangra_school.subject: history
hist_kangra_school.detail:
Founded after Nadir Shah's 1739 invasion drove Mughal artists to Himalayan foothills. Soft colours including cool blues and greens. Lyrical treatment of Vaishnavite themes. Breathed new spirit into miniature painting.

Founded under Raja Govardhan Singh 1774 when Mughal-trained artists migrated from post-Nadir-Shah Delhi. Peak under Raja Sansar Chand (r. 1775-1823). Dominant themes: Gita Govinda, Bhagavata Purana, Satsai of Biharilal, Nala-Damayanti. 'Twelve Months' series depicts seasonal emotions. Soft blues + greens predominate; sensual yet restrained treatment. First developed at Guler (Nainsukh and Manaku tradition) before migrating to Kangra. Parent to sister Pahari ateliers at Kullu, Chamba, Mandi.

hist_battle_panipat_1526.label: First Battle of Panipat (1526)
hist_battle_panipat_1526.subject: history
hist_battle_panipat_1526.detail: Babur's victory over Ibrahim Lodi, Sultan of Delhi, on 21 April 1526. Babur fielded ~12,000 vs Lodi's ~100,000 but used superior tactics: tulughma (flanking divisions), araba (carts chained together as field fortification), and matchlock firearms plus field artillery under Ustad Ali Quli — first significant use of gunpowder in North Indian warfare. Ibrahim Lodi killed. Babur captured Delhi and Agra; founding battle of Mughal Empire.

hist_battle_khanwa_1527.label: Battle of Khanwa (1527)
hist_battle_khanwa_1527.subject: history
hist_battle_khanwa_1527.detail: Babur's victory over Rana Sanga of Mewar and confederated Rajput-Afghan forces on 17 March 1527 near Agra. Declared jihad and took title Ghazi. Used similar artillery-and-carts tactics as Panipat-I. Sanga was defeated but survived; died 1528. Decisive for Mughal security in Rajputana — broke back of organised Rajput opposition for a generation.

hist_battle_chanderi_1528.label: Battle of Chanderi (1528)
hist_battle_chanderi_1528.subject: history
hist_battle_chanderi_1528.detail: Babur's defeat of Medini Rai, Rajput noble holding the Chanderi fort in Malwa. After the fall, Rajput defenders performed jauhar. Consolidated Mughal control over Malwa; cleared the way to the final Afghan campaign east of the Ganga.

hist_battle_chausa_1539.label: Battle of Chausa (1539)
hist_battle_chausa_1539.subject: history
hist_battle_chausa_1539.detail: Sher Khan Suri's victory over Humayun at Chausa (Bihar) on 26 June 1539. Sher Khan's surprise night attack caught Humayun's camp unprepared. Humayun barely escaped swimming the Ganga on a water-carrier's skin (bhishti). Sher Khan assumed the title Sher Shah afterwards.

hist_battle_kanauj_1540.label: Battle of Kanauj / Bilgram (1540)
hist_battle_kanauj_1540.subject: history
hist_battle_kanauj_1540.detail: Sher Shah's second decisive victory over Humayun on 17 May 1540 at Kanauj (also called Battle of Bilgram). Ended Humayun's first reign — he fled via Sind to Persia. Sher Shah established Sur Empire, ruling Delhi 1540-45. Humayun would not return until 1555.

hist_war_of_succession_1658.label: Mughal War of Succession (1657-1658)
hist_war_of_succession_1658.subject: history
hist_war_of_succession_1658.detail: Four-way war among Shah Jahan's sons during his illness in late 1657. Aurangzeb (Deccan) allied with Murad (Gujarat); Dara Shukoh (heir-apparent, Delhi) backed by Shah Jahan; Shah Shuja (Bengal) moved separately. Key battles: Bahadurpur (Feb 1658) vs Shuja, Dharmat (April 1658) vs Rajput Jaswant Singh, Samugarh (May/June 1658) decisive vs Dara. Aurangzeb imprisoned Shah Jahan at Agra Fort. Dara captured 1659, charged with apostasy, executed. Murad executed 1661. Shuja fled to Arakan, disappeared 1661.

hist_bairam_khan.label: Bairam Khan
hist_bairam_khan.subject: history
hist_bairam_khan.detail:
Turkoman noble who served Babur and Humayun; guardian and regent (wakil) of young Akbar from 1556 to 1560. Won Second Battle of Panipat 1556 against Hemu (Hindu general of Afghan Adil Shah Suri), restoring Mughal rule. Dismissed 1560 when Akbar took personal charge; rebelled briefly, pardoned. Assassinated by Afghan at Patan, Gujarat, 1561, en route to Mecca. His widow married Akbar; son Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan became a leading noble and Hindi poet.

Title Khan-i-Khanan. After Akbar dismissed him 1560 he was treated cordially and offered choice of court / exile / Mecca; chose Mecca. Assassinated at Patan (Gujarat) 1561 by Afghan Mubarak Khan bearing personal grudge. Akbar married his widow Salima Sultan Begum (Akbar's own cousin) and raised Bairam's son as his own — this son became Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan, 7000-mansab noble and major Hindi poet.

hist_mirza_hakim.label: Mirza Hakim
hist_mirza_hakim.subject: history
hist_mirza_hakim.detail: Akbar's half-brother, ruler of Kabul (1554-1585). Invaded Punjab 1581 exploiting Akbar's distraction with Deccan and religious policy; threatened Lahore. Akbar led counter-campaign across Indus, Mirza Hakim submitted. After his death 1585, Kabul directly annexed. His revolt exposed Mughal vulnerability and accelerated Akbar's religious policy consolidation (Sulh-i-Kul, Din-i-Ilahi).

hist_dara_shukoh.label: Dara Shukoh
hist_dara_shukoh.subject: history
hist_dara_shukoh.detail: Shah Jahan's eldest son and designated heir (1615-1659). Sufi-influenced scholar; commissioned Persian translation of 52 Upanishads (Sirr-i-Akbar, 1657) — later basis for Anquetil-Duperron's Latin Oupnek'hat (1801), which shaped European knowledge of Hindu thought. Wrote Majma-ul-Bahrain (Confluence of Two Seas) comparing Sufism and Vedanta. Lost Samugarh 1658 to Aurangzeb; captured fleeing through Sind 1659, paraded in Delhi, executed for apostasy. His death foreclosed the syncretic Mughal path.

hist_amar_singh_mewar.label: Amar Singh I of Mewar
hist_amar_singh_mewar.subject: history
hist_amar_singh_mewar.detail: Sisodiya ruler of Mewar 1597-1620, son of Maharana Pratap. Continued resistance until Jahangir's sustained campaigns (1605-1615) led by Prince Khurram (Shah Jahan) forced submission in February 1615 at Gogunda. Terms were honourable: no personal appearance at Mughal court required (unique concession), hereditary Chittor returned as watan jagir, son Karan Singh attended court in his stead. End of the long Mewar-Mughal war; model for all later watan-jagir relationships.

hist_subadari_system.label: Mughal Provincial Administration (Subadari)
hist_subadari_system.subject: history
hist_subadari_system.detail:
Systematised under Akbar. Empire divided into 12 subas (provinces) initially, later 15 under Akbar and 22 under Aurangzeb. Each suba headed by a subadar (governor) handling political and military matters, paired with a diwan (provincial finance officer reporting directly to imperial diwan — deliberate check on subadar). Other provincial officers: bakhshi (military paymaster + intelligence), sadr (religious endowments/charity), faujdar (district military commander), kotwal (town police), amalguzar (revenue collector), qazi (judicial). Subas subdivided into sarkars, then parganas, then villages.

Pargana-level admin handled by three semi-hereditary officers: qanungo (keeper of revenue records), chaudhuri (revenue collection), qazi (judicial). Three central ministers — independent of each other but occasionally convened as advisory body: mir bakhshi (paymaster-general + recruitment, signs all appointment orders), diwan-i-ala (finance minister), sadr-us-sudur (grants of madad-i-maash + appointment of local qazis). Horse-branding (dagh) and soldier-identification (chehra) prevented muster fraud.

Formalised 1580 (24th regnal year): empire divided into 12 subas — Bengal, Bihar, Allahabad, Awadh, Agra, Delhi, Lahore, Multan, Kabul, Ajmer, Malwa, Gujarat. Each suba had parallel ministerial hierarchy (subadar + diwan + bakhshi + sadr + qazi + waqia-navis) — deliberate check-and-balance on subadar. Increased to 15 under Akbar (later additions), 22 under Aurangzeb.

hist_maktab_khana.label: Maktab Khana (Translation Bureau)
hist_maktab_khana.subject: history
hist_maktab_khana.detail:
Translation bureau established by Akbar at Fatehpur Sikri. Translated major Sanskrit works into Persian to bridge Hindu-Muslim intellectual worlds: Razmnamah (Mahabharata) by Faizi/Abul Fazl team 1584, Ramayana by Abdul Qadir Badauni 1589, Atharva Veda, Lilavati (Bhaskara's mathematics), Yogavashistha, Panchatantra, Raj Tarangini. Razmnamah copies lavishly illustrated in imperial ateliers — landmark cross-cultural project.

Output list: Singhasan Battisi, Atharva Veda, Bible (first into Persian), Mahabharata (Razmnamah — team of Faizi + Naqib Khan + Badauni + Abu'l Fazl), Ramayana (chief translator Badauni), Gita, Panchatantra, Raj Tarangini, Lilavati (Bhaskara math), Yogavashistha, and the Quran (first Persian translation). Project served Akbar's cultural-integration goal.

hist_bijapur_annexation_1685.label: Annexation of Bijapur (1685)
hist_bijapur_annexation_1685.subject: history
hist_bijapur_annexation_1685.detail: Aurangzeb ended the Adil Shahi dynasty of Bijapur in September 1685 after prolonged siege led by Prince Azam. Last ruler Sikandar Adil Shah imprisoned, died 1700. Bijapur absorbed into Mughal subas. Removed a check on Maratha expansion — ironically strengthened Shivaji's successors rather than Mughal authority in Deccan.

hist_golconda_annexation_1687.label: Annexation of Golconda (1687)
hist_golconda_annexation_1687.subject: history
hist_golconda_annexation_1687.detail: Aurangzeb ended the Qutb Shahi dynasty of Golconda in September 1687 after an 8-month siege. Last ruler Abul Hasan Tana Shah imprisoned at Daulatabad. Hyderabad city-fortress absorbed; famous diamond mines (Kollur, Panna) came under Mughal control. The fall was achieved by bribing a Golconda commander to open a gate. Ended the Deccan Sultanates as political entities.

hist_ahom_mughal_wars.label: Ahom-Mughal Wars (1615-1682)
hist_ahom_mughal_wars.subject: history
hist_ahom_mughal_wars.detail: Series of 17-18 military engagements between Ahom kingdom (Brahmaputra valley) and Mughals. Mir Jumla's 1662-63 campaign temporarily captured Garhgaon; disease and terrain forced withdrawal. Most famous: Battle of Saraighat (March 1671) — Ahom naval victory on the Brahmaputra under general Lachit Borphukan and king Chakradhwaj Singha defeated Mughal admiral Ram Singh I of Amber. Ahoms retained independence through 1826 (Yandabo treaty). Lachit celebrated as Assam national hero.

hist_abdul_hamid_lahori.label: Abdul Hamid Lahori
hist_abdul_hamid_lahori.subject: history
hist_abdul_hamid_lahori.detail: Official historian of Shah Jahan, pupil of Abu'l Fazl. Commissioned by Shah Jahan to author Badshah Nama on the Akbar Nama model. Wrote daftars 1-2 covering 1627-47 (first two decades of reign); old age prevented him from completing daftar 3 (taken up by Muhammad Waris). Revised by wazir Sadullah Khan.

hist_faizi.label: Faizi (Abu'l Faiz Faizi)
hist_faizi.subject: history
hist_faizi.detail: Elder brother of Abu'l Fazl; son of Shaikh Mubarak. Appointed Malik-ush-Shuara (poet laureate) by Akbar 1588. Co-translated Mahabharata into Persian as Razmnamah with team of scholars. Composed diwan of ghazals, masnavis (notably Nal-Daman). Sent as diplomatic envoy to Deccan sultanates 1591. Akbar's close companion alongside Abu'l Fazl; died 1595.

hist_mir_sayyid_ali.label: Mir Sayyid Ali Tabrizi
hist_mir_sayyid_ali.subject: history
hist_mir_sayyid_ali.detail: Persian painter brought to India by Humayun from the Safavid court c. 1549. Trained under Bihzad's disciples. Founding master of the imperial Mughal atelier alongside Abdus Samad. Worked on early Akbar-era illustrated manuscripts including Tutinama and Hamzanama. Fused Persian miniature tradition with Indian naturalism that would define Mughal painting.

hist_abdus_samad.label: Khwaja Abdus Samad
hist_abdus_samad.subject: history
hist_abdus_samad.detail: Persian painter (Shirazi, 'Shirin-qalam' — sweet-pen) brought with Mir Sayyid Ali by Humayun from Safavid court c. 1549. Co-founder of Mughal atelier. Personally trained young Akbar in drawing. Supervised the monumental Hamzanama project (1,400 folios, c.1562-1577). Later served as diwan of Multan. His son Muhammad Sharif became noble under Akbar and Jahangir.

hist_gulbadan_begum.label: Gulbadan Begum
hist_gulbadan_begum.subject: history
hist_gulbadan_begum.detail: Daughter of Babur, sister of Humayun, aunt of Akbar (c.1523-1603). Author of Humayun Nama — memoir of Babur's and Humayun's courts commissioned by Akbar via Abu'l Fazl as source material for Akbar Nama. Wrote fluently in Turkish and Persian. Her text is unique: not eulogistic but frank about family tensions and the mediating role of senior women. Led women's Hajj caravan 1575-1582.

hist_jahanara.label: Jahanara Begum
hist_jahanara.subject: history
hist_jahanara.detail: Eldest daughter of Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal (1614-1681). After Mumtaz's death 1631 became Padshah Begum (first lady). Annual income equal to highest mansabdars; received revenues of Surat port. Designed Chandni Chowk bazaar in Shahjahanabad and built a double-storey caravanserai there. Sided with father during succession war; voluntarily joined Shah Jahan's imprisonment at Agra Fort. Disciple of Qadiri sufi Mulla Shah; authored biography of Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti (Munis-ul-Arwah) and of Mulla Shah (Risala-i-Sahibiyah). Buried at Nizamuddin Dargah, Delhi, by her own request.

hist_badauni.label: Abdul Qadir Badauni
hist_badauni.subject: history
hist_badauni.detail: Orthodox theologian and courtier (1540-1615) at Akbar's court. Author of secret history Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh ('Selection of Chronicles', completed 1595) — not published in his lifetime for fear of imperial displeasure. Sharply critical of Akbar's religious experiments, Din-i-Ilahi, and Sulh-i-Kul. Counter-narrative to Abu'l Fazl's Akbar Nama. Also translated Ramayana and Mahabharata portions into Persian in the Maktab Khana.

hist_rodolfo_acquaviva.label: Rodolfo Acquaviva
hist_rodolfo_acquaviva.subject: history
hist_rodolfo_acquaviva.detail: Portuguese Jesuit (1550-1583), leader of the First Jesuit Mission to Akbar's court at Fatehpur Sikri (1580-1583). Accompanied by Antonio Monserrate and Francisco Henriques. Participated in Ibadat Khana debates. Returned to Goa 1583; martyred that July at Cuncolim, Salsette, while attempting conversion work. Later beatified.

hist_antonio_monserrate.label: Antonio Monserrate
hist_antonio_monserrate.subject: history
hist_antonio_monserrate.detail: Catalan Jesuit (1536-1600) of the First Jesuit Mission (1580-1583). Accompanied Akbar on his 1581 Kabul campaign. Wrote Mongolicae Legationis Commentarius — first detailed European description of Mughal court and empire. Prepared first European map of Mughal India. Tutored Prince Murad in Portuguese. Later captured by Arabs in Yemen 1589; ransomed 1596. Works rediscovered by H. Hosten 1906.

hist_thomas_roe.label: Sir Thomas Roe
hist_thomas_roe.subject: history
hist_thomas_roe.detail: English envoy of King James I to Jahangir's court (1615-1619). First formal English ambassador. Refused prostration (sijda) — bowed per European custom and scandalously demanded a chair at court. His gifted ring returned by Asaf Khan as worth only Rs 400. Won trading concessions for English East India Company at Surat. His Embassy Journal is a major European source for Jahangir's court. Later English diplomatic career included Ottoman and Holy Roman Empires.

hist_raja_bharmal_kachhwaha.label: Raja Bharmal Kachhwaha of Amber
hist_raja_bharmal_kachhwaha.subject: history
hist_raja_bharmal_kachhwaha.detail: Rajput raja of Amber (r. 1548-1574); first Rajput ruler to submit to Akbar and enter Mughal service January 1562. Gave his daughter Harkha Bai (Mariam-uz-Zamani) in marriage to Akbar at Sambhar — she became mother of Jahangir (1569). Received high mansab. His submission established the template for all later Rajput-Mughal alliances: marital + military service in exchange for watan jagir and autonomy within hereditary territory. Succeeded by grandson Man Singh.

hist_giovanni_careri.label: Giovanni Francesco Gemelli Careri
hist_giovanni_careri.subject: history
hist_giovanni_careri.detail: Italian adventurer-traveller (1651-1725); passed through Mughal India c. 1695 during Aurangzeb's reign as part of his round-the-world voyage (Giro del Mondo, published Naples 1699-1700). Account drew on Bernier and personal observation; vivid description of global silver flows into India. His work on Mexico and Philippines considered a primary source; Indian chapters describe Mughal wealth and coinage circulation.

hist_jharoka_darshan.label: Jharoka Darshan
hist_jharoka_darshan.subject: history
hist_jharoka_darshan.detail:
Ritual of emperor appearing at sunrise on an east-facing small balcony (jharoka) of the palace to give darshan (view) to a crowd of commoners, soldiers, merchants, craftspersons, peasants and women with sick children. Instituted by Akbar to broaden acceptance of imperial authority as part of popular faith — blending Rajput bhakti darshan tradition with Mughal ceremony. Continued under Jahangir and Shah Jahan. Aurangzeb discontinued it after 1669 on Islamic orthodoxy grounds.

Discontinued by Aurangzeb 1669 as superstitious and un-Islamic — ended Akbar's 90-year ritual of daily sunrise public appearance. Part of Aurangzeb's broader retreat from Akbarian ceremonial syncretism.

hist_mughal_court_etiquette.label: Mughal Court Etiquette
hist_mughal_court_etiquette.subject: history
hist_mughal_court_etiquette.detail: Cluster of ceremonial forms governing Mughal court. Salutations: kornish (right palm on forehead + bow — routine), sijda (complete prostration — highest submission), chahar taslim (Shah Jahan innovation — four back-of-hand-on-ground salutations), zaminbos (ground-kissing). Spatial rule: status = proximity to takht (throne — conceived as axis mundi). Canopy symbolised separation of imperial radiance from the sun's. Three annual celebrations: solar birthday, lunar birthday, Nauroz (Iranian vernal-equinox New Year). Tula-dan ceremony: emperor weighed against gold, silver, grain, silk, cloth, butter, oil — equivalents distributed to the poor. Gift economy: nazr (small monetary gift), peshkash (large gift), khilat (robe of honour), sarapa (head-to-foot set), padma murassa (jewelled lotus, exceptional).

hist_khud_kashta_pahi_kashta.label: Khud-kashta vs Pahi-kashta (Peasant Categories)
hist_khud_kashta_pahi_kashta.subject: history
hist_khud_kashta_pahi_kashta.detail: Two categories of peasants in 17c Mughal sources: khud-kashta — resident cultivators of their own village, with longer-standing land rights. Pahi-kashta — non-resident cultivators belonging to another village, working contractually elsewhere. Pahi-kashta status arose from choice (better revenue terms elsewhere) or compulsion (famine-driven displacement). Other terms used interchangeably for peasants: raiyat / riaya (Indo-Persian standard), muzarian, kisan, asami.

hist_silver_flow_mughal.label: Global Silver Flow into Mughal India
hist_silver_flow_mughal.subject: history
hist_silver_flow_mughal.detail: The 16-17c Mughal, Safavid, Ottoman and Ming empires created a linked Eurasian trading zone. Voyages of discovery brought American silver bullion (from Potosí and Zacatecas mines) into Europe → Ottoman/Persian transit → India (in exchange for textiles, spices, indigo). Japanese silver (Iwami mines) also flowed via Dutch ships. India had no native silver; imports stabilised the silver rupya (introduced by Sher Shah), enabling unprecedented coin-mint expansion and cash-revenue collection. Giovanni Careri's 1690s account: 'all the Gold and Silver which circulates throughout the World at last Centres here'. Underpinned monetisation of village economy and zamindari land market.

hist_qandahar_question.label: Qandahar — Mughal-Safavid Contest
hist_qandahar_question.subject: history
hist_qandahar_question.detail:
Strategic fortress-town guarding routes between Iran/Central Asia and India via the Bolan pass. Originally Humayun's; reconquered by Akbar 1595 from a Safavid governor. Safavid court continued to press claims. Jahangir sent embassy to Shah Abbas 1613 to plead Mughal retention — mission failed. 1622: Shah Abbas's army besieged Qandahar, ill-prepared Mughal garrison surrendered. Shah Jahan launched three sieges (1649, 1652, 1653) — all failed despite enormous expenditure and Prince Aurangzeb's involvement. Qandahar permanently lost to the Safavids. Strategic blow contributed to hardening of Mughal-Safavid relations for decades.

Full timeline recap: Part of Timurid empire until Uzbeks took 1507. Babur regained 1522. Shah Tahmasp captured 1540s post-Humayun-collapse. Akbar reconquered 1595. Shah Abbas I seized 1622 during Jahangir's reign (Prince Shah Jahan refused to lead relief — partially cited as cause of his own rebellion). Ali Mardan Khan defection restored to Shah Jahan 1638. Shah Abbas II seized again 1649 — Shah Jahan's three counter-sieges (Aurangzeb 1649, Aurangzeb 1652, Dara 1653) all failed despite heavy artillery. Aurangzeb abandoned the contest as futile. Loss bruised Mughal prestige more than strategic position.

hist_jizya_policy.label: Jizya Policy (Abolition → Reimposition → Final Abolition)
hist_jizya_policy.subject: history
hist_jizya_policy.detail: Cross-reign religious-policy thread. Akbar abolished pilgrimage tax on Hindus (1563) and jizya (poll-tax on non-Muslims, 1564) as incompatible with sulh-i-kul. Not collected under Jahangir or Shah Jahan. Aurangzeb reimposed jizya on 2 April 1679 as part of religious-orthodoxy turn, alongside pilgrimage-tax restoration and temple-destruction edicts (Vishwanath Kashi 1669, Kesava Deo Mathura 1670). Collection resisted — Delhi's Hindu merchants staged a sit-in protest. Jizya abolished again 1712 by Jahandar Shah (briefly) and definitively by Farrukhsiyar 1713. Key marker of shifting state-religion stance.

hist_kitabkhana.label: Imperial Kitabkhana (Mughal Scriptorium)
hist_kitabkhana.subject: history
hist_kitabkhana.detail: Imperial workshop for manuscript production, not merely a library as literal translation suggests. Held emperor's book collection and actively produced new manuscripts. Workforce: paper-makers (prepared folios), scribes/calligraphers (copied text), gilders (page illumination), painters (miniatures), bookbinders (ornamental covers). Calligraphers and painters held highest status; paper-makers and binders remained anonymous. Standard script: nastaliq (Akbar's favourite, fluid long horizontal strokes). Tools: qalam (trimmed reed, 5-10mm tip, split nib), siyahi (carbon ink). Notable calligrapher: Muhammad Husayn Kashmiri awarded title 'zarrin qalam' (golden pen) by Akbar. Major chronicle manuscripts averaged 150 full- or double-page paintings.

hist_mughal_information_system.label: Mughal Imperial Information System
hist_mughal_information_system.subject: history
hist_mughal_information_system.detail: Organised communication network of Mughal administration. Waqia-nawis (court writers, supervised by mir bakhshi) recorded all applications, farmans, court proceedings. Wakils (agents) of distant nobles and tributary rulers copied the daily Akhbarat-i-Darbar-i-Mualla (News from the Exalted Court) and relayed contents to their masters. Imperial postal service: qasid/pathmar foot-runners in round-the-clock relays carried paper rolled in bamboo containers; reports from distant provincial capitals reached the emperor in days. Akhbarats contained attendance, title grants, diplomatic receipts, emperor's health enquiries about officers — rich source for modern historians reconstructing public and private court life.

hist_first_jesuit_mission_1580.label: First Jesuit Mission to Akbar's Court (1580-1583)
hist_first_jesuit_mission_1580.subject: history
hist_first_jesuit_mission_1580.detail: Three Jesuit priests — Rodolfo Acquaviva (leader), Antonio Monserrate, Francisco Henriques — arrived at Akbar's court at Fatehpur Sikri in February 1580 at Akbar's invitation (via Goa embassy). Stayed ~3 years. Debated Christian doctrine in Ibadat Khana alongside ulama, Brahmans, Jains, Parsis. Accompanied Akbar on campaigns, tutored Prince Murad in Portuguese, companions in leisure hours. Akbar's interest was comparative religion, not conversion. Second Jesuit mission sent 1591 (Lahore), third 1595. Monserrate's Commentarius remained the best European description of Mughal court until Bernier.

hist_chain_of_justice.label: Chain of Justice (Zanjir-i-Adl)
hist_chain_of_justice.subject: history
hist_chain_of_justice.detail: Device instituted by Jahangir immediately after his 1605 accession to bypass corrupt officials. Pure gold chain, 30 gaz (~90 feet) long, with 60 bells attached; strung from a tower of Agra Fort to a stone column on the riverbank. Any petitioner denied justice could ring it — bells attracted imperial attention. Described by Jahangir in his memoirs Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri. Symbol drawn in court paintings (e.g., Abu'l Hasan's allegorical 'Jahangir shooting poverty'). Emblematic of Mughal ideology of just sovereignty as social contract (protecting jan/mal/namus/din) in exchange for obedience.

hist_battle_ghagra_1529.label: Battle of Ghagra (1529)
hist_battle_ghagra_1529.subject: history
hist_battle_ghagra_1529.detail: Babur's last major campaign. Faced combined forces of Afghans under Mahmud Lodi (brother of Ibrahim) + Nusrat Shah of Bengal (Husain Shahi) at confluence of Ghagra and Ganga rivers, May 1529. Crossed the river and forced retreat of Afghan-Bengal armies but could not win decisively. Patched up agreement — left Bihar largely under Afghan control, treaty with Nusrat Shah. Babur died shortly after at Agra December 1530.

hist_battle_second_panipat_1556.label: Second Battle of Panipat (1556)
hist_battle_second_panipat_1556.subject: history
hist_battle_second_panipat_1556.detail: 5 November 1556. Mughal forces under Bairam Khan (young Akbar also present) vs Hemu with 50,000 cavalry, 500 elephants, strong artillery. Hemu's artillery had been captured earlier by Mughal vanguard under Ali Quli Khan Shaibani. Battle swung in Hemu's favour until an arrow struck him in the eye and he fainted — leaderless Afghan army collapsed. Hemu captured and executed. Restored Mughal control over Delhi and Agra; marks beginning of Akbar's real reign.

hist_siege_chittor_1568.label: Siege of Chittor (1568)
hist_siege_chittor_1568.subject: history
hist_siege_chittor_1568.detail: Six-month siege of Chittor fortress by Akbar personally (September 1567 — February 1568). Rana Udai Singh II had evacuated to hills leaving Jaimal Rathore and Patta Sisodiya in charge of fort with ~8,000 Rajput warriors + peasants who had taken shelter. Akbar personally shot Jaimal with a musket named Sangram. After fort breached, 30,000 killed in Akbar's only major massacre of non-combatants. Rajput women performed jauhar. Akbar erected stone elephant-statues of Jaimal + Patta outside Agra Fort main gate. Signal event breaking Rajput confederal resistance.

hist_siege_ranthambhor_1569.label: Siege of Ranthambhor (1569)
hist_siege_ranthambhor_1569.subject: history
hist_siege_ranthambhor_1569.detail: Reputed most powerful fortress in Rajasthan. Akbar besieged March 1569 after Chittor fall. Rao Surjan Hada surrendered the fort after month-long siege with heavy artillery bombardment. Hada clan joined Mughal service (Rao Surjan placed in charge of Garh-Katanga, rose to 2000 mansab). Fall triggered wider Rajput submission — rulers of Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Bundi joined Akbar.

hist_battle_haldighati_1576.label: Battle of Haldighati (1576)
hist_battle_haldighati_1576.subject: history
hist_battle_haldighati_1576.detail: Fought 18 June 1576 below a narrow mountain defile near Kumbhalgarh. Mughal force ~5,000 led by Raja Man Singh + Asaf Khan III vs Rana Pratap's ~3,000 including Afghan contingent under Hakim Khan Sur + Bhil allies under Rana Punja. Pratap's initial onslaught broke Mughal centre; rumour that Akbar himself had arrived rallied Mughal troops. Pratap escaped on his horse Chetak (which died of wounds). Not a Hindu-Muslim battle — Afghans commanded Rana's van; Rajput Man Singh led Akbar's side. Last pitched battle; Pratap switched to guerrilla war thereafter. Mughals occupied Gogunda after but could not hold hill country long-term.

hist_conquest_gujarat_1572.label: Akbar's Conquest of Gujarat (1572-1573)
hist_conquest_gujarat_1572.subject: history
hist_conquest_gujarat_1572.detail: Ahmedabad surrendered without fight 1572. Akbar crossed the river Mahi with only 200 men (including Man Singh and Bhagwant Das of Amber) and routed Mirzas at Sarnal. At Cambay Akbar saw the sea for the first time — rode a boat; Portuguese merchants met him formally here. When rebellions broke out after Akbar's return to Agra, he made his famous forced march: 9 days across Rajasthan using camels/horses/carts; reached Ahmedabad on 11th day (journey normally took 6 weeks); defeated force of 20,000 with only 3,000 soldiers who could keep pace (Battle of Ahmedabad 1573). Gujarat added rich maritime trade + Surat port to Mughal control, frustrated Portuguese designs for territorial empire.

hist_bengal_conquest_1576.label: Conquest of Bengal & End of Afghan Rule (1574-1576)
hist_bengal_conquest_1576.subject: history
hist_bengal_conquest_1576.detail: Daud Khan Karrani declared independence from Akbar — last Afghan kingdom in north India. Akbar captured Patna 1574 to secure Bihar communications, left Khan-i-Khanan Munim Khan in charge of subsequent Bengal campaign. Daud forced to sue for peace, then rebelled again. Final defeat in Bihar 12 July 1576 — Daud Khan executed on the spot. Ended Afghan ascendancy that had begun under Sher Shah. Bengal became Mughal suba; Raja Man Singh later conquered Cooch-Bihar and parts of east Bengal including Dacca as governor.

hist_kashmir_annexation_1586.label: Kashmir Annexation (1586)
hist_kashmir_annexation_1586.subject: history
hist_kashmir_annexation_1586.detail: Akbar sent Raja Bhagwant Das + Qasim Khan to annex Kashmir in context of Uzbek Abdullah Khan threat. Yusuf Shah Chak surrendered after short campaign; his son Yaqub Shah continued resistance briefly. Ladakh (called Tibet Khurd — 'Little Tibet') and Baltistan (Tibet Buzurg — 'Greater Tibet') came under Mughal suzerainty; daughter of Baltistan chief married to Salim. Brought Himalayan trade routes under Mughal control. Kashmir became a favourite royal retreat under Jahangir and Shah Jahan (Shalimar Bagh, Nishat Bagh).

hist_sindh_annexation_1590.label: Sindh Annexation (1590)
hist_sindh_annexation_1590.subject: history
hist_sindh_annexation_1590.detail: Mirza Jani Beg Tarkhan of Thatta (lower Sindh) defeated by Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan 1590. Mirza Jani submitted 1593, joined Mughal service. Opened trade down the Indus river for Punjab produce. Upper Sindh (Bakhar) had been acquired earlier. Completed Mughal control of the entire Indus basin.

hist_hemu.label: Hemu (Hem Chandra Vikramaditya)
hist_hemu.subject: history
hist_hemu.detail: Rajput (Dhusar / Baniya caste origin) from Rewari. Started as superintendent of markets under Islam Shah Sur. Rose rapidly under Adil Shah (Sher Shah's nephew) to become wazir with title Vikramajit. Undefeated in 22 prior battles. Captured Agra from Mughal governor 1556; then defeated Mughal forces near Tughlaqabad and occupied Delhi. Proclaimed himself Raja Vikramaditya — last attempt at Hindu rule of Delhi before Mughal consolidation. At Second Panipat November 1556 commanded 50,000 cavalry + 500 elephants + artillery. Arrow-in-eye fluke cost him victory; captured and executed by Bairam Khan.

hist_rana_pratap.label: Maharana Pratap
hist_rana_pratap.subject: history
hist_rana_pratap.detail: Sisodiya ruler of Mewar 1572-1597 (1540-1597). Son of Rana Udai Singh II (founder of Udaipur). Refused to accept Mughal suzerainty despite embassies from Man Singh, Bhagwant Das, Todar Mal. Commanded at Battle of Haldighati 1576; his horse Chetak died carrying him to safety. Adopted guerrilla warfare thereafter; Mughal pressure relaxed post-1585 when Akbar moved to Lahore for 12-year Uzbek frontier vigil. Recovered most of Mewar including Kumbhalgarh and areas around Chittor (but not Chittor fort). Built new capital Chavand near Dungarpur c. 1585. Died June 1597 at age 51 from internal injury drawing a stiff bow. His son Amar Singh I settled with Jahangir 1615. Symbol of Rajput resistance; celebrated by later Rajput tradition.

hist_bahadur_shah_gujarat.label: Bahadur Shah of Gujarat
hist_bahadur_shah_gujarat.subject: history
hist_bahadur_shah_gujarat.detail: Gujarat Sultan 1526-1537, near-exact contemporary of Humayun. Overran and annexed Malwa. Besieged Chittor twice (1533 and 1534-35). Story of Rani Karnavati sending a rakhi to Humayun during the second siege appears in later legends but not contemporary sources. Financed Sher Khan's rise with heavy subsidies against the Mughals. Humayun's Gujarat campaign 1535 ousted him from Mandu and Champaner; he fled to Ahmedabad, then Kathiawar. Drowned 14 February 1537 in a scuffle with the Portuguese aboard a Portuguese ship near Diu — ended Gujarat's challenge to Mughal power.

hist_maham_anaga.label: Maham Anaga
hist_maham_anaga.subject: history
hist_maham_anaga.detail: Akbar's chief wet-nurse and foster-mother. Politically powerful in early reign 1556-1562 as virtual regent alongside Bairam Khan (then after his dismissal). Her clan included foster-brother Adham Khan. Withdrew from politics after Adham's execution 1562; died shortly after 1562. Built Khair-ul-Manazil mosque opposite Purana Qila in Delhi. Typical case of female political influence in Mughal harem that did not survive crises.

hist_adham_khan.label: Adham Khan
hist_adham_khan.subject: history
hist_adham_khan.detail: Son of Maham Anaga. Led expedition against Baz Bahadur of Malwa 1561, defeated him but committed notorious cruelties — death-forcing of Rupmati of Mandu into his harem, which led her suicide. Removed from Malwa command. Claimed the post of wazir when refused, stabbed acting wazir Atgah Khan in his own office on 16 May 1561. Akbar had him thrown twice off the Agra Fort parapet until dead. First major assertion of Akbar's personal authority over Maham Anaga's faction.

hist_abdur_rahim_khanan.label: Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan
hist_abdur_rahim_khanan.subject: history
hist_abdur_rahim_khanan.detail: Son of Bairam Khan (1556-1627). Raised as Akbar's ward after father's assassination 1561. Rose to 7000 mansab (rare honour). Khan-i-Khanan title held across Akbar's and Jahangir's reigns. Led Gujarat campaign 1583, Thatta 1590 (annexed Sindh), Deccan campaigns 1593-1601. Translated Babur Nama from Turkish to Persian 1589. Major Hindi poet — composed devotional dohas in Brajbhasha still popular today. Patron of poets, Sanskrit scholars, Hindu artisans. One of the 'Navaratna' of Akbar's court. Fell out of Jahangir's favour late in career; died in penury 1627 in Delhi, buried in own tomb in Nizamuddin.

hist_birbal_raja.label: Raja Birbal (Mahesh Das)
hist_birbal_raja.subject: history
hist_birbal_raja.detail: Born Mahesh Das (c. 1528-1586), Brahman poet from Kalpi; joined Akbar's court 1562. Gained favour through wit and poetry; given title Raja Birbal (or Kavi Raj). Constant personal companion of Akbar. Among very few Hindus to join Din-i-Ilahi (Birbal was reportedly the only Hindu noble of stature to accept initiation). Killed February 1586 in disastrous Yusufzai Pashtun campaign in Khyber Pass — 8,000 Mughal troops lost. Akbar mourned him deeply. Subject of vast popular folklore in Hindi/Urdu as the witty Hindu counterpart at the Muslim court.

hist_tansen.label: Mian Tansen
hist_tansen.subject: history
hist_tansen.detail: Born Ramtanu Pandey/Trilochan (c. 1500-1589) near Gwalior; trained under sufi Shaikh Muhammad Ghaus and dhrupad master Swami Haridas of Vrindavan. Court musician of Raja Ramchandra of Bandhavgarh (Baghelkhand) before Akbar summoned him 1562. Given title Mian. One of the nine 'jewels' of Akbar's court. Credited with developing or popularising ragas Miyan ki Todi, Miyan ki Malhar, Miyan ki Sarang, Darbari Kanada. Considered founder of the Senia gharana of Hindustani classical music; his descendants (Bilas Khan, etc.) founded important gharanas. Buried at Gwalior next to his teacher.

hist_bhagwant_das.label: Raja Bhagwant Das
hist_bhagwant_das.subject: history
hist_bhagwant_das.detail: Raja of Amber 1574-1589. Son of Raja Bharmal Kachhwaha. Rose to 5000 mansab. Jointly governed Lahore late in his career. Led embassy to Rana Pratap in 1573 attempting to negotiate submission. Gave his daughter Man Bai in marriage to Prince Salim (future Jahangir) 1585. Father of Raja Man Singh. Died 1589 at Lahore.

hist_raja_man_singh.label: Raja Man Singh I of Amber
hist_raja_man_singh.subject: history
hist_raja_man_singh.detail: Kachhwaha Rajput (1550-1614); grandson of Bharmal. Son of Bhagwant Das. 7000 mansab — highest Rajput rank, only one of two (with Aziz Koka). Joined Mughal service young. Commanded at Haldighati 1576. Defended Lahore against Mirza Hakim 1581; escorted Akbar on Kabul campaign. Governor successively of Kabul, Bihar (1587), Bengal (1594-1606). Conquered Orissa (from remaining Afghans) 1590-92 and parts of east Bengal including Dacca. Built the famous Govind Dev temple in Vrindavan (1590) and much of Amber palace (Kesar Kyari). Strained relations with Jahangir after Akbar's death (had supported rival succession candidate Khusrau). Died 1614 Gwalior.

hist_jaimal_patta.label: Jaimal Rathore and Patta Sisodiya
hist_jaimal_patta.subject: history
hist_jaimal_patta.detail: Paired heroes of the 1568 Chittor defence. Jaimal Fatta Rathore (Bednor) commanded fort after Rana Udai Singh evacuated to hills — killed by Akbar's personal musket shot (named Sangram). Patta Sisodiya (of Kelwa) led the second defence after Jaimal's death. Both died in the final Rajput charge as Mughals breached the walls. Akbar, struck by their valour, commissioned life-size stone statues of the two warriors seated on elephants at the main gate of Agra Fort (Akbari Darwaza) — visible to every court visitor. Rare Mughal tribute to an enemy. Celebrated together in Rajput heroic memory; invoked repeatedly in later Rajput poetry.

hist_navaratna.label: Akbar's Navaratna (Nine Jewels)
hist_navaratna.subject: history
hist_navaratna.detail: Legendary assembly of nine preeminent figures at Akbar's court — cultural trope symbolising Akbar's syncretic brilliance. Historiographically the exact list varies, but canonical nine: (1) Abu'l Fazl Allami — vizier and historian, author of Akbar Nama and Ain-i-Akbari; (2) Faizi — poet laureate, Mahabharata translator; (3) Raja Birbal (Mahesh Das) — witty courtier and Akbar's personal favourite; (4) Raja Todar Mal — revenue minister, architect of dahsala bandobast; (5) Raja Man Singh — general, 7000-mansab, governor of Bihar/Bengal/Kabul; (6) Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan — warrior-poet, 7000-mansab, Hindi doha master; (7) Mian Tansen — musician, Senia gharana founder; (8) Fakir Aziao-Din — sufi advisor; (9) Mullah Do-Piyaza — jester (possibly apocryphal). Reflects Akbar's cosmopolitan court combining Hindu and Muslim talent.

hist_akbar_social_reforms.label: Akbar's Social Reforms
hist_akbar_social_reforms.subject: history
hist_akbar_social_reforms.detail: Cluster of social-welfare measures by Akbar, many rarely successful but pioneering in formulation. Raised minimum marriage age to 14 (girls) and 16 (boys). Banned sati unless the widow clearly insisted of her own free will; absolutely forbidden for widows of tender age who had not shared husband's bed. Legalised widow remarriage. Discouraged polygamy unless first wife barren. Restricted sale of wines and spirits. Banned forcible conversion of war prisoners to Islam. Abolished jizya 1564 and pilgrimage tax 1563. Revised educational syllabus — added arithmetic, agriculture, household economy, geometry, history alongside theology. Stopped personally to dissuade a woman from performing sati at Bikaner 1593. Though limited in implementation, these measures framed a template that later reformers (Rammohan Roy, Bentinck) would revisit.

hist_ibadat_khana.label: Ibadat Khana (House of Worship)
hist_ibadat_khana.subject: history
hist_ibadat_khana.detail: Hall built by Akbar at Fatehpur Sikri 1575 for religious debates. Initially only Muslim theologians — proceedings became acrimonious (mullahs shouting, abusing each other in Akbar's presence). 1578 opened to all religions: Portuguese Jesuits (Acquaviva, Monserrate from 1580), Hindus (Purushottam, Devi), Jains (Hira Vijaya Suri from Kathiawar), Zoroastrians (Maharji Rana), Christians, even atheists. Discussions extended to fundamental questions — whether the Quran was the last revealed book, nature of God, resurrection. Horrified orthodox theologians; rumours of Akbar's apostasy spread. Closed 1582. Akbar shifted to bilateral consultations with religious representatives. Stepping-stone between Sulh-i-Kul doctrine (already implicit) and Din-i-Ilahi (1582).

hist_mahzar_1579.label: Mahzar (Infallibility Decree, 1579)
hist_mahzar_1579.subject: history
hist_mahzar_1579.detail: Declaration drafted by Shaikh Mubarak (father of Abu'l Fazl) and signed by leading ulama September 1579 at Fatehpur Sikri. Gave Akbar, as a 'most just and wise king' whose rank was 'higher in the eyes of God than the mujtahids', the authority to choose among conflicting Quranic interpretations by qualified interpreters (mujtahids) on matters beneficial to the nation. Empowered him to issue new orders in conformity with the Quran that would be binding on all. Wrongly termed 'Decree of Infallibility' in older colonial scholarship — actually a limited conflict-resolution device enabling Akbar to navigate sectarian disputes (Shia/Sunni/Mahdawi). Stabilised religious governance in the empire.

hist_din_i_ilahi.label: Din-i-Ilahi / Tauhid-i-Ilahi
hist_din_i_ilahi.subject: history
hist_din_i_ilahi.detail: 'Divine Monotheism' — new Sufi-style order promulgated by Akbar 1582 after closing Ibadat Khana debates. No sacred book, no priestly class, no place of worship, no rituals except initiation. Sunday fixed as initiation day: novice placed head at emperor's feet, emperor raised him and gave the shast (Sufi formula) incorporating Akbar's motto 'Allah-u-Akbar' (can be read either as 'God is great' or 'Akbar is God'). Initiates abstained from meat where possible (at least in month of birth), gave alms and a feast on their birthday. Only about 18 formally joined; Birbal was the only major Hindu noble initiate. Badauni called it apostasy; modern historians (R.P. Tripathi, Athar Ali) argue it was a Sufi order not a new religion. Akbar's motive partly political — bound nobles in personal loyalty beyond religious faction. Died with Akbar; ceremonial continuations under Jahangir (shast giving) soon faded.

hist_bijapur_sultanate.label: Bijapur Sultanate (Adil Shahi)
hist_bijapur_sultanate.subject: history
hist_bijapur_sultanate.detail: Adil Shahi dynasty founded by Yusuf Adil Khan (1490), former Bijapur governor under Bahmanids. Shia-inclined early, oscillated between Shia and Sunni later. Capital: Bijapur. Major rulers: Ali Adil Shah I (1558-80) of Talikota; Ibrahim Adil Shah II (1580-1627) 'Jagat Guru'; Muhammad Adil Shah (1627-56, Gol Gumbaz); Ali Adil Shah II (1656-72). Accepted Mughal suzerainty via 1636 treaty with Shah Jahan. Finally annexed by Aurangzeb 1686.

hist_golconda_sultanate.label: Golconda Sultanate (Qutb Shahi)
hist_golconda_sultanate.subject: history
hist_golconda_sultanate.detail: Qutb Shahi dynasty founded by Sultan Quli Qutb Shah (1518), Turkoman governor under Bahmanids. Shia state. Telangana-Andhra base, capital Golconda; new city Hyderabad founded by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah 1591. Famed for diamond mines (Kollur, Panna) which produced Koh-i-Noor. Major rulers: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah (1580-1612); Abdullah Qutb Shah (1626-72); Abul Hasan Tana Shah (1672-87, the last). Dominated in final decades by Madanna + Akkanna. Annexed by Aurangzeb 1687.

hist_ahmadnagar_sultanate.label: Ahmadnagar Sultanate (Nizam Shahi)
hist_ahmadnagar_sultanate.subject: history
hist_ahmadnagar_sultanate.detail: Nizam Shahi dynasty founded by Malik Ahmad Bahri (1490), son of a Brahmin convert Bahmani wazir Nizam-ul-Mulk Bhairi. Claimed primary Bahmani succession. Capital: Ahmadnagar, later Khirki (built under Malik Ambar). Major rulers: Burhan Nizam Shah I; Murtaza Nizam Shah I; Bahadur Nizam Shah (boy-king under Chand Bibi); Murtaza Nizam Shah II (Malik Ambar's puppet). Extinguished by Shah Jahan 1633 after Daulatabad siege — last Nizam Shah imprisoned at Gwalior.

hist_chand_bibi.label: Chand Bibi
hist_chand_bibi.subject: history
hist_chand_bibi.detail: Daughter of Hussain Nizam Shah I of Ahmadnagar; married to Ali Adil Shah I of Bijapur. After Ali's assassination 1580 served as regent for nephew Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur for ~10 years — remarkable period of female rule. Visited Ahmadnagar 1595 to mourn brother Burhan Nizam Shah; stayed to lead cause of young nephew Bahadur Nizam Shah. Personally commanded fort during first Mughal siege 1595-96 against Prince Murad + Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan — valiant defence forced negotiated cession of Berar. During second Mughal siege 1600 her own nobles accused her of treachery for seeking peace; murdered by hostile faction. Ahmadnagar fell days later.

hist_ibrahim_adil_shah_ii.label: Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur
hist_ibrahim_adil_shah_ii.subject: history
hist_ibrahim_adil_shah_ii.detail: Bijapur Sultan 1580-1627. Ascended at age 9 under Chand Bibi's regency. Titled 'Jagat Guru' ('Teacher of the World') for broad religious tolerance — granted endowments to Hindu Pandharpur (Vithoba), patronised Hindu temples. Author of Kitab-i-Nauras — songs in Dakhini Urdu and Persian set to nine musical modes (ragas), freely invoking Saraswati the Hindu goddess of music. Built new capital Nauraspur as musicians' city near Bijapur (later burnt by Malik Ambar 1624). Employed ~30,000 Marathas as bargis; introduced Marathi in revenue accounts at all levels. Titled 'abla baba' (Friend of the Poor). Major patron of Deccani painting school.

hist_malik_ambar.label: Malik Ambar
hist_malik_ambar.subject: history
hist_malik_ambar.detail: Habshi (Ethiopian, 1548-1626) born Chapu; sold at Baghdad slave market; purchased by a merchant who brought him to Deccan. Rose in service of Changez Khan (Habshi noble of Murtaza Nizam Shah I). After Mughal capture of Ahmadnagar 1600, Malik Ambar revived the state — installed Murtaza Nizam Shah II as puppet, took Peshwa title himself. Pioneered large-scale Maratha guerrilla partnership against Mughals; harassed Mughals in Berar, Balaghat, Ahmadnagar 1600-26. Battle of Nander 1601 — beaten by Khan-i-Khanan. Attacked Mughals again 1607-16; lost Khirki (his new capital) to Mahabat Khan 1616; submitted to Prince Khurram 1618. Recovered territories 1622+ during Shah Jahan's rebellion. Attacked Bijapur 1624, burnt Nauraspur. Introduced zabti revenue system in Ahmadnagar (modelled on Todar Mal's), abolished ruinous ijara (contract-farming). Died 1626 aged 80. Direct ideological ancestor of Shivaji's guerrilla warfare.

hist_muhammad_quli_qutb_shah.label: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah
hist_muhammad_quli_qutb_shah.subject: history
hist_muhammad_quli_qutb_shah.detail: Golconda Sultan 1580-1612. Major poet — wrote in Dakhini Urdu, Persian, Telugu; left an extensive diwan (collected poems). First to introduce secular themes into Urdu poetry (nature, love, social life alongside praise of God). Founded the city of Hyderabad 1591 on the banks of the Musi; constructed Char Minar 1591-92 as its ceremonial centrepiece (commemorating end of a plague). Patron of literature, music and architecture. Named the city after his beloved Bhagmati (renamed Hyder Mahal).

hist_shahji_bhonsle.label: Shahji Bhonsle
hist_shahji_bhonsle.subject: history
hist_shahji_bhonsle.detail: Maratha sardar (1594-1664), father of Shivaji. Son of Maloji Bhonsle. Son-in-law of Lakhuji Jadhav Rao (Nizam Shahi noble treacherously murdered 1629). After father-in-law's death, Shahji defected to Mughals, received 5000 mansab + Poona jagir from Shah Jahan. Switched back to Ahmadnagar cause after Fath Khan's 1632 betrayal transferred his jagir. Following 1636 treaty entered Bijapur service; given Bangalore jagir. His Maharashtra (Poona) jagir passed to son Shivaji under wife Jijabai's guardianship — foundation of Maratha state. Died in hunting accident 1664 Karnataka.

hist_itimad_ud_daulah.label: Mirza Ghiyas Beg (Itimad-ud-Daulah)
hist_itimad_ud_daulah.subject: history
hist_itimad_ud_daulah.detail: Persian émigré, father of Nur Jahan and Asaf Khan. Entered Akbar's service c. 1577. Made joint diwan by Jahangir on his accession 1605. Brief eclipse due to son's involvement in Khusrau's rebellion, restored. After daughter's marriage to Jahangir 1611, appointed chief diwan — served competently till his death 1622. Wielded considerable administrative influence as part of the 'junta' alongside daughter and son Asaf Khan. His marble tomb at Agra (built by Nur Jahan 1622-28 on the Yamuna) pioneered pietra-dura inlay on marble; stylistic prototype for the Taj Mahal — often called the 'Baby Taj'.

hist_asaf_khan.label: Asaf Khan (Mirza Abul Hasan)
hist_asaf_khan.subject: history
hist_asaf_khan.detail: Brother of Nur Jahan, son of Itimad-ud-Daulah. Served as khan-i-saman (master of imperial household) under Jahangir. Married his daughter Arjumand Banu Begum (the future Mumtaz Mahal) to Prince Khurram 1612 — thereby Shah Jahan's father-in-law. Appointed wakil (chief minister) by Jahangir 1625. After Jahangir's death near Lahore October 1627, Asaf Khan outmanoeuvred Nur Jahan: made her virtual prisoner, sent urgent summons to Shah Jahan in Deccan, oversaw Shah Jahan's enthronement at Agra. Continued as Shah Jahan's wakil till his own death 1641.

hist_mahabat_khan.label: Mahabat Khan
hist_mahabat_khan.subject: history
hist_mahabat_khan.detail: Afghan noble, major general under Jahangir and Shah Jahan. Early career: defeated Prince Khusrau 1606 near Lahore. Led major operations against Shah Jahan's 1622-26 rebellion. Mahabat Khan's coup June 1626: feeling harassed by court rivals after the rebellion, he summoned a trusted 4,000-strong Rajput body and seized Jahangir at a Jhelum river crossing en route to Kabul. Nur Jahan escaped across the river, then surrendered herself to be close to emperor; over 6 months she gradually won back nobles, isolated Mahabat Khan, who fled to join Shah Jahan in Deccan. Under Shah Jahan: appointed viceroy of Deccan; captured Daulatabad 1633 ending Nizam Shahi dynasty. Died 1634.

hist_islam_khan_chishti.label: Islam Khan Chishti
hist_islam_khan_chishti.subject: history
hist_islam_khan_chishti.detail: Shaikh Alauddin (1570-1613), grandson of Shaikh Salim Chishti (patron saint of the Mughals). Appointed Bengal subadar by Jahangir 1608 despite youth. Pacified the region's Afghan chiefs and Hindu zamindars: defeated Barah Bhuiyan confederacy (12 zamindars, led by Musa Khan) after 3-year campaign; captured Sonargaon 1611; annexed Jessore and Kamrup (western Assam). Transferred the Bengal provincial capital from Rajmahal to Dacca 1610 — Dacca grew rapidly thereafter, becoming Jahangirnagar. Conciliatory policy: restored Musa Khan's estates; inducted defeated Afghans into Mughal service.

hist_khusrau.label: Prince Khusrau
hist_khusrau.subject: history
hist_khusrau.detail: Eldest son of Jahangir (1587-1622). Favoured by Akbar and Raja Man Singh in succession politics — Man Singh was his father-in-law. Rebelled immediately after Jahangir's accession April 1606; sought support from Guru Arjan (Sikh) in Punjab — Jahangir's retaliation led to Guru Arjan's execution 1606. Defeated near Lahore, captured at the Chenab, blinded partially, imprisoned. Carried around as hostage with the court for years. Executed 1622 on Shah Jahan's orders during the latter's rebellion — set precedent for Mughal fratricide that Shah Jahan himself would practice on Dara Shukoh.

hist_mir_jumla.label: Mir Jumla (Mohammad Syed)
hist_mir_jumla.subject: history
hist_mir_jumla.detail: Persian diamond merchant (d. 1663) who rose to become wazir of Golconda under Abdullah Qutb Shah. Commanded Qutb Shahi campaigns conquering Karnataka; controlled fabulous wealth from Golconda diamond mines. Defected to Aurangzeb 1656 during Golconda crisis, bringing troops and treasure — gifted the Koh-i-Noor diamond to Aurangzeb. One of Aurangzeb's top generals. Governor of Bengal 1660-63. Led 1662-63 campaign against the Ahoms — temporarily captured Garhgaon (Ahom capital). Died 1663 returning from Assam campaign.

hist_madanna_akkanna.label: Madanna and Akkanna (Golconda)
hist_madanna_akkanna.subject: history
hist_madanna_akkanna.detail: Brothers — Madanna chief minister (wazir) and Akkanna commander — who dominated Golconda 1672-1687 under Abul Hasan Tana Shah. Brahmin Hindu ministers of a Muslim state. Pursued pro-Maratha foreign policy: alliance with Shivaji (and later Sambhaji) against Mughal and Bijapur pressure. Their resistance contributed to Aurangzeb's 1687 siege. Murdered 1686 by dissenting nobles during the siege — Golconda surrendered 1687. Significant as Hindu governors of a Deccani Shia state and architects of anti-Mughal Deccan bloc.

hist_berar_annexation_1596.label: Berar Annexation (1596)
hist_berar_annexation_1596.subject: history
hist_berar_annexation_1596.detail: Chand Bibi's treaty with Prince Murad + Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan ceded Berar to the Mughals in return for Mughal recognition of Bahadur Nizam Shah's claim to the Ahmadnagar throne. First permanent Mughal foothold in Deccan. Alarmed all Deccani states — within a year a combined Bijapur+Golconda+Ahmadnagar force invaded Berar and was defeated by Mughals despite 3:1 numerical superiority. Led directly to 1600 Mughal capture of Ahmadnagar fort.

hist_khandesh_annexation_1601.label: Khandesh Annexation — Asirgarh Siege (1601)
hist_khandesh_annexation_1601.subject: history
hist_khandesh_annexation_1601.detail: Akbar personally directed the siege of Asirgarh ('strongest fort in Deccan') in Khandesh after its ruler failed to pay respects to Prince Daniyal. The Faruqi dynasty (1382-1601) ended; Khandesh absorbed into Mughal empire as a suba. Capture reputedly combined close siege, pestilence outbreak inside fort, and bribery. Opened Mughal route deeper into Deccan.

hist_ahmadnagar_fall_1633.label: Extinction of Ahmadnagar (1633)
hist_ahmadnagar_fall_1633.subject: history
hist_ahmadnagar_fall_1633.detail: End of the Nizam Shahi dynasty under Shah Jahan. Viceroy Mahabat Khan besieged Daulatabad (Nizam Shahi capital after Khirki burnt). Fath Khan (Malik Ambar's son, then Peshwa) opened secret negotiations, murdered his own puppet Nizam Shah, surrendered fort 1633. Last Nizam Shah imprisoned at Gwalior. Shahji Bhonsle then raised another Nizam Shahi prince as puppet with Bijapur support, prolonging resistance until 1636 treaty settled Deccan.

hist_treaty_1636_deccan.label: Shah Jahan's Deccan Treaty (1636)
hist_treaty_1636_deccan.subject: history
hist_treaty_1636_deccan.detail: Twin Mughal treaties with Bijapur (ahdnama) + Golconda settling Deccan politics. Bijapur: accepted Mughal suzerainty, paid Rs 20 lakh indemnity, agreed non-interference in Golconda affairs, cooperated against Shahji. Golconda: khutba read in Shah Jahan's name, annual tribute of 2 lakh huns replacing older tribute to Bijapur. In return: Mughals ceded parts of Ahmadnagar (worth 20 lakh huns annually) to Bijapur. Treaty enabled Bijapur-Golconda expansion into Karnataka 1636-56 (2:1 division of spoils). Realised Akbar's ultimate Deccan goal via diplomacy. Shah Jahan pressed palm-print on treaty as oath of inviolability — later broken by Aurangzeb.

hist_balkh_campaign_1646.label: Shah Jahan's Balkh Campaign (1646-1647)
hist_balkh_campaign_1646.subject: history
hist_balkh_campaign_1646.detail: Central Asian intervention: Nazr Muhammad, Uzbek ruler of Balkh, appealed for Mughal help against his rebel son Abdul Aziz. Shah Jahan moved Lahore → Kabul; sent 50,000 cavalry + 10,000 infantry under Prince Murad mid-1646. Murad's impetuous march on Balkh drove Nazr Muhammad to flee; Mughals forced to garrison hostile Balkh. Prince Aurangzeb replaced Murad 1647; won decisive Battle of Balkh vs Abdul Aziz's claimed 1,20,000 Uzbeks. But Mughals retreated October 1647 facing impossible winter logistics + Uzbek insurgency — heavy losses. Aurangzeb held the retreat together. Strategic failure despite tactical victory; Shah Jahan's 'Mughal homeland' recovery dream ended.

hist_shah_jahan_rebellion_1622.label: Shah Jahan's Rebellion (1622-1626)
hist_shah_jahan_rebellion_1622.subject: history
hist_shah_jahan_rebellion_1622.detail: Prince Khurram refused to lead the Qandahar relief campaign vs Shah Abbas I, fearing court intrigues during his absence. Open breach with Jahangir; rebel march on Agra defeated by Mahabat Khan near Delhi — saved by Mewar Rajput contingent from complete rout. Fled Gujarat → Deccan → Orissa (surprise attack) → captured Bengal/Bihar → forced back to Deccan → allied with Malik Ambar → abject submission letters 1626. Sent Dara + Aurangzeb as hostages to Jahangir's court. Shah Jahan's earlier execution of Khusrau during this rebellion set precedent for his own later fratricide by Aurangzeb.

hist_char_minar.label: Char Minar (Hyderabad)
hist_char_minar.subject: history
hist_char_minar.detail: Built 1591-92 by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah as ceremonial centrepiece of newly-founded Hyderabad city. Four lofty arches facing cardinal directions; 4-storeyed minarets 48m high at each corner. Reputedly commemorates end of a plague epidemic. Double-screen arches with fine carvings. Iconic example of Qutb Shahi architecture combining Persian plan with Indo-Islamic decoration. Symbol of Hyderabad to this day.

hist_gol_gumbaz.label: Gol Gumbaz (Bijapur)
hist_gol_gumbaz.subject: history
hist_gol_gumbaz.detail: Mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah of Bijapur (r. 1627-56), built 1626-1656, completed post-his-death 1660 by architect Yaqut of Dabul. Single unsupported dome ~44m internal diameter — among largest pre-modern domes in the world. Famous 'Whispering Gallery' acoustics: whispers at one side audible 37m across. Harmonious proportions balanced by tall tapering corner towers. Apex of Adil Shahi architecture, distinct from Mughal idiom.

hist_ibrahim_rauza.label: Ibrahim Rauza (Bijapur)
hist_ibrahim_rauza.subject: history
hist_ibrahim_rauza.detail: Mausoleum complex of Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur, c. 1626, architect Malik Sandal. Paired tomb and mosque on a single raised plinth with garden. Exquisitely carved stonework — intricate Islamic geometric and calligraphic patterns. Called the 'Taj Mahal of the Deccan'; reportedly inspired the architect of the Taj Mahal (commissioned 1632). Exemplifies refined late-Adil-Shahi style and cross-Deccan architectural cross-pollination.

hist_du_aspah_sih_aspah.label: Du-aspah Sih-aspah System
hist_du_aspah_sih_aspah.subject: history
hist_du_aspah_sih_aspah.detail: Mansabdari modification introduced by Jahangir (developed c. 1611 onward). Literally 'trooper with two (du) or three (sih) horses'. Allowed select nobles to maintain a doubled quota of sawars (cavalrymen) without a corresponding rise in zat rank — i.e., a mansabdar with 3000 zat + 3000 sawar du-aspah sih-aspah rank was required to maintain 6,000 troopers at double the pay scale. Raised effective strike power of favoured nobles (notably Mahabat Khan, Prince Khurram/Shah Jahan) while keeping fiscal establishment numerically stable. Contrasts with normal rule that sawar rank could not exceed zat rank.

hist_guru_arjan.label: Guru Arjan Dev
hist_guru_arjan.subject: history
hist_guru_arjan.detail:
Fifth Sikh Guru (1563-1606), son of Guru Ram Das. Compiled the Adi Granth (first compilation of Sikh scripture) at Ramsar pool in Amritsar 1604 — incorporated hymns of Nanak's four successors + Kabir, Namdev, Shaikh Farid, Ravidas, Mirabai. Built the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) at Amritsar; laid its foundation 1589 reportedly by sufi Hazrat Mian Mir. Gave shelter and financial support to rebel Prince Khusrau 1606. Summoned by Jahangir, refused to expunge a hymn with supposed reference to Muhammad, fined Rs 2 lakh then executed by torture at Lahore May 1606 — first Sikh martyrdom. His death radicalised Sikh community under son Guru Hargobind (introduced Miri-Piri doctrine, militarisation).

Foundation stone of Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) at Amritsar laid 1589 reportedly by Sufi saint **Miyan Mir** of Lahore (Qadariya silsila) at Guru Arjan's invitation — iconic gesture of Sikh-Sufi cross-tradition respect. Completed 1604 when Guru Arjan installed the Adi Granth. Instituted the **daswandh** (tithe) — fixed one-tenth of income contribution by every Sikh to the Guru's treasury. Lived in aristocratic style (fine clothes, Central Asian horses, retainers) to emphasise Guru's combined spiritual + worldly authority (miri-piri precursor).

hist_sambhaji.label: Sambhaji
hist_sambhaji.subject: history
hist_sambhaji.detail: Shivaji's eldest son (1657-1689). Succeeded Shivaji April 1680 after defeating half-brother Rajaram's supporters. Sheltered rebel Prince Akbar (Aurangzeb's son) 1681 — direct provocation that forced Aurangzeb south. Continued Shivaji's policy of raids + Deccani-state alliance; extended to Portuguese Goa 1683. Captured at Sangameshwar January 1689 via betrayal by brother-in-law Ganoji Shirke; paraded before Aurangzeb at Tulapur, refused to embrace Islam or reveal treasures; tortured and executed March 1689. His execution became rallying cry — 'instead of destroying Maratha state, Aurangzeb made Maratha opposition all-pervasive' (Satish Chandra). Wife Yesubai and son Shahu captured at Satara.

hist_rajaram.label: Rajaram
hist_rajaram.subject: history
hist_rajaram.detail: Shivaji's younger son (1670-1700) by second wife Soyarabai. Crowned at Raigarh 1689 after Sambhaji's execution. Mughals stormed Raigarh; Rajaram escaped south, reached Jinji fort on east coast 1690. Held out at Jinji for 8 years under Zulfiqar Khan's siege (1690-98). Escaped 1698 before Jinji fell; returned to Satara. Died 1700 at Sinhagad. Wife Tarabai continued the struggle in his name on behalf of their son Shivaji II — leader of the so-called 'second swarajya' 1700-1707.

hist_shahu.label: Shahu I
hist_shahu.subject: history
hist_shahu.detail: Son of Sambhaji (1682-1749). Captured with mother Yesubai at Satara age 7 during 1689 Mughal storm. Raised at Aurangzeb's court as mansabdar 7,000 — treated well; married two Maratha girls of respectable families. Aurangzeb negotiated his release in 1703 but recanted; finally released 1707 by Bahadur Shah I's rival Azam Shah. Fought Tarabai (Rajaram's widow, regent for Shivaji II) for succession; won Battle of Khed 1708. His Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath (from 1713) and successors (Bajirao I, Balaji Bajirao/Nanasaheb) built the Maratha Confederacy and drove continental expansion.

hist_jijabai.label: Jijabai
hist_jijabai.subject: history
hist_jijabai.detail: Shivaji's mother (c.1598-1674). Daughter of Lakhuji Jadhav Rao, Nizam Shahi noble of Sindkhed (murdered 1629 by Nizam Shah on conspiracy charge). Married Shahji Bhonsle. After husband moved to Karnataka service, she raised Shivaji at Poona with guardian Dadaji Kondadeo — instilled Hindu dharma mission and political aspirations. Steadfast advisor to Shivaji throughout his rise. Died days after Shivaji's Raigarh coronation June 1674.

hist_ram_das_samarth.label: Samarth Ramdas
hist_ram_das_samarth.subject: history
hist_ram_das_samarth.detail: Marathi bhakti saint (1608-1681); originator of 'Maharashtra Dharma' activist political philosophy. Established a math at Sajjangad (on fort given by Shivaji) near Satara. Spiritual guru of Shivaji from c. 1672. Composed Dasbodh (philosophical treatise on dharmic activism + good governance) and Manache Shlok (advice on right living). Devotee of Rama — built Rama temples across Maharashtra. Contrasted with Tukaram's pure devotional path; offered a politicised bhakti suited to Maratha state-building.

hist_afzal_khan.label: Afzal Khan
hist_afzal_khan.subject: history
hist_afzal_khan.detail: Bijapur premier noble (d. 10 November 1659). Sent by Sultan Ali Adil Shah II with 10,000 troops to crush Shivaji late 1659. Plundered Shivaji's ancestral temples in Konkan to provoke. Invited Shivaji to 'personal interview' at Pratapgarh under safe-conduct pretext; Shivaji came armed with concealed bagh-nakh (tiger-claws) + dagger; killed Afzal Khan during the ceremonial embrace. Maratha signal triggered simultaneous attack on waiting Bijapur force — routed leaderless. Shivaji captured Khan's artillery, elephants, treasure; took Panhala fort soon after. Founding legendary moment of Shivaji's career.

hist_shaista_khan.label: Shaista Khan
hist_shaista_khan.subject: history
hist_shaista_khan.detail: Mughal noble (1600-1694, extraordinary 94-year lifespan). Maternal uncle of Mumtaz Mahal (brother of Asaf Khan). Deccan viceroy 1660-63; occupied Poona, made it his headquarters. Famous Shivaji Lal Mahal night raid April 1663 killed Khan's son + bodyguard, cut off the viceroy's own fingers — he lost face; Aurangzeb refused him even a farewell audience on transfer. Bengal subadar 1664-76 and 1679-88: built navy that routed Magh (Arakanese) pirates, captured Sondip island then Chittagong 1666 — freed east Bengal from 60 years of piracy, opened commerce that drove Bengal's 17c prosperity. Founded Jahangirnagar Dacca's growth.

hist_raja_jai_singh_amber.label: Mirza Raja Jai Singh I of Amber
hist_raja_jai_singh_amber.subject: history
hist_raja_jai_singh_amber.detail: Kachhwaha Rajput (1611-1667), grandnephew of Raja Man Singh. Top general of Shah Jahan (7000 mansab) + Aurangzeb. Foremost proponent of a unified Deccan-forward policy — wrote to Aurangzeb 'The conquest of Bijapur is the preface to the conquest of all Deccan and Karnataka.' Besieged Purandar 1665, forced Shivaji's Treaty of Purandar. Persuaded Shivaji to visit Agra 1666 — which ended disastrously. Led failed 1665 Bijapur campaign. Died 1667 disappointed by Aurangzeb's distrust. [NB: distinct from Sawai Jai Singh II, his grandson who founded Jaipur 1727.] Long-serving patron of Sanskrit scholars; built Govind Dev temple Jaipur.

hist_jaswant_singh_marwar.label: Maharaja Jaswant Singh of Marwar
hist_jaswant_singh_marwar.subject: history
hist_jaswant_singh_marwar.detail: Rathor ruler of Marwar (1626-1678). 7000 mansab under Shah Jahan. Commanded Malwa army at Dharmat 15 April 1658 — defeated by Aurangzeb+Murad despite dishonourable retreat-resistance. Defected mid-campaign against Shuja 1659; then invited Dara to Marwar during his flight — but then treacherously withdrew support under Aurangzeb pressure, forcing Dara's capture. Pardoned and reinstated by Aurangzeb — Gujarat governor, later Kabul subadar dealing with Afghan revolts. Died at Jamrud December 1678 without surviving male heir — triggered Marwar succession crisis.

hist_ajit_singh_marwar.label: Ajit Singh of Marwar
hist_ajit_singh_marwar.subject: history
hist_ajit_singh_marwar.detail: Posthumous son of Jaswant Singh (b. February 1679 at Lahore). Rathor sardars under Durgadas smuggled infant + mother out of Agra through a fighting diversion 1679; proclaimed raja at Jodhpur. Aurangzeb refused recognition, declared him 'pretender'; Mughals occupied Jodhpur for 30 years. Reared in Abu hills under Durgadas's protection. Recognised as Marwar ruler 1698 (though Jodhpur fort held by Mughals till 1707). After Aurangzeb's death, installed as Maharaja with Jodhpur restored. Murdered 1724 by his own son Bakht Singh.

hist_durgadas_rathore.label: Durgadas Rathore
hist_durgadas_rathore.subject: history
hist_durgadas_rathore.detail: Veer Durgadas Rathore (1638-1718); Rathor military commander and de facto leader of Marwar resistance 1679-1707. Son of Jaswant Singh's trusted noble Askaran. Organised Ajit Singh's escape from Agra 1679 — loyalty embodied. Allied with rebel Prince Akbar 1681; hosted him in Marwar then escorted his family to Maratha territory. Fought 30-year guerrilla war against Mughal occupation; celebrated as savior of Rathor lineage. Fell out with Ajit Singh 1707 and died in exile 1718. Iconic figure of Rajput loyalty in Rajasthani tradition.

hist_guru_har_govind.label: Guru Har Govind
hist_guru_har_govind.subject: history
hist_guru_har_govind.detail: Sixth Sikh Guru (1595-1644), son of Guru Arjan. Adopted Miri-Piri doctrine after father's martyrdom 1606 — wore two swords symbolising temporal (miri) + spiritual (piri) authority. Built the Akal Takht opposite Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar 1609 — seat of Sikh temporal sovereignty, facing the spiritual Harmandir. Imprisoned briefly at Gwalior Fort by Jahangir (reportedly on debt charges); freed 1620 along with 52 Hindu rajas (commemorated as Bandi Chhor Divas). Four inconsequential skirmishes with Shah Jahan's officials over hawks/city/horses (1628-34) per historian R.P. Tripathi. Retired to Kiratpur in Punjab foothills. Militarised the Sikh community.

hist_guru_har_rai.label: Guru Har Rai
hist_guru_har_rai.subject: history
hist_guru_har_rai.detail: Seventh Sikh Guru (1630-1661), grandson of Guru Har Govind. Peaceful, scholarly Guru — maintained the 2,200-strong armed Sikh force inherited from grandfather but avoided confrontation. Helped rebel Prince Dara Shukoh flee Mughal pursuit 1658 (reportedly gave medical aid); Aurangzeb summoned Guru to court for this; Guru sent elder son Ram Rai as his representative. Ram Rai altered a verse of Adi Granth to please Aurangzeb; Guru Har Rai disinherited him and nominated younger son Har Kishan as successor. Patron of Ayurveda.

hist_guru_har_kishan.label: Guru Har Kishan
hist_guru_har_kishan.subject: history
hist_guru_har_kishan.detail: Eighth Sikh Guru (1656-1664); youngest to hold the office (age 5). Aurangzeb summoned him to Delhi 1664 to arbitrate the Ram Rai succession dispute; arrived at Raja Jai Singh's residence (site of present-day Gurudwara Bangla Sahib). Contracted smallpox helping epidemic patients there; died March 1664 age 8. His last words — 'Baba Bakala' — pointed to his successor at Bakala village: Tegh Bahadur (his granduncle).

hist_guru_tegh_bahadur.label: Guru Tegh Bahadur
hist_guru_tegh_bahadur.subject: history
hist_guru_tegh_bahadur.detail: Ninth Sikh Guru (1621-1675), youngest son of Guru Har Govind. Lived in meditative seclusion at Bakala till chosen successor 1664. Travelled extensively — Assam accompanying Raja Ram Singh's Ahom campaign 1668-71, Bihar, Bengal, Punjab hills. Founded Anandpur Sahib town 1665 on Punjab-hill frontier. Summoned by Aurangzeb 1675; tradition (from Bachittar Natak by son Guru Gobind Singh) says defended Kashmiri Pandits against Governor Iftekhar Khan's forced conversion; refused to convert himself or perform miracle; beheaded at Chandni Chowk Delhi 11 November 1675. Second Sikh martyrdom; radicalised Sikh community under Guru Gobind Singh. Gurudwara Sis Ganj Sahib marks execution site.

hist_guru_gobind_singh.label: Guru Gobind Singh
hist_guru_gobind_singh.subject: history
hist_guru_gobind_singh.detail: Tenth and last human Sikh Guru (1666-1708), only son of Guru Tegh Bahadur. Succeeded at age 9 after father's execution. Established Khalsa at Anandpur on Baisakhi 13 April 1699. Fought Mughal armies + allied hill rajas. Battle of Anandpur 1704 — besieged, retreated on Wazir Khan's promise of safe conduct, then attacked while crossing swollen Sarsa river. Battle of Chamkaur 1705 — lost elder sons Ajit Singh + Jujhar Singh in battle; two younger sons (Zorawar Singh age 9, Fateh Singh age 7) bricked alive at Sirhind by faujdar Wazir Khan. Retreated to Talwandi. Composed Dasam Granth (Zafarnama ode to Aurangzeb, Chandi di Var, Jaap Sahib). On Aurangzeb's invitation moved to Nanded (Deccan) 1708 — reconciled with new Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah I. Assassinated at Nanded October 1708 by Pathan allegedly hired by Wazir Khan. Declared the Guru Granth Sahib as eternal Guru, ending the human-Guru lineage.

hist_shaikh_ahmad_sirhindi.label: Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi
hist_shaikh_ahmad_sirhindi.subject: history
hist_shaikh_ahmad_sirhindi.detail: 'Mujaddid Alf-i-Thani' ('Renewer of the Second Millennium', 1564-1624). Naqshbandi Sufi. Opposed Akbar's Sulh-i-Kul and the prevalent Wahdat-ul-Wujud (unity-of-being) doctrine of the Chishtis as pantheistic/un-Islamic; propounded Wahdat-ul-Shuhud (unity-of-witnessing) — God is distinct from creation, mystical unity is experiential only. Demanded jizya reimposition, anti-Hindu state posture, minimal Muslim-Hindu social contact. Wrote polemical Maktubat (letters) to Jahangir's nobles arguing for orthodox turn. Jahangir imprisoned him at Gwalior 1619 for claiming status above the Prophet; released 1620 after retraction. Ideological ancestor of later Indian Islamic revivalism — Shah Waliullah of Delhi (18c), Deobandi school (19c), all trace lineage to him.

hist_tukaram.label: Sant Tukaram
hist_tukaram.subject: history
hist_tukaram.detail: Marathi bhakti saint (c. 1608-1650) of the Varkari movement at Pandharpur. Shudra (kunbi) by birth, grocer by trade. Composed vast body of abhanga devotional poetry in vernacular Marathi — later collected as Gatha. Rejected caste hierarchy, Brahmin intermediary, temple priests. Intense personal devotion to Vithoba of Pandharpur. Contemporary of Eknath (1533-1599), Ramdas, Shivaji. Disappeared mysteriously 1650 (Varkari tradition: ascended bodily to Vaikuntha). Contrasts with Ramdas's activist Maharashtra-Dharma; together shaped 17c Marathi religious consciousness underpinning Maratha political awakening.

hist_battle_pratapgarh_1659.label: Battle of Pratapgarh (1659)
hist_battle_pratapgarh_1659.subject: history
hist_battle_pratapgarh_1659.detail: 10 November 1659. Shivaji's killing of Afzal Khan at Pratapgarh fort. Shivaji met Khan at a specially-constructed ceremonial tent armed with concealed bagh-nakh (tiger-claws) + dagger — killed him during the formal embrace. Maratha signal triggered simultaneous ambush of the waiting Bijapur force (10,000) — routed. Shivaji captured all Afzal Khan's artillery, horses, elephants, and accumulated treasure. Founding legendary moment of Shivaji's military reputation; became template Maratha tactical model (surprise + guerrilla).

hist_surat_sack_1664.label: Sack of Surat (1664, 1670)
hist_surat_sack_1664.subject: history
hist_surat_sack_1664.detail: Shivaji's twin raids on Surat — Mughal Empire's premier western port. First raid January 1664: looted for 4 days, netted ~Rs 1 crore; English + Dutch factories defended with only limited losses. Second raid October 1670: netted further ~Rs 66 lakh. Exposed Mughal failure to defend key trade hubs; funded Maratha state-building; demonstrated Maratha reach deep into Mughal territory. Mughal response to second sack included Battle of Dindori 1670 where Maratha Moropant routed pursuing Daud Khan Qureshi.

hist_treaty_purandar_1665.label: Treaty of Purandar (1665)
hist_treaty_purandar_1665.subject: history
hist_treaty_purandar_1665.detail: 11 June 1665 between Shivaji and Mirza Raja Jai Singh I of Amber at Purandar fort. Terms: Shivaji surrendered 23 of 35 forts (revenue Rs 4 lakh hun/year) to Mughals; retained 12 forts worth 1 lakh hun on condition of loyalty; Mughals compensated with 4 lakh hun Konkan territory (already Shivaji-controlled) + 5 lakh hun Bijapuri Balaghat (to-be-conquered) territory. Shivaji exempted from personal Mughal service; son Sambhaji given 5,000 mansab. Shivaji pledged to join Mughal Deccan campaigns personally. Failure of joint Mughal-Maratha Bijapur campaign immediately after voided the compensation clause — seed of 1670 breach.

hist_shivaji_agra_escape_1666.label: Shivaji's Agra Visit and Escape (1666)
hist_shivaji_agra_escape_1666.subject: history
hist_shivaji_agra_escape_1666.detail: May 1666. Shivaji + son Sambhaji (age 9) came to Agra under Jai Singh's safe-conduct assurance for Aurangzeb audience. Placed in the 5,000-zat mansabdar row during imperial birthday durbar 12 May 1666 — same rank as his own minor son; emperor did not speak to him. Shivaji walked out angrily, refused imperial service. Detained at Kunwar Ram Singh's (Jai Singh's son) house in Agra. Escaped 19 August 1666 hidden in bamboo baskets of sweets/fruit meant for distribution to holy men + Brahmins, with Sambhaji (disguised as servant's son). Returned to Raigarh via disguise as sannyasi through Mathura, Allahabad, Banaras, Gaya, Golconda. Turning point: thereafter Aurangzeb treated him as permanent mortal enemy. Aurangzeb later said 'by my neglect (in allowing Shivaji's escape) I have undertaken a harassing war'.

hist_battle_salher_1672.label: Battle of Salher (1672)
hist_battle_salher_1672.subject: history
hist_battle_salher_1672.detail: Shivaji's first major pitched-battle victory against Mughals, February 1672 near Salher fort in Baglana (north Maharashtra). Maratha forces under Prataprao Gujar + Moropant Pingle (Peshwa) defeated Mughal force under Diler Khan + Ikhlas Khan — ~20,000 Mughal casualties including Ikhlas Khan. Broke with traditional Maratha guerrilla-only mode; demonstrated readiness for and success in conventional set-piece warfare. Contributed to Maratha confidence ahead of 1674 coronation.

hist_satnami_revolt_1672.label: Satnami Revolt (1672)
