hist_satnami_revolt_1672.subject: history
hist_satnami_revolt_1672.detail: March-May 1672 near Narnaul (south of Delhi). Satnamis were a low-caste religious sect — 'goldsmiths, carpenters, sweepers, tanners and other ignoble beings' per contemporary historian — rejecting caste distinctions and Hindu-Muslim divide (resembling earlier Kabir-panthi tradition but distinct); maintained strict moral code. Revolt triggered by clash with local Mughal official; 5,000 Satnamis briefly captured Narnaul, defeated two Mughal detachments. Aurangzeb marched in person from Delhi to crush, reportedly with Quranic verses inscribed on flags to counter alleged Satnami magic powers. Local Hindu (Rajput) zamindars sided with Mughals. Demonstrates that revolts were not Hindu-vs-Muslim but class-economic.

hist_shivaji_coronation_1674.label: Shivaji's Coronation at Raigarh (1674)
hist_shivaji_coronation_1674.subject: history
hist_shivaji_coronation_1674.detail: 6 June 1674 at Raigarh fort. Officiated by Brahmin priest Gaga Bhatta (Vishveshvar Bhatt) of Banaras after extensive genealogical research — Gaga Bhatta declared Shivaji a high-class kshatriya of solar-dynasty lineage descended from Sisodiyas, overcoming objections that Shivaji's Bhonsle lineage lacked kshatriya credentials. Shivaji paid Gaga Bhatta ~Rs 40 lakh for the validation. Titles assumed: Chhatrapati (paramount sovereign), Haindava-Dharmoddharak (Protector of Hindu faith), Kshatriya Kulavatamsa. Established Hindu kingship framework independent of Bijapur-Mughal political order. Enabled Shivaji to enter treaties with Deccani sultans on equal footing (no longer rebel). Mother Jijabai died 12 days later. Second coronation 1674 performed in tantrik style by Nischal Puri Goswami since first was felt to have defects.

hist_marwar_mewar_war_1679.label: Marwar-Mewar Rajput War (1679-1698)
hist_marwar_mewar_war_1679.subject: history
hist_marwar_mewar_war_1679.detail: Twin Rajput uprising triggered by Aurangzeb's handling of Jaswant Singh's Marwar succession 1679. Aurangzeb had proposed dividing Marwar between Inder Singh (Jaswant's nephew) and posthumous infant Ajit Singh. Durgadas Rathore smuggled Ajit Singh out of Agra; Rathors occupied Jodhpur; Aurangzeb declared Marwar khalisa, demolished many old and new temples. Mewar under Rana Raj Singh joined November 1679 over Ajit's cause + pargana-for-jizya surrender issue. Aurangzeb attacked Udaipur; war stalled in hill guerrilla terrain. Prince Akbar's rebellion January 1681 forced Aurangzeb's retreat; treaty with Mewar 1681 surrendered parganas in lieu of jizya + gave 5,000 mansab to Rana Jagat Singh. Marwar war desultory till 1698 — Ajit Singh recognised then, but Jodhpur fort remained Mughal till 1707. Damaged Mughal-Rajput alliance irreversibly; scholarly consensus: Aurangzeb's biggest political blunder among Rajput dealings.

hist_jinji_siege_1690.label: Siege of Jinji (1690-1698)
hist_jinji_siege_1690.subject: history
hist_jinji_siege_1690.detail: Mughal siege of Jinji fort in Tamil Nadu 1690-1698 — longest single siege of Aurangzeb's reign. Rajaram had reached Jinji 1690 after Sambhaji's execution, establishing Maratha capital-in-exile on eastern seaboard. Mughal siege led by Zulfiqar Khan (son of wazir Asad Khan) + Prince Kam Bakhsh — repeatedly bogged down. Rajaram escaped 1698 just days before fall. Signalled Mughal inability to eliminate Maratha leadership even with overwhelming force. Shows Maratha resistance had become dispersed and structural, no longer dependent on single capital.

hist_ashtapradhan.label: Shivaji's Ashtapradhan (Eight Ministers)
hist_ashtapradhan.subject: history
hist_ashtapradhan.detail: Shivaji's cabinet of eight ministers (ashta = eight, pradhan = minister), each directly responsible to the Chhatrapati (not a collective body): (1) Peshwa / Mukhya Pradhan — finance + general administration (later became hereditary under Shahu I); (2) Amatya / Majumdar — accounts and revenue records; (3) Mantri / Waqenavis — intelligence + household affairs; (4) Senapati / Sar-i-Naubat — army commander (usually senior Maratha chief); (5) Sumant / Dabir — ceremonies + foreign affairs; (6) Sachiv / Surnavis/Chitnis — correspondence + royal orders; (7) Panditrao / Danadhyaksha — religious affairs + charitable grants; (8) Nyayadhish — judicial head. Most titles in Sanskrit (not Persian) — deliberate cultural statement of Hindu revivalism distinct from Mughal/Deccani Islamic bureaucracy.

hist_sardeshmukhi.label: Sardeshmukhi
hist_sardeshmukhi.subject: history
hist_sardeshmukhi.detail: Additional Maratha tribute levy of 9-10% of land revenue, claimed on hereditary rights as the 'chief deshmukh' (sardeshmukh) of an area. Charged on top of chauth (25%). Together (total ~34-35%) formed the Maratha tribute system over non-Maratha territory. Originally a traditional Deccan feudal right transformed by Shivaji into a political instrument: paid chauth + sardeshmukhi freed an area from Maratha raids. Under the Peshwas, became the financial backbone of Maratha Confederacy's continental expansion. Mughal emperor Shahu bargained for sardeshmukhi-over-Deccan recognition from Delhi in 1719 treaty with Sayyid brothers.

hist_muhtasib.label: Muhtasib (Aurangzeb's Morality Police)
hist_muhtasib.subject: history
hist_muhtasib.detail: 'Censor of public morals' — provincial officials appointed by Aurangzeb from 1666 onwards to enforce shariat-compliance in public. Duties: regulated consumption of wine + bhang, brothels, gambling dens; inspected weights and measures; enforced zawabits (secular decrees); ensured shops closed during prayer times. Aurangzeb stressed the state's obligation for Muslim moral welfare but explicitly instructed muhtasibs NOT to enter private homes or interfere in private lives. In practice, enforcement was patchy and uneven; muhtasibs were routinely bribed or defied. Emblem of Aurangzeb's shift towards Islamic state-theory.

hist_fatawa_i_alamgiri.label: Fatawa-i-Alamgiri
hist_fatawa_i_alamgiri.subject: history
hist_fatawa_i_alamgiri.detail: Monumental compendium of Hanafi fiqh (Islamic jurisprudence) commissioned by Aurangzeb c. 1667. Compiled by a team of ~500 ulama under Shaikh Nizam of Burhanpur over ~8 years, completed c. 1675. 30 volumes covering personal law, ritual, commerce, criminal law, state administration. Most comprehensive pre-modern legal text of Indian Sunni Islam. Served as reference in Mughal qazi courts; later used in colonial and post-colonial Muslim personal law. Companion work: Zawabit-i-Alamgiri (Aurangzeb's secular decrees supplementing shariat). Reflects systematisation of Islamic governance analogous to Akbar's Ain-i-Akbari but with religious-legal rather than administrative focus.

hist_moti_masjid_agra.label: Moti Masjid (Agra Fort)
hist_moti_masjid_agra.subject: history
hist_moti_masjid_agra.detail: 'Pearl Mosque' built inside Agra Fort by Shah Jahan 1647-1654. Pure white marble. Three bulbous domes on octagonal drums; inlaid black-marble calligraphy bands; minimal ornamentation. Considered stylistic pinnacle of Shah Jahan's imperial mosque idiom — all marble, refined proportions. Distinct from Aurangzeb's later Moti Masjid inside Delhi Red Fort (1659-1660). Built for private Mughal family prayer.

hist_jama_masjid_delhi.label: Jama Masjid (Delhi)
hist_jama_masjid_delhi.subject: history
hist_jama_masjid_delhi.detail: Masjid-i-Jahan-Numa ('Mosque Commanding View of the World') — Shah Jahan's grand Friday mosque of Shahjahanabad, built 1650-1656. Largest mosque in India. Red sandstone base + white marble striping. Three bulbous domes with black-marble inlay. Two 40m-high tapering minarets. Vast prayer courtyard (~75,000 sq ft, capacity 25,000). Three gateways (north/south/east). Completed by architects Ustad Khalil + team of 5,000 workers. Symbol of Mughal imperial Islam at Shahjahanabad's heart. Bahadur Shah Zafar II delivered his final khutba here 1857 before British exile.

hist_ustad_mansur.label: Ustad Mansur
hist_ustad_mansur.subject: history
hist_ustad_mansur.detail: 'Nadir-ul-Asr' ('Wonder of the Age') — Jahangir's master painter active c. 1595-1625. Celebrated for natural-history studies of birds, animals, flowers commissioned personally by Jahangir (himself a keen amateur naturalist). Famous works: Siberian Crane, Dodo (one of only four contemporary dodo paintings), zebra (Jahangir's 1621 gift from Turkish governor of Abyssinia), turkey from Goa, tulips of Kashmir. Scientific accuracy rivalled Dutch natural-history painters of the period. Pinnacle of Mughal naturalist tradition; his style influenced later Deccani and Rajasthani natural-history painting.

hist_wahdat_ul_wujud_vs_shuhud.label: Wahdat-ul-Wujud vs Wahdat-ul-Shuhud
hist_wahdat_ul_wujud_vs_shuhud.subject: history
hist_wahdat_ul_wujud_vs_shuhud.detail: Two Sufi metaphysical positions with major political consequence in Mughal India. **Wahdat-ul-Wujud** (Unity of Being) — doctrine of Ibn Arabi (13c Andalusian Sufi): all existence is a single reality; God and creation are ontologically one. Favoured by Chishti Silsila, embraced by Akbar (underpinned Sulh-i-Kul), Dara Shukoh (wrote Majma-ul-Bahrain comparing it with Vedanta), and the Muslim-Hindu liberal synthesis. **Wahdat-ul-Shuhud** (Unity of Witnessing) — doctrine of Alauddoullah Simnani (14c Persian Sufi) + Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi (17c): God is ontologically distinct from creation; apparent unity in mystical experience is only 'witnessing' not ontological identity. Favoured by Naqshbandi Silsila, supported by orthodox ulama, aligned with Aurangzeb's religious turn. The Wujud-Shuhud rift underlay the Akbar-Aurangzeb policy divergence and shaped later Indo-Muslim intellectual traditions (Shah Waliullah attempted synthesis in 18c; Deobandis and Barelvis still divide on the issue).

hist_itmad_ud_daulah_tomb.label: Itmad-ud-Daulah's Tomb (Baby Taj)
hist_itmad_ud_daulah_tomb.subject: history
hist_itmad_ud_daulah_tomb.detail: Agra tomb of Mirza Ghiyas Beg (Itimad-ud-Daulah), built by his daughter Nur Jahan 1622-1628 on the east bank of the Yamuna. **First Mughal monument entirely in white marble** (prototype for Taj Mahal). **First Mughal use of pietra-dura inlay** — semi-precious stones (cornelian, jasper, topaz, lapis lazuli, onyx) in fine arabesque and floral patterns. Elegant small pavilion on a chahar-bagh garden. Known as the 'Baby Taj' or 'Jewel Box' for its jewel-like quality. Direct stylistic ancestor of Shah Jahan's Taj Mahal built a decade later.

hist_akbar_tomb_sikandra.label: Akbar's Tomb at Sikandra
hist_akbar_tomb_sikandra.subject: history
hist_akbar_tomb_sikandra.detail: Tomb of Akbar at Sikandra (10 km NW of Agra). Begun by Akbar himself c. 1605 on site he selected; completed by Jahangir 1613 after several redesigns (father-son rift over plans reportedly caused delay). Unique 5-storey pyramidal structure — no dome. Trabeate chhatris, open terraces, central cenotaph chamber with actual grave in basement. Massive four-minaret southern gateway faced with mosaic. Blends Hindu-Buddhist-Islamic architectural elements in Akbar's syncretic idiom. Surrounding chahar-bagh was once stocked with deer, hares, black-buck. Looted by Jats under Rajaram 1691, and later by Nadir Shah 1739.

hist_jahangir_tomb.label: Jahangir's Tomb at Shahdara (Lahore)
hist_jahangir_tomb.subject: history
hist_jahangir_tomb.detail: Tomb of Jahangir at Shahdara, across the Ravi from Lahore. Built by Shah Jahan 1627-1637 on grounds Jahangir himself selected (died near Lahore October 1627). Single-storey rectangular structure with **no central dome** — tradition holds Jahangir forbade it in his will. Four octagonal corner minarets, each ~30m high, faced with marble inlay. Interior: white-marble cenotaph chamber with pietra-dura inlay listing 99 names of Allah in black. Paired with Nur Jahan's own tomb nearby (she outlived him 18 years). Baoli Sarai forecourt with four gateways.

hist_bibi_ka_maqbara.label: Bibi-ka-Maqbara (Aurangabad)
hist_bibi_ka_maqbara.subject: history
hist_bibi_ka_maqbara.detail: 'Tomb of the Lady'. Mausoleum at Aurangabad built by Prince Azam Shah (Aurangzeb's son) 1651-1661 for his mother Dilras Banu Begum (titled Rabia-ud-Daurani posthumously). Deliberate replica of Taj Mahal at reduced scale and cheaper materials — only lower plinth and mausoleum base in marble; rest in plaster simulating marble. Cost ~7 lakh rupees vs Taj's ~32 million. Hence nicknames 'Poor Man's Taj' / 'Dakkhani Taj'. Only significant Aurangzeb-era imperial architectural monument — reflects Aurangzeb's economy-mindedness.

hist_peacock_throne.label: Peacock Throne (Takht-i-Tawus)
hist_peacock_throne.subject: history
hist_peacock_throne.detail: Shah Jahan's fabled jewelled throne, installed in Diwan-i-Khas of Red Fort Delhi 1635 after 7 years of work by royal goldsmith Bebadal Khan. Solid gold base ~1,150 kg; ~230 kg of precious gems. Twelve-pillared canopy surmounted by two jewel-studded peacock figures (hence the name). Major stones: **Koh-i-Noor diamond**, **Timur Ruby** (actually a balas ruby/spinel), Akbar Shah Diamond, Great Table Diamond. Cost ~100 lakh rupees — approximately twice the Taj Mahal. Looted by **Nadir Shah during 1739 Delhi sack** — carried to Iran; dismantled after Nadir Shah's assassination 1747. Gems dispersed: Koh-i-Noor reached British crown jewels; Timur Ruby in British Crown; Nadirs of remaining parts replicated in later Iranian and Ottoman thrones.

hist_shalimar_bagh_kashmir.label: Shalimar Bagh (Kashmir)
hist_shalimar_bagh_kashmir.subject: history
hist_shalimar_bagh_kashmir.detail: Mughal pleasure garden laid out by Jahangir 1619 for wife Nur Jahan on shores of Dal Lake, Srinagar. Three ascending terraces connected by a central canal (Shah Nahar) with fountains: (1) **Diwan-i-Am** — ordinary public; (2) **Diwan-i-Khas** — emperor's private terrace; (3) **zenana terrace** reserved for imperial ladies. Black-marble pavilion on upper terrace. Classic chahar-bagh layout with fountains, fruit orchards (apple, pear, mulberry), chinar trees. Shah Jahan later built a distinct Shalimar Bagh at Lahore 1641 following similar template. Both are UNESCO World Heritage components.

hist_hamzanama.label: Hamzanama
hist_hamzanama.subject: history
hist_hamzanama.detail: Dastan-i-Amir-Hamza (Romance of Amir Hamza — the Prophet's uncle). Monumental illustrated Persian manuscript commissioned by Akbar c. 1562 and completed c. 1577 after 15 years. **14 volumes with ~1,400 folios** — one of the largest Islamic illustrated manuscript projects ever. Each folio ~68×55 cm — unusually large; paintings on cotton cloth, text on reverse. Supervised by Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad. Employed 100+ artists including Daswant, Basawan, Kesav Das, Miskin, Mukund, Lal. Fusion of Persian composition with Indian colour and naturalistic figures — synthesised the Mughal style. Only ~200 folios survive today (major holdings: MAK Vienna, Victoria & Albert Museum London). Foundational project of Mughal painting tradition.

hist_tutinama.label: Tutinama
hist_tutinama.subject: history
hist_tutinama.detail: 'Tales of a Parrot'. Persian version of Sanskrit Suka Saptati (Seventy Tales of the Parrot) commissioned by Akbar c. 1560-65. Early formative work of Mughal atelier under Mir Sayyid Ali + Abdus Samad — bridging Persian miniature style to emerging Mughal synthesis. ~250 folios with ~200 miniatures, smaller format than Hamzanama. Major version in Cleveland Museum of Art (US). Shows the transitional moment when Persian techniques (flat planes, stylised landscape) began absorbing Indian colour and figure traditions.

hist_mewar_painting.label: Mewar School of Painting
hist_mewar_painting.subject: history
hist_mewar_painting.detail: Rajasthani school centred at Udaipur (Sisodiya patronage), peak in 17-18c. Mewar resisted Mughal suzerainty longest — acceded only under Shah Jahan (via 1615 Jahangir treaty's spirit still honoured). Paintings continued throughout wilderness-capital years. Master **Sahibdin** (active c. 1628-1655) depicted Rasikapriya, Ramayana, Bhagavata Purana. Post-Sahibdin: court-life scenes + unique 'tamasha' paintings showing royal ceremony + city views in unprecedented architectural detail. Characterised by bold colour, devotion to Krishna-Radha + royal portraiture subjects, strong linear rhythm. → closely related to Pre-Mughal Chaurapanchasika tradition of Western India.

hist_kishangarh_painting.label: Kishangarh School — Bani Thani
hist_kishangarh_painting.subject: history
hist_kishangarh_painting.detail: 18c Rajasthani school in the small Kishangarh kingdom (Rajasthan). Trio of creators: Raja **Sawant Singh** (r. 1748-57) + his alter-ego Nagari Das (Krishna bhakti poet who abdicated to live at Vrindavan) + court painter **Nihal Chand**. Signature style: the iconic 'Bani Thani' female figure — stylised with elongated arched eyebrows, pronounced lotus-petal eyes, thin lips, pointed chin, graceful neck, elegant pointed headgear — reputedly modelled on Sawant Singh's beloved companion and poet Bani Thani. Depicts Radha-Krishna devotional scenes + idealised feminine figure. Often called 'the Mona Lisa of India'.

hist_ragamala_paintings.label: Ragamala Paintings
hist_ragamala_paintings.subject: history
hist_ragamala_paintings.detail: 'Garland of Ragas' — illustrative painting tradition personifying Indian classical musical ragas as visual scenes. Emerged 16-17c. Each raga depicted as nayaka-nayika (hero-heroine) figure, with associated colour, season, time of day/night, and Hindu deity (e.g. Bhairava ↔ Shiva, Bhairavi ↔ Devi, Sri ↔ Devi). Six principal ragas: Bhairava, Deepak, Sri, Malkaus, Megha, Hindola — plus 36 raginis and sub-raginis in typical set of 36 or 42 paintings. Produced across schools: **Pahari Ragamala, Rajasthani/Rajput Ragamala, Deccan Ragamala, Mughal Ragamala** — each with distinct stylistic treatment. Classical amalgamation of music + poetry + visual art; popular subject across all 17c-18c Indian painting traditions.

hist_bundi_painting.label: Bundi-Kota School (Hadoti)
hist_bundi_painting.subject: history
hist_bundi_painting.detail: Twin-kingdom school — Bundi (parent) + Kota (split c. 1631). Collectively called Hadoti. 18c royal patrons declared themselves mere regents ruling on behalf of the god Krishna as true king. Krishna-bhakti central to painting. Bundi style: detailed local vegetation, round faces with pointed noses, distinctive sky-treatment with red-ribbon accents, colourful palette. Kota school famous for hunting scenes + Rao Ram Singh II-era (early-19c) court portraits. Bundi produced Rasikapriya, Barahmasa, Ragamala series. Some of the finest Rajput hunting-scene compositions.

hist_amber_jaipur_painting.label: Amber-Jaipur (Dhundar) School
hist_amber_jaipur_painting.subject: history
hist_amber_jaipur_painting.detail: Rajasthani school in Kachhwaha kingdom — earliest evidences in wall paintings at Bairat (Rajasthan) and Amer palace murals. Zenith under **Sawai Pratap Singh** (r. 1778-1803) — deeply religious, passionate patron. His suratkhana (painting department) produced miniatures of Bhagavata Purana, Ramayana, Ragamala + portraits. Mughal-influenced clothing and headgear on figures but folk-styled overall finish. Also called 'Dhundar School' after the Dhundar region. Closely tied to Amber-Mughal cultural exchange.

hist_marwar_painting.label: Marwar-Jodhpur School
hist_marwar_painting.subject: history
hist_marwar_painting.detail: Rathor-patronised Rajasthani school spanning Jodhpur + Bikaner + Jaisalmer (Bhati). Prospered through close Mughal ties in 16-17c. Peak during reign of Maharaja **Man Singh** of Jodhpur (1803-1843) who commissioned extensive series: Shiva Purana, Natacharitra, Durgacharitra, Panchatantra. 15-16c paintings featured colourful clothing on men and women. Post-18c: Rajput element became predominant — linear rhythm + bright colours + less Mughal influence. Desert-kingdom palette (earth tones dominant) distinguishes from Mewar's richer colour scheme.

hist_naqshbandi_silsila.label: Naqshbandi Silsila
hist_naqshbandi_silsila.subject: history
hist_naqshbandi_silsila.detail: Sunni-orthodox Sufi order established in India by Khwaja Baqi Billah of Kabul c. 1600 (order traces to Bahauddin Naqshband, 14c Central Asia). Distinctive practices vs Chishtis: strict shariat compliance; silent zikr (not loud/musical); rejection of sama (music in religious gatherings); no bowing to pir; emphasis on inner mental discipline. Most famous Indian exponent **Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi** — propounded Wahdat-ul-Shuhud against Chishti Wahdat-ul-Wujud. Order aligned with Mughal political revivalism — influenced Aurangzeb's orthodox turn. Later Naqshbandi lineage: Shah Waliullah of Delhi (18c ideological fountainhead of Indian Islamic revivalism); Deobandi school (19c) traces partial intellectual descent.

hist_qadariya_silsila.label: Qadariya Silsila
hist_qadariya_silsila.subject: history
hist_qadariya_silsila.detail: Sufi order founded by Abdul Qadir Gilani (Pir Dastagir, 11-12c Baghdad). Introduced to India by Shah Niamatullah c. 15c. Flourished in Punjab (especially Sindh). Supported Wahdat-ul-Wujud doctrine (unity of being) — contrasting with orthodox Naqshbandis. Most famous Indian pir: **Miyan Mir** of Lahore, spiritual guide to Dara Shukoh. Later Qadariya-influenced Urdu poets: Hasrat Mohani, Muhammad Iqbal. Integrated Chishti-like openness to Hindu mystic traditions. Supported the syncretic intellectual current that produced Dara Shukoh's Upanishad translations + Majma-ul-Bahrain.

hist_miyan_mir.label: Miyan Mir
hist_miyan_mir.subject: history
hist_miyan_mir.detail: Qadariya Sufi saint of Lahore (1550-1635), born Mir Mohammed in Sindh. Spent most life in Lahore. **Laid the foundation stone of Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar in 1589** at Guru Arjan's invitation — iconic gesture of Sikh-Sufi cross-tradition respect. Pir of **Dara Shukoh** — initiated him into the Qadariya path. Taught syncretic fusion of Sufism and Hindu mysticism that deeply shaped Dara's Majma-ul-Bahrain (Confluence of Two Seas) comparing Sufi and Vedantic metaphysics. Also respected by Jahangir who visited him. Buried at Lahore (tomb now in Pakistan) — tomb a pilgrimage site for both Sikhs and Muslims.

hist_tudor_arch.label: Tudor Arch (Akbari Architecture)
hist_tudor_arch.subject: history
hist_tudor_arch.detail: Four-centred arch architectural element introduced by Akbar in Mughal buildings. Name borrowed from roughly coincident English Tudor-era architecture, though independently developed. Lower and wider than earlier two-centred Islamic pointed arches (used in Delhi Sultanate). Allowed lighter structural loads, broader openings, and more ornamental gateways. Used extensively at Fatehpur Sikri (Jama Masjid, Diwan-i-Khas) and Agra Fort. Characteristic of Akbari architectural phase alongside red sandstone construction, jharokha balconies, chhatris borrowed from Rajput idiom, and decorative tile work with Persian glazed-blue pattern.

hist_tavernier.label: Jean-Baptiste Tavernier
hist_tavernier.subject: history
hist_tavernier.detail: French jeweller-traveller (1605-1689). Made six voyages to the East including India 1631-1668 — more than any European contemporary. Visited every major Mughal city + Deccan sultanates + Hindu courts. Trader in precious stones — identified and brought back the 'Tavernier Blue' diamond (later recut as the Hope Diamond) plus the Great Mogul Diamond. Published Les Six Voyages 1676 (widely translated) — most detailed European account of 17c Indian trade, diamond mines (Golconda, Panna), royal workshops. Compared India favourably with Iran and Ottoman Empire. Received title Baron d'Aubonne by Louis XIV for services.

hist_manucci.label: Niccolao Manucci
hist_manucci.subject: history
hist_manucci.detail: Venetian traveller (1638-1717) who settled permanently in India. Arrived 1656 as teenager; served as artilleryman in Dara Shukoh's army during 1658 succession war; witnessed Dara's defeat. Later gunner for Raja Jai Singh's 1665 Bijapur campaign. Physician to Dara's sister Jahanara, then at Shah Alam's court. Settled at Madras post-1686. Wrote monumental **Storia do Mogor** (Story of the Mughals, 1701-1711) covering Mughal history from Timur to Aurangzeb — rich eyewitness detail on Deccan wars, court intrigues, daily life. Illustrated with 60+ miniatures. Never returned to Europe. Among most comprehensive European sources for late-17c Mughal India — translated into English only 1907 (William Irvine).

hist_eknath.label: Sant Eknath
hist_eknath.subject: history
hist_eknath.detail: Marathi bhakti saint (1533-1599) of the Varkari tradition (worshipper of Vithoba of Pandharpur). Wrote **Bhavarth Ramayana** in Marathi + **Eknathi Bhagavata** (commentary on the 11th canto of Bhagavata Purana). Asserted vernacular dignity: 'Marathi is worthy of expressing the highest sentiments... God is no partisan of tongues.' Opened his house to Dalits; argued against caste-based discrimination. Bridge figure between medieval Jnandev-Namdev tradition and the Tukaram-Ramdas era that fed Maratha political awakening. Celebrated Eknathi Bharud (bhakti-dramatic-songs) form.

hist_dadu_dayal.label: Dadu Dayal
hist_dadu_dayal.subject: history
hist_dadu_dayal.detail: Rajasthani Nirguna bhakti saint (1544-1603), born in Ahmedabad (possibly originally a Muslim cotton-carder by caste). Follower of Kabir-like Sant tradition. Refused identification with either Hindus or Muslims — preached nipakh ('non-sectarian') path. Asserted indivisibility of Brahma (Supreme Reality). Composed in Hindi/Braj (his compositions gathered as Dadu-Bani). Contemporary of Akbar who reportedly respected and visited him. Established order called **Dadu Panth** at Naraina, Rajasthan 1585 — the sect continues to this day with ~100,000 followers across Rajasthan. His disciples included Sundar Das and Rajab.

hist_galileo.label: Galileo Galilei
hist_galileo.subject: history
hist_galileo.detail: Italian astronomer and physicist (1564-1642), called the 'father of modern science'. Used the telescope to observe moons of Jupiter, phases of Venus, and sunspots, supporting Copernican heliocentrism. Tried by the Inquisition (1633) and forced to recant. Pioneered the experimental method in physics.

pol_hobbes.label: Thomas Hobbes
pol_hobbes.subject: polity
pol_hobbes.detail: English philosopher (1588-1679). 'Leviathan' (1651). State of nature as war of all against all. Social contract creates absolute sovereign for security. Individual rights surrendered for protection. Life without government: 'nasty, brutish, and short'.

pol_locke.label: John Locke
pol_locke.subject: polity
pol_locke.detail: English philosopher (1632-1704). Father of liberalism. Natural rights: life, liberty, property. Social contract: people form government to protect rights. Government that violates rights can be overthrown. Influenced American constitution.

hist_enclosure_movement.label: Enclosure Movement
hist_enclosure_movement.subject: history
hist_enclosure_movement.detail: Process by which common lands were fenced off and consolidated into private farms, particularly in 18th-century England. Parliamentary Enclosure Acts accelerated this. Large landowners benefited while smallholders and cottagers lost access to commons. Displaced rural population migrated to industrial towns, providing factory labour.

hist_agricultural_revolution.label: Agricultural Revolution (Britain)
hist_agricultural_revolution.subject: history
hist_agricultural_revolution.detail: 18c British farming transformation: crop rotation (turnip + clover), selective livestock breeding, Jethro Tull's seed drill, enclosures. Food surplus freed labour for industrial employment.

pol_rousseau.label: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
pol_rousseau.subject: polity
pol_rousseau.detail: French philosopher (1712-1778). Argued inequality is not natural but created by society and private property. 'Man is born free and everywhere he is in chains.' Social contract theory emphasizing popular sovereignty and general will.

hist_counter_reformation.label: Counter-Reformation
hist_counter_reformation.subject: history
hist_counter_reformation.detail: The Catholic Church's response to the Protestant Reformation, spanning roughly 1545-1648. The Council of Trent (1545-1563) reaffirmed Catholic doctrine while reforming abuses. The Jesuit order (founded 1540) led educational and missionary efforts. The Inquisition was strengthened to combat heresy. Art was used to inspire faith (Baroque).

hist_coal_iron.label: Coal and Iron Industries
hist_coal_iron.subject: history
hist_coal_iron.detail: Coal powered the steam engines and heated iron furnaces. Abraham Darby's coke-smelting process (1709) and Henry Cort's puddling process (1784) revolutionised iron production. Britain's abundant coal and iron deposits were critical advantages. These industries underpinned railway construction, shipbuilding, and machine manufacturing.

hist_proto_industrialisation.label: Proto-Industrialisation
hist_proto_industrialisation.subject: history
hist_proto_industrialisation.detail: Pre-factory production system where merchants gave advances to rural producers. Large-scale production for international market existed before factories. Challenges view of a sudden factory revolution.

hist_calico_act_1720.label: Calico Act (1720)
hist_calico_act_1720.subject: history
hist_calico_act_1720.detail: British Parliament banned use of printed cotton (chintz) in England to protect English wool and silk industries from Indian textile competition. Early protectionist law against Indian textiles.

hist_diseases_and_depopulation.label: Diseases and Indigenous Depopulation
hist_diseases_and_depopulation.subject: history
hist_diseases_and_depopulation.detail: European diseases -- smallpox, measles, influenza, typhus -- devastated indigenous populations who had no immunity. In the Americas, an estimated 90% of the indigenous population died within a century of contact. In Australia, smallpox epidemics decimated Aboriginal communities. Disease was the single largest cause of indigenous population decline.

hist_council_of_trent.label: Council of Trent
hist_council_of_trent.subject: history
hist_council_of_trent.detail: Ecumenical council of the Catholic Church (1545-1563) convened in response to the Protestant Reformation. Reaffirmed key Catholic doctrines (transubstantiation, seven sacraments, role of tradition alongside scripture). Reformed clerical abuses, established seminaries for priest training, and standardised the Latin Vulgate Bible.

hist_cricket_origins.label: Origins of Cricket
hist_cricket_origins.subject: history
hist_cricket_origins.detail: Evolved from stick-and-ball games in England 500 years ago. First written Laws of Cricket in 1744 specified 22-yard pitch, stumps 22 inches high. World's first cricket club formed at Hambledon in 1760s. MCC at Lord's became guardian of rules.

hist_scientific_revolution.label: Scientific Revolution
hist_scientific_revolution.subject: history
hist_scientific_revolution.detail: Transformation in understanding of the natural world from the 16th-17th centuries. Copernicus proposed heliocentrism (1543), Galileo used the telescope to confirm it, Kepler described planetary motion, and Newton formulated laws of gravity and motion. Shifted authority from ancient texts and the Church to observation and experiment.

hist_rise_of_novel.label: Rise of the Novel in Europe
hist_rise_of_novel.subject: history
hist_rise_of_novel.detail: Novel emerged in 18th century Europe with growing middle class and print culture. Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe (1719), Samuel Richardson's Pamela (1740). Novels explored individual choices, social relationships and everyday life.

hist_english_agricultural_revolution.label: English Agricultural Revolution
hist_english_agricultural_revolution.subject: history
hist_english_agricultural_revolution.detail: New crop rotations replacing fallow with turnip and clover increased productivity. Enclosures enabled large-scale farming. Population growth from 7 million (1750) to 30 million (1900) drove demand for grain.

hist_copernicus.label: Nicolaus Copernicus
hist_copernicus.subject: history
hist_copernicus.detail: Polish astronomer (1473-1543) who proposed the heliocentric model of the solar system in his work 'De Revolutionibus' (1543). Challenged the geocentric (Earth-centred) view held since Ptolemy and endorsed by the Church. His theory was revolutionary but initially had limited impact; it was taken forward by Galileo and Kepler.

hist_jesuits.label: Jesuits (Society of Jesus)
hist_jesuits.subject: history
hist_jesuits.detail: Catholic religious order founded by Ignatius of Loyola in 1540. Known for rigorous education, missionary activity, and intellectual engagement. Established schools and universities across Europe and in missions worldwide (including India, China, Japan, Americas). Were the spearhead of the Counter-Reformation.

hist_qing_dynasty.label: Qing Dynasty (1644-1912)
hist_qing_dynasty.subject: history
hist_qing_dynasty.detail: Manchu dynasty, last imperial dynasty of China. Zenith under Kangxi + Qianlong. From 19c: Opium Wars, Taiping, Boxer Rebellion. Failed to modernise adequately; overthrown 1911.

hist_samurai.label: Samurai
hist_samurai.subject: history
hist_samurai.detail: Warrior class of feudal Japan serving daimyo lords. Bushido code: loyalty, martial arts, self-discipline. Many became bureaucrats during Tokugawa peace. Meiji Restoration abolished their special status — though many samurai led the modernisation effort.

hist_tokugawa_japan.label: Tokugawa Shogunate (1603-1868)
hist_tokugawa_japan.subject: history
hist_tokugawa_japan.detail: Military government ruling Japan. Rigid social hierarchy (samurai/farmers/artisans/merchants). Sakoku isolation limited foreign contact. Internal tensions + Perry's 1853 arrival led to collapse.

hist_suleyman_magnificent.label: Suleyman the Magnificent
hist_suleyman_magnificent.subject: history
hist_suleyman_magnificent.detail: Ottoman Sultan 1520-1566, known in Turkish as 'Kanuni' (the Lawgiver) for standardising administrative law. Ruled at Ottoman apogee — conquered Belgrade 1521, Rhodes 1522, defeated Hungary at Mohács 1526, besieged Vienna 1529, took Baghdad 1534, Yemen 1538, much of North Africa to Morocco. Rebuilt Ottoman navy under Barbarossa Hayreddin Pasha; contested Portuguese in Red Sea and Arabian Sea. Contemporary of Babur and Humayun. Patron of architect Sinan (Suleymaniye Mosque 1557). Died campaigning in Hungary.

hist_shah_abbas_safavid.label: Shah Abbas I (Safavid)
hist_shah_abbas_safavid.subject: history
hist_shah_abbas_safavid.detail: Safavid Shah of Persia 1588-1629 ('the Great'). Re-established Persian power after Ottoman/Uzbeg reverses — modernised army with cannon corps (ghulam slaves from Caucasus), reformed administration. Captured Qandahar from Mughals 1622 during Jahangir's reign; Qandahar lost again by Shah Jahan 1649 after three unsuccessful sieges. Moved capital to Isfahan (1598), built Naqsh-e-Jahan Square, Shah Mosque, Chehel Sotoun. Received Sherley brothers and other European envoys. Direct Mughal contemporary; Humayun had received asylum from his grandfather Shah Tahmasp.

hist_queen_elizabeth_i.label: Queen Elizabeth I of England
hist_queen_elizabeth_i.subject: history
hist_queen_elizabeth_i.detail: Queen of England and Ireland 1558-1603. Akbar's near-exact contemporary. Protestant settlement (Church of England), defeat of Spanish Armada 1588, Elizabethan cultural flowering (Shakespeare, Spenser, Marlowe). Granted Royal Charter to East India Company 31 December 1600. Sent William Hawkins and Thomas Roe as ambassadors to Mughal court. Virgin Queen — died without issue, ending Tudor line; succeeded by Stuart James I.

hist_ivan_iv_russia.label: Ivan IV "the Terrible" of Russia
hist_ivan_iv_russia.subject: history
hist_ivan_iv_russia.detail: First crowned Tsar of All Russia (1547-1584). Expanded Russia eastward — conquered Khanate of Kazan 1552 and Astrakhan 1556 (ending Mongol/Tatar successor states on the Volga), opened Siberia to Russian colonisation. Oprichnina terror (1565-1572). Long Livonian War (1558-1583) weakened Russia. Founded first Russian printing press. Reign coincided with Humayun's second reign and most of Akbar's; no direct India contact but long-term Russian presence in Central Asia would later intersect with Great Game.

period_babur_humayun.label: Babur & Humayun
period_babur_humayun.subject: history
period_babur_humayun.detail: Founding phase of the Mughal Empire (1526-1556). Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat-I 1526 — first major gunpowder use in North India via Ottoman master-gunners Ustad Ali + Mustafa. Defeated Rana Sanga at Khanwa 1527, Medini Rai at Chanderi 1528. Battle of Ghagra 1529 vs Afghans + Nusrat Shah of Bengal. Babur died 1530, leaving memoirs Tuzuk-i-Baburi in Chaghtai Turkish. Humayun (1530-40, 1555-56) lost empire to Sher Shah Sur at Chausa 1539 + Kanauj 1540; regained Delhi 1555 from Sur civil war with Safavid help. Ruinous Timurid tradition of partition among brothers (Kamran took Punjab/Multan; Askari and Hindal rebelled). Bahadur Shah of Gujarat and his ally Sher Khan loomed as rivals.

period_akbar.label: Akbar
period_akbar.subject: history
period_akbar.detail: Akbar's reign (1556-1605) — consolidation of Mughal power. Crowned at Kalanaur age 13 after Humayun's death; Second Battle of Panipat 1556 by Bairam Khan vs Hemu restored Mughal Delhi. Period of three phases: regency (Bairam Khan, 1556-60), consolidation (Chittor 1568, Ranthambhor 1569, Gujarat 1572-73, Bengal 1576), expansion (Qandahar 1595, Kashmir 1586, Sindh 1590, Deccan). Raja Bharmal Kachhwaha of Amber — first Rajput to join Mughal service 1562 — established the watan-jagir model. Administrative reforms: subadari system (12 subas 1580), dahsala land revenue via Todar Mal + team, mansabdari system institutionalised (zat+sawar 1594-95), Akbar Nama + Ain-i-Akbari by Abu'l Fazl. Religious experiments: Ibadat Khana debates 1575-82, Sulh-i-Kul doctrine, Mahzar 1579, Din-i-Ilahi 1582, Maktab Khana translated Sanskrit classics into Persian. Abolished jizya 1564 + pilgrimage tax 1563. Capital shifted Agra → Fatehpur Sikri (1571) → Lahore (1585). Navaratna court: Abu'l Fazl, Faizi, Birbal, Todar Mal, Man Singh, Abdur Rahim, Tansen, et al.

period_jahangir_nur_jahan.label: Jahangir & Nur Jahan
period_jahangir_nur_jahan.subject: history
period_jahangir_nur_jahan.detail: Jahangir's reign (1605-1627). Zanjir-i-Adl (Chain of Justice) instituted to bypass corrupt officials. Painting reached its zenith — Ustad Mansur's naturalistic studies; Mughal atelier's portrait mastery. Wife Nur Jahan (married 1611) + father Itimad-ud-Daulah + brother Asaf Khan formed the disputed 'junta' influence over court. Itimad-ud-Daulah's tomb (1622-28) by Nur Jahan was the first pure-marble + first pietra-dura Mughal work — prototype for the Taj Mahal. Bengal pacified 1608-13 by Islam Khan Chishti (Barah Bhuiyan defeated, capital moved Rajmahal → Dacca). Jesuit missions (Acquaviva, Monserrate) continued. Thomas Roe, English envoy 1615-19. Mughal-Safavid contest over Qandahar — lost to Shah Abbas I 1622. Shah Jahan's rebellion 1622-26 disrupted the final years. Mahabat Khan's June 1626 coup on the Jhelum; Nur Jahan rescued situation within 6 months.

period_shah_jahan.label: Shah Jahan
period_shah_jahan.subject: history
period_shah_jahan.detail: Shah Jahan's reign (1628-1658) — Mughal architectural and cultural climax. Taj Mahal commissioned 1632 for Mumtaz Mahal; Shahjahanabad founded 1639 with Red Fort and Jama Masjid (completed 1656); Moti Masjid at Agra Fort. Peacock Throne (1635) — symbol of imperial wealth, later looted by Nadir Shah 1739. Badshah Nama by Abdul Hamid Lahori. Expanded Mughal control into Deccan: extinction of Ahmadnagar 1633 (Daulatabad fall); Treaties of 1636 secured Bijapur + Golconda as Mughal vassals. Foreign policy: Qandahar regained via Ali Mardan Khan's defection 1638, then permanently lost to Safavids 1649 despite three sieges by Aurangzeb/Dara. Balkh campaign 1646-47 under Prince Murad then Aurangzeb — tactical victory but strategic failure. War of Succession 1657-58 among sons — Aurangzeb triumphed at Samugarh; Shah Jahan imprisoned at Agra Fort till death 1666.

period_aurangzeb.label: Aurangzeb
period_aurangzeb.subject: history
period_aurangzeb.detail: Aurangzeb's reign (1658-1707) — 50 years, territorial climax of the Mughal empire. Orthodox Sunni ruler ('zinda pir'). Zawabit-i-Alamgiri secular decrees; Fatawa-i-Alamgiri 30-volume Hanafi compendium. Discontinued jharoka darshan 1669; reimposed jizya 1679. Temple destruction at Vishwanath Kashi 1669 + Kesava Deo Mathura 1670. Guru Tegh Bahadur executed 1675 — radicalised Sikh community under Guru Gobind Singh (Khalsa founded 1699). North India revolts: Jats (Gokla 1669, Rajaram 1685, Churaman), Satnamis 1672 at Narnaul, Afghan Raushanai/Yusufzai 1667, Afridi 1672. Marwar-Mewar war 1679-1698 damaged Rajput alliance. Ahom-Mughal wars lost at Saraighat 1671 under Lachit Borphukan. Deccan: annexation of Bijapur 1686 + Golconda 1687 ended Deccan Sultanates. Sambhaji executed 1689 — triggered expanded Maratha resistance. Personal 1698-1707 Deccan campaign vs Maratha guerrilla warfare — siege after siege in the fort-country. Died at Aurangabad March 1707. Nobility count tripled (2069→11456) producing the jagirdari crisis.

period_mughal_decline.label: Mughal Decline & Successor States
period_mughal_decline.subject: history
period_mughal_decline.detail: Decline and successor states (1707-1757). Rapid weakening after Aurangzeb's death: multiple successions, faction fighting at court. Banda Bahadur's Sikh revolt 1708-1715. Regional autonomies crystallised: Bengal (Murshid Quli Khan 1717), Awadh (Saadat Khan 1722), Hyderabad (Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah 1724), Jaipur (Sawai Jai Singh II from 1727), Jat state (Churaman/Suraj Mal at Bharatpur). Ijaradari (revenue farming) replaced zabti as administration loosened. Nadir Shah's sack of Delhi 1739 carried off the Peacock Throne + Koh-i-Noor; devastated imperial prestige. Textile economy continued: Dacca mulmul, jamdani; Kangra + Basohli painting schools thrived post-Mughal-atelier dispersal. European East India Companies expanded factories. The era ends with Plassey 1757, marking transition to Company rule (era 7).

period_maratha_rise.label: Maratha Rise
period_maratha_rise.subject: history
period_maratha_rise.detail: Rise of the Marathas (1630-1757). Shivaji (1630-80) built an independent Maratha kingdom: Javli 1656, Afzal Khan killed at Pratapgarh 1659, Shaista Khan's fingers cut at Lal Mahal 1663, Surat sack 1664 + 1670, Treaty of Purandar 1665 with Raja Jai Singh, Agra escape 1666, Battle of Salher 1672, coronation at Raigarh 1674 by Gaga Bhatta (Chhatrapati + Haindava-Dharmoddharak), Karnataka expedition 1676 via Qutb Shahi alliance. Ashtapradhan (8 ministers) system. Chauth (25%) + sardeshmukhi (10%) tribute model. Sambhaji (1680-89) executed by Aurangzeb. Rajaram held Jinji 1690-98. Tarabai led resistance from 1700. Shahu released 1707 by Bahadur Shah — defeated Tarabai at Khed 1708 with Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath; foundation of 18c Maratha Confederacy. Ideological foundation from Samarth Ramdas (Maharashtra Dharma, Dasbodh) and Tukaram's bhakti. Included at the end: contemporary Jijabai (Shivaji's mother) and Shahji Bhonsle's career.

period_mughal_economy.label: Economy, Society & Trade
period_mughal_economy.subject: history
period_mughal_economy.detail: Economy, society and trade under the Mughals (1526-1757) — thematic span across all reigns. Agrarian structure: 85% rural population; khud-kashta (resident) vs pahi-kashta (migrant) peasants; zamindars held milkiyat lands + collected revenue; Ain's 8-column mulk-abadi schema. Land revenue: polaj/parauti/chachar/banjar classification; kankut/batai/khet-batai/lang-batai collection methods. Dahsala bandobast (Akbar) = 10-yr average produce + prices × 1/3 state share. Mughal irrigation: Persian wheel (rehat), shahnahr canals. Jins-i-kamil cash crops (cotton, sugarcane, oilseeds). New World crops adopted 17c (maize, chilli, potato, tomato, tobacco, pineapple). Surat = premier western port; Masulipatnam = Golconda's eastern port. Hundi banking network. Silver rupya stable via global silver flow (Americas → Ottoman/Persia → India). Village panchayat + jajmani system governed local artisan-peasant exchange. Population grew ~50M (1600-1800). Cotton + textile trade (chintz, muslin, Dacca mulmul) was the world's largest. Proto-industrialisation in 18c Bengal. Jagirdari crisis from mid-17c drove decline. European EIC expanded from 1600.

period_mughal_culture.label: Culture, Art & Religion
period_mughal_culture.subject: history
period_mughal_culture.detail: Culture, Art and Religion under the Mughals (1526-1757) — thematic span. Architecture: evolved from red sandstone (Akbar: Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri, Humayun's Tomb, Buland Darwaza) through first marble + pietra-dura (Itimad-ud-Daulah's tomb 1628) to climax marble style (Taj Mahal 1653, Shahjahanabad 1648, Moti Masjid, Jama Masjid). Tudor arch, jharoka, chahar-bagh. Painting: Mughal atelier under Akbar (Hamzanama, Tutinama), Jahangir's naturalism (Ustad Mansur), Shah Jahan's formalism; dispersal seeded Rajasthani (Mewar, Kishangarh, Bundi, Amber, Marwar) + Pahari (Basohli, Kangra, Guler) + Deccan schools + Ragamala tradition. Literature: Persian court language; Akbar Nama, Badshah Nama, Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, Razmnama, Ain-i-Akbari; Hindi Tulsidas (Ramcharitmanas), Surdas; Marathi Eknath, Tukaram; Sikh Adi Granth (1604); Ramdas Dasbodh; Gulbadan Begum's Humayun Nama. Religion: Akbar's Sulh-i-Kul → Din-i-Ilahi; jizya timeline (abolished 1564 → reimposed 1679 → abolished 1712); Chishti silsila (Salim Chishti), Naqshbandi (Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi), Qadariya (Miyan Mir, Dara Shukoh's pir); Sikh gurus Arjan → Gobind Singh; Khalsa 1699; bhakti Tulsidas, Surdas, Mirabai, Eknath, Tukaram, Dadu Dayal. Ibadat Khana, Maktab Khana translation bureau, Mughal kitabkhana. Classical music: Tansen, dhrupad + khayal foundations.

period_deccan_sultanates_tail.label: Deccan Sultanates (post-Talikota)
period_deccan_sultanates_tail.subject: history
period_deccan_sultanates_tail.detail: Deccan Sultanates post-Talikota (1565-1687). Three sultanates dominant: Bijapur (Adil Shahi, 1490-1686) — Ibrahim Adil Shah II 'Jagat Guru' (1580-1627) with Kitab-i-Nauras; Golconda (Qutb Shahi, 1518-1687) — Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah founded Hyderabad + Char Minar 1591; Ahmadnagar (Nizam Shahi, 1490-1633) — Chand Bibi's defence 1595-1600, revived by Ethiopian general Malik Ambar (d. 1626) who pioneered Maratha-guerrilla partnership. Mughal advance: Berar annexation 1596, Khandesh (Asirgarh) 1601, Ahmadnagar extinction 1633, Shah Jahan's 1636 treaties with Bijapur + Golconda, final annexations by Aurangzeb 1686-87. Architecture: Char Minar, Gol Gumbaz (1660, largest single dome of its age), Ibrahim Rauza ('Deccan Taj'). Deccani Urdu poetry, Bijapuri painting school. 30,000-strong Maratha bargis in Bijapur. Major Maratha families (Bhonsles, Mores, Nimbalkars, Ghatges) rose in Sultanate service — seedbed for Shivaji's kingdom.

period_parallel_islamic_west.label: Safavid Persia & Ottoman Empire (parallel)
period_parallel_islamic_west.subject: history
period_parallel_islamic_west.detail: Safavid Persia + Ottoman Empire (1501-1722) — parallel Islamic-world context. **Safavid dynasty** (Shah Ismail from 1501, Shah Tahmasp, **Shah Abbas I 1588-1629**): established Shiism as state religion; rivalry with Sunni Uzbeks and Ottomans; Humayun took refuge there 1544. Contest with Mughals over Qandahar: Akbar reconquered 1595; Shah Abbas seized 1622; Shah Jahan regained 1638 (Ali Mardan defection) then lost 1649. Shah Abbas moved capital to Isfahan (Naqsh-e-Jahan Square, Shah Mosque). **Ottoman Empire** under **Suleyman the Magnificent 1520-1566** (Kanuni/Lawgiver): conquered Hungary at Mohács 1526, besieged Vienna 1529, seized Baghdad 1534; rebuilt Ottoman navy; contested Portuguese in Red Sea + Arabian Sea. Direct Ottoman-Mughal contact via Suleyman + Babur/Humayun (Ottoman master-gunners at Panipat). Ottoman sultan sent embassy to Aurangzeb 1680. Pilgrimage + Red Sea trade routes underlay Mughal-Ottoman economic cooperation.

hist_portuguese_in_india.label: Portuguese Arrival (1498)
hist_portuguese_in_india.subject: history
hist_portuguese_in_india.detail: Portuguese arrived on west coast of India from 1498, establishing trading and military stations. Superior military technology (muskets) made them important in regional politics. Travellers like Duarte Barbosa, Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz documented Vijayanagara.

hist_east_india_companies.label: European East India Companies
hist_east_india_companies.subject: history
hist_east_india_companies.detail: English, Dutch and French companies formed to expand commercial activities in the east. Used naval power to control sea trade. Forced Indian traders to work as agents. English emerged dominant.

hist_black_towns.label: Black Towns
hist_black_towns.subject: history
hist_black_towns.detail: Settlements established by European companies within new cities for native traders and craftspersons. 'Blacks' were confined here while 'whites' occupied Fort St. George (Madras) or Fort St. William (Calcutta).

hist_wajid_ali_shah.label: Wajid Ali Shah
hist_wajid_ali_shah.subject: history
hist_wajid_ali_shah.detail: Last Nawab of Awadh whose patronage helped Kathak grow into a major art form. The Lucknow gharana of Kathak developed under his court. Important patron of arts and culture.

hist_colonial_presidency_cities.label: Presidency Cities
hist_colonial_presidency_cities.subject: history
hist_colonial_presidency_cities.detail: Bombay, Calcutta and Madras became major colonial cities and capitals of three Presidencies. Originally fishing/weaving villages that grew into commercial and administrative centres under British rule. Each had distinct 'white' and 'black' town segregation.

hist_calcutta_colonial.label: Colonial Calcutta
hist_calcutta_colonial.subject: history
hist_calcutta_colonial.detail: Capital of British India until 1911. Fort William built 1757. Black Hole incident (1756). Maidan created as military open space. White Town and Black Town segregation. Became centre of commerce, administration and intellectual life. Bengali renaissance began here.

hist_fort_william.label: Fort William (Calcutta)
hist_fort_william.subject: history
hist_fort_william.detail: Built after Battle of Plassey (1757), massive fort with large open areas around it (Maidan). Symbol of British military power. Earlier Fort William was scene of the Black Hole incident (1756). New fort designed to withstand any future attack.

hist_bombay_colonial.label: Colonial Bombay
hist_bombay_colonial.subject: history
hist_bombay_colonial.detail: Acquired from Portugal in 1661 as part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry. Developed as major port. Cotton textile mills established from 1850s. Great Indian Peninsular Railway terminus (Victoria Terminus, now CST). Gateway of India built 1911. Massive land reclamation projects.

hist_presidency_towns.label: Presidency Towns
hist_presidency_towns.subject: history
hist_presidency_towns.detail: Calcutta, Bombay and Madras were three major colonial cities (Presidency towns) that grew as centres of trade, administration and military power. Each developed distinct colonial urban character.

hist_industrial_revolution.label: Industrial Revolution
hist_industrial_revolution.subject: history
hist_industrial_revolution.detail: Fundamental transformation in manufacturing, technology, and society that began in Britain around 1760 and spread globally through the 19th century. Shifted production from hand tools and home workshops to machine-based factory production. Transformed economy, society, urbanisation, and eventually global power relations. Began ~1760 in Britain, spread globally through 19c. Shifted production from hand tools and home workshops to machine-based factory production.

hist_why_britain.label: Why Britain Led Industrialisation
hist_why_britain.subject: history
hist_why_britain.detail: Britain had unique advantages: abundant coal and iron deposits, colonial markets and raw materials, a strong navy and merchant fleet, political stability after the Glorious Revolution, a patent system encouraging innovation, agricultural revolution freeing labour, and financial institutions (Bank of England, stock exchanges).

hist_canal_system.label: Canal System
hist_canal_system.subject: history
hist_canal_system.detail: Network of artificial waterways built in Britain from the 1760s to transport heavy goods (coal, iron, pottery) cheaply. The Bridgewater Canal (1761) halved the price of coal in Manchester. By 1830, over 4,000 miles of canals existed. Canals were superseded by railways but were crucial in early industrialisation.

hist_third_battle_panipat.label: Third Battle of Panipat (1761)
hist_third_battle_panipat.subject: history
hist_third_battle_panipat.detail: Decisive battle between Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali. Maratha expansion had made other rulers hostile, so they lacked support. Ended Maratha ambitions of replacing Mughal authority at Delhi.

hist_thomas_munro.label: Thomas Munro
hist_thomas_munro.subject: history
hist_thomas_munro.detail: Governor of Madras Presidency who developed the ryotwari system with Alexander Read. Settled revenue directly with individual peasant cultivators without intermediary zamindars. Revenue demand could be revised periodically based on productivity assessment.

hist_history_painting.label: History Painting
hist_history_painting.subject: history
hist_history_painting.detail: Imperial art tradition dramatising British victories in India, like Francis Hayman's 1762 painting of Clive meeting Mir Jafar after Plassey, and numerous paintings of the Battle of Seringapatam against Tipu Sultan.

hist_impact_on_india.label: Industrial Revolution's Impact on India
hist_impact_on_india.subject: history
hist_impact_on_india.detail: British industrialisation devastated India's traditional textile industry. Machine-made British cloth flooded Indian markets while raw cotton was exported from India. Indian artisans and weavers were ruined. India was transformed from a manufacturing economy into a supplier of raw materials and a captive market for British goods.

hist_rousseau_social_contract.label: Rousseau and Social Contract
hist_rousseau_social_contract.subject: history
hist_rousseau_social_contract.detail: Jean Jacques Rousseau proposed government based on social contract between people and representatives. Along with Locke's ideas on individual rights and Montesquieu's separation of powers, shaped revolutionary thought.

hist_cotton_industry.label: Cotton Textile Industry
hist_cotton_industry.subject: history
hist_cotton_industry.detail: The leading sector of early industrialisation in Britain. Raw cotton imported from colonies (India, Americas) was processed in Lancashire mills. Key inventions: spinning jenny (Hargreaves, 1764), water frame (Arkwright, 1769), spinning mule (Crompton, 1779), power loom (Cartwright, 1785). Production increased enormously while Indian textiles were destroyed.

hist_spinning_jenny.label: Spinning Jenny
hist_spinning_jenny.subject: history
hist_spinning_jenny.detail: Multi-spindle spinning frame invented by James Hargreaves around 1764. Allowed one worker to operate eight spindles simultaneously (later expanded to 120). Dramatically increased yarn production. One of the key inventions that mechanised the cotton textile industry and shifted production from homes to factories.

hist_james_watt.label: James Watt
hist_james_watt.subject: history
hist_james_watt.detail: Scottish inventor and engineer (1736-1819) who transformed the steam engine from a crude pump into an efficient power source. His separate condenser (1769) and rotary motion mechanism revolutionised industry. Partnered with Matthew Boulton for manufacturing. The unit of power 'watt' is named after him.

hist_richard_arkwright.label: Richard Arkwright
hist_richard_arkwright.subject: history
hist_richard_arkwright.detail: English inventor and entrepreneur (1732-1792) who developed the water frame for spinning cotton (1769) and built the first water-powered cotton mill at Cromford (1771). Often called the 'father of the factory system'. His mills employed hundreds of workers including children. Became one of the wealthiest men in Britain.

hist_steam_engine.label: Steam Engine
hist_steam_engine.subject: history
hist_steam_engine.detail: Thomas Newcomen built an early steam engine for pumping water from mines (1712). James Watt dramatically improved it (1769), making it efficient and versatile. Applied to factories, railways, and ships. Freed industry from dependence on water power and location near rivers. The defining technology of the Industrial Revolution. Newcomen's early mine-pump engine 1712; Watt's separate condenser 1769 made it efficient and rotary. Applied to factories, railways, ships.

hist_eic_textile_revenue.label: EIC Revenue for Textile Purchase
hist_eic_textile_revenue.subject: history
hist_eic_textile_revenue.detail: After gaining political power in Bengal, the English East India Company no longer imported silver to buy Indian goods. Instead they collected revenues from peasants and zamindars and used this revenue to purchase Indian textiles.

hist_factory_system.label: Factory System
hist_factory_system.subject: history
hist_factory_system.detail: New mode of production replacing cottage industry and artisan workshops. Workers gathered in large buildings with powered machinery, working fixed hours under supervision. Richard Arkwright's Cromford Mill (1771) was an early example. Enabled mass production, division of labour, and employer control over the work process.

hist_opium_cultivation_bengal.label: Opium Cultivation in Bengal
hist_opium_cultivation_bengal.subject: history
hist_opium_cultivation_bengal.detail: British forced Bengal peasants to grow opium for export to China through advance system. Peasants lost food crop land. EIC used opium trade to balance Chinese tea purchases. Caused Opium Wars with China. British opium monopoly 1773. Peasants tied to system via mahato (headman) advances. Pykars (travelling traders) offered higher prices from princely states (Central India, Rajasthan) — British tried to suppress as smuggling.

hist_louis_xvi.label: Louis XVI
hist_louis_xvi.subject: history
hist_louis_xvi.detail: Bourbon king who ascended French throne in 1774 at age 20. Found empty treasury due to wars. Called Estates General in 1789 which led to revolution. Executed publicly on 21 January 1793 for treason. Bourbon king, ascended 1774 at age 20. Empty treasury from wars. Called Estates General 5 May 1789. Tried and executed by guillotine 21 January 1793.

hist_bahadur_shah_zafar.label: Bahadur Shah Zafar II
hist_bahadur_shah_zafar.subject: history
hist_bahadur_shah_zafar.detail: Last Mughal emperor, declared leader of the revolt by sepoys who marched from Meerut to Delhi in May 1857. Had no real military power but provided symbolic legitimacy. After suppression, tried and exiled to Rangoon (Myanmar) where he died in 1862. Tried by British military commission and exiled to Rangoon where he died in 1862. Captured at Humayun's Tomb after Delhi fell 20 Sept 1857. Tried by British military commission; deported to Rangoon (Burma) where he died 1862.

hist_adam_smith.label: Adam Smith
hist_adam_smith.subject: history
hist_adam_smith.detail: Scottish economist and philosopher (1723-1790), author of 'An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations' (1776). Argued for free markets, division of labour, and minimal government intervention (laissez-faire). Concept of the 'invisible hand' guiding economic activity. Called the father of modern economics.

hist_capitalism.label: Capitalism
hist_capitalism.subject: history
hist_capitalism.detail: Economic system that emerged alongside industrialisation, based on private ownership of the means of production, wage labour, and production for profit. Adam Smith's 'Wealth of Nations' (1776) provided its theoretical foundation with ideas of free markets and division of labour. Generated unprecedented wealth but also stark inequality.

hist_kunwar_singh.label: Kunwar Singh
hist_kunwar_singh.subject: history
hist_kunwar_singh.detail: Zamindar from Jagdishpur (Bihar) who was nearly 80 years old when he led the rebellion in Bihar. Despite his age, fought effectively against British forces. One of the most notable non-sepoy leaders of the revolt, representing zamindar resentment.

hist_indigo_plantation.label: Indigo Plantation System
hist_indigo_plantation.subject: history
hist_indigo_plantation.detail: European planters in Bengal forced peasants to grow indigo through advances (dadon) that trapped them in debt cycles. Two systems: nij (planter's own land) and ryoti (peasant's land under contract). Planters used coercion, fraud and intimidation. System collapsed after 1860 rebellion. Two systems: nij (planter own land) and ryoti (peasant contract under dadon advance). Collapsed after Blue Mutiny 1859-60.

hist_paharias.label: Paharias
hist_paharias.subject: history
hist_paharias.detail: Hill people of Rajmahal hills in Bengal-Bihar who lived by shifting cultivation, hunting and gathering forest produce. British initially tried to 'pacify' them, then encouraged Santhals to settle in the plains below, marginalising Paharias from their traditional lands. Rajmahal hills. British policy shifted from pacification to displacement by settling Santhals in the plains below.

hist_print_french_revolution.label: Print Culture and French Revolution
hist_print_french_revolution.subject: history
hist_print_french_revolution.detail: Historians argue print popularised Enlightenment ideas of Voltaire and Rousseau, created culture of dialogue and debate, and literature mocking royalty eroded legitimacy of social order. Prepared conditions for revolution.

hist_tipu_mural_paintings.label: Tipu Sultan's Mural Paintings
hist_tipu_mural_paintings.subject: history
hist_tipu_mural_paintings.detail: Tipu Sultan resisted British cultural traditions and encouraged local art. Had walls of his Seringapatam palace covered with murals by local artists celebrating his father Haidar Ali's victory at Polilur in 1780.

hist_calcutta_madrasa.label: Calcutta Madrasa
hist_calcutta_madrasa.subject: history
hist_calcutta_madrasa.detail: Set up in 1781 to promote study of Arabic, Persian and Islamic law. Warren Hastings supported its establishment as part of the Orientalist approach to education.

hist_industrial_revolution_britain.label: Industrial Revolution in Britain
hist_industrial_revolution_britain.subject: history
hist_industrial_revolution_britain.detail: Cotton and iron industries led early industrialisation. Richard Arkwright's cotton mill (1781) introduced new discipline. But even in 1840s, hand labour dominated. New technology adopted slowly and unevenly.

hist_orientalism.label: Orientalism
hist_orientalism.subject: history
hist_orientalism.detail: Scholarly tradition represented by William Jones and Colebrooke who respected ancient Indian cultures, discovered and translated Sanskrit and Persian texts, and believed British should promote Indian rather than Western learning. Sought to promote Indian rather than Western learning; translated Sanskrit and Persian texts into English.

hist_william_jones.label: William Jones
hist_william_jones.subject: history
hist_william_jones.detail: Arrived in Calcutta in 1783 as a junior judge. A linguist who studied Sanskrit with pandits, discovered ancient Indian texts on law, philosophy and science. Set up the Asiatic Society of Bengal with Colebrooke.

hist_asiatic_society_bengal.label: Asiatic Society of Bengal
hist_asiatic_society_bengal.subject: history
hist_asiatic_society_bengal.detail: Founded by William Jones and Henry Thomas Colebrooke in Calcutta. Started a journal called Asiatick Researches to publish discoveries about ancient Indian heritage and translations.

hist_portrait_painting_colonial.label: Colonial Portrait Painting
hist_portrait_painting_colonial.subject: history
hist_portrait_painting_colonial.detail: Life-size oil portraits became popular among both British and Indian elite. Johann Zoffany was one of the most famous visiting European painters. Portraits displayed lavish lifestyles and imperial power.

hist_picturesque_landscape.label: Picturesque Landscape Painting
hist_picturesque_landscape.subject: history
hist_picturesque_landscape.detail: Imperial art tradition depicting India as quaint and untamed. Thomas and William Daniell were most famous practitioners, arriving in India in 1785. Their paintings contrasted ancient decaying India with modern British-ruled Calcutta.

hist_lord_cornwallis.label: Lord Cornwallis
hist_lord_cornwallis.subject: history
hist_lord_cornwallis.detail: Governor-General who introduced the Permanent Settlement in Bengal (1793). Believed that fixed revenue would encourage zamindars to invest in land improvement. Also introduced the Cornwallis Code separating revenue and judicial administration.

hist_mcc_lords.label: Marylebone Cricket Club
hist_mcc_lords.subject: history
hist_mcc_lords.detail: MCC founded in 1787 at Lord's cricket ground in London. Became the custodian of cricket's rules and traditions. Revised laws periodically including allowing wider bats and overarm bowling.

hist_australian_aborigines.label: Australian Aborigines
hist_australian_aborigines.subject: history
hist_australian_aborigines.detail: Indigenous peoples of Australia with over 65,000 years of continuous habitation, making them one of the oldest surviving cultures. Practised a sophisticated hunter-gatherer lifestyle adapted to the Australian environment. After British colonisation from 1788, they suffered land dispossession, massacres, forced removal of children (Stolen Generations), and near-destruction of their cultures.

hist_british_colonisation_australia.label: British Colonisation of Australia
hist_british_colonisation_australia.subject: history
hist_british_colonisation_australia.detail: Britain established a penal colony at Sydney in 1788 under Captain Arthur Phillip. Free settlers followed, particularly after the wool industry developed. Six colonies were established by the 1850s. The indigenous Aboriginal population suffered massive decline from disease, violence, and dispossession. Federation into the Commonwealth of Australia occurred in 1901.

hist_terra_nullius.label: Terra Nullius
hist_terra_nullius.subject: history
hist_terra_nullius.detail: Legal doctrine meaning 'land belonging to nobody', used by the British to justify colonisation of Australia from 1788. Denied Aboriginal land ownership despite over 65,000 years of habitation. Overturned by the Australian High Court in the Mabo judgment (1992), which recognised native title.

hist_bastille_storming.label: Storming of the Bastille
hist_bastille_storming.subject: history
hist_bastille_storming.detail: On 14 July 1789, about 7,000 citizens stormed the fortress-prison Bastille in Paris, symbol of despotic royal power. Commander killed, prisoners released. Followed by peasant revolts and abolition of feudal system. 14 July 1789, ~7,000 citizens attacked fortress-prison Bastille. Commander killed; symbolic end of despotic power. Triggered peasant revolts and abolition of feudalism.

hist_declaration_rights_man.label: Declaration of Rights of Man and Citizen
hist_declaration_rights_man.subject: history
hist_declaration_rights_man.detail: Established natural and inalienable rights: life, freedom of speech, equality before law. Constitution of 1791 made France a constitutional monarchy but gave voting rights only to propertied men above 25. August 1789. Proclaimed natural and inalienable rights: liberty, property, security, resistance to oppression. Constitution 1791 = constitutional monarchy with voting for propertied men over 25.

hist_estates_general.label: Estates General
hist_estates_general.subject: history
hist_estates_general.detail: Political body with representatives from three estates. Last met in 1614 before Louis XVI called it on 5 May 1789 to pass new taxes. Third estate demanded voting by head not by estate, walked out when refused. Three-estate body. Had not met since 1614. Summoned 5 May 1789 to approve new taxes. Third Estate demanded voting by head, walked out, declared itself National Assembly 17 June, Tennis Court Oath 20 June.

hist_french_revolution.label: French Revolution
hist_french_revolution.subject: history
hist_french_revolution.detail: Began with storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789. Led to end of monarchy, execution of Louis XVI in 1793, and establishment of a republic. Ideas of liberty, equality and fraternity became its lasting legacy. Storming Bastille 14 July 1789. Execution Louis XVI 21 Jan 1793. Liberty, Equality, Fraternity became lasting legacy. Abolished feudal privileges, declared Rights of Man.

hist_french_revolution_clothing.label: French Revolution and Clothing
hist_french_revolution_clothing.subject: history
hist_french_revolution_clothing.detail: Revolution abolished sumptuary laws. Jacobins called themselves sans-culottes (without knee breeches). Blue-white-red national colours, red cap of liberty, long trousers became symbols of patriotic citizenship and equality.

hist_national_assembly_france.label: National Assembly of France
hist_national_assembly_france.subject: history
hist_national_assembly_france.detail: Third Estate declared itself National Assembly on 20 June 1789 at tennis court in Versailles. Led by Mirabeau and Abbe Sieyes. Swore not to disperse till a constitution limiting monarchy was drafted.

hist_nationalism_europe.label: Nationalism in 19th Century Europe
hist_nationalism_europe.subject: history
hist_nationalism_europe.detail: Emerged as a force bringing sweeping changes, replacing multi-national dynastic empires with nation-states. Driven by shared identity, common history and culture. French Revolution was the first clear expression.

hist_three_estates.label: Three Estates of France
hist_three_estates.subject: history
hist_three_estates.detail: French society divided into First Estate (clergy), Second Estate (nobility) both exempt from taxes, and Third Estate (peasants, artisans, merchants, lawyers). Peasants were 90% of population but only Third Estate paid taxes.

hist_wootz_steel.label: Wootz Steel
hist_wootz_steel.subject: history
hist_wootz_steel.detail: Special high-carbon steel produced all over south India, used to make Tipu Sultan's legendary swords. The process fascinated European scientists including Michael Faraday. The technique was completely lost by mid-nineteenth century due to British conquest. Fascinated European scientists including Michael Faraday. Production technique lost by mid-19c after British conquest disrupted Indian smelters.

hist_benaras_sanskrit_college.label: Benaras Sanskrit College
hist_benaras_sanskrit_college.subject: history
hist_benaras_sanskrit_college.detail: Hindu College established in Benaras (Varanasi) in 1791 to encourage study of ancient Sanskrit texts useful for administration of the country.

hist_olympe_de_gouges.label: Olympe de Gouges
hist_olympe_de_gouges.subject: history
hist_olympe_de_gouges.detail: Wrote Declaration of Rights of Woman and Citizen in 1791 protesting women's exclusion from basic rights. Criticised Jacobin government for closing women's clubs. Tried for treason and executed in 1793. Wrote Declaration of the Rights of Woman and the Female Citizen (1791) answering the male-only Rights of Man. Criticised Jacobin closure of women's clubs. Guillotined November 1793.

hist_jacobins.label: Jacobins
hist_jacobins.subject: history
hist_jacobins.detail: Political club led by Robespierre, mainly from less prosperous sections - shopkeepers, artisans, servants. Known as sans-culottes (without knee breeches). Stormed Tuileries Palace in August 1792, established republic. Club led by Robespierre, drew from less-prosperous sections (shopkeepers, artisans). Known as sans-culottes. Stormed Tuileries August 1792, established republic September 1792.

hist_bengal_zamindars.label: Bengal Zamindars under Company
hist_bengal_zamindars.subject: history
hist_bengal_zamindars.detail: Under Permanent Settlement, many old zamindari families lost lands at revenue auctions. New purchasers were often urban moneylenders. Zamindars' power limited - could not evict peasants easily. Jotedars (rich peasants) emerged as powerful figures controlling local resources.

hist_colonial_agrarian_laws.label: Colonial Agrarian Legislation
hist_colonial_agrarian_laws.subject: history
hist_colonial_agrarian_laws.detail: Series of laws reshaping Indian agrarian relations: Bengal Regulation (1793), various Tenancy Acts, Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act (1879). These defined property rights, revenue obligations and debtor-creditor relations in ways that transformed traditional rural society.

hist_permanent_settlement.label: Permanent Settlement (1793)
hist_permanent_settlement.subject: history
hist_permanent_settlement.detail: Introduced by Lord Cornwallis in Bengal in 1793. Fixed revenue demand permanently with zamindars as intermediaries. Zamindars who failed to pay lost lands in auctions. Aimed to create loyal class of landowners. Led to rack-renting of peasants and sub-infeudation. Sunset Law fixed payment deadlines; defaulting zamindars lost lands at auction, often to Calcutta absentee purchasers (urban moneylenders).

hist_reign_of_terror.label: Reign of Terror
hist_reign_of_terror.subject: history
hist_reign_of_terror.detail: Period 1793-94 under Robespierre marked by severe repression. Ex-nobles, clergy, political opponents arrested and guillotined by revolutionary tribunal. Wages and prices fixed, white flour banned, churches shut.

hist_robespierre.label: Maximilian Robespierre
hist_robespierre.subject: history
hist_robespierre.detail: Leader of Jacobins who implemented the Reign of Terror (1793-94) with severe control and punishment. Guillotined opponents, rationed bread, shut churches. Ultimately arrested and guillotined by his own party in July 1794. Led Jacobin Reign of Terror 1793-94. Fixed wages and prices, rationed bread, shut churches. Arrested and guillotined by his own party July 1794.

hist_abolition_slavery_france.label: Abolition of Slavery in French Colonies
hist_abolition_slavery_france.subject: history
hist_abolition_slavery_france.detail: Convention legislated in 1794 to free all slaves in French overseas possessions. Slave trade had linked Europe, Africa and Americas. Napoleon reintroduced slavery. Final abolition in French colonies only in 1848. Convention legislated emancipation 1794 in French colonies. Napoleon reinstated slavery 1802. Final abolition 1848.

hist_ranjit_singh.label: Maharaja Ranjit Singh
hist_ranjit_singh.subject: history
hist_ranjit_singh.detail: Reunited Sikh groups and established capital at Lahore in 1799. Sikh territories extended from the Indus to the Jamuna. Created a powerful kingdom that lasted until British annexation.

hist_tipu_sultan_sword.label: Tipu Sultan's Sword
hist_tipu_sultan_sword.subject: history
hist_tipu_sultan_sword.detail: Made of Wootz steel with incredibly hard and sharp edge. Gold quotations from the Koran were inscribed on the handle. Tipu fought four wars with the British and died fighting in 1799. Tipu died defending Seringapatam in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799).

hist_company_paintings.label: Company Paintings
hist_company_paintings.subject: history
hist_company_paintings.detail: Hybrid painting style (late 18th-19th C) that emerged when British East India Company officers employed Indian painters trained in Mughal/Rajput styles to produce works in European tastes. Used water colour; linear perspective; shading. Centres: Kolkata, Patna, Varanasi, Delhi, Madras, Thanjavur. Famous painters: Sewak Ram, Ishwari Prasad, Ghulam Ali Khan. Subject matter: exotic Indian flora/fauna, courtly portraits, everyday Indian scenes.

hist_de_urbanisation.label: De-urbanisation in 19th Century
hist_de_urbanisation.subject: history
hist_de_urbanisation.detail: Many pre-colonial cities like Machilipatnam, Surat and Seringapatam declined as trade routes shifted and colonial policies drained traditional industries. Handloom weavers and artisans were ruined. Population of old trading centres fell while port cities grew.

hist_factory_discipline.label: Factory System and Discipline
hist_factory_discipline.subject: history
hist_factory_discipline.detail: Factories imposed new work discipline: fixed hours, supervised labour, fines for lateness. Workers resisted through strikes and absenteeism. Women and children exploited in early factories with long hours and low wages.

hist_francis_buchanan.label: Francis Buchanan
hist_francis_buchanan.subject: history
hist_francis_buchanan.detail: Employed by East India Company to survey eastern India in early 19th century. His reports provide detailed accounts of local communities, agriculture and natural resources. Used by historians to understand pre-colonial and early colonial rural society in Bengal and Bihar. Surveyed Mysore 1807; Bengal-Bihar early 19c. Ethnographic + ecological reports extensively used by later historians.

hist_jotedars.label: Jotedars
hist_jotedars.subject: history
hist_jotedars.detail: Rich peasants in Bengal who controlled much of local trade and moneylending. Exercised more effective authority than zamindars over peasants. Resisted zamindars' attempts to increase revenue. Could prevent zamindars from exercising power by lending land to peasants. Actively resisted zamindar authority; held more effective power on the ground than many zamindars.

hist_serampore_mission.label: Serampore Mission
hist_serampore_mission.subject: history
hist_serampore_mission.detail: Christian missionary centre established by William Carey near Calcutta in area under Danish East India Company. Set up printing press in 1800 and college in 1818 to promote moral education.

hist_urban_planning_colonial.label: Colonial Urban Planning
hist_urban_planning_colonial.subject: history
hist_urban_planning_colonial.detail: British imposed new urban visions: wide roads, public buildings, clock towers, parks. Segregation between European and Indian quarters. Improvement Trusts established (Bombay 1898). Plague and fire used as pretexts for demolition and replanning of Indian areas. Bombay Improvement Trust established 1898. Plague and fire used as pretexts for demolition and replanning of Indian quarters.

hist_american_frontier.label: American Frontier
hist_american_frontier.subject: history
hist_american_frontier.detail: The moving boundary of European-American settlement westward across North America. The frontier experience shaped American identity, democracy, and individualism (as argued by historian Frederick Jackson Turner). But it came at the cost of indigenous displacement, environmental destruction, and violence.

hist_manifest_destiny.label: Manifest Destiny
hist_manifest_destiny.subject: history
hist_manifest_destiny.detail: 19th-century ideology asserting that the United States was destined to expand across the North American continent. Justified the displacement of Native Americans and the annexation of Mexican territory. Combined nationalism, racial superiority, and religious mission. Used to legitimise territorial expansion and settler colonialism.

hist_westward_expansion.label: Westward Expansion (USA)
hist_westward_expansion.subject: history
hist_westward_expansion.detail: The expansion of the United States from the Atlantic coast to the Pacific Ocean during the 19th century.
