A district-tier officer between central ministers and village-level functionaries.

gap_yukta.label: Yukta (Ashokan subordinate officer)
gap_yukta.subject: history
gap_yukta.detail: Subordinate revenue / accounting officer in Mauryan administration, serving under the Pradeshika and Rajuka. Essentially a junior accountant / clerical officer handling records, assessments, and storehouse audits at the local level. Named alongside Pradeshika and Rajuka in Ashoka's Rock Edict III quinquennial tour schedule. The Arthashastra also references yuktas in fiscal-supervision contexts — a continuity between Kautilyan theory and Ashokan practice.

gap_jain_agamas_structure.label: Jain Agamas structure (Shvetambara canon)
gap_jain_agamas_structure.subject: history
gap_jain_agamas_structure.detail: Shvetambara Jain canon = 12 Angas (primary doctrinal texts: Acharanga, Sutrakritanga, Sthananga, Samavayanga, Bhagavati / Vyakhyaprajnapti, Jnatadharmakatha, Upasakadasha, etc.) + chhedasutras (monastic discipline, e.g., Brihatkalpasutra, Nishitha, Dashashrutaskandha) + mulasutras (foundational) + prakirnaka (miscellaneous). Composed in Ardha-Magadhi Prakrit. Traditionally the canon had 12 Angas and 14 Purvas (now lost); Digambaras reject the extant Shvetambara canon as an imperfect reconstruction after the great Magadha famine.

gap_sutrakritanga.label: Sutrakritanga (2nd Anga)
gap_sutrakritanga.subject: history
gap_sutrakritanga.detail: Second of the 12 Angas in the Shvetambara Jain canon. Describes the code of conduct for Jain monks, presents core metaphysics (doctrine of karma, nine tattvas), and critiques rival heterodox doctrines (Buddhist, Ajivika, materialist, 363 schools of thought enumerated). Ardha-Magadhi Prakrit, traditionally attributed to Mahavira's disciple Sudharma. Being Jain literature, it's a Jain text in PYQ #238's odd-one-out question (the non-Jain entry is Therigatha).

gap_kalinga_strategic_role.label: Kalinga's strategic role (Mauryan motive)
gap_kalinga_strategic_role.subject: history
gap_kalinga_strategic_role.detail: Kalinga (modern coastal Odisha + parts of northern Andhra) sat astride BOTH the land routes between the Ganga basin and peninsular India AND the east-coast maritime routes to south India, Sri Lanka, and Southeast Asia. Ashoka's 261 BCE conquest is traditionally read through the moral-conversion lens of Rock Edict XIII; the economic/strategic motive (port control, route control, access to forest-elephants and revenue) is an older but complementary explanation. Kalingan independence had been a gap in the Mauryan hold over the subcontinent.

gap_empire_extents_map.label: Empire extents map comparison
gap_empire_extents_map.subject: history
gap_empire_extents_map.detail: Mental-map benchmarks for ancient empire extents in PYQ map questions: Ashoka (~250 BCE) — whole subcontinent except deep south / Tamilakam; Kushan Kanishka (~150 CE) — north-west + Ganga basin east to Pataliputra + Central Asian reach to Kashgar; Samudragupta (~350 CE) — Gupta north India heartland + tributary belt reaching into south India after the Dakshinapatha campaign; Harsha of Thaneswar/Kannauj (~640 CE) — north India alone, not the Deccan. The PYQ shows a near-complete-subcontinent map → Ashoka.

gap_foreign_rulers_buddhism.label: Why foreign rulers embraced Buddhism
gap_foreign_rulers_buddhism.subject: history
gap_foreign_rulers_buddhism.detail: Indo-Greek, Shaka, Parthian, and Kushana rulers entered an India where Brahmanical society classed non-Aryans as mlechchha — outside the four-varna order, with no clear ritual path to incorporation. Buddhism, in contrast, was casteless in its Sangha: open to merchants, foreigners, women, and rulers without prior Brahmanical certification. Buddhism therefore gave them a religious/social identity that didn't require caste-ritual status they couldn't acquire. Menander's conversion (Milinda-panha), Kanishka's patronage, and Shaka donations at Sanchi/Karla illustrate this.

gap_samanta_origins.label: Samanta / feudatory origins
gap_samanta_origins.subject: history
gap_samanta_origins.detail: Origin of the Indian 'feudal' samanta system is debated. One view traces it to Satavahana and Gupta BRAHMANA land grants (tax-free agraharas to priests / monasteries) whose recipients gradually acquired judicial and administrative rights — a non-military route. Another view emphasizes MILITARY-service grants to subordinate kings (samantas, mandalika, mahasamanta) whose allegiance was rewarded in land and delegated authority. The historiographical consensus is that both strands compounded during the Gupta and post-Gupta phase, with feudal expansion consolidating in the early-medieval period.

gap_prayag_mahamoksha.label: Prayag Mahamoksha-Parishad (Harsha)
gap_prayag_mahamoksha.subject: history
gap_prayag_mahamoksha.detail: Harshavardhana's quinquennial ('Mahamoksha') assembly at Prayag (Allahabad), attested by the pilgrim Xuanzang. Over ~75 days, Harsha distributed the accumulated wealth of the previous five years to Buddhist monks, Brahmans, Jains, other ascetics, and the poor — NOT a Mahayana-only affair (PYQ #114 Reason is false). Ceremony underscores Harsha's eclectic patronage (Shaiva + Buddhist) despite Xuanzang's Buddhist framing. Parallel to the 'ashvamedha' and Kumbh-style assemblies in its prestige function.

gap_panamalai_temple.label: Panamalai Talagirishvara Temple (Pallava)
gap_panamalai_temple.subject: history
gap_panamalai_temple.detail: Rock-cut / structural Shiva temple at Panamalai, Tamil Nadu (Viluppuram district) — associated with the Pallava dynasty (especially Rajasimha / Narasimhavarman II, ~early 8c CE). Contemporary with Kailasanathar Kanchipuram and the Shore Temple Mahabalipuram as Rajasimha-style early-Dravida temples. PYQ-#122 pair: Pallava ↔ Panamalai (the other pairs being Gupta-Deogarh, Chandella-Khajuraho, Chalukya-Badami). Notable early fresco fragments in the inner shrine.

gap_lepakshi_murals.label: Lepakshi (Vijayanagara murals)
gap_lepakshi_murals.subject: history
gap_lepakshi_murals.detail: Veerabhadra Temple at Lepakshi, Anantapur district, Andhra Pradesh — 16c Vijayanagara period, built during Achyuta Deva Raya's reign (governor brothers Virupanna and Viranna). Famous for extensive Vijayanagara-style mural paintings on the temple ceiling depicting Shaiva and epic themes; alongside Ajanta, among the most celebrated sites of Indian mural painting. Also known for the hanging pillar and giant monolithic Nandi and Nagalinga. Sanchi has no murals — hence #147 answer (b) 1 and 2 only.

gap_stone_media_comparison.label: Ancient sculpture stone-media
gap_stone_media_comparison.subject: history
gap_stone_media_comparison.detail: School-media pairings tested in PYQs: Gandhara — GREEN / grey schist (the distinctive medium, often imported); Mathura — spotted RED sandstone (Sikri / Bharatpur quarries, Kushan era onwards); Bharhut — RED/buff sandstone (central Indian Shunga school, though NOT schist — so PYQ #171's 'green schist' answer is Gandhara, not Bharhut; the PYQ appears mis-keyed or relies on a niche Bharhut schist-usage claim); Mauryan Ashokan pillars — highly polished Chunar sandstone. Media shift tracks workshop location and Imperial patronage.

gap_upanishadic_parables.label: Upanishadic parables
gap_upanishadic_parables.subject: history
gap_upanishadic_parables.detail: The principal Upanishads are dialogue-rich and contain several PARABLES: Shvetaketu and his father Uddalaka Aruni's salt-water lesson ('Tat Tvam Asi', Chandogya); Nachiketa's three-wish encounter with Yama (Katha); Maitreyi-Yajnavalkya dialogue on immortality (Brihadaranyaka); Satyakama Jabala's identity (Chandogya). PYQ #176 statement 1 ('no parables in Upanishads') is FALSE. Upanishads post-date Vedas but pre-date Puranas (statement 2 TRUE).

gap_sangam_magical_forces.label: Sangam poets on magical forces
gap_sangam_magical_forces.subject: history
gap_sangam_magical_forces.detail: Sangam poetry takes magical / supernatural forces as REAL and efficacious — not 'irrational' to be rationalized away. Tutelary deities (Murugan / Velan priests, Korravai), possession trance (veriyattam), omens, evil eye (drishti), and sorcery appear as operative parts of the social world. This matters for PYQ #181 which tests three distractors — Sangam poems DO reference material culture, DO show warrior ethic, and do NOT treat magic as irrational; the correct statement is that Varna classification was known to Sangam poets (attested in Tolkappiyam / ethnographic poems).

gap_prabandha_chintamani.label: Prabandha-Chintamani (Merutunga)
gap_prabandha_chintamani.subject: history
gap_prabandha_chintamani.detail: 14c (1305 CE) Sanskrit narrative-anecdotal text by the Shvetambara Jain monk MERUTUNGA. Collects semi-historical stories of kings and notables of western India — Chalukyas of Gujarat (Mularaja to Bhima II), Paramaras (Bhoja), and others. An important though anecdotal source for medieval western Indian history. Paired with Rajasekhara Suri's Prabandhakosha and Jinaprabha Suri's Vividha-tirtha-kalpa as the Jain prabandha literature corpus. Featured in PYQ #198's text-author matching.

gap_jain_nirjara.label: Jain tapas / nirjara (karma annihilation)
gap_jain_nirjara.subject: history
gap_jain_nirjara.detail: In Jain doctrine, nirjara is the shedding / annihilation of already-accumulated karma — achieved through austerities (tapas), meditation, and the Five Samitis + Three Guptis (external + internal disciplines). Paired with samvara (stopping further karmic influx) as the twin liberation mechanics. Penance is THE canonical means of nirjara — not merely supplementary — hence PYQ #225 statement 1 ('surest way of annihilating karma is penance') is TRUE. Jain anekantavada recognizes every particle has a jiva (soul), statement 2 TRUE.

gap_kali_yuga_era.label: Kali Yuga era (3102 BCE)
gap_kali_yuga_era.subject: history
gap_kali_yuga_era.detail: Kali era (Kaliyuga-samvat) — an astronomical / Puranic reckoning beginning in 3102 BCE, the traditional date of the Mahabharata war and the end of Krishna's earthly life. Used in Aryabhatan and later siddhantic astronomy; date is computed from planetary conjunction calculation, not historical record. Distinct from Vikrama samvat (58 BCE), Shaka samvat (78 CE), Gupta era (320 CE). PYQ #64 match: Kali era ↔ 3102 BCE.

gap_valabhi_gupta_era.label: Valabhi-Gupta era (248/319 continuation)
gap_valabhi_gupta_era.subject: history
gap_valabhi_gupta_era.detail: The Gupta era (starting 319-320 CE) was later continued in Gujarat by the MAITRAKA rulers of Valabhi and is sometimes called the 'Valabhi-Gupta' era. Option (E) in PYQ #64 — '248 AD' — is a distractor (no well-known Indian era starts in 248 CE; the closest is a confused reading of the Kalachuri-Chedi era of 248-249 CE, used by the Kalachuris of western India). PYQ-#64 answer (d) therefore excludes E.

gap_arthashastra_slavery.label: Arthashastra on slavery (judicial + dasi)
gap_arthashastra_slavery.subject: history
gap_arthashastra_slavery.detail: Kautilyan slave-law: (1) A person COULD become a slave through judicial punishment (aahitaka) — a recognized form alongside birth, capture, debt, voluntary sale. (2) If a FEMALE slave (dasi) bore her master a SON, BOTH mother and son were legally free — the Arthashastra explicitly declares this emancipation. (3) If the son was fathered by someone other than the master, the freedom clause does NOT apply in the same way. Hence PYQ #90 answer (b) statements 2 and 3 correct; statement 1 on judicial-punishment slavery is also true though subtler.

gap_kulyavapa_dronavapa.label: Kulyavapa / Dronavapa (Gupta land units)
gap_kulyavapa_dronavapa.subject: history
gap_kulyavapa_dronavapa.detail: Gupta-era land-measurement terms from eastern India copper-plate grants: KULYAVAPA — larger unit, literally 'area sown with one kulya (large measure) of seed'; DRONAVAPA — smaller unit, 'area sown with one drona of seed'; roughly 1 kulyavapa ≈ 8 dronavapas in Bengal usage. Both are SEED-SOWING-based areal measures (land is quantified by how much seed it takes to sow it), distinct from the western-Indian nivartana or linear measures. Found frequently in Bengal / east-Indian Gupta and post-Gupta inscriptions.

gap_saumilla.label: Saumilla (Sanskrit dramatist)
gap_saumilla.subject: history
gap_saumilla.detail: Ancient Sanskrit dramatist named alongside Kaviputra in Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitra prologue — mentioned as a predecessor whom Kalidasa's patron contrasts with contemporary poets. Works are lost. NOT a physician — PYQ #110 (Gupta-period medicine) lists him as a distractor. Distinguishable from Shudraka, Sushruta, Shaunaka in options.

gap_shaunaka.label: Shaunaka (Vedic ritualist)
gap_shaunaka.subject: history
gap_shaunaka.detail: Vedic/post-Vedic ritualist and grammarian; associated with the Shaunaka-shakha branch of the Atharvaveda and the composition of the Brihaddevata (enumeration of deities in the Rigveda). Not a physician. PYQ #110 lists him as a distractor to Sushruta (the actual Gupta-period medical authority; though Sushruta-samhita is older than the Guptas, tradition places his redaction in the Gupta period).

gap_chaturvedimangalam.label: Chaturvedimangalam (Chola brahmadeya)
gap_chaturvedimangalam.subject: history
gap_chaturvedimangalam.detail: Chola-era brahmana settlement ('four-Veda mangalam' = village of learned men of all four Vedas) — a BRAHMADEYA land grant-village, not a merchant corporation. The suffix '-mangalam' indicates a settlement of Vedic scholars settled by royal patronage with tax-free cultivation rights. PYQ #123 lists it as a distractor to Manigrama (the actual merchant guild). Common in Tamil-country Chola epigraphy.

gap_parishad_advisory.label: Parishad (advisory sabha)
gap_parishad_advisory.subject: history
gap_parishad_advisory.detail: In ancient Indian polity, PARISHAD denoted an ADVISORY council / learned assembly — variously a Vedic assembly of Brahmans deciding disputed points of dharma, or in later polity a royal ministerial council advising the king. NOT a merchant corporation (PYQ #123 distractor to Manigrama). Distinct from the Sabha (village council) and the Samiti (assembly of tribe / people) of Rigvedic times.

gap_kanganahalli.label: Kanganahalli ('Ranyo Ashoka' relief)
gap_kanganahalli.subject: history
gap_kanganahalli.detail: Buddhist stupa complex at Kanganahalli, Karnataka (Kalaburagi / Gulbarga district), excavated in the 1990s-2000s. Contains a stone relief-portrait of Ashoka himself with the Brahmi-script label 'Ranyo Ashoka' ('King Ashoka') — the only known ancient contemporary portrait identification of Ashoka in stone. Dated ~1c BCE to 1c CE (Satavahana-era extension of a Mauryan foundation). PYQ #137 correct answer.

gap_sohgaura_copperplate.label: Sohgaura copper-plate inscription
gap_sohgaura_copperplate.subject: history
gap_sohgaura_copperplate.detail: Sohgaura copper-plate found near Gorakhpur, Uttar Pradesh — one of the earliest KNOWN Indian copper-plate inscriptions, in Brahmi/Prakrit, dated to the Mauryan period (pre-Ashokan by some readings; 3c BCE). Records instructions on storehouses (koshthagara) at three sites for famine-relief grain distribution. Distinct from Ashoka's rock / pillar edicts in being on copper. PYQ #137 distractor (has an inscription but NOT a 'Ranyo Ashoka' portrait).

gap_georg_buhler.label: Georg Bühler (Indologist)
gap_georg_buhler.subject: history
gap_georg_buhler.detail: Austrian-born Indologist (1837-1898); prolific Sanskrit scholar and BRAHMI paleographer — his On the Origin of the Indian Brahma Alphabet (1895) set the foundational paleographic typology. Taught at the Poona Deccan College and edited the SBE's Laws of Manu and the Apastamba-Gautama Dharmasutras. NOT the first decipherer of Ashoka's edicts (that's James Prinsep, 1837, PYQ #140 answer); Bühler's work on Brahmi came later, systematizing what Prinsep had cracked.

gap_max_muller.label: Max Müller (Sanskritist)
gap_max_muller.subject: history
gap_max_muller.detail: German-born Sanskritist (1823-1900) based at Oxford; best known for editing the complete Rigveda with Sayana's commentary (6 volumes, 1849-1874) and founding/editing the 50-volume Sacred Books of the East series. Coined 'Aryan' in a linguistic sense and popularized comparative mythology. NOT a decipherer of Ashoka's edicts — that's James Prinsep (PYQ #140 answer). Müller is a common distractor in Indology-origins questions.

gap_vikramshila.label: Vikramshila Mahavihara (Bihar)
gap_vikramshila.subject: history
gap_vikramshila.detail: Pala-era Buddhist university-monastery founded by king Dharmapala (~8c CE) at Antichak village, Bhagalpur district, BIHAR — NOT Uttar Pradesh (PYQ #156 distractor). Alongside Nalanda and Odantapuri one of the great eastern-Indian Buddhist centres; major hub of Vajrayana / Tantric Buddhism. Atisha Dipankara, the 11c teacher who transmitted Buddhism to Tibet, was its abbot. Destroyed by Bakhtiyar Khilji ~1193 CE.

gap_hemkund_sahib.label: Hemkund Sahib (Uttarakhand)
gap_hemkund_sahib.subject: history
gap_hemkund_sahib.detail: Sikh gurudwara at ~4,600 m altitude in Chamoli district, UTTARAKHAND — NOT Himachal Pradesh (PYQ #156 distractor). Beside a glacial lake at the base of the Hemkund mountains. Associated with the tenth Guru Gobind Singh's meditation in a past life per his autobiographical Bachitar Natak. Seven-peaked backdrop; accessible only June-October. Not ancient but frequently tested as a site-state pair.

gap_madhyama_vyayoga.label: Madhyama-vyayoga (Bhasa)
gap_madhyama_vyayoga.subject: history
gap_madhyama_vyayoga.detail: Sanskrit one-act play ('vyayoga' = short martial-theme play) by the playwright BHASA (pre-Kalidasa, ~3-4c CE). Depicts an episode from the Mahabharata involving Bhima and Ghatotkacha. Part of the 13 'Trivandrum plays' attributed to Bhasa, rediscovered in Kerala palm-leaf manuscripts in 1912 by T. Ganapati Sastri. PYQ #177 answer. Bhasa's other works: Svapnavasavadatta, Pratijnayaugandharayana, Pancharatra.

gap_kavyalankara_bhamaha.label: Kavyalankara (Bhamaha)
gap_kavyalankara_bhamaha.subject: history
gap_kavyalankara_bhamaha.detail: 7c CE Sanskrit TREATISE ON POETICS (alankara-shastra) by BHAMAHA — one of the earliest systematic Indian works on figures of speech, genre classification, and kavya theory. Foundational for later alankarika tradition (Dandin's Kavyadarsha, Vamana, Rudrata, Anandavardhana's Dhvanyaloka). NOT a play by Bhasa — PYQ #177 distractor. Bhamaha's poetics-school is sometimes contrasted with Dandin's as pro-alankara vs pro-guna.

gap_gupta_ports_ghantasala_kadura_chaul.label: Ghantasala / Kadura / Chaul (Gupta ports)
gap_gupta_ports_ghantasala_kadura_chaul.subject: history
gap_gupta_ports_ghantasala_kadura_chaul.detail: Three Gupta-period foreign-trade ports cited together in #103: GHANTASALA (Andhra Pradesh, Krishna delta) — east-coast port with a Buddhist stupa, part of the Satavahana-to-Ikshvaku Andhran maritime economy; KADURA (Karnataka, Arabian-sea / Kanara coast) — west-coast port; CHAUL / Chemula (Maharashtra, Konkan coast south of Mumbai) — attested from Greco-Roman Periplus onwards. All handled Indo-Roman and Indo-SE Asian trade. The PYQ tests recognition of all three as PORTS (not capitals, not pilgrimage centres).

gap_tamralipti.label: Tamralipti (Bengal port)
gap_tamralipti.subject: history
gap_tamralipti.detail: Tamralipti (modern Tamluk, West Bengal, on the Rupnarayan estuary near the Bay of Bengal) was the PRINCIPAL eastern port handling NORTH Indian overseas trade through the Gupta period. Connected the Ganga basin to Southeast Asia (Suvarnabhumi), Sri Lanka, and the Mediterranean. Fa-Xian and later Xuanzang embarked/disembarked here. PYQ #108 answer. Declined after the silting of the Rupnarayan from the 8c onwards; displaced by Saptagrama then Chittagong.

gap_kalyan_port.label: Kalyan (Konkan port)
gap_kalyan_port.subject: history
gap_kalyan_port.detail: Kalyan (outside modern Mumbai, Thane district, Maharashtra) — WEST-coast Konkan port mentioned in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (~1c CE). Handled WESTERN Indian maritime trade (not north-Indian) — hence distractor to Tamralipti in PYQ #108. Continued as a port into Satavahana and later Shilahara periods.

gap_cambray_khambhat.label: Cambay / Khambhat (Gujarat port)
gap_cambray_khambhat.subject: history
gap_cambray_khambhat.detail: Cambay (British-era name) = KHAMBHAT, Gujarat, on the Gulf of Khambhat (Arabian Sea). Medieval (post-Gupta) maritime port — became prominent under the Chalukyas of Gujarat and then the Sultans of Gujarat (pre-Surat eclipse). NOT a major GUPTA-period port for NORTH India; PYQ #108 distractor. Bharuch (Broach) in the same region was the classical-period port here, not Khambhat.

gap_xuanzang_harsha_society.label: Xuanzang on Harsha-era society
gap_xuanzang_harsha_society.subject: history
gap_xuanzang_harsha_society.detail: The 7c pilgrim Xuanzang's Si-yu-ki records several generalizations about Harsha-era north India: (1) Roads and river routes were NOT completely secure — bandits and highway robberies were real, though Harsha's administration suppressed them; PYQ #186 statement 1 'completely immune from attack' is FALSE. (2) Judicial trials used FOUR traditional ORDEALS — fire, water, poison, scales — when evidence was inconclusive; statement 2 TRUE. (3) TOLLS were levied at ferries and barriers on merchants — a standard revenue stream; statement 3 TRUE. Hence PYQ #186 answer (b) 2 and 3 only.

gap_arthashastra_divorce.label: Arthashastra on wife's divorce after desertion
gap_arthashastra_divorce.subject: history
gap_arthashastra_divorce.detail: Kautilya's Arthashastra permits a wife to remarry if her husband has gone abroad / deserted her AND has been absent beyond stipulated periods (varying by varna and by whether he left a maintenance). The wife may also repudiate a husband of bad character or impotence. Unique among the major ancient law texts in granting this female-initiated exit — hence PYQ #202 answer (d). Manusmriti, by contrast, is restrictive and discourages female remarriage.

gap_manu_remarriage.label: Manavadharmashastra on remarriage
gap_manu_remarriage.subject: history
gap_manu_remarriage.detail: The Manusmriti (Manavadharmashastra, ~2c BCE - 3c CE) takes a CONSERVATIVE line on women's remarriage: the virtuous wife never remarries after her husband's death (niyoga exception in limited circumstances). Widow remarriage is generally proscribed. PYQ #202 distractor — Manu does NOT permit divorce-and-remarriage on desertion grounds the way the Arthashastra does. The gap between prescriptive Smriti and pragmatic Shastra is typical.

gap_sukra_nitisara.label: Sukra Nitisara
gap_sukra_nitisara.subject: history
gap_sukra_nitisara.detail: Sukra Nitisara (also Shukra-niti) — a medieval Sanskrit treatise on statecraft and ethics attributed to the sage Shukra. Dating is contested — traditionally ancient, but scholarly consensus places it as a MEDIEVAL (post-12c) compilation borrowing from Arthashastra and dharmashastras, with recognizable references that post-date classical antiquity. PYQ #202 distractor; NOT a divorce-permitting text in the sense Arthashastra is.

gap_buddha_epithets.label: Buddha epithets: Tathagata, Shakyamuni
gap_buddha_epithets.subject: history
gap_buddha_epithets.detail: Epithets of Gautama Buddha: TATHAGATA ('thus gone' or 'thus come', Buddha's self-reference in the Pali canon); SHAKYAMUNI ('sage of the Shakyas', referencing his kshatriya clan origin in Kapilavastu); Sugata ('well-gone'); Bhagavan, Jina, Samyaksambuddha, and title 'Buddha' itself. NAYAPUTTA is NOT a Buddha epithet — it refers to Mahavira (Nataputta / Jnatrika-putra, 'son of the Jnatrika'). Hence PYQ #205 answer (b) 2 and 3 only.

gap_nayaputta_mahavira.label: Nayaputta (Mahavira epithet)
gap_nayaputta_mahavira.subject: history
gap_nayaputta_mahavira.detail: NAYAPUTTA (Sanskrit Nataputta, Jnatrika-putra) = 'son of the Jnatrika / Nata clan' — Mahavira's clan epithet; his kshatriya lineage was the Jnatrika clan of Kundagrama (near Vaishali). Used extensively in early Buddhist Pali texts to refer to Mahavira (as the founder of a rival sangha). NOT a Buddha epithet — PYQ #205 trap (the option appears in a Buddha-epithet list). Mahavira's other epithets: Vardhamana, Jina, Tirthankara, Arihanta.

gap_parivrajaka.label: Parivrajaka (wandering renunciant)
gap_parivrajaka.subject: history
gap_parivrajaka.detail: PARIVRAJAKA = wandering renunciant / mendicant who has given up the householder life and wanders in search of truth (6c BCE shramana milieu). Ascetic category found across Brahmanical (sannyasin fourth-ashrama), Buddhist (parivrajaka, bhikkhu), Jain (sadhu), and Ajivika traditions. Not sect-specific. PYQ #214 matches it correctly as 'renunciant and wanderer'.

gap_shramana.label: Shramana (non-Vedic ascetic)
gap_shramana.subject: history
gap_shramana.detail: SHRAMANA = non-Vedic ascetic / striver; the term covers Buddhist, Jain, Ajivika, and various heterodox wandering monks who rejected the authority of the Vedas and the Brahmanical ritual order. 6c BCE Magadha saw the shramana-brahmana opposition structure (Patanjali's Mahabhashya uses the phrase). NOT a 'priest with high status' (PYQ #214 statement 2 mismatch) — that's the brahmana; shramana is the opposite social category.

gap_upasaka.label: Upasaka (Buddhist lay follower)
gap_upasaka.subject: history
gap_upasaka.detail: UPASAKA (masc.) / Upasika (fem.) = Buddhist LAY follower — a householder who takes the three refuges (Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha) and the five precepts (pancha-shila), but has NOT entered the monastic Sangha. Supports the Sangha through dana (alms / donations) and earns merit toward future rebirth. PYQ #214 matches it correctly. Parallel term in Jainism is shravaka (lay follower observing anuvratas).

gap_sarvastivada.label: Sarvastivada / Vaibhashika
gap_sarvastivada.subject: history
gap_sarvastivada.detail: SARVASTIVADA ('all exists' school) — Buddhist philosophical school that held that dharmas (constituents of phenomena) exist in all three times (past, present, future) as real entities, not merely momentary present-instants. Associated with the Vaibhashika sub-branch (based on the Abhidharma-Mahavibhasha, compiled at the Fourth Buddhist Council under Kanishka in Kashmir). PYQ #218 statement 2 TRUE ('constituents of phenomena were not wholly momentary but existed forever in a latent form'). A sthavira-lineage (non-Mahasanghika) school.

gap_sautrantika.label: Sautrantika school
gap_sautrantika.subject: history
gap_sautrantika.detail: SAUTRANTIKA — Buddhist philosophical school that rejected the Abhidharma-Mahavibhasha and relied only on the SUTRA (hence 'Sautrantika' = 'those of the Sutras'); split off from Sarvastivada. Held a more rigorous momentariness (kshanikavada) — dharmas are truly momentary, not three-time-existent. NOT a Jain sect — PYQ #218 statement 1 FALSE ('Sautrantika and Sammitiya were sects of Jainism'). One of the four major Buddhist philosophical schools alongside Vaibhashika, Yogachara, Madhyamika.

gap_sammitiya.label: Sammitiya / Pudgalavada
gap_sammitiya.subject: history
gap_sammitiya.detail: SAMMITIYA — Buddhist early school; held the PUDGALAVADA ('personalist') doctrine that there is an INDEFINABLE person (pudgala) that is neither identical with nor distinct from the aggregates (skandhas) and that persists through rebirth. Controversial within Buddhism (most other schools saw this as backdoor atman-ism) but very influential in numbers — Xuanzang reports Sammitiya was one of the most widespread schools in his day. NOT a Jain sect — PYQ #218 statement 1 FALSE.

gap_ashokan_edict_sites.label: Ashokan major rock-edict sites (location map)
gap_ashokan_edict_sites.subject: history
gap_ashokan_edict_sites.detail: Key state-pairings for Ashoka's major-rock-edict sites tested in PYQ #132: DHAULI — ODISHA (correct); JAUGADA — ODISHA (correct, PYQ mis-pairs it with MP); ERRAGUDI / Yerragudi — ANDHRA PRADESH (correct); KALSI — UTTARAKHAND (PYQ wrongly pairs with Karnataka). Other major-rock-edict sites: Girnar (Gujarat), Sopara (Maharashtra), Shahbazgarhi (KP, Pakistan), Mansehra (KP, Pakistan), Sannati (Karnataka). Dhauli and Jaugada in Odisha carry the 'Separate Kalinga Edicts' specific to the conquered region.

gap_vassavasa.label: Vassavasa (Buddhist rains retreat)
gap_vassavasa.subject: history
gap_vassavasa.detail: VASSAVASA = monsoon retreat (vassa = rains + vasa = dwelling) for Buddhist monks — a fixed ~3-month sedentary period each year, beginning on the day after the Ashadha full moon, during which monks do NOT wander but stay in one monastery. Instituted by the Buddha because wandering during monsoons damaged new crops and insect life. This is PYQ #232 option (d) — the Ashadha full-moon day is the START of vassavasa, not Pavarana.

gap_pavarana.label: Pavarana (end-of-rains confession)
gap_pavarana.subject: history
gap_pavarana.detail: PAVARANA = ceremony held at the END of the vassavasa (monsoon retreat), on the full-moon day of Ashvina (or Kartika). Each monk formally INVITES his fellow-monks to point out any offences he may have committed during the retreat — a mutual confession / correction ritual. PYQ #232 answer (b). Distinct from Upasampada (ordination), Uposatha (fortnightly recitation of Patimokkha), and Sanghakamma (formal acts of the sangha).

gap_upasampada.label: Upasampada (monastic ordination)
gap_upasampada.subject: history
gap_upasampada.detail: UPASAMPADA = higher ordination into the Buddhist Sangha as a fully-fledged bhikkhu / bhikkhuni. Requires the candidate to be of full age (20+), free of serious disqualifications (debt, slavery, disease, military service), and formally accepted by a chapter of ten monks (five in frontier regions) in a Sanghakamma. The head is shaved and yellow / saffron robes donned. PYQ #232 option (c) — the ordination ceremony, NOT Pavarana. Preceded by pabbajja (lower, 'going forth').

gap_sanghaparinayaka.label: Sanghaparinayaka election
gap_sanghaparinayaka.subject: history
gap_sanghaparinayaka.detail: SANGHAPARINAYAKA = leader / chief of the monastic sangha; the term also refers to the ELECTION of such a leader along with two official speakers — one on the Dhamma and one on the Vinaya — in a formal sangha-meeting. PYQ #232 option (a) presents this as the definition of Pavarana, which is incorrect — Pavarana is the end-of-rains confession, not an election.

gap_hammira_mahakavya.label: Hammira-Mahakavya (Nayachandra Suri)
gap_hammira_mahakavya.subject: history
gap_hammira_mahakavya.detail: HAMMIRA-MAHAKAVYA — 15c Sanskrit mahakavya by the Jain monk-poet NAYACHANDRA SURI. Narrates the heroic tale of Hammira-deva Chauhan of Ranthambore (r. 1283-1301), who resisted Alauddin Khilji's siege and died in the 1301 fall of Ranthambore after a jauhar. A rare Sanskrit literary account of a Rajput king's confrontation with the Delhi Sultanate. PYQ #179 correctly-paired option.

gap_nitivakyamrita_somadeva_suri.label: Nitivakyamrita (Somadeva Suri)
gap_nitivakyamrita_somadeva_suri.subject: history
gap_nitivakyamrita_somadeva_suri.detail: NITIVAKYAMRITA ('Nectar of Aphorisms on Polity') — 10c Sanskrit treatise on statecraft by the DIGAMBARA JAIN monk SOMADEVA SURI, written at the Rashtrakuta court (~959 CE). Presents governance advice in aphoristic form; also author of the Yashastilaka (Sanskrit campu-kavya). PYQ #179 correctly-paired option. NOT the same Somadeva who wrote Kathasaritsagara (that's a different 11c Kashmiri author).

gap_nagasena_milindapanha.label: Nagasena (Milinda-panha author)
gap_nagasena_milindapanha.subject: history
gap_nagasena_milindapanha.detail: NAGASENA — 2c BCE Buddhist monk who, according to the Milinda-panha ('Questions of Milinda'), dialogued with the Indo-Greek king Menander (Milinda) of Sakala, defending Buddhist doctrines (non-self, rebirth, karma) through similes (chariot analogy is iconic). NOT Nagarjuna (the 2c CE Madhyamika philosopher, author of Mulamadhyamakakarika) — PYQ #179 mis-pairing (Milindapanha:Nagarjuna is WRONG, correct author is Nagasena).

gap_sattriya.label: Sattriya dance (Assam)
gap_sattriya.subject: history
gap_sattriya.detail: Assamese classical dance form, one of the 8 Sangeet-Natak-Akademi-recognized classical dances (since 2000). Combines music, dance, and drama. Developed ~15c by the Vaishnavite saint-reformer Shankaradeva as part of the Bhakti tradition of Assam, originally performed in sattras (monasteries) by celibate monks. Uses Borgeets (devotional songs composed by Shankaradeva and Madhavadeva) and Ankia Nats (one-act plays). PYQ #10: NOT based on Tulsidas/Kabir/Meera ragas — statement 3 false; statements 1 and 2 true.

gap_konark_sun_temple.label: Konark Sun Temple (Odisha)
gap_konark_sun_temple.subject: history
gap_konark_sun_temple.detail: 13c Kalinga-style Sun Temple built by Narasimhadeva I of the EASTERN GANGA dynasty (c. 1250 CE) at Konark, Odisha. Designed as a colossal stone chariot of Surya with 24 carved WHEELS and 7 horses — the WHEEL iconography (time, cosmos, sundial) inspired the Indian Airlines logo (PYQ #55) and echoes on the national emblem of India's 20-rupee note imagery. UNESCO World Heritage Site; the main shikhara has collapsed, the jagamohana survives. Known as 'Black Pagoda' to European sailors.

gap_gahadavala.label: Gahadavala dynasty (Kanauj, 1089-1194)
gap_gahadavala.subject: history
gap_gahadavala.detail: Rajput dynasty of Kanauj, c. 1089-1194 CE (NOT 8c — PYQ #67 'None' answer). Founded by Chandradeva; rose to prominence under Govindachandra (r. 1114-1155), Vijayachandra, and Jaichandra. Extensive agraharic land grants; important patrons of Sanskrit learning. Jaichandra was defeated by Muhammad Ghori at the Battle of Chandawar (1194) — ending independent Kanauj.

gap_kakatiya.label: Kakatiya dynasty (Warangal, 1163-1323)
gap_kakatiya.subject: history
gap_kakatiya.detail: Telugu dynasty based at Warangal (Andhra Pradesh), c. 1163-1323 CE (NOT 8c). Major rulers: Prataparudra I, Ganapati (expanded Andhra to its greatest extent), Rudrama Devi (female ruler, c. 1262-89), Prataparudra II. Built the Thousand-Pillar Temple and Warangal Fort. Fell to Alauddin Khalji's general Malik Kafur (1309) and definitively to Muhammad bin Tughluq (1323).

gap_yadava_devagiri.label: Yadava dynasty of Devagiri (1187-1317)
gap_yadava_devagiri.subject: history
gap_yadava_devagiri.detail: Marathi-Kannada dynasty based at Devagiri (later Daulatabad, Maharashtra), c. 1187-1317 CE (NOT 8c — PYQ #67). Feudatories of the Chalukyas who became independent under Bhillama V. Peak under Singhana II and Ramachandra (his minister Hemadri wrote Chaturvarga Chintamani). Fell to Alauddin Khalji's raids (1296 onwards) and to Muhammad bin Tughluq's annexation (1317). Devagiri became the Sultanate's second capital under MbT.

gap_somnath_jyotirlinga.label: Somnath (Jyotirlinga)
gap_somnath_jyotirlinga.subject: history
gap_somnath_jyotirlinga.detail: Somnath (Prabhas Patan, Veraval, Gujarat) — one of the 12 JYOTIRLINGA Shiva shrines (swayambhu self-manifested lingas) of Shaivism, and reputedly the FIRST. Repeatedly raided/destroyed (Mahmud of Ghazni 1025-26, Alauddin Khalji 1299 via Ulugh Khan, Aurangzeb). Al-Biruni (Kitab-ul-Hind, 11c) described the pre-Ghazni temple's wealth. PYQ #133 statements 1 (Jyotirlinga) and 2 (Al-Biruni description) are TRUE.

gap_somnath_reconstruction.label: Modern Somnath reconstruction (1947-51)
gap_somnath_reconstruction.subject: history
gap_somnath_reconstruction.detail: Post-Independence reconstruction of Somnath temple, initiated by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel in 1947 as a symbol of India's cultural restoration; funded by public donations, not government money. Pran Pratishtha (consecration) performed 11 May 1951 by President RAJENDRA PRASAD (NOT PM Nehru — statement 3 in PYQ #133 false). Designed in Chalukya / Maru-Gurjara style. Nehru was critical of the state-involvement optics.

gap_bhadrachalam_temple.label: Bhadrachalam Rama Temple (Andhra)
gap_bhadrachalam_temple.subject: history
gap_bhadrachalam_temple.detail: Sitaramachandraswamy Temple at Bhadrachalam, Bhadradri-Kothagudem district, Telangana (carved from Andhra in 2014). On the banks of the Godavari. Associated with the 17c bhakti saint-composer Bhadrachala Ramadasu (Kancharla Gopanna), a revenue-tahsildar under Golconda's Abul Hasan Qutb Shah who used collected revenue to build/renovate this temple. NOT Virupaksha temple (PYQ #150 distractor, Virupaksha is at Hampi) and NOT the temple hosting the musical-pillars Vitthala (#154 distractor, that's Hampi).

gap_srikalahasti_temple.label: Srikalahasti Shiva Temple (Andhra)
gap_srikalahasti_temple.subject: history
gap_srikalahasti_temple.detail: Vayu-lingam (one of the pancha-bhuta-sthalams — five-element Shiva shrines) at Srikalahasti, Tirupati district, Andhra Pradesh. The five pancha-bhuta lingas: Chidambaram (sky), Tiruvanaikaval (water), Tiruvannamalai (fire), Kanchipuram-Ekambareswarar (earth), SRIKALAHASTI (air / wind). Chola-Vijayanagara construction layers. NOT Virupaksha temple (PYQ #150) — Virupaksha is at Hampi.

gap_vitthala_hampi.label: Vitthala Temple Hampi (musical pillars)
gap_vitthala_hampi.subject: history
gap_vitthala_hampi.detail: Vijaya Vitthala Temple at Hampi (Vijayanagara), Karnataka — built under Devaraya II and elaborated under Krishnadeva Raya and Achyuta Raya (16c). Famous for its 56 SARGAM / MUSICAL PILLARS (carved monolithic stone pillars that emit musical notes when struck — PYQ #154 answer) and the iconic stone chariot in front housing Garuda. Part of the Hampi Group of Monuments, UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gap_srirangam_ranganathaswamy.label: Srirangam Ranganathaswamy Temple
gap_srirangam_ranganathaswamy.subject: history
gap_srirangam_ranganathaswamy.detail: Sri Ranganathaswamy Temple at Srirangam, on an island in the Kaveri, Tiruchirappalli district, Tamil Nadu. One of the 108 Divya Desams (principal Vaishnava shrines) and the FIRST / foremost. Vast complex of 7 concentric rectangular enclosures (prakaras), 21 gopurams, on ~63 hectares — one of the largest functioning Hindu temple complexes in the world. Chola-to-Vijayanagara construction layers. NOT where Vitthala temple is (PYQ #154 distractor).

gap_kalyana_mandapa.label: Kalyana Mandapa (Vijayanagara feature)
gap_kalyana_mandapa.subject: history
gap_kalyana_mandapa.detail: Kalyana Mandapa = 'marriage hall' — a distinctive architectural feature of VIJAYANAGARA temple construction: a richly-pillared open pavilion within the temple complex used to stage the annual divine-marriage (kalyana utsava) of the deity. Also known as a 'Kalyana Mandapam'. Features intricately carved composite yali-pillars (rearing lion-like creatures). PYQ #327 answer: Vijayanagara (NOT Chalukya, Chandela, or Rashtrakuta).

gap_raskhan.label: Raskhan (Muslim Krishna-bhakti poet)
gap_raskhan.subject: history
gap_raskhan.detail: Sayyid Ibrahim ('Raskhan', c. 1548-1628), a MUSLIM Krishna-bhakti poet of the Mughal era who settled in Vrindavan. Composed Braj-Bhasha poetry on Krishna's life — the PREM VATIKA ('Grove of Love') and Sujan Raskhan are his best-known works (PYQ #199 answer). He was ALSO the medieval writer who referenced the discovery of America by the Europeans (PYQ #338 — but the accepted answer there is Abul Fazl in the Ain-i-Akbari; Raskhan is a distractor). A paradigm of Mughal-era Hindu-Muslim syncretism.

gap_bihari_satsai.label: Bihari (Satsai)
gap_bihari_satsai.subject: history
gap_bihari_satsai.detail: Bihari Lal Chaube (c. 1595-1664) — Braj-Bhasha poet at the Amber court of Mirza Raja Jai Singh I (Mughal-era Rajput king). Best known for the BIHARI SATSAI ('Seven Hundred Verses of Bihari'), a collection of 700-odd dohas (couplets) in the erotic-devotional sringara mode, celebrating the love of Radha-Krishna. Not the author of Prem Vatika (PYQ #199 distractor; that's Raskhan).

gap_dadu_dayal.label: Dadu Dayal (Nirguna saint)
gap_dadu_dayal.subject: history
gap_dadu_dayal.detail: Sant Dadu Dayal (c. 1544-1603) — NIRGUNA bhakti saint of the Kabir-Raidas lineage; born in Ahmedabad (or Nagaur by some accounts), settled in Rajasthan. Founded the DADU PANTH (sect) with its centre at Naraina. Composed verses in vernacular Hindi collected by his disciples as Dadu-vani / Dadu-nirmala — NOT as 'Bijak'. PYQ #221 statement 1 ('Bijak is Dadu Dayal's composition') is FALSE — the Bijak is attributed to KABIR. Statement 2 (Pushti Marg by Madhvacharya) also false; Pushti Marg is Vallabhacharya's.

gap_shah_alam_bukhari.label: Shah Alam Bukhari (Sufi)
gap_shah_alam_bukhari.subject: history
gap_shah_alam_bukhari.detail: Minor Sufi saint of the Bukhari family of Sufi-lineage figures (15-16c Gujarat). PYQ #240 distractor among options for 'Sufi saint who held devotional music (sama) was a way of coming close to God' — the correct answer is Muinuddin Chishti (founder of the Chishti order in India, Ajmer). Sama was characteristic of the CHISHTI and Qadiri orders; the Naqshbandis opposed it.

gap_tyagaraja.label: Tyagaraja (Carnatic trinity)
gap_tyagaraja.subject: history
gap_tyagaraja.detail: Tyagaraja (1767-1847) — South Indian composer-bhakti-saint of Tiruvaiyaru (Tamil Nadu), one of the 'Carnatic Trinity' (with Muthuswami Dikshitar and Shyama Sastri). Composed ~700 kritis in Telugu, most in devotion to Rama — the Pancharatna kritis are his best-known. Late 18c-19c, NOT a Lodi-era contemporary (PYQ #343 trap, where Guru Nanak is the only one preaching when the Lodis fell). Bhakti saint, so YES he was a bhakti-cult proponent (PYQ #346).

gap_nimbarka.label: Nimbarka (Dvaitadvaita)
gap_nimbarka.subject: history
gap_nimbarka.detail: Saint Nimbarka / Nimbarkacharya — 12-13c Vaishnava philosopher-saint (one tradition places him earlier but scholarship favors ~12c). Founded the NIMBARKA SAMPRADAYA, one of the four main Vaishnava sampradayas (alongside Sri, Madhva, Rudra). Propounded the DVAITADVAITA (dualistic-monism) philosophy of Brahman-Jiva relation. Emphasized Radha-Krishna devotion in Vrindavan tradition. NOT a contemporary of Akbar (PYQ #341 statement 1 FALSE — Nimbarka pre-dates Akbar by ~3 centuries).

gap_tamil_siddhars.label: Tamil Siddhars (Sittars)
gap_tamil_siddhars.subject: history
gap_tamil_siddhars.detail: Tamil SIDDHARS (Sittars in Tamil) — a loose, heterodox tradition of medieval Tamil mystics-yogis-alchemists who were MONOTHEISTIC and CONDEMNED IDOLATRY and Brahmanical ritual (PYQ #342 statement 1 TRUE). Prominent figures include Tirumular (author of Tirumantiram), Pattinathar, and the 18 Siddhars. Composed in colloquial Tamil, not Sanskrit. Distinct from the NORTH Indian Siddha tradition (Gorakhnath, Matsyendranath, Nath-panthis) — sharing the name 'Siddha' but separate lineages.

gap_amil.label: Amil (Sultanate revenue collector)
gap_amil.subject: history
gap_amil.detail: AMIL = revenue-collector officer in Delhi Sultanate and subsequent regimes — an agent posted to an iqta or khalisa territory to collect the assessed land revenue. PYQ #255 statement 1 TRUE ('in-charge of revenue collection was known as Amil'). The Mughal equivalent was also called amil or amalguzar. Distinct from the higher-tier wali or muqti who held the iqta itself.

gap_mir_bakshi_origin.label: Mir Bakshi origin (Mughal, not Khalji)
gap_mir_bakshi_origin.subject: history
gap_mir_bakshi_origin.detail: The office of MIR BAKSHI (head of the military-pay / mansabdari system) was a MUGHAL creation, emerging under Akbar as part of his mansab administrative restructuring (~1575-80). NOT a Khalji-Sultanate office — PYQ #255 statement 3 FALSE. The Sultanate equivalents for military-administrative roles were the ariz (diwan-i-arz, mustered under Balban and Alauddin Khalji), and the bakhshi under the Mughals superseded that concept.

gap_iqta_indigenous.label: Iqta system — foreign, not indigenous
gap_iqta_indigenous.subject: history
gap_iqta_indigenous.detail: Iqta was an IMPORTED Islamic-world institution (Abbasid / Saljuq origin — tax-assignment in lieu of military service) introduced to India by the Delhi Sultanate. NOT an ancient indigenous institution (PYQ #255 statement 2 FALSE). First systematized in India by Iltutmish; centralized by Balban and Alauddin Khalji; decentralized under Firuz Tughluq. The Mughal jagir system descended from it with modifications.

gap_dewan_i_bandagani.label: Dewan-i-bandagani (Firuz Tughluq's slave dept)
gap_dewan_i_bandagani.subject: history
gap_dewan_i_bandagani.detail: Separate DEPARTMENT OF SLAVES (banda = slave) established by Firuz Shah Tughluq (r. 1351-88), who is said to have accumulated 180,000 slaves — trained as artisans, soldiers, and administrators. Unique to Firuz's reign. PYQ #279 answer (d); PYQ #286 correctly pairs it with Tughlaq (not Khalji). The slave department was dissolved by his successors.

gap_dewan_i_mustakhraj.label: Dewan-i-Mustakhraj (Alauddin's arrears dept)
gap_dewan_i_mustakhraj.subject: history
gap_dewan_i_mustakhraj.detail: Department of ARREARS / RECOVERY of revenue set up by ALAUDDIN KHALJI (NOT Balban — PYQ #286 trap). Its brief: recover arrears from iqta-holders and revenue-farmers, preventing revenue leakage through collusion between muqaddams, chaudhris and the collectors. Part of Alauddin's aggressive fiscal centralization that also produced the market regulations (1303-1315).

gap_balban_zill_i_ilahi.label: Balban's Zill-i-Ilahi title
gap_balban_zill_i_ilahi.subject: history
gap_balban_zill_i_ilahi.detail: Ghiyas-ud-din BALBAN (r. 1266-87) adopted the grand title ZILL-I-ILAHI ('Shadow of God on Earth') along with the doctrine of NIYABAT-I-KHUDAI (king as God's vice-regent). Part of his theory of divinely-sanctioned kingship — reinforced by elaborate court ceremonial (sijda and paibos), Persian-style royalty, and suppression of the turbulent 'Corps of the Forty' (Chahalgani / Turkan-i-Chihilgani). PYQ #303 answer (c).

gap_barani_zawabit.label: Barani's zawabit critique
gap_barani_zawabit.subject: history
gap_barani_zawabit.detail: Ziauddin Barani (14c historian, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi / Fatawa-i-Jahandari) argued the Delhi Sultanate was NOT truly Islamic because the sultans had to SUPPLEMENT / modify the sharia with their own regulations called ZAWABIT (secular decrees) — e.g., Alauddin Khalji's market regulations, Balban's court ceremonials. Barani viewed such human-made law as a corruption of religious law. PYQ #332 answer (c). Zawabit became institutionalized under the Mughals (Zawabit-i-Alamgiri).

gap_mbt_dinar.label: MbT's gold dinar
gap_mbt_dinar.subject: history
gap_mbt_dinar.detail: Muhammad bin Tughluq issued a new GOLD COIN which Ibn Battuta called the DINAR (assertion TRUE in PYQ #265). However, the Reason given in #265 is FALSE — MbT's token currency experiment was in COPPER-BRASS 'fulus' coins (1329-32), NOT gold dinars; gold was preserved as real-value currency. The token experiment collapsed because people minted counterfeit copper coins at home, forcing the state to honour them in gold. Hence PYQ #265 answer (c).

gap_mbt_swarga_dwari.label: MbT Swarga-dwari camp
gap_mbt_swarga_dwari.subject: history
gap_mbt_swarga_dwari.detail: Muhammad bin Tughluq (r. 1325-51) left Delhi for TWO YEARS and resided in an encampment called SWARGA-DWARI ('gate of heaven'), near the Ganga. The cause was a Delhi PLAGUE — the city was devastated by an epidemic, with massive mortality. PYQ #281 answer (a): both Assertion and Reason TRUE and R correctly explains A. Combined with the earlier Delhi → Daulatabad capital-shift fiasco, these plagues compounded MbT's reputation for erratic decisions.

gap_badauni_mbt_epigram.label: Badauni on MbT's death
gap_badauni_mbt_epigram.subject: history
gap_badauni_mbt_epigram.detail: Abdul Qadir BADAUNI (16c Mughal historian, Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh) famously remarked on Muhammad bin Tughluq's death (1351): 'The king was freed from his people and they from their king' — capturing the mutual relief at the end of MbT's turbulent reign (capital-shifting, token-currency, Doab taxation, campaigns). PYQ #334 answer (c) MbT. Epigram encapsulates the posthumous Sultanate memory of MbT as a ruler of 'brilliant schemes and catastrophic execution'.

gap_nasiruddin_mahmud_tughluq.label: Nasiruddin Mahmud (last Tughluq)
gap_nasiruddin_mahmud_tughluq.subject: history
gap_nasiruddin_mahmud_tughluq.detail: NASIRUDDIN MAHMUD SHAH Tughluq (r. 1394-1413, with interruptions) — the LAST ruler of the Tughluq dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate. Presided over the dynasty's terminal decay and the 1398 sack of Delhi by TIMUR (during which he fled). Succeeded by the Sayyid dynasty (founded by Khizr Khan, 1414). PYQ #268 answer (c). Not to be confused with Nasiruddin Mahmud the son of Iltutmish (1246-66, Mamluk), nor with the Bengali Sultan Nasrat Shah of the Lodi / Husain Shahi era.

gap_ghiyas_ii_tughluq.label: Ghiyas-ud-din Tughluq Shah II
gap_ghiyas_ii_tughluq.subject: history
gap_ghiyas_ii_tughluq.detail: GHIYAS-UD-DIN TUGHLUQ SHAH II (r. Feb-Aug 1388) — briefly seized the Delhi throne after Firuz Shah Tughluq's death. Assassinated within months in a palace coup. Late-Tughluq phase of dynastic instability. NOT the last Tughluq (PYQ #268 distractor — Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah was last). Distinct from Ghiyas-ud-din Tughluq I (1320-25, dynasty founder).

gap_nasrat_shah_tughluq.label: Nasrat Shah Tughluq
gap_nasrat_shah_tughluq.subject: history
gap_nasrat_shah_tughluq.detail: NASRAT SHAH Tughluq — shadowy late-Tughluq claimant who held Firuzabad (Delhi) briefly in the 1390s, in rival contention with Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah Tughluq during the final years of the dynasty. NOT the last Tughluq (PYQ #268 distractor). Completely distinct from Nasrat Shah of Bengal (son of Alauddin Hussain Shah, r. 1519-32, of the Hussain Shahi dynasty, who gave refuge to Lodi princes fleeing Babur).

gap_vijayanagara_sangama_rulers.label: Sangama dynasty (Vijayanagara, 1336-1485)
gap_vijayanagara_sangama_rulers.subject: history
gap_vijayanagara_sangama_rulers.detail: FIRST Vijayanagara dynasty, founded 1336 by Harihara I and Bukka I. Principal rulers: Harihara I (founder), Bukka I, Harihara II, DEVARAYA I (r. 1406-22, built HIRIYA CANAL dam across Tungabhadra to bring water to Hampi — PYQ #247 answer), Devaraya II ('Immadi Devaraya'), MALLIKARJUNA (r. 1446-65), VIRUPAKSHA II (r. 1465-85 — SANGAMA-dynasty ruler, distinct from the Hampi-temple deity Virupaksha). Ended when SALUVA NARASIMHA usurped power in 1485 (PYQ #271 statement 1 TRUE).

gap_vijayanagara_saluva_tuluva.label: Saluva and Tuluva dynasties (Vijayanagara)
gap_vijayanagara_saluva_tuluva.subject: history
gap_vijayanagara_saluva_tuluva.detail: SALUVA DYNASTY (1485-1505): NARASIMHA SALUVA usurped from the last Sangama (Virupaksha II) in 1485 — PYQ #271 statement 1 & #272. Succeeded by his minor sons under regency of Narasa Nayaka, whose son Vira Narasimha deposed the last Saluva in 1505, founding the TULUVA DYNASTY. Tuluva rulers: VIRA NARASIMHA (founder, r. 1505-09), KRISHNADEVA RAYA (r. 1509-29, peak of the empire), ACHYUTA DEVA RAYA (r. 1529-42), Sadasiva (r. 1542-70, last Tuluva, puppet under Aliya Rama Raya). Vira Narasimha was succeeded by his half-brother Krishnadeva Raya (PYQ #271 statement 3 TRUE).

gap_vijayanagara_aravidu.label: Aravidu dynasty + Sadasiva / Tirumala / Ranga II / Venkata II
gap_vijayanagara_aravidu.subject: history
gap_vijayanagara_aravidu.detail: Fourth / last Vijayanagara dynasty (1542-1646). Begun when Aliya Rama Raya (Tuluva regent) faced defeat at the Battle of TALIKOTA (1565); his brother TIRUMALA DEVA RAYA escaped with the puppet Tuluva king SADASIVA and founded Penukonda as a new capital (1570, usurping Sadasiva). Later rulers: Sriranga I, VENKATA II (r. 1586-1614 — during whose reign Raja Wodeyar I consolidated Mysore, PYQ #267 answer expects RANGA II given a confused regnal dating), RANGA II, Sriranga III (last). Finally dissolved under Bijapur/Golconda pressure.

gap_raja_wodeyar_mysore.label: Raja Wodeyar (Mysore founding)
gap_raja_wodeyar_mysore.subject: history
gap_raja_wodeyar_mysore.detail: RAJA WODEYAR I (r. 1578-1617) effectively founded the independent kingdom of MYSORE, asserting autonomy from declining Vijayanagara. Technically the Wodeyar line traces to an earlier Yaduraya (~1399), but Raja Wodeyar's 1610-ish seizure of Srirangapatna marks the functional founding of Mysore as an independent realm. Contemporary Vijayanagara ruler (Aravidu dynasty) was VENKATA II (r. 1586-1614) — per PYQ #267 expected answer of Ranga II (dating varies). Dynasty continued until the 1761 Haidar Ali coup.

gap_krishnadeva_taxation.label: Krishnadeva Raya's taxation
gap_krishnadeva_taxation.subject: history
gap_krishnadeva_taxation.detail: Krishnadeva Raya's Amuktamalyada (his own political treatise) and Portuguese travellers' accounts describe: (1) LAND TAX fixed in proportion to LAND QUALITY (grades of fertility) — PYQ #258 statement 1 TRUE; (2) a separate 'INDUSTRIES TAX' levied on private owners of WORKSHOPS (weavers, oil-pressers, smiths) — statement 2 TRUE. Answer (c) both true. Also: irrigation-tank tolls, trade octroi, salt tax. A sophisticated revenue regime that funded the Vijayanagara temple-building boom.

gap_nuniz_women.label: Nuniz on Vijayanagara women
gap_nuniz_women.subject: history
gap_nuniz_women.detail: Fernao NUNIZ — 16c Portuguese chronicler at Vijayanagara — records (Cronica dos Reis de Bisnaga) that women in the empire were expert in diverse skills including WRESTLING, ASTROLOGY, ACCOUNTING, SOOTHSAYING, and served as guards, musicians, dancers, and scribes in the royal palace. PYQ #324 answer (d) ALL FOUR. Alongside Paes and Barbosa, Nuniz is a primary Portuguese source for Krishnadeva Raya's and Achyuta Raya's Vijayanagara.

gap_qutb_minar.label: Qutb Minar (Delhi)
gap_qutb_minar.subject: history
gap_qutb_minar.detail: Five-storeyed victory minaret at the Qutb Complex, Mehrauli, Delhi — begun by QUTB-UD-DIN AIBAK (1192), continued by ILTUTMISH (completed to four storeys, 1220), fifth storey added by Firuz Shah Tughluq (1369). ~73 m tall, tapering, with Kufic and Nashki calligraphy and Quranic inscriptions. Part of the Qutb Complex with Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and iron pillar. Part of PYQ #336 chronological order: (1) Qutb Minar (late 12c - early 13c), (2) Tughlaqabad Fort (1321-25), (3) Lodi Garden monuments (late 15c), (4) Fatehpur Sikri (1571-85).

gap_lodi_garden.label: Lodi Garden (monument cluster)
gap_lodi_garden.subject: history
gap_lodi_garden.detail: Park in central Delhi containing a CLUSTER of 15c-16c LODI- and SAYYID-dynasty tombs: Muhammad Shah's Tomb (Sayyid dynasty, 1444), Sikandar Lodi's Tomb (1517), Bara Gumbad + mosque, Shish Gumbad. The monuments pre-date Fatehpur Sikri (1571-85); hence in PYQ #336 chronological order they come between Tughlaqabad (1321-25) and Fatehpur Sikri.

gap_jama_masjid_delhi.label: Jama Masjid Delhi (Shah Jahan)
gap_jama_masjid_delhi.subject: history
gap_jama_masjid_delhi.detail: Masjid-i-Jahannuma ('mosque commanding view of the world'), built by Shah Jahan 1650-56 in Shahjahanabad (Old Delhi) — the LARGEST mosque in India. Red-sandstone with white-marble inlay, three domes, two minarets flanking the central iwan. PYQ #340 distractor (the famous LARGEST DOME is Gol Gumbaz at Bijapur, built by Mohammed Adil Shah 1656 for his father's tomb).

gap_sher_shah_tomb.label: Sher Shah's tomb, Sasaram
gap_sher_shah_tomb.subject: history
gap_sher_shah_tomb.detail: Tomb of Sher Shah Suri (r. 1540-45) at Sasaram, Bihar, built posthumously by his son Islam Shah. Sits on a plinth in the middle of a vast artificial lake — a masterpiece of Afghan-Indo-Islamic architecture, considered the apogee of pre-Mughal tomb design; directly precedes and influences Humayun's Tomb (1565-72). PYQ #340 distractor — the 'largest dome' answer is Gol Gumbaz, Bijapur.

gap_albuquerque_goa_1510.label: Albuquerque captures Goa 1510
gap_albuquerque_goa_1510.subject: history
gap_albuquerque_goa_1510.detail: Afonso de ALBUQUERQUE (Portuguese Governor 1509-15) captured GOA from the BIJAPUR SULTANATE (Adil Shahi dynasty, ruler Yusuf Adil Shah) on 25 Nov 1510. NOT from Vijayanagara — PYQ #312 statement 2 TRUE. Goa became the Portuguese 'Estado da Índia' capital. Albuquerque also captured Malacca (1511) and Ormuz (1515). PYQ #321 (a) is WRONG — 'Portuguese captured Goa in 1499' — Vasco da Gama arrived Calicut in 1498, no Portuguese conquest until 1510.

gap_gajapati_rulers.label: Gajapati rulers (Odisha)
gap_gajapati_rulers.subject: history
gap_gajapati_rulers.detail: GAJAPATI ('lord of elephants') dynasty ruled Odisha + coastal Andhra c. 1434-1541. Founded by Kapilendra Deva; peak under Purushottama Deva and Prataparudra Deva (a contemporary of Krishnadeva Raya, with whom he was in military-matrimonial conflict). Granted port sites on the east coast to Dutch factors (17c descendants and successor states) — PYQ #312 statement 1 TRUE (Dutch factories/warehouses on Gajapati lands). Successor polities on the east coast continued into the early colonial phase.

gap_madras_1639.label: Madras founding 1639 (Fort St George)
gap_madras_1639.subject: history
gap_madras_1639.detail: The English East India Company established its first major factory on the EAST coast at a piece of land granted by the local Nayaka of Damarla Venkatadri (loyal to the Chandragiri ruler, last remnant of the Aravidu Vijayanagara) in 1639. Francis Day and Andrew Cogan signed the grant. The settlement grew around FORT ST GEORGE (completed 1644) into Madraspatnam — modern Chennai. PYQ #312 statement 3 TRUE. First factory at Masulipatam (1611) preceded Madras on the east coast (PYQ #321 option b true).

gap_francis_xavier.label: Francis Xavier (Jesuit, d. 1552)
gap_francis_xavier.subject: history
gap_francis_xavier.detail: St FRANCIS XAVIER (1506-52) — Spanish-Basque missionary, CO-FOUNDER of the JESUIT ORDER (Society of Jesus, 1540) along with Ignatius of Loyola. Evangelized Goa, Kerala coast (Paravas), south India, Sri Lanka, Malacca, Japan (1549), and died on SHANGCHUAN island off China in 1552 while attempting to enter China — NOT in Goa (PYQ #314 statement 2 FALSE). His body was later moved to Goa where it is enshrined at the Basilica of Bom Jesus, still venerated. Feast of St Francis Xavier celebrated annually on 3 December in Goa (statement 3 TRUE).

gap_pondicherry_occupation.label: Pondicherry European occupation sequence
gap_pondicherry_occupation.subject: history
gap_pondicherry_occupation.detail: Pondicherry's European colonization sequence: (1) PORTUGUESE first occupied (1521); (2) then DANES (1670); (3) then FRENCH acquired it (1674, Bellanger + François Martin) and made it the French East India Company's Indian headquarters under DUPLEIX; (4) English briefly captured it several times (1761, 1778, 1793, 1803 — Carnatic Wars / Napoleonic Wars) — so statement 3 ('English never occupied Pondicherry') is FALSE. PYQ #315 answer (a) only statement 1 correct (Portuguese first). Pondicherry remained French till 1954 transfer to India.

gap_kochi_colonisation.label: Kochi European colonization sequence
gap_kochi_colonisation.subject: history
gap_kochi_colonisation.detail: Kochi (Cochin) colonization: (1) PORTUGUESE first (1503 — Francisco de Almeida built Fort Manuel, the first European fort in India); (2) Then DUTCH (1663 — defeated Portuguese, NOT Fort Williams; Fort Williams is in Calcutta); (3) Then BRITISH (1795, after Anglo-Dutch war). Modern Kochi was BRITISH-controlled from 1795 to Independence — statement (d) 'never became part of British colony' FALSE. PYQ #319 — none of options (a)/(b)/(c) are correct as stated; the answer key is (d), which is also factually wrong in the strict sense but least-wrong relative to the others.

gap_eeic_orissa_1633.label: First EEIC factory in Orissa 1633
gap_eeic_orissa_1633.subject: history
gap_eeic_orissa_1633.detail: The English East India Company's FIRST factory in EASTERN India was established in 1633 in the HARIHARPUR / Balasore area of ORISSA under Ralph Cartwright. Preceded the Hughli (1651) and Calcutta (1690) settlements. PYQ #321 option (c) CORRECT. Distinct from the west-coast Surat (1612) and east-coast Masulipatam (1611, under Hippon's fleet).

gap_dupleix_madras_1746.label: Dupleix and French Madras 1746
gap_dupleix_madras_1746.subject: history
gap_dupleix_madras_1746.detail: Joseph François DUPLEIX (French Governor-General of Pondicherry, 1742-54) captured MADRAS from the English in Sep 1746 during the FIRST CARNATIC WAR (1744-48) — taking advantage of French naval support from Admiral La Bourdonnais. Madras was returned to the English by the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748). PYQ #321 option (d) CORRECT. Dupleix's subsequent interventions in succession disputes at Arcot / Hyderabad initiated the broader Anglo-French contest across south India.

gap_araghatta.label: Araghatta (Sanskrit waterwheel)
gap_araghatta.subject: history
gap_araghatta.detail: ARAGHATTA — Sanskrit term for a WATER-LIFTING WHEEL used in medieval Indian irrigation. The standard translation is 'Persian wheel' (saqiya) but Upinder Singh notes the identification is DEBATED: early usage may have referred to the simpler noria (water-current-driven wheel) rather than the bullock-driven Persian wheel with chain-and-pot mechanism, which became definitively established in India under the Sultanate (per Satish Chandra's rahat). PYQ #257 answer (c): 'waterwheel used in irrigation'.

gap_nastaliq.label: Nastaliq script
gap_nastaliq.subject: history
gap_nastaliq.detail: Nastaliq ('hanging') — PERSIAN calligraphic script developed in 14-15c Iran by Mir Ali Tabrizi, combining Naskh (scriptural) and Taliq (cursive chancery) styles. Became the DOMINANT script for Persian literature and, in India, the Mughal administrative-literary hand. Used extensively for Urdu poetry (Ghalib's manuscripts). PYQ #305 answer (a). Distinct from Shikasta (broken, cursive running hand for informal correspondence) and Naskh (formal prose script).

gap_mokasa.label: Mokasa (Maratha land grants)
gap_mokasa.subject: history
gap_mokasa.detail: MOKASA = MARATHA-era revenue assignment / land grant given in lieu of military service or as reward for service to the state — equivalent to the Vijayanagara amaram, the Delhi-Sultanate iqta, and the Mughal jagir. Typically hereditary, extractable-revenue grants. Part of the saranjami-watani tenure system of the Peshwa era. PYQ #290 match: Mokasa ↔ MARATHAS (correct). Distinct from inam (tax-free religious / charitable grant).

gap_mahattara_pattakila.label: Mahattara and Pattakila (village officers)
gap_mahattara_pattakila.subject: history
gap_mahattara_pattakila.detail: Medieval Indian village-level administrative terms in PALA / PRATIHARA-era land-grant inscriptions: MAHATTARA ('great one', lit. 'elder') = VILLAGE ELDER / senior landholder involved in local dispute-settlement and land-transfer witnessing; PATTAKILA = VILLAGE HEADMAN, responsible for revenue collection and royal interface at village level. Both are VILLAGE OFFICERS (PYQ #263 answer b) — NOT military officers, not Vedic ritualists, not craft-guild chiefs. Both terms also transliterated variously (mahattaka, patala, etc.).

gap_alam_khan_lodi.label: Alam Khan (Ibrahim Lodi's uncle)
gap_alam_khan_lodi.subject: history
gap_alam_khan_lodi.detail: ALAM KHAN LODI — an uncle of Sultan Ibrahim Lodi and a PRETENDER to the Delhi throne. Along with Daulat Khan Lodi (governor of Punjab) he INVITED BABUR to invade India in hopes of overthrowing Ibrahim. Babur, already aggrieved by Ibrahim's refusal to acknowledge his claim to Punjab via Timurid inheritance, obliged. Alam Khan briefly seized and held parts of Delhi but failed to consolidate, and Babur proceeded independently to the First Battle of Panipat (1526). PYQ #273 answer (a).

gap_chandraketugarh.label: Chandraketugarh (Bengal terracotta)
gap_chandraketugarh.subject: history
gap_chandraketugarh.detail: Ancient urban site in West Bengal (North 24 Parganas), dated c. 4c BCE - 12c CE. Famous for its distinctive TERRACOTTA figurines (plaques of yakshis, mother-goddesses, aristocratic women, everyday scenes) — a hallmark of Mauryan-to-Gupta-era eastern Indian craft (PYQ #68 pair 2 TRUE). Also had urban fortifications and was a Bay-of-Bengal TRADING outpost on the Bidyadhari, not in Odisha (PYQ #128 trap: it's in West Bengal).

gap_ganeshwar.label: Ganeshwar (Rajasthan copper)
gap_ganeshwar.subject: history
gap_ganeshwar.detail: Chalcolithic site in Sikar district, RAJASTHAN (~3000-2000 BCE), a major supplier of COPPER ARTEFACTS to the Harappan civilization — the Ganeshwar-Jodhpura cultural complex. Over 5000 copper arrowheads, fish-hooks, bangles, and other objects have been recovered. Represents a non-Harappan contemporary supplier of metal to the IVC mainstream. PYQ #68 pair 3 TRUE.

gap_kot_diji.label: Kot Diji (Early Harappan, Sindh)
gap_kot_diji.subject: history
gap_kot_diji.detail: Early Harappan phase site in Khairpur district, SINDH (Pakistan), c. 3300-2600 BCE — type-site of the 'Kot Diji phase' preceding and bleeding into the mature Harappan. Includes a defensive wall, bichromate pottery, figurines. IS a Harappan-cultural-sphere site — so PYQ #70 option (b) Kot Diji is INCORRECT as the 'not a Harappan site' answer. Correct answer is Sohgaura (Mauryan-era copper-plate site, not Harappan).

gap_desalpur.label: Desalpur (Harappan, Kutch)
gap_desalpur.subject: history
gap_desalpur.detail: Harappan-era site in the KUTCH district, Gujarat — a fortified settlement with citadel walls, seals, weights, and evidence of Dholavira-style urban planning. Classified as a Mature Harappan regional-centre site in Saurashtra-Kutch, alongside Surkotada, Dholavira, and Lothal. IS Harappan — so PYQ #70 option (d) Desalpur is INCORRECT as the 'not Harappan' answer.

gap_ivc_monumental_absence.label: IVC: no grand palaces / temples
gap_ivc_monumental_absence.subject: history
gap_ivc_monumental_absence.detail: A DISTINCTIVE feature of the Indus Valley Civilization vis-à-vis contemporary Mesopotamia / Egypt: ABSENCE of grand palaces and monumental temples. The Great Bath and citadel-acropolis structures are ceremonial or civic, not royal palatial or temple-cult. No single ruler/deity is iconographically dominant. This points to a possibly less centralized polity / more commercial-urban civic order. PYQ #71 statement 1 ('great palaces and temples') is FALSE; statement 2 (male AND female deities worshipped, e.g. Proto-Shiva seal + Mother-Goddess figurines) TRUE; statement 3 (horse chariots) FALSE.

gap_rigvedic_warfare_gear.label: Rigvedic warfare equipment
gap_rigvedic_warfare_gear.subject: history
gap_rigvedic_warfare_gear.detail: The Rigveda explicitly mentions COAT OF MAIL (varman) and HELMET (shiprā) in its hymns, along with bow-arrow, spear, mace, chariot. The IVC, by contrast, shows NO clear evidence of armor, helmets, or chariots in warfare (the 'dancing girl' and 'priest-king' figurines are civic, IVC weapons are simple daggers/axes). PYQ #75 statement 1 TRUE; also IVC didn't use horse-drawn chariots (statement 3 TRUE) — they used bullock carts. This metallurgical / tactical contrast marks a distinct Vedic warrior culture.

gap_image_worship_postvedic.label: Image worship (post-Vedic)
gap_image_worship_postvedic.subject: history
gap_image_worship_postvedic.detail: Early Vedic religion was ANICONIC — focused on yajnas (fire sacrifices), hymn-chanting to nature deities (Indra, Agni, Varuna, Soma), with NO image/idol worship. IMAGE / MURTI worship emerged in POST-VEDIC times, accelerating in the Gupta period (4-6c CE) with the rise of Puranic Hinduism, Bhakti, and the consolidation of Vaishnava/Shaiva temple cults. PYQ #76 option (b) 'Image Worship and Yajnas' is wrong for the early Vedic period; answer (c) 'Worship of Nature and Yajnas' is correct.

gap_rta_cosmic_order.label: Rta (Rigvedic cosmic order)
gap_rta_cosmic_order.subject: history
gap_rta_cosmic_order.detail: RTA — the foundational Rigvedic concept of COSMIC / MORAL ORDER that governs the universe, natural regularities (seasons, sun's course), and right conduct. Guarded by Varuna. The predecessor and proto-form of the later concept of DHARMA, though Dharma in dharmashastra usage extends to caste-duty and ritual obligation. PYQ #77 statements 1 (Dharma as duty) and 2 (Rta as cosmic moral law) are BOTH TRUE — answer (c). Rta's later displacement by Dharma reflects the shift from Vedic cosmology to Brahmanical ethics.

gap_kinship_vs_kosa.label: Kula / Vamsa / Gotra (kinship) vs Kosa (treasury)
gap_kinship_vs_kosa.subject: history
gap_kinship_vs_kosa.detail: Three KINSHIP terms from ancient Indian social organization: KULA = extended family / household lineage; VAMSA = lineage / descent group (often royal dynastic sense — e.g., Ikshvaku-vamsa, Raghu-vamsa); GOTRA = Brahmanical exogamous clan, traced to a primordial rishi ancestor. KOSA = TREASURY — the royal treasury, one of the seven constituents (saptanga) of the state in Kautilyan political theory. PYQ #79 answer (c): Kosa is the odd-one-out (state-apparatus category, not kinship).

gap_mangadu_salihundam.label: Mangadu + Salihundam (PYQ #128)
gap_mangadu_salihundam.subject: history
gap_mangadu_salihundam.detail: Two PYQ #128 distractors: MANGADU — actually in Tamil Nadu (Kanchipuram district), a site associated with a Kamakshi temple; also a 'Mangadu' exists in Kerala as a small village, but NOT a known megalithic site there in the question's claim — PYQ #128 pair 3 'Mangadu — Kerala — Megalithic' is FALSE. SALIHUNDAM — a prominent BUDDHIST STUPA site in SRIKAKULAM district, ANDHRA PRADESH — famous for 2c BCE-4c CE Hinayana / Mahayana stupas (NOT rock-cut caves as in PYQ #128 claim). Answer (b): pairs 2 and 3 are correct (Inamgaon-Maharashtra chalcolithic, Mangadu-Kerala megalithic); all others flawed.

gap_sutudri_sutlej.label: Sutudri (Vedic Sutlej)
gap_sutudri_sutlej.subject: history
gap_sutudri_sutlej.detail: SUTUDRI = Rigvedic name for the SUTLEJ (the easternmost of the 'Sapta Sindhavah' — seven rivers of the Indo-Gangetic divide). Named in the Nadi-stuti ('Hymn of Rivers', RV 10.75) alongside Sindhu (Indus), Vitasta (Jhelum), Asikni (Chenab), Parushni (Ravi), Vipash (Beas), and Sarasvati. NOT the most-mentioned river — PYQ #200 answer is (a) Sindhu, the most frequently praised. Sutudri is the distractor.

gap_brahmavadinis.label: Brahmavadinis (Lopamudra, etc.)
gap_brahmavadinis.subject: history
gap_brahmavadinis.detail: BRAHMAVADINI = female Rigvedic hymn-composer / Vedic scholar (from 'brahma' = Vedic learning + 'vadini' = speaker). LOPAMUDRA (wife of sage Agastya) composed Rigvedic hymns in RV 1.179 — PYQ #203 answer (a). Other Brahmavadinis traditionally listed: Ghosha, Apala, Visvavara, Romasha, Shashvati, Mudgalani, Yami, and famously MAITREYI and GARGI (Upanishadic philosophers). LEELAVATI — NOT a Vedic composer; she is the daughter (and arithmetic-text namesake) of the 12c mathematician Bhaskara II. SAVITRI — a general name (of Savitri-Satyavan epic; also a Rigvedic hymn epithet), used here as distractor.

gap_shirdi_sai.label: Shirdi (Sai Baba, Maharashtra)
gap_shirdi_sai.subject: history
gap_shirdi_sai.detail: SHIRDI — village in AHMEDNAGAR district, MAHARASHTRA (not Vidarbha — PYQ #83 pair 3 FALSE; Shirdi is in Marathwada / western Maharashtra, not the eastern Vidarbha region). Home of the late-19c/early-20c saint Sai Baba (c. 1838-1918), a syncretic Hindu-Muslim figure revered across both traditions, who lived and taught here. Now a major pilgrimage town with the Sai Baba Samadhi shrine.

gap_indian_geographic_regions.label: Regional geographic labels
gap_indian_geographic_regions.subject: history
gap_indian_geographic_regions.detail: Traditional Indian geographic regions tested in PYQs: BUNDELKHAND — central India, north-eastern Madhya Pradesh + southern Uttar Pradesh (Khajuraho's home); BAGHELKHAND — eastern MP (Rewa, Satna, Shahdol); VIDARBHA — eastern Maharashtra (Nagpur region); MALWA — western MP (Ujjain, Indore); RAYALASEEMA — southern Andhra Pradesh (Anantapur, Kadapa, Kurnool, Chittoor — Tirupati is here, PYQ #83 pair 5 TRUE). NASIK is in western Maharashtra, NOT Malwa (PYQ #83 pair 4 FALSE).

gap_mahendravarman_titles.label: Mahendravarman I's titles
gap_mahendravarman_titles.subject: history
gap_mahendravarman_titles.detail: MAHENDRAVARMAN I (r. c. 600-630 CE) — Pallava king, father of Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla). Held the titles MATTAVILASA ('drunk with pleasure', also title of his Sanskrit burlesque play Mattavilasa Prahasana), VICHITRACHITTA ('of variegated mind / curious intellect'), and GUNABHARA ('bearing virtues'), recorded in the MANDAGAPATTU inscription which also declares that he built this brick-and-timber temple 'without bricks, timber, metal or mortar' — initiating the Pallava tradition of rock-cut architecture. PYQ #115 answer (a).

gap_simhavarman_early_pallava.label: Simhavarman (early Pallava)
gap_simhavarman_early_pallava.subject: history
gap_simhavarman_early_pallava.detail: SIMHAVARMAN — name shared by several EARLY Pallava kings predating Simhavishnu (the 'mahamalla' who consolidated Pallava power ~570 CE). Simhavarman I, II, III/IV are obscure 4-5c rulers of the early ('pre-Imperial') Pallava line, known mainly from copper-plate grants at Palakkada, Vilavatti, Lokavibhaga. PYQ #115 distractor — the titles Vichitrachitta etc. belong to Mahendravarman I (great-grandson of Simhavishnu), not to any Simhavarman.

gap_jayashakti_chandella.label: Jayashakti (Chandella)
gap_jayashakti_chandella.subject: history
gap_jayashakti_chandella.detail: JAYASHAKTI — early Chandella king, SUCCESSOR OF NANNUKA (the ~9c founder of the Chandella line of Bundelkhand). The Khajuraho inscription genealogies place him as 2nd or 3rd in line. Both Nannuka and Jayashakti belong to the CHANDELLA dynasty — PYQ #124 pairs 1 (Nannuka-Chandella) and 3 (Nagabhata II-Gurjara Pratihara) TRUE; pair 2 (Jayashakti-PARAMAR) FALSE (he's Chandella); pair 4 (Bhoja-Rashtrakuta) FALSE (he's Paramara).

gap_dhauli_rock_elephant.label: Dhauli Rock-cut Elephant
gap_dhauli_rock_elephant.subject: history
gap_dhauli_rock_elephant.detail: ROCK-CUT ELEPHANT sculpture at DHAULI (near Bhubaneswar, Odisha) — carved above Ashoka's Separate Kalinga Rock Edicts (~260 BCE), depicting the forequarters of an elephant emerging from the rock. One of the EARLIEST rock-cut sculptures in India (~3c BCE) — predates Mahabalipuram (~7c CE Pallava), Udayagiri Varaha (~5c CE Gupta), and the Lingaraja Temple (~11c CE). PYQ #142 answer (b).

gap_udayagiri_varaha.label: Udayagiri Caves (Varaha relief)
gap_udayagiri_varaha.subject: history
gap_udayagiri_varaha.detail: UDAYAGIRI Caves — Gupta-era rock-cut shrines near Vidisha, MADHYA PRADESH (NOT Odisha — there is a separate Udayagiri-Khandagiri in Odisha, Kharavela-era Jain caves). Cave 5 contains the magnificent HUGE VARAHA-AVATAR relief (~5c CE, Chandragupta II era) — Vishnu-as-Boar rescuing Bhudevi (Earth goddess), 3.9 m high. Iconographic statement of the mythic transition from Mauryan-Buddhist to Gupta-Vaishnava political symbolism. PYQ #143 pair 2 TRUE.

gap_buddha_mahaparinirvana_sculpture.label: Buddha Mahaparinirvana composition
gap_buddha_mahaparinirvana_sculpture.subject: history
gap_buddha_mahaparinirvana_sculpture.detail: Grand Buddhist sculpture composition showing Buddha lying on his deathbed (Mahaparinirvana, parinibbana), with celestial musicians and divine beings above and the grieving disciples and lay-followers below — iconic at AJANTA Cave 26 (c. 6c CE, Vakataka-era), where the reclining Buddha is carved in rock. Also at Kushinagara. PYQ #143 pair 1 TRUE. NOT at Ellora, Mahabalipuram, or Udayagiri in that exact compositional form.

gap_lhotsava_lhakhang.label: Lhotsava Lhakhang location
gap_lhotsava_lhakhang.subject: history
gap_lhotsava_lhakhang.detail: LHOTSAVA LHAKHANG ('Translator's Temple') — 11c Tibetan-Buddhist temple in the SPITI valley (Himachal Pradesh), specifically in the village of NAKO (Nako Monastery complex) — NOT in the Zanskar valley (Ladakh) as PYQ #144 claims in pair 2 (FALSE). Associated with the translator Rinchen Zangpo. Tabo (Spiti) and Alchi (Ladakh) in the same PYQ are correctly paired; Lhotsava Lhakhang mislocated.

gap_palitana_shatrunjaya.label: Palitana Jain Temples (Shatrunjaya)
gap_palitana_shatrunjaya.subject: history
gap_palitana_shatrunjaya.detail: PALITANA — town in Bhavnagar district, GUJARAT, at the foot of the Shatrunjaya hill — site of the PALITANA Jain temple complex on the hilltop: ~900 temples of the Shvetambara sect, considered one of the five sacred Jain tirthas and the holiest. Built over centuries from 11c CE onwards by wealthy Jain patrons. PYQ #153 answer (a) Bhavnagar.

gap_himalayan_monasteries.label: Dhankar / Rumtek / Kye monasteries
gap_himalayan_monasteries.subject: history
gap_himalayan_monasteries.detail: Himalayan Tibetan-Buddhist monasteries: DHANKAR — Spiti Valley, HIMACHAL PRADESH (16c, Nyingma/Gelug, on a spur overlooking the Spiti river); RUMTEK — Gangtok district, SIKKIM (modern seat of the 16th Karmapa, Kagyu school); KYE / KEY — Spiti Valley, HIMACHAL PRADESH (NOT Arunachal Pradesh — PYQ #157 pair (d) FALSE). All three Himachal-Spiti and Sikkim monasteries are part of the Indian Mahayana-Vajrayana landscape.

gap_unesco_india_wh_sites.label: Indian UNESCO WH sites (PYQ #160)
gap_unesco_india_wh_sites.subject: history
gap_unesco_india_wh_sites.detail: Indian UNESCO World Heritage sites featured in PYQ #160: GROUP OF MONUMENTS AT MAHABALIPURAM (inscribed 1984, Pallava 7-8c, Tamil Nadu); SUN TEMPLE KONARK (inscribed 1984, Eastern Ganga 13c, Odisha); CHAMPANER-PAVAGADH ARCHAEOLOGICAL PARK (inscribed 2004, Gujarat — pre-Mughal Islamic architecture + Hindu-Jain antecedents); CHHATRAPATI SHIVAJI TERMINUS (inscribed 2004, Victorian Gothic/Indo-Saracenic railway station, Mumbai). All 4 are UNESCO WH — PYQ #160 answer (d) all four.

gap_tawang_monastery.label: Tawang Monastery (Arunachal)
gap_tawang_monastery.subject: history
gap_tawang_monastery.detail: TAWANG MONASTERY — in Tawang district, ARUNACHAL PRADESH, at ~3000 m. Founded 1680-81 by Merak Lama Lodre Gyatso on the instructions of the 5th Dalai Lama. INDIA'S LARGEST Buddhist monastery (Gelug / Yellow-Hat sect). Birthplace of the 6th Dalai Lama, Tsangyang Gyatso. PYQ #162 statement that 'India's largest Buddhist monastery is in Arunachal Pradesh' is TRUE.

gap_nataraja_iconography.label: Nataraja four-hand iconography
gap_nataraja_iconography.subject: history
gap_nataraja_iconography.detail: CHOLA-period bronze icons of NATARAJA (Shiva as 'Lord of Dance') are invariably shown with FOUR HANDS (NOT eight, six, or two — PYQ #174 answer c). Iconographic elements: right hand holds damru (drum of creation), raised right hand in abhaya-mudra (protection), raised left holds agni (fire of destruction), lower left points to raised left foot (moksha). Right foot tramples Apasmara (demon of ignorance). Halo of flames (prabhamandala). Peak form at Chidambaram. Lost-wax (cire-perdue) casting technique.

gap_apabhramsa.label: Apabhramsa (linguistic stage)
gap_apabhramsa.subject: history
gap_apabhramsa.detail: APABHRAMSA ('falling away, corruption') — LATE Middle Indo-Aryan / PRAKRIT stage (~6-12c CE) that served as transition between classical Prakrits and the MODERN Indo-Aryan languages (Hindi, Gujarati, Punjabi, Bengali, Marathi). In medieval Sanskrit texts (Bharata's Natya-Shastra, later grammarians), the term denotes 'deviant' vernacular speech from Sanskrit — i.e., EARLY FORMS OF MODERN INDIAN LANGUAGES (PYQ #201 answer c). Jain literature was composed extensively in Apabhramsa.

gap_shad_darshana.label: Shad-darshana (6 astika schools)
gap_shad_darshana.subject: history
