gap_shad_darshana.detail: The SIX astika ('orthodox, Veda-accepting') schools of Indian philosophy (Shad-darshana), traditionally paired: (1) SAMKHYA (dualism, purusha/prakriti) + YOGA (Patanjali, practical meditation); (2) NYAYA (logic, Gautama) + VAISHESHIKA (atomism, Kanada); (3) MIMAMSA (Vedic ritual-interpretation, Jaimini) + VEDANTA (Upanishadic metaphysics, Badarayana). LOKAYATA (materialism) and KAPALIKA (Shaiva tantric ritual) are NASTIKA / heterodox, NOT part of shad-darshana — PYQ #222 answer (c): 'Lokayata and Kapalika' is the pair NOT forming part of the six.

gap_jahandar_farrukhsiyar.label: Jahandar Shah / Farrukhsiyar
gap_jahandar_farrukhsiyar.subject: history
gap_jahandar_farrukhsiyar.detail: JAHANDAR SHAH (r. 1712-13) — Later Mughal emperor, son of Bahadur Shah I. Incompetent; dominated by his mistress Lal Kunwar and minister Zulfiqar Khan. DEFEATED IN BATTLE by his NEPHEW FARRUKHSIYAR (son of Azim-ush-Shan) at Agra in January 1713 — captured, imprisoned, and strangled shortly after. PYQ #275 answer (c) 'defeated by his nephew'. Farrukhsiyar (r. 1713-19) was himself later deposed and killed by the SAYYID BROTHERS in 1719.

gap_eeic_charter_1600.label: EEIC Royal Charter 1600
gap_eeic_charter_1600.subject: history
gap_eeic_charter_1600.detail: The English East India Company received its ROYAL CHARTER from Queen ELIZABETH I on 31 DECEMBER 1600 — granting monopoly rights on English trade with the 'East Indies' (broadly, everything east of the Cape of Good Hope). Original name: 'The Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies'. Capital £68,373, 125 shareholders. The charter was renewed repeatedly by subsequent monarchs and parliaments until the company's 1858 dissolution after the Revolt.

gap_gondwana_garha_katanga.label: Gondwana / Garha-Katanga
gap_gondwana_garha_katanga.subject: history
gap_gondwana_garha_katanga.detail: GONDWANA — region of central India (broadly central-eastern MP + parts of Chhattisgarh + Maharashtra) inhabited by Gond tribes. Organized as the independent GARHA-KATANGA kingdom (~1500-64) in the Mughal-era. Famous ruler: RANI DURGAVATI (r. 1550-64), widow of Gond ruler Dalpat Shah, fought bravely against Asaf Khan's Mughal invasion in 1564 and died on the battlefield at Narrai. Gondwana was INDEPENDENT during early Akbar's reign — PYQ #298 map option (d), Akbar 1605 shaded portion NOT including Gondwana. Lahore (B-marker) was a major Mughal city.

gap_fatehpur_sikri_khankah.label: Khankah at Fatehpur Sikri
gap_fatehpur_sikri_khankah.subject: history
gap_fatehpur_sikri_khankah.detail: KHANKAH — Sufi lodge / retreat, a hospice for itinerant Sufi disciples and travellers. The Khankah at FATEHPUR SIKRI (inside Akbar's 1571-85 walled city) is built of RED SANDSTONE (not white marble — PYQ #328 statement 1 FALSE). The Buland Darwaza (1575) is also RED SANDSTONE with white-marble INLAY, not 'made of white marble'. Akbar's Fatehpur Sikri used red sandstone as its signature material; Shah Jahan's later Agra/Delhi monuments shifted to white marble.

gap_lucknow_nawabi_monuments.label: Bara Imambara + Rumi Darwaza
gap_lucknow_nawabi_monuments.subject: history
gap_lucknow_nawabi_monuments.detail: BARA IMAMBARA — in LUCKNOW, built 1784 by Nawab ASAF-UD-DAULAH (as a famine-relief project) in Nawabi-style; houses a vast central hall (50×16 m) with an unsupported arched roof and the Bhul-Bhulaiya labyrinth. RUMI DARWAZA — 1784 'Turkish Gate' nearby, modelled on the Sublime Porte of Istanbul, serves as the western entrance to the Bara Imambara complex. Built mainly of LAKHAURI BRICK + LIME STUCCO / PLASTER, NOT red sandstone and marble (PYQ #328 statement 2 FALSE).

gap_jama_masjid_srinagar.label: Jama Masjid Srinagar (Zain-ul-Abidin)
gap_jama_masjid_srinagar.subject: history
gap_jama_masjid_srinagar.detail: Jama Masjid at SRINAGAR, Kashmir — originally begun by Sultan Sikandar Shah Miri (1394), COMPLETED / ENLARGED under his son Sultan ZAIN-UL-ABIDIN (r. 1420-70, known as 'Bud Shah', the Great King). Distinctive Kashmir architectural synthesis: wooden construction with ~370 deodar pillars, pagoda-style tiered turrets echoing BUDDHIST PAGODAS (Kashmiri-Buddhist heritage), with PERSIAN / Timurid planning influences. PYQ #333 answer (b): all three — turret, Buddhist-pagoda similarity, Persian style — are correct.

gap_urdu_poetry_origin_khusrau.label: Urdu poetry origin — Amir Khusrau
gap_urdu_poetry_origin_khusrau.subject: history
gap_urdu_poetry_origin_khusrau.detail: AMIR KHUSRAU (1253-1325) — poet-musician at the Delhi Sultanate courts from Balban to Ghiyas-ud-din Tughluq, disciple of the Chishti Sufi Nizam-ud-din Auliya. Credited as the FIRST to use URDU ('Hindavi' / 'Dehlavi', early Khari-Boli Hindustani) as a medium of poetic expression — pioneering the ghazal, qawwali, and blending Persian and Indic elements. PYQ #335 answer (a). Major works: Tughluqnama, Khamsa-i-Nizami in Persian; riddles and dohas in Hindavi. Also credited with inventing the sitar and tabla (traditional attribution).

gap_mirza_ghalib.label: Mirza Ghalib
gap_mirza_ghalib.subject: history
gap_mirza_ghalib.detail: MIRZA ASADULLAH KHAN GHALIB (1797-1869) — pre-eminent 19c Urdu and Persian ghazal poet of the Mughal twilight. Lived through the 1857 Revolt in Delhi. Known for his ghazals (Diwan-e-Ghalib), letters, and tart wit. Nearly 200 years AFTER Urdu's birth with Amir Khusrau (NOT the 'first' Urdu poet — PYQ #335 distractor). Took a pension from the Mughal court (Bahadur Shah Zafar) and later applied for a British pension post-1857.

gap_bahadur_shah_zafar.label: Bahadur Shah Zafar (poet-emperor)
gap_bahadur_shah_zafar.subject: history
gap_bahadur_shah_zafar.detail: BAHADUR SHAH ZAFAR (1775-1862) — last Mughal emperor (r. 1837-57), also an accomplished Urdu GHAZAL POET under the takhallus 'Zafar' (famous couplet 'Lagta nahin hai ji mera ujde dayar mein...'). Figurehead leader of the 1857 Revolt; tried by the British, exiled to Rangoon where he died 1862. NOT the first Urdu poet (PYQ #335 distractor — that's Amir Khusrau). His patronage kept the Urdu court tradition alive in its dying Mughal-court phase.

gap_faiz_ahmed_faiz.label: Faiz Ahmed Faiz
gap_faiz_ahmed_faiz.subject: history
gap_faiz_ahmed_faiz.detail: FAIZ AHMED FAIZ (1911-84) — 20c PAKISTANI Urdu poet (born in Sialkot, pre-Partition Punjab), Marxist / Progressive Writers' Movement, nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature. Celebrated ghazals and nazms of resistance and socialist humanism (Hum Dekhenge). Exiled under Ayub Khan's regime. 20c figure — NOT the origin of Urdu poetry (PYQ #335 distractor — that's Amir Khusrau in the 13-14c).

gap_sikh_gurus_ramdas_amardas_angad.label: Sikh Gurus: Angad, Amar Das, Ram Das, Manji system
gap_sikh_gurus_ramdas_amardas_angad.subject: history
gap_sikh_gurus_ramdas_amardas_angad.detail: (2) GURU ANGAD (1504-52) — 2nd Sikh Guru; standardized the GURUMUKHI SCRIPT (though Punjabi had been written in earlier letterforms; Guru Angad systematized it for the Adi Granth tradition). NOT Guru Arjan Dev (PYQ #348 statement 3 FALSE). (3) GURU AMAR DAS (1479-1574) — 3rd Guru; established the MANJI SYSTEM of 22 preaching seats across north India to spread Sikh teachings. Miri-Piri is Guru Hargobind's (6th), NOT Guru Amar Das's — PYQ #352 option (a) FALSE. (4) GURU RAM DAS (1534-81) — 4th Guru; founded Amritsar / Chak Ram Das; PRECEDED Guru Arjan Dev (his son, 5th Guru, 1563-1606) — PYQ #348 statement 2 TRUE. Guru Arjan Dev compiled the Adi Granth — PYQ #352 option (b) TRUE.

gap_nizamat_of_arcot.label: Nizamat of Arcot (Carnatic Nawabdom)
gap_nizamat_of_arcot.subject: history
gap_nizamat_of_arcot.detail: NIZAMAT OF ARCOT / CARNATIC NAWABDOM — a Mughal subahdari that emerged as SEMI-INDEPENDENT under Sa'adatullah Khan I (c. 1710s), then fully under Dost Ali. FORMALLY a subordinate of the Nizam of Hyderabad's Deccan Subah — so PYQ #354 statement 1 (Arcot emerged 'out of Hyderabad State') is TRUE in the nominal succession sense, but strictly Arcot was a Mughal creation that passed through Hyderabad's overlordship. Venue of the Anglo-French Carnatic Wars (1744-63). Anwar-ud-din, Chanda Sahib, Muhammad Ali Walajah. Annexed by British 1801.

gap_rohilkhand.label: Rohilkhand (Rohilla Afghans)
gap_rohilkhand.subject: history
gap_rohilkhand.detail: ROHILKHAND — independent state formed ~1720-40 in the region north of Delhi / east of Delhi between the Ganga and the terai (modern Bareilly, Moradabad, Rampur districts of UP), by Afghan (Rohilla) settlers who took advantage of Mughal decline. Founding figures: Ali Muhammad Khan (d. 1749), later Hafiz Rahmat Khan. NOT formed out of Ahmad Shah Durrani's occupied territory — PYQ #354 statement 3 FALSE. Ultimately broken in the ROHILLA WAR of 1774 (British + Oudh against the Rohillas); Rampur survived as a small princely Rohilla state into 1947.

gap_first_anglo_burmese_war.label: First Anglo-Burmese War (1824-26)
gap_first_anglo_burmese_war.subject: history
gap_first_anglo_burmese_war.detail: First Anglo-Burmese War (1824-26) — fought between the British East India Company and the Burmese Konbaung dynasty (King Bagyidaw) over Assam, Manipur, and Arakan, which the Burmese had been encroaching upon. British victory; ended by the TREATY OF YANDABO (24 Feb 1826): Burma ceded ASSAM, MANIPUR, ARAKAN, and TENASSERIM to the British, paid an indemnity of Rs 1 crore, and accepted a British resident. One of the most expensive wars in EIC history (£13 million, 15,000 British casualties). PYQ #372 and #386 pairings.

gap_second_anglo_sikh_war.label: Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848-49)
gap_second_anglo_sikh_war.subject: history
gap_second_anglo_sikh_war.detail: Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848-49) — NOT 1845-46 (that's the First Anglo-Sikh War, which ended with the Treaty of Lahore 1846). PYQ #372 pair 4 ('1845-46 — Second Sikh War') is FALSE. The Second war was triggered by the Multan revolt under Diwan Mulraj (April 1848), spread across Punjab; key battles Ramnagar, Chillianwala (Jan 1849, near-stalemate), Gujrat (Feb 1849, British decisive victory). Governor-General Dalhousie ANNEXED PUNJAB outright in March 1849 — the last major Indian annexation by the British.

gap_ali_mardan_khan.label: Ali Mardan Khan
gap_ali_mardan_khan.subject: history
gap_ali_mardan_khan.detail: ALI MARDAN KHAN — Persian-origin Mughal noble (d. 1657). Served as governor of Kandahar under Safavid Persia until defecting to Shah Jahan (1638), bringing Kandahar to the Mughals. Later Mughal governor of KASHMIR and PUNJAB, celebrated as a HYDRAULIC ENGINEER — built the Shalimar Bagh canals and the CANAL OF ALI MARDAN (Nahr-i-Shah) from the Yamuna. Did NOT introduce revenue-farming in Bengal — PYQ #375 option (a) is the INCORRECT statement; revenue farming in Bengal was instituted under Murshid Quli Khan (early 18c) and expanded by the EIC post-Plassey.

gap_tipu_shringeri.label: Tipu Sultan & Shringeri Sharada
gap_tipu_shringeri.subject: history
gap_tipu_shringeri.detail: TIPU SULTAN (r. 1782-99) of Mysore famously sent financial and artisanal help to the SHRINGERI MATHA (Karnataka) when a Maratha raid (1791 by Parashurambhau Patwardhan) sacked the matha and desecrated the SHARADA idol. Tipu's correspondence with the Shankaracharya of Shringeri — requesting Pran Pratishtha (consecration) of a new Sharada idol + funding its reconstruction — is famous for complicating the image of Tipu as purely anti-Hindu. PYQ #375 option (d) CORRECT.

gap_ranjit_singh_lahore_foundries.label: Ranjit Singh's Lahore foundries
gap_ranjit_singh_lahore_foundries.subject: history
gap_ranjit_singh_lahore_foundries.detail: Maharaja RANJIT SINGH (r. 1799-1839) of the Sikh Empire set up MODERN CANNON FOUNDRIES at LAHORE under European supervision (Italian Ventura, French Allard, French Court) — part of his Europeanization of the Khalsa Army (Fauj-i-Khas). Produced heavy artillery using European-trained Sikh / Muslim artisans; the Zamzama cannon at Lahore is a famous Mughal-era piece Ranjit used. PYQ #375 option (b) CORRECT. His army was considered the most formidable indigenous force the British faced in India.

gap_jai_singh_euclid.label: Sawai Jai Singh's Euclid translation
gap_jai_singh_euclid.subject: history
gap_jai_singh_euclid.detail: SAWAI JAI SINGH II of Amber (r. 1699-1743) — founder of Jaipur (1727), astronomer, built the JANTAR MANTAR observatories (Jaipur, Delhi, Mathura, Ujjain, Varanasi). Had Euclid's ELEMENTS of Geometry (the medieval Arabic / Persian versions of the Greek classic) TRANSLATED into SANSKRIT — along with other Arab / Greek astronomical works — in order to reconcile and improve Indian siddhantic astronomy. PYQ #375 option (c) CORRECT. Patron of the Zij-i-Muhammad-Shahi astronomical tables.

gap_tribhanga_pose.label: Tribhanga (Dance/Sculpture pose)
gap_tribhanga_pose.subject: history
gap_tribhanga_pose.detail: Classical Indian pose where the body bends in three places — neck, waist, hips — creating an S-curve. Waist and neck bend in OPPOSITE directions (not same-direction, a common trap). Seen from ancient Didarganj Yakshi (Maurya-Shunga) through Kushana/Gupta sculpture into classical dance (Odissi especially). Distinct from Samabhanga (straight), Abhanga (slight bend), Atibhanga (dramatic). Widely used in Krishna flute-playing iconography and devis. NOT a facial-expression or hand-gesture concept — that's Abhinaya/Mudra (PYQ #14 trap distractors).

gap_traditions_community_pairs.label: Chaliha Sahib / Nanda Raj Jaat / Wari-Warkari
gap_traditions_community_pairs.subject: history
gap_traditions_community_pairs.detail: Three tradition-community pairings PYQ-tested (2017 #40). Chaliha Sahib: 40-day Sindhi festival honouring Jhulelal (water deity); observed July-Aug by Sindhis (CORRECT pairing). Nanda Raj Jaat Yatra: Uttarakhand pilgrimage (every 12 years, Chamoli-district Himalayas to Nanda Devi) — belongs to Garhwalis/Kumaonis, NOT Gonds (central-Indian Adivasi). Wari-Warkari: Maharashtra bhakti pilgrimage to Pandharpur's Vithoba shrine on Ashadhi Ekadashi, dindis carrying Tukaram/Dnyaneshwar palanquins — NOT Santhals (eastern-Indian Adivasi). Community-misattribution is the classic UPSC trap.

gap_changpa_community.label: Changpa community (Ladakh)
gap_changpa_community.subject: history
gap_changpa_community.detail: Nomadic pastoral community of eastern Ladakh's Changthang plateau — NOT Uttarakhand (PYQ #42 trap). Recognised as Scheduled Tribe. Primary livelihood: rearing Changra goats yielding fine Pashmina wool (~10 microns) that feeds the Kashmir Pashmina/shahtoosh shawl industry. Also keep yaks and sheep. Semi-nomadic; seasonal altitudinal migration (4,000-5,000 m). Tibetan Buddhist; originate from Tibet. UPSC-favourite community for tribal-geography PYQs. Separate from Dards (Ladakh) and Gaddi shepherds (Himachal) — each asked independently in different years.

gap_bnhs.label: Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS)
gap_bnhs.subject: history
gap_bnhs.detail: Founded 1883 in Bombay — oldest natural-history research organisation in India. NOT an autonomous body under MoEFCC (PYQ #45 trap) — it is a registered charitable society (NGO). Core activities: conservation research, publications (Journal of BNHS, Hornbill magazine), bird atlases, India's largest natural-history specimen collection. Runs nature-education programmes, trails, camps for the public. Custodian of Salim Ali's legacy. Designated Scientific & Industrial Research Organisation by DSIR. BirdLife International partner. Key work on bird-ringing, IBA mapping, Great Indian Bustard and vulture conservation.

gap_colonial_commerce_terms.label: Aurang / Banian / Mirasidar
gap_colonial_commerce_terms.subject: history
gap_colonial_commerce_terms.detail: Three Company-era economic terms PYQ-tested (2020 #253). Aurang: Persian-origin warehouse or workshop where weavers/craftsmen produced goods for EIC under gomasta supervision — NOT a treasury official (PYQ trap). EIC set up aurangs across Bengal for textile production. Banian (also banyan): Indian merchant/agent of a European trader or Company factor — credit-broker and intermediary with local markets; became a distinct Bengali propertied class in 18c Calcutta (Dwarkanath Tagore was one such). Mirasidar: Tamil-country customary-right cultivator holding miras — hereditary revenue-paying status; designated revenue payer under the Ryotwari settlement.

gap_abdali_panipat_motive.label: Abdali's casus belli for Third Panipat (1761)
gap_abdali_panipat_motive.subject: history
gap_abdali_panipat_motive.detail: Immediate reason for Ahmad Shah Abdali's 1759-61 India campaign culminating in Third Panipat: Marathas under Raghunath Rao expelled Abdali's son Timur Shah (his appointed viceroy of Lahore) from Punjab in 1758. Abdali returned to avenge this loss and reassert Durrani control. Distractor traps from PYQ #264: invitation by Adina Beg (false — Adina Beg was Maratha-aligned; anyway died 1758), Chahar Mahal revenue dispute (false, earlier issue), pure annexation of Punjab plains (ambition existed but not the immediate trigger). Result: 14 January 1761 — Maratha defeat, Bhau killed, Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao died shortly after from shock.

gap_shah_alam_ii.label: Shah Alam II (Mughal emperor 1759-1806)
gap_shah_alam_ii.subject: history
gap_shah_alam_ii.detail: Nominal Mughal emperor during Company ascendancy. Son of Alamgir II. Proclaimed emperor in exile 1759; spent early years away from Delhi due to Afghan/Maratha/Jat threats and unstable capital politics (PYQ #277 assertion). Commanded Bengal coalition (with Mir Qasim + Shuja-ud-daula) defeated by British at Buxar 1764. Signed Treaty of Allahabad 1765 — granted EIC the diwani of Bengal-Bihar-Orissa, formalising Company revenue-gathering role. Lived on British pension. Blinded by Rohilla Ghulam Qadir at Delhi 1788. Returned under Maratha protection 1772-1803, then under British after 2nd Anglo-Maratha War. Died 1806; succeeded by Akbar II. Titular only.

gap_surat_factory_1613.label: EIC Surat factory (1613)
gap_surat_factory_1613.subject: history
gap_surat_factory_1613.detail: First English East India Company factory in India, permitted at Surat in 1613 under Mughal emperor Jahangir. Preceded by William Hawkins' diplomatic mission to Agra (1608-11). Formal establishment followed Captain Thomas Best's naval victory against Portuguese at the Battle of Swally (Suvali, 1612), which convinced Jahangir of English naval strength. Surat remained the principal EIC factory on the west coast through 17c, before Bombay (acquired 1661, fortified 1668) superseded it. Madras 1639, Calcutta 1690 follow. PYQ #318 answer: Surat.

gap_bengal_commerce_18c.label: Bengal exports mid-18c (EIC)
gap_bengal_commerce_18c.subject: history
gap_bengal_commerce_18c.detail: Staple commodities the English East India Company exported from Bengal in mid-18c: cotton textiles (muslin, calico), raw silk, saltpetre (potassium nitrate for gunpowder — key strategic export fuelling European wars), opium (forcibly cultivated for China trade), indigo (blue dye). NOT copper/gold/spices/tea (PYQ #357 trap — these were imports or traded differently). Post-Diwani 1765, EIC used Bengal revenue to finance purchase of these 'investment goods' for European auction — classic drain-of-wealth pattern.

gap_cornwallis_dc_judicial_1793.label: Cornwallis 1793 — DC stripped of judicial powers
gap_cornwallis_dc_judicial_1793.subject: history
gap_cornwallis_dc_judicial_1793.detail: Cornwallis Code regulation 1793: the District Collector was deprived of judicial powers and reduced to pure revenue-collecting agent. PYQ #364 answer: Cornwallis was alarmed at the concentration of absolute power (revenue + magistracy + judicial) in one European officer and felt such power could be abused (distractor: efficiency, race-based separation, Indian law training — all rejected). Judicial duties transferred to separate district judges and courts. This is the origin of the revenue-judicial separation in Indian district administration that largely persists today.

gap_carnatic_wars.label: Carnatic Wars (3, 1744-63) + Wandiwash/Ambur
gap_carnatic_wars.subject: history
gap_carnatic_wars.detail: Three Anglo-French wars in South India. 1st Carnatic War (1744-48): French Dupleix captured Madras 1746, returned at Aix-la-Chapelle 1748. 2nd Carnatic War (1749-54): Battle of Ambur (1749, first battle of 2nd war) — French-backed Chanda Sahib won Arcot throne; Clive's brilliant defence of Arcot (1751) broke French momentum; Treaty of Pondicherry 1754 recalled Dupleix. 3rd Carnatic War (1757-63): Battle of Wandiwash (22 Jan 1760) — Sir Eyre Coote decisively defeated Comte de Lally's French force, effectively ending French political ambitions in India; Treaty of Paris 1763 left Pondicherry as a purely commercial French outpost. Chronology order (PYQ #369): Ambur 1749 → Plassey 1757 → Wandiwash 1760 → Buxar 1764.

gap_khasi_early_contact.label: Khasi tribe — first EIC contact post-Diwani
gap_khasi_early_contact.subject: history
gap_khasi_early_contact.detail: Khasis of the Khasi-Jaintia hills (modern Meghalaya) were the first mountain tribe the EIC came into contact with after the grant of the Diwani of Bengal-Bihar-Orissa in 1765 (PYQ #378). Initial encounters as British revenue officers moved through northeast frontier; expanded in the 1820s-30s when Assam was annexed post-First Anglo-Burmese War (1824-26, Treaty of Yandabo). Distractors: Garos (reached via Kamrup/Goalpara slightly later), Kukis (further east in Manipur-Lushai hills, mid-19c contact), Tipperahs (Tipperah State, also later). Khasis known for matrilineal society, jhum cultivation.

gap_imperial_preference.label: Imperial Preference
gap_imperial_preference.subject: history
gap_imperial_preference.detail: British colonial-economic doctrine: tariff preferences favouring imports from Britain into India (and other Empire territories), over non-Empire goods. Institutionalised especially post-Ottawa Conference 1932 (though the term was used earlier). Meant: low or nil duties on British imports entering India, higher duties on non-British imports — protecting British manufacturers against Japanese/American competition in the Indian market. Not to be confused with (PYQ #387 trap options): racial discrimination generally, subordination of Indian interests generally, or preference to political agents. Key grievance of Indian nationalists / INC economic critique.

gap_danish_tranquebar.label: Danish Tranquebar (Tamil Nadu)
gap_danish_tranquebar.subject: history
gap_danish_tranquebar.detail: Tranquebar (Tharangambadi, Tamil Nadu coast) — the principal Danish East India Company outpost in India, established 1620 under Ove Gjedde by treaty with Tanjore Nayak. Built Fort Dansborg. Hosted the first Protestant Christian mission in India (Ziegenbalg and Plütschau, 1706). Ceded to British 1845. Also: Serampore (Bengal) was another Danish settlement (hist_serampore_mission ✓). Quaint colonial town today with New Jerusalem church, fort, empty beaches (PYQ #390). Distractors: Kerala/Goa were Portuguese, Karnataka coast had no Danish outpost.

gap_modi_script.label: Modi Script (Marathas)
gap_modi_script.subject: history
gap_modi_script.detail: Cursive form of Marathi script used extensively by the Marathas for administrative and revenue documents from the Peshwa period through early British rule in Maharashtra. Reputedly developed/popularised by Hemadpant under Yadavas, refined under Shivaji's chief-accountant Balaji Avji Chitnis. Running cursive form — faster writing, preferred over Devanagari Balbodh for bureaucratic correspondence. Declined in 20c as standard Devanagari replaced it. PYQ #393 answer: Marathas (not Wodeyars/Zamorins/Hoysalas). Large corpus of Modi manuscripts survives in Pune/Satara archives.

gap_maratha_confederacy_clans.label: Maratha Confederacy sardar-seats
gap_maratha_confederacy_clans.subject: history
gap_maratha_confederacy_clans.detail: Four major sardar-families forming the Maratha Confederacy under Peshwa nominal authority (18c): Scindias (Shinde) — seat at Gwalior; Holkars — seat at Indore; Gaekwads — seat at Baroda; Bhonsles — seat at Nagpur (distinct from Shivaji's Bhonsle line at Satara). PYQ #394 map tests these pairings. The Peshwa held authority from Pune but the sardars operated with substantial autonomy, especially after the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) weakened the Peshwa. Each was defeated separately in the three Anglo-Maratha Wars (1775-82, 1803-05, 1817-18).

gap_lord_canning.label: Lord Canning (GG 1856-62, first Viceroy 1858)
gap_lord_canning.subject: history
gap_lord_canning.detail: Governor-General 1856-58 and first Viceroy 1858-62 after the Government of India Act 1858 transferred rule from EIC to Crown. Presided during the Revolt of 1857 — nicknamed 'Clemency Canning' for his policy of relative leniency towards rebels (controversial in Britain). Issued Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1 November 1858). Introduced the Indian Councils Act 1861, Indian High Courts Act 1861, Indian Penal Code (enacted 1860 on Macaulay's draft). Reorganised army and finances post-Mutiny. PYQ #396 answer.

gap_covenanted_civil_service.label: Covenanted Civil Service of India
gap_covenanted_civil_service.subject: history
gap_covenanted_civil_service.detail: Civil service established by Lord Cornwallis in 1793 — 'covenanted' because entrants signed a bond/covenant with the EIC Court of Directors. Staffed exclusively by Europeans initially (Indians excluded until 1864 when Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian ICS). Trained at Haileybury College (founded 1806, shut 1857). Later renamed Indian Civil Service (ICS); recruitment became competitive exam after 1853 Charter Act (exam held in London until 1922). Distinct from uncovenanted service (Indian subordinate clerks/officials). PYQ #363 answer: Cornwallis (not Hastings, Wellesley, Bentinck).

gap_ics_charter_1833_law_member.label: Charter Act 1833 — provisions list
gap_ics_charter_1833_law_member.subject: history
gap_ics_charter_1833_law_member.detail: Key provisions of the Charter Act 1833 (PYQ #376 asks which is NOT a provision): (i) EIC's trading activities abolished — became purely administrative body; (ii) Governor-General of Bengal became Governor-General of India with centralised authority over Bombay/Madras; (iii) All law-making power vested in Governor-General in Council; (iv) FIRST Law Commission appointed under Macaulay (led to IPC draft 1837); (v) Chinese trade monopoly also ended (last piece of 1813 carve-out removed); (vi) Hindu/Muslim law codification directive. NOT in the Act: Indian as Law Member (that came only in 1861 Indian Councils Act under Canning — Sir Sunkey/Raja of Benares admitted). The 1833 Act explicitly opened service to Indians in principle ('no native shall be excluded by reason of religion, place of birth, descent, colour') but this remained dead-letter until 1861/1864.

gap_middle_class_1857.label: Educated middle class and Revolt of 1857
gap_middle_class_1857.subject: history
gap_middle_class_1857.detail: The English-educated Indian middle class (the incipient intelligentsia — journalists, teachers, clerks, landlords' lawyers) broadly remained NEUTRAL to the Revolt of 1857 (PYQ #401 answer). They neither actively supported the rebels (whom they saw as reactionary/feudal, restoring old Mughal/Maratha order) nor actively supported the British. Figures like Rammohun Roy's successors, early Brahmo Samaj members, Dadabhai Naoroji's circle, saw British rule as an agent of modernisation even while pressing for reform. Aitchison's remark (PYQ #400 on Hindu-Muslim unity — couldn't be 'played off') captures British surprise at cross-community rebel unity; Aitchison was a Punjab-frontier official.

gap_english_education_pipeline.label: English Education pipeline (1813-35)
gap_english_education_pipeline.subject: history
gap_english_education_pipeline.detail: Four-stage colonial path to English-medium higher education in India. (1) Charter Act 1813 imposed Rs 1 lakh/year education obligation on EIC — first parliamentary commitment to Indian education. (2) General Committee of Public Instruction established 1823 under William Bentinck predecessor era — staffed initially by Orientalists (H.T. Prinsep, H.H. Wilson) who wanted to promote Sanskrit/Arabic/Persian learning. (3) Orientalist-Anglicist Controversy 1830s: Anglicists (led by Macaulay from 1834, with Trevelyan, Alexander Duff) pushed English + Western science vs Orientalists defending classical Indian languages. (4) Macaulay's Minute 2 Feb 1835 + English Education Act 1835 under Bentinck — resolved controversy in favour of Anglicists; English became medium of higher education; state funding for Calcutta Madrasa + Benaras Sanskrit College ended. All three (Charter 1813, GCPI 1823, controversy) led to the outcome (PYQ #653 answer: all three correct).

gap_sarvodaya_samaj.label: Sarvodaya Samaj (Vinoba, 1948)
gap_sarvodaya_samaj.subject: history
gap_sarvodaya_samaj.detail: Organisation founded by Vinoba Bhave in March 1948 as a voluntary association continuing Gandhian constructive work after Gandhi's assassination. Initial focus included relief and resettlement work for Partition refugees (PYQ #614 statement IV), plus rural uplift. Evolved into the Bhoodan movement from 1951 (Vinoba's padyatra starting from Pochampally, Telangana) and Gramdan (1952+). Philosophical foundation: Gandhi's Sarvodaya ('welfare of all') from his 1908 paraphrase of Ruskin's Unto This Last. Jayaprakash Narayan was closely associated. Distinct from Sarvodaya movements of individual leaders later.

gap_factories_act_1881.label: Factories Act 1881 (and 1891 amendment)
gap_factories_act_1881.subject: history
gap_factories_act_1881.detail: Bipin Chandra records the Factories Act of 1881 (and its 1891 amendment) as legislation regulating working conditions in Indian factories — passed during Lord Ripon's viceroyalty. Early cotton-mill owners and Moderate nationalists were largely indifferent to or opposed the Act, not wanting to 'create any divisions in the fledgling anti-imperialist movement' and viewing factory legislation as a British-led intrusion while broader structural reforms were being sought. Act did NOT fix wages nor authorise trade unions (PYQ #404 S1 FALSE; PYQ #411 answer: Ripon).

gap_vpa_repeal_ripon_1881.label: Vernacular Press Act repealed by Ripon (1881)
gap_vpa_repeal_ripon_1881.subject: history
gap_vpa_repeal_ripon_1881.detail: Bipin Chandra records: the Vernacular Press Act of 1878, directed only against Indian-language newspapers, was 'conceived in great secrecy and passed at a single sitting of the Imperial Legislative Council.' It provided for confiscation of press plant and paper and for imprisonment of editors. It was REPEALED IN 1881 BY LORD RIPON (PYQ #413 answer) after a sustained Indian Press campaign against the Act. (Standard PYQ keys give 1882; Bipin Chandra's text gives 1881 — used here as the corpus-authoritative source.)

gap_lytton_forward_policy_afghanistan.label: Lytton's Afghan adventure / Second Afghan War 1878-80
gap_lytton_forward_policy_afghanistan.subject: history
gap_lytton_forward_policy_afghanistan.detail: Bipin Chandra records: 'The Second Afghan War was waged in 1878-80.' The Indian nationalists opposed 'the Afghan adventure of Lord Lytton' and later 'compelled the British Government to contribute towards the cost of the Second Afghan War.' Surendranath Banerjee publicly branded the war as 'an act of sheer aggression and as one of the most unrighteous wars that have blackened the pages of history.' Lytton (Viceroy 1876-80, hist_arms_act_1878 / hist_vernacular_press_act_1878) pursued the aggressive forward policy towards Afghanistan that PYQ #418 names.
